ADDENDUM

Pages 427-433

The following was omitted among the preparations of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. g. Carbonas Ferri præcipitatus, E. Precipitated carbonate of iron. Prepared by decomposing a solution of sulphate of iron by a solution of carbonate of soda; washing and drying the precipitate. Similar in its virtues to 961. Dose five to 30 grains. The space allotted to this article was so small, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> for preparing it so short, that it is, of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, much less full and complete than it might otherwise have been. As it was impossible, under such circumstances, to produce any thing like an original and complete treatise, the compiler has endeavoured to render as useful as possible the selection that he found it necessary to make, and to supply the unavoidable deficiencies by a reference to the most respectable works on the subject. | **<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia DRARGYRUS MURIATUS

Pages 420-423

L. Muriate of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>. Corrosive muriated mercury. Corrosive sublimate. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, No 1736. Prepared by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> two pounds of purified quicksilver in two pounds and a half of sulphuric acid, in a glass vessel, over a sand bath, to dryness, triturating the dried <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> with four pounds of dried muriate of soda, then subliming in a glass <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUCURBIT">cucurbit</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> gradually increased, and separating the sublimed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> from the scoriae. Used as a salagogue; dose one-eighth to one-fourth of a grain; as an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> stimulus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> eucharotic to venereal ulcers, chancres, and herpetic eruptions, in the proportion of about a grain or more to the ounce of liquid. d. Submuriatas Hydrargyri, E. Hydrargyrum muriatum mite sublimatum, D. Calomelas, L. Submuriate of mercury. Sublimed mild muriate of mercury. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALOMEL">Calomel</a>. See Chemistry, No 1742, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is much the same as that of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. Given in most <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> where mercury is indicated. Dose, as a diaphoretic or alternative, about a grain; as a cathartic or anthelmintic, three to 10 grains; as a salagogue, one or two grains twice a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. e. Submuriatas Hydrargyri precipitatum, E. Precipitated hydrargyrum muriatum mite præcipitatum, D. Hydrargyri muriatus mite, L. Precipitated submuriate of mercury. Precipitated mild muriate of mercury. Procured by adding to a solution of half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of purified quicksilver in the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of diluted nitrous acid, a solution of four pounds and a half of muriate of soda in eight pounds of boiling <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; washing and drying the precipitate. Much the same in its effects and doses as the foregoing. f. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">Calx</a> Hydrargyri <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBA">alba</a>, L. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">White</a> calx of white calx of mercury. White precipitate. Prepared by dissolving first half a pound of sal ammoniac, and then half a pound of muriated mercury, in distilled water, adding to the mixed solution half a pound of water of prepared kall, filtering and washing and drying the precipitate. See Duncan's Dispensatory. g. Unguentum calcis hydrargyri albae, L. Ointment of ointment of white calx of mercury. Prepared by mixing a dram of the foregoing with an ounce and a half of ointment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOG">hog</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a>. Used to destroy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a>, and in some cutaneous eruptions. h. Oxidum hydrargyri cinereum, E. Pulvis hydrargyri cinereus, D. Cinereous oxide of mercury. Prepared by dissolving four parts of purified quicksilver in five parts of diluted nitrous acid; then gradually adding 15 parts of distilled water, and pouring in a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water of carbonate of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMONIA">ammonia</a> to precipitate the whole of the oxide, which is to be washed and dried. A mild salagogue and alterative. Dose from one to five grains. Used also as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUMIGATION">fumigation</a> in syphilitic eruptions, &c. i. Unguentum Oxidi Hydrargyri Cinerei, E. Ointment of cinerous oxide of mercury. Composed of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the foregoing, and three parts of hog's lard. Used for mercurial inunction. k. Hydrargyrum cum Creta, L. Quicksilver with chalk. Prepared by triturating together three parts of purified quicksilver and five parts of prepared chalk, till the globules disappear. A mild alterative. Dose from 10 to 30 grains. l. Hydrargyrum Calcinatum, D. Hydrargyrum Calcinatus, L. Calcined mercury. See Chemistry, No 1709. A violent salagogue. Dose half a grain to a grain. m. Oxidum Hydrargyri Rubrum per Acidum Nitricum, E. Hydrargyrum Nitratus Ruber, L. Hydrargyrum Subnitratum, D. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> oxide of mercury by nitric acid. Red nitrated mercury. Red precipitate. See Chemistry, No 1709. Used as a stimulant or an efaractive in fungous ulcers, &c. n. Unguentum Oxidi Hydrargyri Rubri, E. Ointment of red oxide of mercury. Composed of one part of the foregoing reduced to fine powder, and eight parts of hog's lard. o. Subsulphas Hydrargyri Flavus, E. Hydrargyrum Subvitriolatum, D. Hydrargyrum Vitriolatus, L. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">Yellow</a> subfulphate of mercury. Subvitriolated mercury. Turpeth mineral. See Chemistry, No 1720. Employed chiefly as an erthine, mixed with liquorice powder or cephalic snuff. p. Sulphuretum Hydrargyri Nigrum, E. Hydrargyrum Sulphuratum Nigrum, D. Hydrargyrum Cum Sulphure, L. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> sulphuret of mercury. Mercury with sulphur. Ethiops mineral. Prepared by triturating together in a glass <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> with a glass pestle, equal weights of purified quicksilver, and sublimed sulphur, till the globules of the former disappear. See Chemistry, No 1712. Employed chiefly as an alternative in cutaneous diseases and glandular affections. Dose from five or 10 grains to a dram or more. q. Hydrargyrum Sulphuratum Rubrum, D. Hydrargyrum Sulphuratius Ruber, L. Red sulphuret of mercury. Facitios cinnabar. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMILION">Vermilion</a>. See Chemistry, No 1713. Used principally as a fumigation for venereal ulcers in the nose, mouth, and throat, and as an ingredient in an ointment for the itch. r. Pilulae Hydrargyri, E. L. D. Mercury pills. Prepared by triturating an ounce of purified quicksilver with the same weight of conserve of red roses in a glass mortar, till the globules completely disappear, adding occasionally a little mucilage of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> arabic, then adding two ounces of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STARCH">starch</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> the whole with a little water into a mass, to be immediately divided into 480 equal pills (E.). The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> pills are composed of two drams of purified quicksilver, three drams of conserve of roses, and one dram of powdered liquorice; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a> pills of three drams of quicksilver, the same of extract of liquorice, and a dram and a half of purified liquorice root. Four grains of the Edinburgh mass, three of the London, and two and a half of the Dublin, contain about one grain of mercury, so that the last are nearly twice as strong as the first. Dose of the Edinburgh pills as a salagogue, from three to six, once or twice a day. s. Unguentum Hydrargyri, E. Mercurial ointment. Blue ointment. Prepared by triturating together one part of quicksilver with a little hog's lard, till the globules disappear; then adding one part of mutton fat, and as much hog's lard as, with the first quantity, is equal to three parts. Also formed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> or treble the quantity of mercury. Used for mercurial inunction. Quantity to be used at once about four scruples or drams every other night, or every night. t. Unguentum Hydrargyri Fortius, L. D. Stronger mercurial ointment. Composed of two pounds of purified quicksilver, 23 ounces of prepared hog's lard, and an ounce of prepared mutton fat. Quantity used at once, about two scruples or a dram. u. Unguentum Hydrargyri Mitius, L. D. Mild mercurial ointment. Trooper's ointment. Formed of one part of the foregoing, and two of prepared hog's lard. Used chiefly to destroy vermin, or for some cutaneous affections. v. Emplastrum Hydrargyri, E. Mercurial <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>. Formed by melting one part of olive <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and the same of white rosin together; and when the mixture is cold, rubbing with it three parts of quicksilver till the globules disappear, afterwards adding by degrees six parts of melted plaster of semivitrified oxide of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and mixing the whole carefully together. w. Emplastrum Ammoniaci cum Hydrargyro, L. Plaster of gum ammoniac with mercury. Prepared by triturating together three ounces of purified quicksilver, with about a dram of sulphurated oil, till the globules disappear, and then adding gradually one pound of strained gum ammoniac melted. **<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, &c.** **Part IV.** **a. Emplastrum Lithargyri cum Hydrargyro, L. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LITHARGE">Litharge</a> plaster with mercury.** Composed of three ounces of purified quicksilver, about a dram of sulphurated oil, and a pound of melted litharge plaster. These three last are employed as resolvents and diuretics, in cases of venereal nodes and beginning inductions. **b. Unguentum nitratis hydrargyri, E. Unguentum hydrargyri nitrati, L.D. Unguentum citrinum.** Ointment of nitrate of mercury. Citrine ointment. Prepared by first dissolving one part of quicksilver in two of nitrous acid, and beating up the solution in a glass mortar, with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> parts of olive oil, and three of hog's lard, previously melted together (or with 12 parts of hog's lard, L.D.) till the whole is formed into an ointment. A powerful stimulant and detergent ointment, useful in inflammation and ulceration of the eyelids, and in cutaneous affections. **c. Sulfas Zinci, E. Zincum vitriola.** Sulphate of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a>, L.D. Sulphate of zinc. Vitriolated zinc. White vitriol. See Chemistry, No 1764. Employed internally as an emetic, in the dose of from 10 to 30 grains, and as an astringent and tonic in a dose of from two to five grains, several times a day. Externally as a stimulant and astringent, in the form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOTION">lotion</a>, collyrium, or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJECTION">injection</a>. **d. Solutio sulphatis zinci, E. Solution of sulphate of zinc.** Prepared by dissolving 16 grains of sulphate of zinc in eight ounces of water; then adding 16 drops of diluted sulphuric acid, and filtering through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>. Used in most cases where the sulphate of zinc is employed externally. **e. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUA">Aqua</a> zinci vitriolati cum camphora, L. Water of vitriolated zinc with camphor.** Composed of half an ounce of vitriolated zinc, half an ounce by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of camphorated spirit, and two pints of boiling water, mixed together, and filtered through paper. Used for an astringent lotion and collyrium. **f. Solutio acetitis zinci, E. Solution of acetic acid of zinc.** Prepared by mixing together a solution of one dram of sulphate of zinc, in 10 ounces of distilled water, and a solution of four scruples of acetate of lead in 10 ounces of distilled water, allowing them to stand for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> at rest, and filtering. An excellent astringent collyrium. **279. Oxidum Zinci impurum, E. Tutia, L. Impure oxide of zinc. Tutty. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a>.** **Officinal Preparations.** **a. Oxidum Zinci impurum praeparatum, E. Prepared Tutia praeparata, L.D. Prepared impure oxide of zinc. Prepared tutty.** Prepared in the same way as chalk, and other hard substances. **b. Unguentum oxidii zinci impuri, E. Unguentum tutiae, L.D. Ointment of impure oxide of zinc. Tutty ointment.** Composed of one part of the foregoing, and five parts of simple liniment (E.), or of any quantity of the foregoing, and as much ointment of spermaceti, or of hog's Part IV.

MAHWAH

Pages 19-19
or MAWEE, in Botany; an East Indian tree, so called by the natives of Bahar and the neighbouring countries, but of which the Sanscrit name is Madhuca or Madhuradruma. According to Lieut. C. Hamilton, by whom a very particular account of this tree is given in the Asiatic Researches*, it is of the class of the polyandria-monogynia of Linnæus, but of a genus not described by him. The tree, when full grown, is about the size of a common mango tree, with a bushy head and oval leaves a little pointed; its roots spreading horizontally, are sunk but little in the earth; the trunk, which is often of a considerable thickness, rises seldom to any great height, without giving off branches; it is, however, not uncommon to see it shoot up clear to the length of eight or ten feet; the wood itself is moderately hard, fine grained, and of a reddish colour. By incision the tree affords a resinous gum from the bark. The flowers are of a nature very extraordinary, differing essentially (says Mr Hamilton) from those of any other plant with which I am acquainted, as they have not, in any respect, the usual appearance of such, but rather resemble berries; and I, like many others, had long conceived them to be the fruit of the Mahwah." The tree drops its leaves in the month of February, and early in March these flowers begin to come out in clusters of thirty, forty, or fifty, from the extremity of every small branch; and, from this period till the latter end of April, as the flowers come to maturity (for they never open or expand), they continue falling off, with their anthera, in the mornings, a little after sunrise; when they are gathered; and afterwards dried by an exposure of a few days in the sun: when thus prepared, they very much resemble a dried grape, both in taste and flavour. Immediately after the flowers drop off, fresh shoots are made for the new leaves, which soon make their appearance, coming presently to their full growth. The fruit (properly so called) is of two sorts in shape; the one resembling a small walnut, the other somewhat larger and pointed: it is ripe towards the middle of May; and continues dripping from the tree till the whole fall, which is generally about the beginning or towards the middle of June. The outer covering, or pericarpium, which is of a soft texture, commonly bursts in the fall, so that the seeds are very easily squeezed out of it: the seeds are somewhat of the shape, but longer than an olive. These seeds are replete with a thick oil, of the consistence of butter or ghee, which is obtained by expression. From this description it may easily be conceived, that the Mahwah tree and its productions are of singular and general use, especially in those dry and barren countries, which, from the nature of their situation, are not so well calculated for producing in plenty or perfection the other necessaries of life. The corolla or flowers, after being dried as before described, are eaten by the natives raw or dressed with their curries; and, when even simply boiled with rice, they afford a strengthening and wholesome nourishment. They are indeed, our author tells us, often ap. Mahwah, plied to a less laudable purpose; for being fermented, they yield by distillation a strong spirit, which the people here sell for very cheap, that for one pice (about a halfpenny) may be purchased no less than a eucalyptus (above a pint English) with which any man may get completely drunk. These flowers make an article of trade; being exported from this country to Patna and elsewhere in no inconsiderable quantities. The oil yielded by the fruit, as before mentioned, resembles ghee so much, that, being cheaper, the natives often mix it with that commodity. They use it the same as ghee in their victuals, and in the composition of some sorts of sweetmeats; and burn it in their lamps. It is also regarded as a salutary remedy, applied externally to wounds and all cutaneous eruptions. It is at first of the consistence of common oil, but soon coagulates: after being kept for some time, it acquires a bitterish taste and rancid smell, which renders it somewhat less agreeable as an article of food: but this is an inconvenience which, by the oil being properly clarified and prepared at first, might be perhaps avoided. This oil is also exported both in its adulterated and original state to Patna and other parts of the low country. The gum has not been applied to any use: but might be collected in large quantities in the months of March and April, about the time the flowers come out.

MAI INDUCTIO

Pages 21-21

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> and people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>-villages to go in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> to some adjoining wood on a May-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> morning; and return in a kind of triumph, with a May pole, boughs, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, garlands, and other tokens of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. This May-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rejoicing at the coming of the spring, was for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> observed, and still is in some parts of England; but there was thought to be so much heathen vanity in it, that it was condemned and prohibited within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a> by the good old Bishop Grofthead.

MAIDEN

Pages 19-20

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for beheading criminals. Of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and form of this instrument Mr Pennant gives the following account: "It seems to have been confined to the limits of the forest of Hardwick, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the 18 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and hamlets within its precincts. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is unknown; whether <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> Warren, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of this forest, might have established it among the fugitive laws then in use against the invaders of the hunting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, or whether it might not take place after the woollen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a> began to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> strength, is uncertain. The last is very probable; for the wild <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> around the town was inhabited by a lawless set, whose depredations on the cloth-tenters might soon stifle the efforts of infant industry. For the protection of trade, and for the greater terror of offenders by speedy execution, this custom seems to have been established, so as at last to receive the force of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, which was, 'That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a felon be taken within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of the forest of Hardwick, with goods stolen out, or within the said precincts, either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>-habend, back-bearand, or confessed, to the value of thirteen pence halfpenny, he shall, after three market days or meeting-days within the town of Halifax, next after such his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>, and being condemned, be taken to the gibbet, and there have his head cut from his body.'" "The offender had always a fair <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>; for as soon as he was taken, he was brought to the lord's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a> at Halifax: he was then exposed on the three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> (which here were held thrice in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>), placed in a stocks, with the goods stolen on his back, or, if the theft was of the cattle kind, they were placed by him; and this was done both to strike terror into others, and..." and to produce new informations against him. The bailiff then summoned four freeholders of each town within the forest to form a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a>. The felon and prosecutors were brought <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> to face; and the goods, the cow or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, or whatsoever was stolen, produced. If he was found guilty, he was remanded to prison, had a week's time allowed for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>, and then was conveyed to this spot, where his head was struck off by this machine. I should have premised, that if the criminal, either after apprehension, or in the way to execution, could escape out of the limits of the forest (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the town), the bailiff had no farther power over him; but if he should be caught within the precincts at any time after, he was immediately executed on his former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>. "This privilege was very freely used during the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>: the records before that time were lost. Twenty-five suffered in her reign, and at least 12 from 1623 to 1650; after which I believe the privilege was no more exerted. "This machine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> is now destroyed; but I <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> one of the same kind in a room under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, where it was introduced by the regent Morton, who took a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of it as he passed through Halifax, and at length suffered by it himself. It is in form of a painter's easel, and about ten feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>: at four feet from the bottom is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> on which the felon lays his head, which is kept <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by another placed above. In the inner edges of the frame are grooves; in these is placed a sharp axe, with a vast <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, supported at the very summit with a peg: to that peg is fastened a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, which the executioner <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a>, the axe falls, and does the affair effectually, without suffering the unhappy criminal to undergo a repetition of strokes, as has been the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> method. I must add, that if the sufferer is condemned for stealing a horse or a cow, the string is tied to the beast, which, on being whipped, pulls out the peg, and becomes the executioner." This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> is now in possession of the Scottish Antiquarian <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>. MAIDEN is also the name of a machine first used in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, and since introduced into other places, for washing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>; consisting of a tub 19 inches high, and 27 inches diameter at the top, in which the linen is put, with hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, to which is adapted a cover, fitting it very closely, and fastened to the tub by two wedges; through a hole in the middle of the cover passes an upright piece of wood, kept at a proper height by a peg above, and furnished with two handles, by which it is turned backward and forward: to the lower end of this upright piece is fastened a round piece of wood, in which are fixed several pieces, like cogs of a wheel. The operation of this machine is to make the linen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> and repass quick through the water. MAIDEN-Rents, in our old writers, a noble paid by the tenants of some manors on their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. This was said to be given to the lord for his omitting the custom of marcheta, whereby he was to have the first night's lodging with his tenant's wife; but it seems more probably to have been a fine for a license to marry a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>.

MAIDENHEAD

Pages 20-20

a town of Berks, 26 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>. It is governed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, a mayor, a steward, and 19 aldermen, out of which last two bridgemasters are chosen every year. Here is a gaol both for debtors and felons. The town stands partly in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Bray and partly in that of Cookham; and here is a chapel peculiar to the corporation, the minister whereof is chosen by the inhabitants, and not obliged to attend the bishop's visitation. Here are several almshouses and charities. This town, now so considerable, did not begin to flourish till, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of its bridge, travellers were brought this way, who before used a ferry at that called Babham's End, two miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of it. The barge pier bridge is maintained by the corporation, for which they are allowed the tolls both over and under it. The bridge-pier divides Berks from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUCKS">Bucks</a>. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade here in malt, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, which they carry in their barges to London. As this is the great thoroughfare from thence to Bath, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, and other south-west parts of England, the adjacent wood <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> thicket has been noted for many robberies. The market here is on Wednesdays; there are three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>; and here are frequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> races.

MAIDSTONE

Pages 20-20

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, in England, 36 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, seated on the river Medway, a branch of which runs through it. It is a corporation, and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> trade, besides <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>-thread, which is made in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> perfection, is in hops; of which there are great plenty of plantations about the town, as well as orchards of cherries. The tide flows quite up to the town, and brings up barges, &c., of 50 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 60 tons. It has a fine <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. One of the public gaols for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> is kept in this town; and the custody of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WEIGHTS_AND_MEASURES">weights and <a class</a>="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, renewed by the standard of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VII., was committed to it by parliament, as being in the centre of Kent; for which reason the knights of the shire are always elected, and the courts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> always held here, and generally the assizes. The archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> is constant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>, which is his peculiar, and served by his curate. Here are four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, in which are above 100 boys and girls, who are visited once a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> and catechized by the minister. This is such a plentiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and the lands hereabouts are so rich, that London is supplied with more commodities from hence than from any market-town in England; particularly with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> bullocks that come from the Weald of Kent, which begins but six miles off; with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, wheat, and great quantities of hops, apples, and cherries; with a fort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVING">paving</a>-stone, eight or ten inches <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, that is exceeding durable; and with the fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> sand for glasshouses and stationers. There are so many gentlemen's seats within 10 miles, that it is rare to find a town of so much trade and business, so full of gentry and good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>.

MAIENNE

Pages 20-20

a considerable, handsome, and populous town in France, formerly having the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>; seated on a river of the same name, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 35' N. Lat. 48° 18'.

MAIGNAN

Pages 20-21

EMANUEL, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINIM">Minim</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> of considerable eminence, was born of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and noble family at Thouleuf in 1601. Like the famous Pascal, he became a complete mathematician without the assistance of a teacher; and filled the professor's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> at Rome in 1636, where, at the expense expence of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Spada, he published his book *De Perspectiv Horaria*. He returned to Thoulouse in 1650, and was created <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> who in 1660 entertained himself with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> and curiosities in his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a>, made him offers by Cardinal Mazarine, to draw him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; but he humbly desired to spend the remainder of his days in a cloister. He published a course of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, 4 vols 8vo, at Thoulouse; to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition of which he added two treatises, one against the vortices of Descartes, and the other on the speaking <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a> invented by Sir Samuel Morland. He is said to have studied even in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, his very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a> being employed in theorems, the demonstrations of which would awaken him with joy. He died in 1676.

MAIL

Pages 21-22

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> primarily applied to the meshes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> holes in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. **Coat of Mail.** See Coat. It is called also a haubergeon. Anciently they also wore shirts of mail under the waistcoat, to serve as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> against swords and poniards. We also read of gloves of mail. **Mail**, or **Mall**, also signifies a round <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; whence the play of pall-mall, from *palla* "a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>," and *maille* "the round ring through which it is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>." **Mail**, or **Maille**, in our old writers, a small kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. Silver halfpence were likewise termed *Mailles*, 9 Henry V. By indenture in the mint, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of old <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> silver was to be coined into 360 sterlings or pennies, or 720 mails or half-pennies, or 1440 farthings. Hence the word mail was derived, which is now vulgarly used in Scotland to signify an annual rent. **Mail**, or **Mail**, on ship-board, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> machine composed of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of rings interwoven net-wise, and used for rubbing off the loose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> which remains on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> cordage after it is made. Mail is likewise used for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> bag wherein letters are carried by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>. **Mail-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COACH">Coach</a>.** See Coach. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">Action</a> of Mails and Duties, in Scots <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>.** See Law, p. 689, § 20. **Mail, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a>.** See Black-Mail. **Maillet, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>-Marie de Moyriac de,** a learned Jesuit, was born in the castle of Mailiac in the Bugey, and appointed a missionary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, whither he went in 1703. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 28 he had acquired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a skill in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, arts, sciences, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> books of the Chinese, as to astonish even the learned. He was greatly beloved and esteemed by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Kham-Hi, who died in 1722. He, together with other missionaries, was employed by that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> to draw a chart of China and Chinese <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, which was engraved in France in the year 1732. He drew likewise particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTS">charts</a> of some of the provinces of this vast empire; with which the emperor was so pleased, that he settled the author at his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. The great annals of China were also translated into French by Father Maillet, and his manuscript was transmitted to France in 1737. This work was published in 12 volumes quarto, under the inspection of M. Grofier, and is the first complete <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of that extensive empire. The style, which was full of hyperbole and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOMBAST">bombast</a>, has been revised by the editor, and the speeches which extended to too great a length, and had too much sameness in them, have been omitted. Father Maillet, after having resided 45 years in China, died at Pekin on the 28th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1748, in the 79th year of his age. Kien-Lung the reigning emperor paid the expenses of his funeral. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of a lively and gentle character, capable of the most persevering labour and the most unremitting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>. **Maillet, Benoît de,** descended from a noble family in Lorraine, was born in 1659, and appointed, at the age of 33, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> general for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. He fulfilled this office for 16 years with great ability, supported the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s authority against the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANIZARIES">janizaries</a>, and greatly extended the trade of France into that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. As a recompense for his services, the king bestowed upon him the consulship of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a>, which is the first and most considerable consulship in his gift. Being at last appointed in 1715 to visit the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-ports Maillet, sea-ports in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a> and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Barbary, he was so successful in the execution of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, that he obtained permission to retire with a considerable pension. He settled at Marseille; where he died in 1738, in the 79th year of his age. He was a man of a lively imagination, and gentle manners; in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> he was very amiable, and he possessed the strictest probity. He was fond of praise, and very anxious about the reputation of genius. During the whole of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he paid particular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> history; and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> object was to become acquainted with the origin of our globe. On this important subject he left some curious observations, which have been published in octavo under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Telliamed, which is the name de Maillet written backwards. The editor Abbé Malcrier has given to this work the form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a>. An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> is introduced as explaining to a French missionary his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the globe, and the origin of mankind; and, which is very incredible, he supposes it to have come out of the waters, and makes an abode uninhabitable by man the birthplace of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>. His great object is to prove, that all the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of which this globe is composed, even to the tops of the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, have come from the bottom of the waters; that they are the work of the sea, which continually retires to allow them gradually to appear. Telliamed dedicated his book to the illustrious Cyrano de Bergerac, author of the imaginary "Travels to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>." In the humorous epistle which is addressed to him, the Indian philosopher informs us that these dialogues are nothing but a collection of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a> and fancies. He cannot be accused of having broken his word; but he may well be reproached with not having written them in the same style with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Cyrano, and with not having displayed equal liveliness and humour. A subject the most extravagant is handled in the gravest manner, and his ridiculous opinion is delivered with all the serious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of a philosopher. Of the six dialogues which compose the work, the four first contain many curious observations truly philosophical and important; in the other two we find nothing but conjectures, fancies, and fables, sometimes amusing, but always absurd. To Maillet we are indebted also for "A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">Description</a> of Egypt;" collected from his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> by the editor of Telliamed, 1743, 4to, or in 2 vols. 12mo.

MAIMONIDES

Pages 22-22

Moses, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Moses the son of Maimon, a celebrated rabbi, called by the Jews the eagle of the doctrine, was born of an illustrious family at Cordova in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in 1131. The early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> was undertaken by his father, who afterwards placed him under the tuition of Rabbi <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, the son of Megas, a person of whose profound learning he has bestowed the highest praise; and, according to Leo Africanus, he had also among his tutors the learned Arabians Ibn Thophail and Averroes. He is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> named Moses Egyptian, because he settled in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, where he spent his whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of physician to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a>. Here he opened a school, which was soon filled with pupils from all parts, from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> and Damascus especially, whose proficiency under him spread his fame all over the world. He was no less eminent in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, than in medicine. Calaubon affirms it may be truly said of him, as Pliny of old said of Diodorus Siculus, that "he was the first of his tribe who ceased to be a trifle." It would be tedious to enumerate all the works of Maimonides; some were written originally in Arabic, but are now extant only in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> translations. "Those (says Collier) who desire to learn the doctrine and the canon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> contained in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALMUD">Talmud</a>, may read Maimonides's compendium of it in good Hebrew, in his book entitled Yad; wherein they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> find <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of the fables and imbecilities in the Talmud entirely discarded. But the More Nevochim is the most valued of all his works; designed to explain the obscure words, phrases, metaphors, &c., in scripture, which, when literally interpreted, have either no meaning or appear absurd.

MAIN

Pages 22-22

an epithet usually applied by sailors to whatever is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>, as opposed to whatever is inferior <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> secondary. Thus the main <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> is used in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>; and the main mast, the main wale, the main <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>, and the main hatchway, are in like manner distinguished from the fore and mizen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, the channel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">wales</a>, the false keel, and the fore and after hatchways, &c.

MAINOUR

Pages 22-23

Manour, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Meinour (from the French, manier, i.e. manu tractare), in a legal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> denotes the thing that a thief taketh away or flealeth: As to be taken with the mainour (Pl. Cor. fol. 179.), is to be taken with the thing stolen about him: And again (fol. 194.) it was pretended, that a thief was delivered to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> or viscount, together with the mainour: And again (fol. 186.), <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> be indicted, that he feloniously stole the goods of another, where, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, they are his own goods, and the goods be brought into the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> as the mainour; and if it be demanded of him, what he <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> to the goods, and he disclaim them; though he be acquitted of the felony, he shall lose the goods: And again (fol. 149.), if the defendant were taken with the mainour, and the mainour be carried to the court, they, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times, would arraign him upon the mainour, without any <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a>. Cowell. See Blackst. Comment. vol. iii. p. 71. vol. iv. p. 303. MAINPRIZE. See False Imprisonment. The writ of mainprize, manucapio, is a writ directed to the sheriff (either generally, when any man is imprisoned for a bailable offence, and bail hath been refused; or specially, when the offence or cause of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMITMENT">commitment</a> commitment is not properly bailable below), commanding him to take sureties for the prisoner's appearance, usually called mainpernors, and to let him at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>. Mainpernors differ from bail, in that a man's bail may imprison or surrender him up before the stipulated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of appearance; mainpernors can do neither, but are barely sureties for his appearance at the day: bail are only sureties for which the parties be answerable for the special <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> for which they stipulate, mainpernors are bound to produce him to answer all charges whatever. See HABERAS CORPUS.

MAINTENANCE

Pages 23-23

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, bears a near relation to BARBETRY; being an officious intermeddling in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> that no way belongs to one, by maintaining <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> afflicting either party with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> or otherwise, to prosecute or defend it; a practice that was greatly encouraged by the first introduction of usfs. This is an offence against public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, as it keeps alive strife and contention, and perverts the remedial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of the law into an engine of oppression. And therefore, by the Roman law, it was a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the crimen falsi, to enter into any confederacy, or do any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> to support another's law suit, by money, witnessefs, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> may, however, maintain the suit of his near kinsman, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> neighbour, out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> and compassion, with impunity. Otherwise the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law is fine and imprisonment; and by the statute 32 Henry VIII. c. 9, a forfeiture of 10l.

MAINTENON

Pages 23-23

MADAME DE, a French lady of extraordinary fortune, descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family, and whose proper name was Frances d'Aubigné, was born in 1635. Her parents by misfortunes being ill able to support her, she fell to the care of her mother's relations; to escape which state of dependence, she was induced to marry that famous old buffoon the Abbé Scarron, who subsisted himself only on a pension allowed him by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> for his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and parts. She lived with him many years, which Voltaire makes no scruple to call the happiest years of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; but when he died in 1660, she found herself as indigent as she had been before her <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. Her friends indeed endeavoured to get her husband's pension <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to her, and presented so many petitions to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> about it, all beginning with "The widow Scarron most humbly prays your majesty's," &c. that he was quite weary of them, and has been heard to exclaim, "Must I always be pestered with the widow Scarron?" At last, however, through the recommendation of Madame de Montespan, he settled a much larger pension on her, with a genteel apology for making her wait so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; and afterward made choice of her to take care of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of the young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, his son by Madame de Montespan. The letters she wrote on this occasion charmed the king, and were the origin of her advancement; her personal merit effected all the rest. He bought her the lands of Maintenon, the only estate she ever had; and finding her pleased with the acquisition, called her publicly Madame de Maintenon; which was of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to her in her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>, by releasing her from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> attending that of Scarron. Her elevation was to her only a retreat; the king came to her apartment every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> after dinner, before and after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>, and continued there till midnight; here he did business with his ministers, while Madame de Maintenon, employed in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> needlework, never showed any desire to talk of state affairs; and carefully avoided all appearance of cabal or intrigue; she did not even make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of her power to dignify her own relations. About the latter end of the year 1685, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. married her, he being then in his 48th and she in her 50th year; and that piety with which she inspired the king to make her a wife instead of a mistress, became by degrees a fettered dilution of mind. She prevailed on Louis to found a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> at St Cyr, for the education of 300 young ladies of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; and here she frequently retired from that melancholy of which she complains so pathetically in one of her letters, and which few ladies <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> suppose she should be liable to in such an elevated situation. But, as M. Voltaire says, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> anything could show the vanity of ambition, it would certainly be this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>. Madame de Maintenon could have no other uneasiness than the uniformity of her manner of living with a great king; and this made her once say to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> D'Aubigné her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, "I can hold it no longer; I wish I was dead." The answer he made to her was, "You have then a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> to marry the Almighty!" Louis, however, died before her in 1715; when she retired wholly to St Cyr, and spent the rest of her days in acts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>; and what is most surprising is, that her husband left no certain provision for her, recommending her only to the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>. She would accept no more than a pension of 80,000 livres, which was punctually paid her till she died in 1719. A collection of her letters has been published, and translated into English; from which familiar intercourse her character will be better known than from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>.

MAIRAN

Pages 25-26

Jean-Jacques d'Ortous de, descended from a noble family at Besiers, was born in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> in 1678, and died at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> of a delusion on the lungs on the 20th of February 1771, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 93. He was one of the most illustrious members of the Academy of Sciences and of the French Academy. Being early connected with the former <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, he, in the year 1741, succeeded Fontenelle in the office of secretary. This station he filled with the most distinguished success till the year 1744; and, like his predecessor, possessed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of placing the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> subjects in the clearest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> which is very rare, but which appears conspicuous in all his works. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of them are, 1. Dissertation sur la Glace, the last edition of which was printed in 1749, 12mo. This excellent little tract has been translated into German and Italian. 2. Dissertation sur la cause de la lumière des Phosphores, 1717, 12mo. 3. Traité historique et physique de l'Aurore Boreale, first published in 12mo, 1733, and afterwards much enlarged and printed in 4to in 1754. The system embraced by the author is liable to be controverted; but the book displays <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and erudition. 4. Lettre au Pere Parennin, contenant diverses questions sur la Chine, 12mo. This is a very curious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and is full of that philosophical spirit which characterizes the author's other publications. 5. A great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of papers in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of the Academy of Sciences (since 1719), of which he published some volumes. 6. Several Dissertations on particular subjects, which form only small pamphlets. 7. The Eloges of the Academicians of the Academy of Sciences, who died in 1741, 1742, 1743, in 12mo, 1747. Without imitating Fontenelle, the author attained almost equal excellence by his talent of discriminating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, appreciating their worth, and giving them their due share of praise, without at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> concealing their defects. Mairan's reputation extended itself into foreign countries. He was a member of the Imperial Academy at Petersburgh, of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Academy of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, of the royal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> and Upsal, &c. The gentleness and sweetness of his manners made him be considered as a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of the social virtues. He possessed that amiable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>, that agreeable gaiety, and that steady firmness, which never fail to procure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and esteem. But we must add, says M. Saverien, that every thing had a reference to himself; self-love and a regard to his own reputation were the motives of all his actions. He was deeply affected with censure <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> applause, and yet he had many friends. Uniting much gentleness of disposition to an ingenious and agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of countenance, he possessed the art of infusing himself into the good graces of others, so as to pave the way to elevation and success. He was honoured with protection and particular marks of regard by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a> the regent, who bequeathed to him his watch in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Conti loaded him with favours; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> Dagueffeau, observing in him great originality and ingenuity of thought, appointed him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the Journal des Sciences: a station which he filled very much to the satisfaction of the public and of the learned. The private and selfish views imputed to him by M. Saverien never made him deficient in what was due to the strictest probity. An expression of his is remembered, which could have proceeded only from sentiment; "An honest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> (said he) is one whose blood is refreshed with the recital of a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>." He was ready at repartee. One <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> he happened to be in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>, and to differ with him in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> upon some point which had no more connexion with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">jurisprudence</a> than with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>. "Sir," said the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, who supposed that a learned man was a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IDIOT">idiot</a> out of his own sphere, "we are not now talking of Euclid or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHIMEDES">Archimedes</a>."—"No, nor of Cujas nor Barthole!" replied the academician.

MAIRE

Pages 26-26

STREIGHTS LE, a passage to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">Horn</a>, situated between Terra del <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEGO">Fuego</a> and Staten <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>; which, being discovered by Le Maire, obtained his name. It is now, however, less made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of than formerly, ships going round Staten island as well as Terra del Fuego.

MAISTRE

Pages 26-26
LOUIS-ISAAC LE, better known by the name of Sacy, was born at Paris in 1613. His genius very early discovered itself. After an excellent course of study under the direction of the abbot of Saint Cyran, he was raised to the priesthood in 1648, and soon after was chosen, on account of his virtues, to be director of the religious of Port Royal des Champs. As this monastery bore the reputation of Jansenism, their enemies were furnished with a pretence for persecuting them. In 1661 the director was obliged to conceal himself; and in 1666 he was committed to the Bastille. During his confinement he composed the book Figures de la Bible; in which, according to the Molinists, allusions are made to the sufferings endured by the Jansenists. If we may believe a Jesuit writer, the gentlemen of Port Royal and those who opposed their errors are represented in the 92d figure, the former by David, the latter by Saul. Rehoboam in the 116th figure, Jezebel in the 130th, Ahaziah in the 148th and 150th, and Darius in the 160th, in the opinion of this author, represent Louis XIV. The writer of these anecdotes, of which we do not answer for the authenticity, adds, that when Sacy wished to reproach his persecutors, he always did it by means of the holy fathers. If this is the key to those enigmatical portraits and allusions, which it is pretended are to be found in that book, certain we are it was not discovered by the spirit of charity. Besides, it is not certain that Sacy was the author of that book; for it is much more probable that it was composed by Nicolas Fontaine his fellow prisoner. To Sacy's confinement the public are indebted for a French translation of the Bible. This work was finished in 1668, the evening before the feast of All Saints; on which day he recovered his liberty, after an imprisonment of two years and a half. He was presented to the king and the minister; and all the favour he asked from them was, that they would send several times a year to examine the state of the prisoners in the Bastille. Le Maistre continued at Paris till 1673, when he retired to Port Royal, which he was obliged to leave in 1679. He went to settle at Pompone, where he died January 4, 1684, at the age of 71. From him we have, 1. La Traduction de la Bible, with explanations of the spiritual and literal meaning taken from the fathers, the greater part of which was done by Du Foë, Huré, and Tourneux. This is the best French translation, which has yet appeared, and the most esteemed edition is that of Paris in 3 vols. 8vo, 1682 and following years. The author translated the New Testament three times, because the first time the style of it appeared too much laboured and too refined, and the second too simple. A counterfeit of the edition in 3 vols. 8vo, was published at Brussel in 40 vols. 12mo. The best editions of this version have been published at Brussel, 1700, in 3 vols. 4to; at Amsterdam, under the name of Paris, 1711, 8 vols. 12mo; at Paris 1713, in 2 vols. 4to; and in 1715, with notes and a concordance, 4 vols folio. 2. Une Traduction des Psaumes selon l'Hebreu et la Vulgate, in 12mo. 3. Une version des Homélies de St Chrysostome sur St Matthieu, in 3 vols 8vo. 4. La Traduction de l'Imitation de Jésus Christ (sous le nom de Beuil, prieur de Saint-Val), Paris 1663, 8vo. 5. Celle de Phèdre, 12mo. (sous le nom de Saint-Aubin). 6. De trois Comédies de Terence, in 12mo. 7. Des Lettres de Bongars (sous le nom de Brianville). 8. Du Piéme de St Prophèr sur les ingrati, 12mo, en vers et en prose. 9. Les Enluminures de l'Almanach des jéfuites, 1654, 12mo, reprinted in 1733. In 1653 there appeared a print representing the overthrow of Jansenism authenticated by the two powers, and the confusion of the disciples of the bishop of Ypres, who are going to seek refuge with the Calvinists. The monks of Port-Royal were greatly provoked at this print, and Sacy thought that he would lower its reputation by means of his Enluminures, which Racine has ridiculed in one of his letters. It is indeed very strange that men of taste and piety should write satires to the injury of one another. 10. Heures de Port-Royal, 12mo. 11. Lettres de Piété, Paris 1690, 2 vols. 8vo.

MAITTAIRE

Pages 26-27

MICHAEL, a learned English writer, was born in 1668. Dr South, canon of Christ-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>, made him a student of that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, where he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of M.A. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 23, 1696. From 1695 till 1699 he was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Westminster school; which was afterwards indebted to him for Grece Linguae Dialecti, in usum Scholae Westmonasteriensis, 1706, 8vo; and for "The English <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, applied to, and exemplified in, the English Tongue, 1712," 8vo. In 1711, he published "Remarks on Mr Whitton's Account of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">Convocation</a>'s proceedings with relation to himself, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> reverend Father in God George <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Bishop of Bath and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a>," 8vo; also "An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> against Arianism, and some other Heresies; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a Reply to Mr William Whitton's Historical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">Preface</a> and Appendix to his Primitive Christianity revived," 8vo. In 1709 he gave the first specimen of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> skill in typographical antiquities, by publishing Stephanorum Historia, vitas totum ac libros complectens, 8vo; which was followed in 1717 by Historia Typographorum aliquot Parisiensium, vitas et libros complectens, 8vo. In 1719, Annales Typographici <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> arte inventa origine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> annum MD, 4to. The second volume, divided into two parts, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to the year 1336, was published at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a> in 1702; introduced by a letter of John Toland, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Conjectura verisimilis de prima Typographiae Inventione. The third volume, from the same press, in two parts, continued to 1557, and (by an Appendix) to 1664, in 1725. In 1733 was published at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> what is usually considered as the fourth volume, under the title of Annales Typographici ab arte inventa origine, ad annum MDCLXIV, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> Mich. Maittaire, A.M. editio nova, auctior et emendator; In 1741 the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was closed at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, by Annalium Typographicorum Tomus quintus et ultimus, indicem in tomos quattuor praecantantes complectens; divided, like the two preceding volumes, into two parts. In the intermediate years, Mr Maittaire was diligently employed on various works of value. In 1713 he published by subscription Opera ad Fragmenta Veterum Poetarum, 1713, two volumes in folio: the title of some copies is dated 1721. In 1714, he was the editor of a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, in 2 vols. The Latin writers, which he published separately, most of them with good indexes, came out in the following order: In 1713, Chrysost Patiens; Juven; Lucretius; Phaedrus; Sallust; Terence. In 1715, Catullus; Tibullus; Propertius; Cornelius Nepos; Florus; Horace; Juvenal; Ovid, 3 vols.; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>. In 1711, Caesar's Commentaries; Martial; Quintus Curtius. In 1718 and 1725, Velleius Paterculus. In 1719, Lucan. In 1720, Boneforni Carmina. In 1721 he published, Batrachomyomachia, Graeci, ad veterum exemplarium fidem recta; glotta Graeca, variabilibus lectionibus, verisimilibus Latinis, commentarius et indicibus, illigata, 8vo. In 1722, Miscellanea Graecorum aliquot Scriporum Carmina, cum verifone Latina et notis, 4to. In 1724 he compiled, at the request of Dr John Freind (at whose expense it was printed), an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> to the works of Arateus, to accompany the splendid folio edition of that author in 1723. In 1725 he published an excellent edition of Anacreon in 4to, of which no more than 100 copies were printed, and the few errata in each copy corrected by his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. A second edition of the like <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> was printed in 1741, with five copies on fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>. In 1726 he published Petri Petili Medici Parisiensis in tres prioris Aratei Cappadoci Libros Commentarii, nunc primum editi, 4to. This learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> was found among the papers of Graevius. From 1728 to 1733 he was employed in publishing Marmorum Arundelionorum, Seldenianorum, aliorumque Academiae Oxoniensis donatorum, una cum Commentariis et Indice, editio secunda, folio; to which an Appendix was printed in 1733. Epistolae D. Mich. Maittaire ad D. P. Des Maizeaux, in qua Indicis in Annales Typographicos methodus explicatur, &c., is printed in "The Present State of the Republic of Letters," August 1733, p. 142. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Robert Stephens in Latin, revised and corrected by the author, with a new and complete <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of his works, is prefixed to the improved edition of R. Stephens's Thesaurus, 4 vols. in folio, in 1734. In 1736 appeared Antique Inscriptiones duae, folio; being a commentary on two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> tables discovered near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERACLEA">Heraclea</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Tarentum. In 1738 were printed at the Hague Graecae Linguae Dialecti in Schola Regiae Westmonasteriensis usum recogniti, opera Mich. Maittaire. In 1739 he addressed to the empress of Russia a small Latin poem, under the title of Carmen Epinicum Auguflffimi Rufforum Imperatrix sacrum. His name not having been printed in the title page, it is not so generally known that he was editor of Plutarch's Apophthegmata, 1741, 4to. The last publication of Mr Maittaire was a volume of poems in 4to, 1742, under the title of Senilia, sive Poetica aliquot in argumentis variis generis tentamina. Mr Maittaire died in 1747, aged 79. His valuable library, which had been 50 years collecting, was sold by auction by Messrs Cock and Langford, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the same year, and the beginning of the following, taking up in all 44 nights. Mr Maittaire, it may be added, was patronized by the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, both before and after that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>'s elevation to the peerage, and continued a favourite with his son the second earl. He was also Latin <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to Mr Stanhope, the earl of Chesterfield's favourite son.

MAIZE
