or INDIAN CORN. See ZEA, BOTANY Index. MAKI. See LEMUR, MAMMALIA Index.

MAJESTY

Pages 21-21

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> given to kings, which frequently serves as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of distinction. The word seems composed of the two Latin words, *<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>* "greater," and *status* "state." The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> is called Sacred Majesty, Imperial Majesty, and Caesarian Majesty. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a> is styled His Apostolic Majesty. The king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> is termed His most Catholic Majesty; and the king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, His most Faithful Majesty. The king of France used to be called His most Christian Majesty; and when he treated with the emperor, the word Sacred was added: He was afterwards called simply, King of the French. Bonaparte assumed the title of Emperor and King of France.—With respect to other kings, the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> is added; as His Britannic Majesty, His Prussian Majesty, &c. Formerly princes were more sparing in giving titles, and more modest in claiming them: before the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. the king of Spain had only the title of Highness; and before that of Henry VIII. the kings of England were only addressed under the titles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a> and Highness. Under the Roman republic, the title Majesty (majestas) belonged to the whole body of the people, and to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> magistrates; so that to diminish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wound the majesty of the commonwealth, was to be wanting in respect to the state or to its ministers. But the power afterwards passing into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of a single person, the appellation of Majesty was transferred to the emperor and the imperial family. Pliny compliments Trajan on his being contented with the title of Greatness; and speaks very indifferently of those who affected that of Majesty. And yet this last seems to be the most modest and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> title that can be attributed to sovereigns, since it signifies no more than the royalty or sovereign power.

MAJOR

Pages 23-24

in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, the name of several officers of very different ranks and functions. Mayor-general. See General. Mayor of a Regiment of Foot, the next officer to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a>, generally promoted from the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>: he is to take care that the regiment be well exercised, to see it <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> in good order, and to rally it in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of being broke in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>: he is the only officer among the infantry that is allowed to be on horseback in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of action, that he may the more readily execute the colonel's orders. Mayor of a Regiment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">Horse</a>, as well as foot, ought to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, integrity, understanding, courage, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>: he should be <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, and keep a detail of the regiment in every particular: he should be skilled in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORSEMANSHIP">horsemanship</a>, and ever attentive to his business: one of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> functions is, to keep an exact roster of the officers for duty: he should have a perfect knowledge in all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> evolutions, as he is obliged by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> to instruct others, &c. Town-Major, the third officer in order in a garrison, and next to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>-governor. He should understand fortification, and has a particular <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the guards, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROUNDS">rounds</a>, patroles, and sentinels. Brigade-Major, is a particular officer appointed for that purpose only in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>: he goes every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> to headquarters to receive orders from the adjutant-general: there he writes exactly whatever is dictated to him: from thence he goes and gives the orders, at the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> appointed for that purpose, to the different majors <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> adjutants. Major adjutants of the regiments which compose that brigade, and regulates with them the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of officers and men which each are to furnish for the duty of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; taking care to keep an exact roster, that one may not give more than another; and that each march in their tour: in short, the major of brigade is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with the particular detail in his own brigade, in much the same way as the adjutant-general is charged with the general detail of the duty of the army. He sends every morning to the adjutant-general an exact return, by battalion and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, of the men of his brigade missing at the retreat, or a report expressing that none are absent: he also mentions the officers absent with or without leave. As all orders <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the majors of brigade, they have infinite occasions of making known their talents and exactness. **Mayor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">Artillery</a>**, is also the next officer to the Lieutenant-colonel. His post is very laborious, as the whole detail of the corps particularly rests with him; and for this reason all the non-commissioned officers are subordinate to him, as his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of **serjeant-major** imports: in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> they must render him an exact account of every thing which comes to their knowledge, either regarding the duty or wants of the artillery and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. He should possess a perfect knowledge of the power of artillery, together with all its evolutions. In the field he goes daily to receive orders from the brigade-major, and communicates them with the parole to his superiors, and then dictates them to the adjutant. He should be a very good mathematician, and be well acquainted with every thing belonging to the train of artillery, &c. **Mayor of Engineers**, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> with us called **Sub-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>**, should be very well skilled in military <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, fortification, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNNERY">gunnery</a>, and mining. He should know how to fortify in the field, to attack and defend all sorts of posts, and to conduct the works in a siege, &c. See **Engineer**. **Aid-Major**, is on sundry occasions appointed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> as major, who has a pre-eminence above others of the same denomination. Our horse and foot guards have their guidons, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> or third majors. **Serjeant-Major**, is a non-commissioned officer, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> merit and capacity, subordinate to the adjutant as he is to the major. See **Serjeant**. **Drum Major**, is not only the first drummer in the regiment, but has the same authority over his drummers as the corporal has over his squad. He instructs them in their different beats; is daily at orders with the serjeants, to know the number of drummers for duty. He marches at their head when they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> in a body. In the day of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, or at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, he must be very attentive to the orders given him, that he may regulate his beats according to the movements ordered. **Fife-Major**, is he that plays the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a> on that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, and has the same authority over the fifers as the drum-major has over the drummers. He teaches them their duty, and appoints them for guards, &c. **Major**, in **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>**, a person who is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> to manage his own affairs. By the civil law a man is not a major till the age of 25 years; in England, he is a major at 21, as in Normandy at 20. **Major**, in **Logic**, is understood of the first proposition of a regular syllogism. It is called major, because it has a more extensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> proposition, as containing the principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>. See **Logic**. **Major** and **Minor**, in **Music**, are applied to concords which differ from each other by a semi-tone. See **Concord**. **Major tone** is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the fifth and fourth; and major semi-tone the difference between the major fourth and the third. The major tone surpasses the minor by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMA">comma</a>. **Mayor-domo**, an Italian term, frequently used to signify a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> or master of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>. The title of mayor-domo was formerly given in the courts of princes to three different kinds of officers. 1. To him who took care of what related to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, or eating; otherwise called eleater, prefectus mensae, architrielinus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAPIFER">dapifer</a>, and principis coquorum. 2. Mayor-domo was also applied to the steward of the household.—3. The title of mayor-domo was also given to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> minister, or him to whom the prince deputed the administration of his affairs, foreign and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a>, relating to war as well as peace. Instances of major domos in the two first senses are frequent in the English, French, and Norman affairs. **Major**, John, a scholastic divine and historian, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HADDINGTON">Haddington</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOTHIAN">Lothian</a> in Scotland. It appears from some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in his writings, that he resided a while both at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. He went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1493, and studied in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARBE">Barbe</a>, under the famous John Boulac. Thence he removed to that of Montacute, where he began to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> under the celebrated Standouk. In the year 1498, he was entered of the college of Navarre. In 1503, he was created <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> in divinity; returned to Scotland in 1519, and taught <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> during several years in the university of St Andrew's. But, at length, being disgusted with the quarrels of his countrymen, he went back to Paris, and resumed his lectures in the college of Montacute, where he had several pupils who afterwards became men of great eminence. About the year 1530, he returned once more to Scotland, and was chosen professor of theology at St Andrew's, of which he afterwards became provost; and there died in 1547, aged 78. His logical treatises form one immense folio; his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s physics makes another; and his theological works amount to several volumes of the same size. These masses of crude and useless disputation were the admiration of his contemporaries. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, less prized in his own age, was to make him known to posterity. His book *De Geftis Scotorum*, was first published at Paris by Radius Afsenius, in the year 1521. He rejects in it some of the fictions of former historians; and would have had greater merit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had rejected more. He intermingles the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of England with that of Scotland; and has incurred the censure of some partial writers, for giving an authority to the authors of the former <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, which he refuses to those of his own. Bede, Caxton, and Froissart, were exceedingly useful to him. What does the greatest honour to this author is, the freedom with which he has censured the rapacity and indolence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, and the strain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> with which he treats the pope's supremacy. The style in which he wrote does not deserve commendation. Bishop Spotifield calls it Sorbonic and barbarous.

MAJORCA

Pages 24-25

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Mediterranean, lying between Yvica on the west and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINORCA">Minorca</a> on the east. These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THREE_ISLANDS">three <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> were anciently called Baleares, supposed to be from the skill of their inhabitants in flinging, for which they were very remarkable. Originally they belonged to the Carthaginians; but during the wars of that people with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> they seem to have regained their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. In 122 B.C., they were subdued by Metellus the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, who treated the inhabitants with such cruelty, that out of 30,000 he scarce left 1000 alive. He then built two cities on Majorca; one called Palma, now Majorca, to the east; the other to the west, named Pollentia, now no longer in being. The island <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> subject to the Romans, and to the nations who overran the western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the empire, for many ages. At last it was subdued by the Moors about the year 800. By them the island was put in a much better condition than it ever was before <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> since. The Moors being very industrious, and also populous, surrounded the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> with fortifications, that is, with a kind of towers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> between them; cultivated every spot in the island that was not either rock or sand; and had no fewer than 15 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, whereas now there are not above three. Neither was it at all difficult for the Moorish monarch to bring into the field an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> much superior in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> to the inhabitants that are now upon it, taking in all ranks, sexes, and ages. In 1229, the island was subdued by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARAGON">Aragon</a>, who established in it a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, feudatory to that of Arragon, which was again destroyed in 1341 by the same monarchs; and ever since, the island hath been subject to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and hath entirely lost its importance. It is about 60 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and 45 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is clear and temperate; and, by its situation, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> is so qualified by the breezes, that it is by far the most pleasant of all the islands in the Mediterranean. There are some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is generally flat, and of such an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, that it produces great quantities of corn as good in its kind as any in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">Oil</a>, wine, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, are very plentiful, as also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle and sheep; but deer, rabbits, and wild-fowl, abound so much, that they alone are sufficient for the subsistence of the inhabitants. There are no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, but a great many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, as well as several good harbours. The inhabitants are robust, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, and good seamen. Majorca, a handsome, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, rich, and strong town, in the island of the same name, with a bishop's see. It contains about 6000 houses, and 22 churches, besides the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>. The squares, the cathedral, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, are magnificent structures. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>-general resides there, who commands the whole island; and there is a garrison against the incursion of the Moors. It was taken by the English in 1706; but was retaken in 1715, since which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it has been in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Spaniards. It is seated on the south-west part of the island, where there is a good harbour, 70 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of Yvica, 120 south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARCELONA">Barcelona</a>, 140 east of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a>, and 300 from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>. E. Long. 2° 55'. N. Lat. 39° 36'.

MALABAR

Pages 27-27

the name given to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of Hindoostan on this side of the Ganges, extending from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Baglala to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Comorin, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> extremity of the kingdom of Canara as far as Cape Comorin, and lying between 9° and 14° N. Lat. It is bounded by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Balaghat on the east; by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECCAN">Deccan</a> on the north; and on the west and south is washed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>.

MALACA

Pages 27-27

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">Ancients</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, furredam Faderaturum by Pliny; a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town of Barica; a Carthaginian colony according to Strabo; so called from Malach, signifying "<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>;" a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> noted for pickled <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> salted meat. Now <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALAGA">Malaga</a>, a port town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 45. N. Lat. 36. 40.

MALACCA

Pages 27-28

the most southerly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> beyond the Ganges, is about 600 miles in length, and contains a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the same name. It is bounded by the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Siam and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean on the east; and by the straits of Malacca, which separate it from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a>, on the south-west. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is more to the south than any other in the East Indies; and comprehends the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and kingdoms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATAN">Patan</a>, Pahan, Ighor, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERA">Pera</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEDA">Queda</a>, Borkelon, Ligor; and to the north the town and kingdom of Tanaffery, where the Portuguese formerly carried on a great trade. This last either does <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> did belong to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Siam. The people of Malacca are in general subject to the Dutch, who possess all the strong places on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, and compel them to trade on their own terms, excluding all other nations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> from having any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with the natives. The Malays are governed by feudal laws. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, who has the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of king or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a>, issues his commands to his great vassals, who have other vassals in subjection to them in a similar manner. A small part of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> live independent, under the title of orangsai or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>. (A) The awkwardness of this title has induced many collectors to dispose of their first volume, as thinking it superseded by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition; but this is by no means the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>; the volume of 1719 being equally necessary to complete the set as that of 1733, which is a revision of all the former volumes. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> when properly bound, consists, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> libitum, either of five volumes or of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>. and fell their services to those who pay them best; while the body of the nation is composed of slaves, and live in perpetual servitude. The generality of these people are restless, fond of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, plunder, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMIGRATION">emigration</a>, colonies, desperate enterprises, adventures, and gallantry. They talk incessantly of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and their bravery; whilst they are universally considered by those with whom they have intercourse, as the most treacherous, ferocious people on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. This ferocity, which the Malays qualify under the name of courage, is so well known to the European companies who have settlements in the Indies, that they have universally agreed in prohibiting the captains of their ships who may put into the Malay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, from taking on board any men from that nation, except in the greatest distresses, and then on no account to exceed two or three. It is not in the least uncommon for a handful of these horrid savages suddenly to embark, attack a vessel by surprise, massacre the people, and make themselves masters of her. Malay batteaux, with 24 or 30 men, have been known to board European ships of 30 or 40 guns, in order to take possession of them, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> with their poniards great part of the crew. Those who are not slaves go always armed: they would think themselves disgraced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they went abroad without their poniards, which they call crit. As their lives are a perpetual round of agitation and tumult, they cannot endure the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> flowing garments in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the other Asiatics. Their habits are exactly adapted to their shapes, and loaded with a multitude of buttons, which fasten them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to their bodies. The country possessed by the Malays is in general very fertile. It abounds with odoriferous woods, such as the aloes, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANDAL">sandal</a>, and caffia. The ground is covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of the greatest fragrance, of which there is a perpetual succession throughout the year. There are abundance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of the most precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, said to be richer even than those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, and in some places are mines of diamonds. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> also abounds with excellent fish, together with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBERGRIS">ambergris</a>, pearls, and those delicate birds-nests so much in request in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, formed in the rocks with the spawn of fishes and the foam of the sea, by a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of small-sized swallow peculiar to those seas. These are of such an exquisite flavour, that the Chinese for a long <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> purchased them for their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, and still buy them at an excessive price. See Birds-Neck. Notwithstanding all this plenty, however, the Malays are miserable. The culture of the lands, abandoned to slaves, is fallen into contempt. These wretched labourers, dragged incessantly from their rustic employments by their restless masters, who delight in war and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> enterprises, have never time or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to give the necessary <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the labouring of their grounds; of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> the lands for the most part are uncultivated, and produce no kind of grain for the subsistence of the inhabitants. The fago tree indeed supplies in part the defect of grain. It is a species of the palm tree, which grows naturally in the woods to the height of about 20 or 30 feet; its circumference being sometimes from five to six. Its ligneous bark is about an inch in thickness, and covers a multitude of long fibres, which being interwoven one with another envelope a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of a gummy kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>. As soon as this tree is ripe, a whitish dust, which transpires through the pores of the leaves, and adheres to their extremities, indicates that the trees are in a state of maturity. The Malays then cut them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> near the root, and divide them into several sections, which they split into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>; they then scoop out the mass of mealy substance, which is enveloped by and adheres to the fibres; they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILUTE">dilute</a> it in pure <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> it through a straining bag of fine cloth, in order to separate it from the fibres. When this paste has lost part of its moisture by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a>, the Malays throw it into a kind of earthen vessel of different shapes, where they allow it to dry and harden. This paste is wholesome nourishing food, and preserves for many years. Malacca, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the country of the same name, is situated in a flat country close to the sea. The walls and fortifications are founded on a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> rock, and are carried up to a great height; the lower part of them is washed by the sea at every tide, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> side is a wide canal or ditch, cut from the sea to the river, which makes it an island. In 1641 it was taken from the Portuguese by the Dutch, since which time it has <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in their possession. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> there are a great many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> streets; but they are very badly paved. The houses are tolerably well built, and some of them have gardens behind or on one side. The inhabitants consist of a few Dutch, many Malaysians, Moors, Chinese, and other Indians, who are kept in awe by a fortress, which is separated from the city by a river, and by good walls and bastions, as well as by strong gates, and a drawbridge that is on the eastern side. The city is well situated for trade and navigation. F. Long, 102. 2. N. Lat. 2. 12.

MALACHI

Pages 28-28
or the prophecy of Malachi, a canonical book of the Old Testament, and the last of the 12 lesser prophets. Malachi prophesied about 300 years before Christ, reproving the Jews for their wickedness after their return from Babylon, charging them with rebellion, sacrilege, adultery, profaneness, and infidelity; and condemning the priests for being scandalously careless in their ministry; at the same time not forgetting to encourage the pious few, who, in that corrupt age, maintained their integrity. This prophet distinctly points at the Messiah, who was suddenly to come to his temple, and to be introduced by Elijah the prophet, that is, John the Baptist, who came in the spirit and power of Elias or Elijah.

MALACIA

Pages 28-28

in Medicine, is a languishing disorder incident to pregnant women, in which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> sometimes for one kind of food and sometimes for another, and eat it with extraordinary greediness.

MALACOPTERYGEOUS

Pages 28-28

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a>, an appellation given to fishes having the rays of their fins <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONY">bony</a> at the extremities, but not pointed, like those of acanthopterygeous fishes. MALACOSTOMOUS fishes, those destitute of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> in the jaws, called in English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>-mouthed, as the tench, carp, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BREAM">bream</a>, &c.

MALAGA

Pages 28-29

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, rich, and strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, with two castles, a bishop's see, and a good harbour, which renders it a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. The advantage of Malagrida of this commerce, according to M. Bozorganne, is entirely in favour of Spain, but almost without any to its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>; of 842 vessels which arrived at this port in 1782, from almost every commercial <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, scarcely 100 were Spanish, even reckoning the ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> which anchored there. The English, who are in possession of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the trade, carry thither woollens and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of small <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>; the Dutch carry spice, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTLERY">cutlery</a> ware, laces, ribbons, thread, &c. These nations, those of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, export to the amount of two millions and a half of piastres in wines, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, surnach, pickled anchovies, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, &c. and all they carry thither amounts only to about a million and a half. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> would be still more advantageous for Malaga <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> of the kingdom of Granada were exported from this port; but these are employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> where they are produced. The streets of Malaga are narrow, but there are some good squares; and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is a superb <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, said to be as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as St Paul's. The only other building of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> is the bishop's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>; which is a large edifice, but looks insignificant from its being situated near the other. Its prelate enjoys a revenue of 16,000l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. Malaga is seated on the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, at the foot of a craggy mountain. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 10' N. Lat. 36° 51'

MALAGRIDA

Pages 29-29

GABRIEL, an Italian Jesuit, was chosen by the general of the order to conduct missions into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. To <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ease and fluency of speech, for which he was indebted to enthusiasm, he added the most ardent zeal for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> to which he belonged. He soon became the fashionable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>; and every one, small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> great, placed himself under his conduct. He was respected as a saint, and consulted as an oracle. When a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> was formed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> d'<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVEIRO">Aveiro</a> against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Portugal, it is asserted by the enemies of the society, that three Jesuits, among whom was Malagrida, were consulted concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>. They add (what is very improbable), that it was decided by these casuists, that it was only a venial crime to kill a king who persecuted the saints. At that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the king of Portugal, spurred on by a minister who had no favour for the Jesuits, openly declared himself against them, and soon after banished them from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Only three of them were apprehended, Malagrida, Alexander, and Mathos, who were accused of having approved this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>. But either the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> could not be proceeded in without the consent of the pope, which was not granted, or no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> could be got sufficient to condemn Malagrida; and therefore the king was obliged to deliver him to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">Inquisition</a>, as being suspected of having formerly advanced some rash <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> which bordered on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>. Two publications which he acknowledged, and which give the fullest indications of complete insanity, were the foundation of these suspicions. The one was written in Latin, and entitled Tractatus de vita et imperio Antichristi; the other in Portuguese, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, composed with the assistance of the blest Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> and her most holy Son." They are full of extravagance and absurdity.—This enthusiast pretended to have the gift of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>. He confessed before the judges of the Inquisition, that God himself had declared him his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a>, and prophet; Malagrida that he was united to God by a perpetual union; and that the Virgin Mary, with the consent of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ and of the whole Trinity, had declared him to be her son. In short, he confessed, as is pretended, that he felt in the prison, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 72, some emotions very uncommon at that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of life, which at first gave him great uneasiness, but that it had been revealed to him by God that these motions were only the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> effect of an involuntary agitation, wherein there was the same merit as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>. It was for such extravagancies, that this unfortunate wretch was condemned by the Inquisition; but his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> was hastened by a vision which he eagerly revealed. Upon occasion of the death of the marquis de Tancourt, commander in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Extremadura, mournful and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> discharges were made in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of him by the castle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, and by all the forts on the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAGUS">Tagus</a>. These being heard by Malagrida in his dungeon, he instantly supposed, from their extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and from their happening during the night, that the king was dead. The next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> he demanded an audience from the members of the Inquisition; which being granted, he told them that he had been ordered by God to show the minister of the holy office that he was not a hypocrite, as was pretended; for the king's death had been revealed to him, and he had seen in a vision the torments to which his majesty was condemned for having persecuted the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> of his order. This was sufficient to accelerate his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>: he was burnt on the 21st of September 1761; not as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCOMPLICE">accomplice</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARRICIDE">parricide</a>, but as a false prophet, for which he deserved to be confined in bedlam rather than tied to the stake. The acts of impiety whereof he was accused were nothing more than extravagancies proceeding from a mistaken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> and an overheated brain.

MALALEUCA

Pages 29-29

the CAYPUTI TREE, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyadelphia class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. This plant, which is a native of the Moluccas, yields the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> called Cayputi.

MALDEN

Pages 29-29

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, 37 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, situated on an eminence at the confluence of the Chalmer and Pant <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Blackwater, where they enter the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It was the first Roman colony in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and the seat of some of the old British kings. It was besieged, plundered, and burnt by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Boudicca; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> repaired it. It was again ruined by the Danes, but rebuilt by the Saxons. It has a convenient haven on an arm of the sea for vessels of 400 tons; and a considerable trade in coals, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, corn, and deals. A little beyond it begins Blackwater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, famous for the Wallicet oysters. The channel called Malden <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is navigable to the town. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Edward the elder (of the Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>) resided here whilst he built Witham and <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol10.html#article-HERTFORD">Hertford</a> castles. On the west side of the town are the remains of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>.

MALDIVIA ISLANDS

Pages 29-30

a cluster of small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean, 500 miles south-west of the continent of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Ceylon. They are about 1000 in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and are very small; extending from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of south latitude to the seventh degree of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. They are generally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> low lands, surrounded by rocks and sands. The natives are of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> with the Arabians, profess the Mahometan Mahometan <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and are subject to one sovereign. The channels between the islands are very narrow, and some of them are fordable. They produce neither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, corn, nor herbage; but the natives live upon cocoanuts, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, roots, and fish. They have little <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> nothing to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARTER">barter</a> with, unless the shells called cowry, or blackmore's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, with which they abound: and these serve instead of small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> in many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>.

MALE

Pages 30-30

among zoologists, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a> of animals which has the parts of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> situated externally. See **Sex** and **Generation**. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> male has also, from some similarity to that sex in animals, been applied to several inanimate things; thus we say, a male flower, a male screw, &c. See **Mas Plania**, **Masculus Flor**, and **Screw**; also **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">Female</a>** and **Flos**.

MALEBRANCHE

Pages 30-30

Nicholas, an eminent French metaphysician, the son of Nicholas Malebranche, secretary to the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, was born in 1638, and admitted into the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of the oratory in 1660. He at first applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of languages and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; but afterwards meeting with Des Cartes's Treatise of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, he gave himself up entirely to the study of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. In 1699, he was admitted an honorary member of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Academy of Sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. Notwithstanding he was of a delicate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, he enjoyed a pretty good state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in 1715, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 77. Father Malebranche read little, but thought a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>. He despised that kind of philosophy which confines only in knowing the opinions of other men, since a person may know the history of other men's thoughts without thinking himself. He could never read ten verses together without difficulty. He meditated with his windows shut, in order to keep out the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, which he found to be a disturbance to him. His conversation turned upon the same subjects as his books; but was mixed with so much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> and deference to the judgment of others, that it was extremely and universally desired. His books are famous; particularly his *Recherche de la Verité*, i.e., "Search after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>;" his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> in which is, to point to us the errors into which we are daily led by our senses, imagination, and passions; and to prescribe a method for discovering the truth, which he does, by starting the notion of seeing all things in God. And hence he is led to think and speak merely of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> knowledge, either as it lies in written books, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in the book of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, compared with that light which displays itself from the ideal world; and, by attending to which, with pure and delicate minds, he supposes knowledge to be most easily had. The fineness of this author's sentiments, together with his fine manner of expressing them, made every body admire his genius and abilities; but he has generally passed for a visionary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. Mr Locke, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of Malebranche's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of seeing all things in God, styles him "an acute and ingenious author;" and tells us, that there are "a great many very fine thoughts, judicious reasonings, and uncommon reflections in his Recherches." But Mr Locke, in that piece, endeavours to refute the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> principles of his system. He wrote many other pieces besides that we have mentioned, all tending some way or other to confirm his main system, established in the *Recherche*, and to clear it from the objections which were brought against it, or from the consequences which were deduced from it; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he has not attained what he aimed at in these several productions, he has certainly shown great abilities and a vast force of genius.

MALESHERBES

Pages 30-31

Christian-William de Lamoignon de, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1721. He was son of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of France, William de Lamoignon, who was descended of an illustrious family. His early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> he received at the Jesuits <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, applying himself afterwards to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> assiduity, as well as <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> economy. He was chosen a councillor of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of Paris at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 24, and succeeded his father as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of aids in the year 1750. With the presidency of the court of aids he received the superintendence of the press, in whose <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> it became the means of promoting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> beyond all former example in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. As he firmly believed that despotism alone had any reason to dread the liberty of the press, he was anxious to give it every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> consistent with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> policy and the state of public <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. Through his favour the French Encyclopedia, the works of Rousseau, and many other free speculations, issued from the press, in defiance of the terrific anathemas of the Sorbonne. This had its own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVING">paving</a> the way to the horrors of the revolution, which Maletherbes did not probably foresee; yet it had also the happy effect of freeing the minds of men from the fetters of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, and of enlightening them respecting their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and duties in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. The superintendence of the press having been taken from him, to confer it on that tool of despotism Maupeou, he was only the more intent on fulfilling the duties of his presidency, and opposing arbitrary power with all his vigour, being thus freed from a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of other cares. When the proceedings of the court of aids were to be prohibited, on account of the spirited conduct of Maletherbes in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of one Monnerat, who had been most unjustly treated by the farmers of the revenue, he presented a remonstrance to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, containing a free protest against the enormous abuses of lettres de cachet, by which every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s liberty was rendered precarious, concluding with these memorable words; "no one is great enough to be secure from the hatred of a minister, nor little enough not to merit that of a clerk." Soon after this he was banished to his country-seat by a lettre de cachet, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> de Richelieu at the head of an armed force abolished the tribunal. In this state of retirement he committed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> a number of observations on the political and judicial state of France, on <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> history, which all perished in the wreck of the revolution. On the accession of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XVI. to the throne in 1774, he received an order to appear at the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the court of aids had sat, and resume the presidency of the tribunal thus restored. He laid before the new sovereign an ample memoir on the calamitous state of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, with a free exposure of the faults by which it had been produced, from a firm conviction that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> at all times should have access to the throne. His sentiments so fully accorded with those of the the young king, whose mind was not yet corrupted, that he was chosen minister of state in the year 1775, in which elevated <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> he was only ambitious to extend the sphere of his usefulness. His first care was to visit the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a>, and restore to liberty the innocent victims of the former reign. His administration was also distinguished by the powerful encouragement of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> and agriculture, being supported in his laudable endeavours by the able and virtuous Turgot, at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> comptroller-general of the revenue, who having lost his place through the intrigues of financiers, Maleherbes did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> retain his office after him. As he failed in his benevolent endeavours to ameliorate the condition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> respecting the solemnization of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> and the legitimating of their children, he resigned his office in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of May 1776. Being fond of travelling, and resolved to mix freely with people of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, in order to acquire an accurate knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, he assumed the humble <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of M. Guillaume, and commenced his journey in a simple, frugal manner. He travelled through France, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, frequently on foot, and lodged in villages, to have a nearer survey of the state of the country. He made memorandums, with the greatest care, of whatever he conceived to be worthy of observation respecting the productions of nature and the operations of industry; and after an absence of four years he returned to his favourite mansion, fully fraught with such a stock of valuable knowledge as his age and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> qualified him to appreciate. Finding on his return that his native country was far advanced in philosophical principles, he drew up two elaborate <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> to the king, one of them on the condition of the Protestants, and the other on civil liberty and toleration in general; and the difficulties with which ministers now found themselves surrounded, induced the king to call him to his councils, being a man who stood <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> in the esteem of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, but he received no appointment to any particular office. In the critical state in which he clearly <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the king stood, he made one effort for opening his eyes, by means of two spirited and energetic memoirs, "On the calamities of France, and the means of repairing them;" but, as the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s party carried everything before it, he was not even permitted to read them, and also denied a private interview with the ill-fated monarch, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which he took his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> leave of the court. When by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the national convention the unfortunate Louis was to be tried for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, Maleherbes generously offered to plead his cause, nobly forgetting the manner in which he had been banished from his councils. He was the person who announced to him his cruel doom, and one of the last who took leave of him, when taken out to suffer. After this eventful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, he withdrew to his retreat with a deeply wounded heart, and refused to hear anything more of what was acting on the bloody <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> of Paris. Walking one morning in his garden, he perceived four men coming towards his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, sent by the convention to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Mad. Lepelletier Rollambo and her husband, once president of the parliament of Paris; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> of Maleherbes was followed, as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of course, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. The truth is, the convention never forgave his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the Malherbes king; an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, however, in which he himself always gloried. On the fatal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, this great man left the prison with a serene countenance; and, happening to stumble against a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, he said (with the pleasantry of Sir Thomas More), "a Roman would have thought this an unlucky <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>, and walked back again." He conversed with his children in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CART">cart</a>, took an affectionate farewell, and received the stroke in April 1794, in the 73rd year of his age. Thus fell, by the infatiable cruelty of a monster, whose hatred to men of virtue and abilities was implacable, one of the most splendid and exemplary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the period at which he lived. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> afterwards made some reparation for the injustice done him, by ordering his bust to be placed among those of the great men who have reflected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> upon their country.

MALHERBE

Pages 31-31

FRANCIS DE, the best French poet of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAEN">Caen</a> about the year 1556, of a noble and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family. He quitted Normandy at 17 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and went into Provence, where he attached himself to the family of Henry Angoulême, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry II. and was in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> till he was killed by Altoviti in 1586. At length <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> de Perron, being informed of his merit and abilities, introduced him to Henry IV. who took him into his service. After that monarch's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> de Medicis settled a pension of 500 crowns upon our poet, who died at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1628. The best and most complete edition of his poetical works is that of 1666, with Menage's remarks. Malherbe to far excelled all the French poets who preceded him, that Boileau considers him as the father of French <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>: but he composed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> difficulty, and put his mind on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACK">rack</a> in correcting what he wrote. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of singular humour, and blunt in his behaviour. When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> used to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> him, that, that they would pray to God for him, he answered them, that "he did not believe they could have any great <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in heaven, since they were left in such a bad condition upon <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; and that he should be better pleased <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> de Luyn, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some other favourite, had made him the same promise." He would often say that "the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of gentlemen was that of their prince." During his last sicknesses he had much ado to resolve to confess to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>; for which he gave this facetious reason, that "he never used to confess but at Easter." And some few moments before his death, when he had been in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETHARGY">lethargy</a> two hours, he awoke on a sudden to reprove his landlady, who waited on him, for using a word that was not good French; saying to his confessor, who reprimanded him for it, that "he could not help it, and he would defend the purity of the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> to the last moment of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>."

MALICE

Pages 31-32

in Ethics and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is a formed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of doing mischief to another; it differs from hatred. In <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, it is malice makes the crime; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, having a malicious intent to kill another, in the execution of his malice kills a person not intended, the malice shall be connected to his person, and he shall be adjudged a murderer. The words ex malitia praecogitata are necessary to an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a> of murder, &c. And this malitia praecogitata, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> malice prepense, Malignant may be either express or implied in law. Express malice is, when one, with a sedate, deliberate mind, and formed design, kills another; which formed design is evidenced by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> circumstances discovering that intention; as lying in wait, antecedent menaces, former grudges, and concerted schemes to do him some bodily harm. Besides, where no malice is expressed, the law <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> imply it; as where a man wilfully poisons another, in such a deliberate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> the law presumes malice, though no particular enmity can be proved. And if a man kills another suddenly, without any, or without a considerable provocation, the law implies malice; for no person, unless of an abandoned heart, would be guilty of such an act upon a slight or no apparent cause.

MALIGNANT

among physicians, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to diseases of a very dangerous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and generally infectious; such are the dysentery, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> fever, &c., in their worst stages.

MALIGNITY AMONG PHYSICIANS

y among physicians signifies much the same with contagion. See CONTAGION.

MALLEABLE

Pages 32-32

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, whereby they are capable of being extended under the hammer. MALLENDERS. See FARRIERY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MALLEOLI

Pages 32-32

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, were bundles of combustible materials, set on fire to give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> in the night, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to annoy the enemy; when they were employed for the latter purpose they were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> out of a bow, or fixed to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JAVELIN">javelin</a>, and thus thrown into the enemies engines, flaps, &c., in order to burn them. Pitch was always a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> ingredient in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. The malleoli had also the name of pyroboli.

MALLET

Pages 32-34

Edme, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MELUN">Melun</a> in 1713, and enjoyed a curacy in the neighbourhood of his native <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> till 1751, when he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> to be professor of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Navarre, of which he was admitted a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>. Boyer, the late bishop of Mirepoix, was at first much prejudiced against him; but being afterwards undeceived, he conferred upon him the see of Verdun as a reward for his doctrine and morals. Janenism had been imputed to him by his enemies with this prelate; and the gazette which went by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a>, accused him of impiety. Either of these imputations was equally undefended by the abbe Mallet: as a Christian, he was grieved at the disputes of the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; and, as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, he was astonished that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> had not, from the very beginning of those dissensions imposed silence on both parties. He died at Paris in 1755, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 42. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of his works are, 1. Principes pour la lecture des Poètes, 1745, 1 vols. 2. Essai sur l'Etude des Belles Lettres, 1747, 12mo. Mallet, 12mo. 3. *Essai sur les bienfaits oratoires*, 1753, 12mo. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALLICOLLO">Mallicollo</a>. 4. *Principes pour la lecture des Orateurs*, 1753, 12mo. 3 vols. 5. *Histoire des Guerres civiles de France sous les règnes de François II., <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> IX., Henri III., et Henri IV.* translated from the Italian of d'<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVILA">Avila</a>.—In Mallet's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> on the Poets, Orators, and the Belles Lettres, his object is no more than to explain with accuracy and precision the rules of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> masters, and to support them by examples from authors <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>. The style of his different writings, to which his mind bore a great resemblance, was neat, easy, and unaffected. But what most rendered his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> estimable, was his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to his friends, his candour, moderation, gentleness, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>. He was employed to write the theological and belles lettres <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> in the Encyclopédie; and whatever he wrote in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a> was in general well composed. Abbé Mallet was preparing two important works when the world was deprived of him by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. The first was *Une Histoire générale de nos Guerres depuis le commencement de la Monarchie*; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, *Une Histoire de Concile de Trente*, which he intended to set in opposition to that of Father Paul translated by Father le Courayer. **Mallet**, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> kind of hammer made of wood; much used by artificers who work with a chisel, as sculptors, masons, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-cutters, whose mallet is ordinarily round; and by carpenters, joiners, &c., who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. There are several sorts of mallets used for different purposes on ship-board. The caking mallet is chiefly employed to drive the oakum into the seams of a ship, where the edges of the planks are joined to each other in the sides, deck, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bottom. The head of this mallet is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and cylindrical, being hooped with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> to prevent it from splitting in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of calking. There is also the serving mallet, used in serving the rigging, by binding the spun-yarn more firmly about it than it could possibly be done by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, which is performed in the following manner; the spun-yarn being previously rolled up in a large <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> or clue, two or three turns of it are patted about the rope, and about the body of the mallet, which for this purpose is furnished with a round channel in its surface, that conforms to the convexity of the rope intended to be served. The turns of the spun-yarn being strained round the mallet, so as to confine it firmly to the rope, which is extended above the deck, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> pats the ball continually above the rope, whilst the other, at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, winds on the spun-yarn by means of the mallet, whose handle acting as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVER">lever</a> strains every turn about the rope as firm as possible. **Mallicollo**, one of the largest of the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific ocean</a>. It extends twenty leagues from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south. Its inland <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and clad with forests. Its vegetable productions are luxuriant, and in great variety; cocoa-nuts, breadfruit, bananas, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-canes, yams, eddoes, turmeric, and oranges. Hogs and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a> are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animals. The inhabitants appear to be of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> totally distinct from those of the Friendly and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. Their form, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and manners, are widely different. They seem to correspond in many particulars with the natives of New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, particularly in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and woolly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. They go almost naked, are of a slender make, have lively but very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> ugly features, and tie a rope fast round their belly. They use bows and arrows as their principal weapons, and the arrows are said to be sometimes poisoned. They keep their bodies entirely free from punctures, which is one particular that remarkably distinguishes them from the other tribes of the Pacific ocean. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, according to Mr Forster, may amount to 50,000, who occupy 600 square miles of ground. The same author informs us that very few women were seen, but that those few were not less ugly than the men, were of small stature, and their heads, faces, and shoulders were painted <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>. They had bundles on their backs containing their children, and the men seemed to have no kind of regard for them. They appeared in fact to be oppressed, despised, and in a state of servility.
