The men use bows and arrows, and a club about 30 inches long, which they hang on their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> shoulder, from a thick rope made of a kind of grass. They live chiefly on vegetables, and apply themselves to hulbandry. Their music had nothing remarkable in it, either for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> or variety, but seemed to Mr Forster to be of a more lively turn than that at the Friendly islands. In some of their countenances he thought he could trace a mischievous, ill-natured disposition, but he confesses that he might mistake jealousy for hatred. It is in 16° 28' S. Lat. and 167° 56' E. Long. **Mallow**, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>, and also a borough town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cork, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, above 118 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, pleasantly situated on the north <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Blackwater, over which there is an excellent stone <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. Not far distant is a fine <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of a moderately tepid <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which bursts out of the bottom of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a> rock, and approaches the nearest in all its qualities to the hot-well waters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a> of any that has been yet discovered in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, which brings a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> there frequently in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> months, and has caused it to be called the Irish Bath. **Mallow**. See Malva, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **Marrow-Mallow**. See Althaea, Botany Index. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> Mallow**. See Sida, Botany Index. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALMSBURY">Malmsbury</a>**, a town of Wiltshire in England, 95 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It stands on a hill, with six bridges over the river Avon at the bottom; with which and a brook that runs into it, it is in a manner encompassed. It formerly had walls and a castle, which were pulled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to enlarge the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, which was the biggest in Wiltshire, and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> sat in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. The Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> Athelstan granted the town large immunities, and was buried under the high altar of the church, and his monument still remains in the nave of it. The memory of Aldhelm, its first abbot, who was the king's great favourite, and whom he got to be canonized after his death, is still kept up by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a> near this town, called Aldhelm's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAD">Mead</a>. By <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of King William III. the corporation consists of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALDERMAN">alderman</a>, who is chosen yearly, 12 <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> burgesses, and 4 assistants, landholders and commoners. Here is an almshouse for 4 men and 4 women, and near the bridge an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> for lepers, where it is supposed there was formerly a nunnery. This town drives a considerable trade in the woollen manufacture; Malmesbury, has a market on Saturday, and three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>. It has sent members to parliament ever since the 26th of Edward I. William of Malmesbury. See William.

MALO

Pages 34-34

MAELOU, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Mahout, SAINT, the son of an Englishman, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> to St Magloire, was educated in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and afterwards chosen bishop of Gui-Caitel, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> which his humility prevented him from accepting. The people wishing to compel him, he went to Brittany, and put himself under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a holy anchorite called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a>, in the neighbourhood of Aleth. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, about the year 541, he was chosen bishop of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and there cultivated piety and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success. He afterwards retired to a solitude near Xaintes, where he died November 15, 565. From him the city of St Malo derives its name; his body having been carried thither, after the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Aleth to a small village called Guidalet or Guichalet, and the transference of the episcopal see to St Malo.

MALOUIN

Pages 34-35

PAUL-JAQUES, born at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAEN">Caen</a> in 1701, was professor of medicine in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, physician in ordinary to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, and a member of the Royal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and of the Academy of Sciences of Paris. These stations were a proper reward for his very extensive information in medicine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>; and his amiable and steady character procured him many friends and protectors. He was very unlike some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> physicians, who put little trust in medicine; and was greatly displeased to hear any ill spoken of his profession. He observed one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> to a young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who took this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, that all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men had respected medicine: Ah! said the young fellow, you must at least except from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> one Moliere. But then, instantly replied the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>, you see he is dead. He is said to have believed the certainty of his art as firmly as a mathematician does that of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>. Having prescribed a great many medicines for a celebrated man of letters, who followed his directions exactly, and was cured, Malouin eagerly embraced him, saying, You deserve to be sick. As he valued the rules of medicine still more on his own account than on that of others, he observed, especially in the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, a very austere regimen. He strictly practised the preservative part of medicine, which is much more certain in its effects than the restorative. To this regimen Malouin was indebted, for what many philosophers have desired in vain, a healthy old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> and an easy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. He was a stranger to the infirmities of age; and died at Paris of an apoplexy, the 3d of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1778, in the 77th year of his age. By his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> he left a legacy to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of medicine, upon condition of their holding a public meeting every year for the purpose of giving the public an account of his labours and discoveries. Malouin was economical, but at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> very disinterested. After two years of very lucrative practice, he left Paris and went to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>, where he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> very few patients, observing that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALPAS">Malpas</a>, that he had retired to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are, 1. Traité de Chimie, 1734, 12mo. 2. Chimie Medicale, 2 vols. 12mo, 1755; a book full of curious observations, and written in a chaste and well adapted style. He had the character of a laborious chemist; and he was a well-informed and even a distinguished one for the age in which he lived: but his knowledge of chemistry, it must be confessed, was very imperfect, compared with the state of the science in the present age, in which it has assumed a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>, that probably will not be the last. 3. Some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> in the Collection published by the Academy of Sciences on the arts and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a>. A circumstance which happened at a meeting of the academy does as much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to his heart, as any of his works do to his understanding. A new treatise on the art of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAKING">baking</a>, wherein some of Malouin's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> were combated, was read by M. Parmentier before his fellows, among whom was the old doctor. The young academician, who knew how easily self-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> is hurt, was afraid to meet his looks; but no sooner was the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> finished, than Malouin went up to him, and embracing him, "Receive my respects (said he), you have seen farther into the subject than I did." 4. He was likewise the author of the chemical articles in the Encyclopédie. Of the same family was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Malouin, who graduated as a doctor of medicine in the university of Caen, and died in 1718 in the flower of his age. He published a Treatise on Solids and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">Fluids</a>, Paris 1718, 12mo.

MALPAS

Pages 35-35

a town of Cheshire, 166 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It stands on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> hill, not far from the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>, on the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a>; has a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school, and an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, and had formerly a castle. It is called in Latin Mala Plaeca, i.e. "Ill Street," and was, for the same reason, by the Normans, called Mal Pas; but its three streets, of which it chiefly consists, are now well paved; and here is a benefice rich enough to support two rectors, who officiate alternately in its lately <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. It has a good market on Mondays, and three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> in the year.

MALPIGHI

Pages 35-35

MARCELLUS, an eminent Italian physician and anatomist in the 17th century. He studied under Massari and Mariano. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> invited him to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a>, to be professor of physic there. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> he contracted an intimate acquaintance with Borelli, to whom he ascribed all the discoveries he had made. He went back to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of Pisa not agreeing with him. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Antonio Pignatelli, who had known him while he was legate at Bologna, being chosen pope in 1691, under the name of Innocent XII, immediately sent for him to Rome, and appointed him his physician. But this did not hinder him from pursuing his studies, and perfecting his works, which have immortalized his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. He died in 1694; and his works, with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> written by himself, prefixed, were first collected and printed at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, in folio, in 1667.

MALPIGHIA

Pages 35-35

BARBADOS CHERRY; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the decandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 23d order, Trihilidae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MALPLAQUET

Pages 35-35

a village of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in Hainault, famous for a most bloody <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought here on the 11th of September 1709, between the French under old Marshal Villars, and the allies commanded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Eugene and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>. The French <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> amounted to 120,000 men; and were posted behind the woods of La Marte and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TENIERS">Teniers</a>, in the neighbourhood of Malplaquet. They had fortified their situation in such a manner with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, hedges, and trees laid across, that they seemed to be quite inaccessible. In this situation they expected certain victory; and even the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> were so eager to engage, that they flung away the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> which had been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> given them, though they had taken no sustenance for a whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> before. The allied army began the attack early in the morning, being favoured by a thick fog. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> fury of their impetuosity was made upon the left of the enemy; and with such success, that notwithstanding their lines and barricades, the French were in less than an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> driven from their entrenchments. But on the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> was sustained with much greater obstinacy. The Dutch, who carried on the attack, drove them from their first line; but were repulsed from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> slaughter. The prince of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, who headed that attack, perished in his efforts with incredible perseverance and intrepidity, though two horses had been killed under him, and the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his officers slain and disabled. At last, however, the French were obliged to yield up the field of battle; but not till after having sold a dear-bought victory. Villars being dangerously wounded, they made an excellent retreat under the conduct of Boufflers, and took <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> near Guénon and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIENNES">Valenciennes</a>. The conquerors took possession of the field of battle, on which above 20,000 of their best troops lay dead. The loss of the French, it is said, did not exceed 8,000; and Marshal Villars confidently asserted, that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had not been disabled, he would have gained an undoubted victory.

MALT

Pages 35-51

T denotes barley cured, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> prepared to fit it for making a potable liquor, under the denomination of beer or ale. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREWING">Brewing</a>. Malt-Liquors have different names as well as different virtues, properties, and uses, both from the different manners of preparing the malt, whence they are distinguished into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>; and from the different manners of preparing or brewing the liquors themselves; whence they are divided into beer and ale, strong and small, new and old. Malt drinks are either pale or brown, as the malt is more or less dried on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KILN">kiln</a>: that which is the flendereft dried tinging the liquor least in brewing, and therefore being called pale; whereas that higher dried, and as it were roasted, makes it of a higher <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. A mixture of both these makes an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a> colour; whence several of these liquors take their name. Now, it is certain, the pale malt has most of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> grain in it, and is therefore the most nourishing; but, for the same reason, it requires a stronger <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> to digest it. Those who drink much of it, are usually fat and fleck in their bloom, but are often cut off by sudden fevers; or, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they avoid this, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> early into a ditempered old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. The brown malt makes a drink much less vicious, and fitter to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the several strainers of the body; but, if very strong, it may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> on to the same inconvenience. Dr Quincy observes, that the best pale malt-liquors are those brewed with hard waters, as those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, because the mineral particles, wherewith these waters are impregnated, help to prevent the cohesions of those drawn from the grain, and enable them to pass the proper secretions the better; as the viscid particles of the grain do likewise defend them from doing the mischief they might otherwise occasion. But softer waters seem best suited to draw out the substance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> dried malts, which retain many fiery particles in their contexture, and are therefore best left in a smooth vehicle. For the differences in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of malt liquors, they chiefly consist in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of hops, as in beer; or in the more sparing use of them, as in ale. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> made by hops is best discovered from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the hops themselves: these are known to be a subtle grateful bitter; in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, therefore, with this liquor, they add somewhat of an alkaline nature, i.e., particles that are sublime, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, and rigid. By which means, the rosy viscid parts of the malt are more divided and lubricated; and are therefore not only rendered more easy of digestion and secretion in the body, but also, while in the liquor, they prevent it from running into such cohesions as would make it rosy, vapid, and sour. For want of this, in unhopped drinks, that clammy sweetness, which they retain after working, soon turns them acid and unfit for use; which happens sooner or later in proportion to the strength they receive from the malt, and the commination that has undergone by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>. The different strengths of malt liquors also make their effects different. The stronger they are, the more viscid parts they carry into the blood; and though the spirituous parts make them imperceptible at first; yet when those are evaporated, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be in a few hours, the other will be sensibly felt by pains in the head, nauseousness at the stomach, and lassitude or listlessness of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. This those are the most sensible of who have experienced the extremes of drinking these liquors and wines; for a debauch of wine they find much sooner worn off, and they are much more lively and brisk afterwards, than after fuddling malt liquors, whose viscid remains will be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before they be thinned off. Malt liquors, therefore, are, in general, the more wholesome for being small; i.e., of such a strength as is liable to carry a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of warmth into the stomach, but not so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> as to prevent their being proper diluters of the necessary food. Indeed, in robust people, or those who labour hard, the viscidities of the drink may be broken into convenient nourishment; but in persons of another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> and way of living, they serve rather to promote obstructions and ill humours. The age of malt liquors is the last thing by which they are rendered more or less wholesome. Age seems to do nearly the same thing as hops; for those liquors which are longest kept are certainly the least viscid; age breaking the viscid parts, and by degrees rendering them smaller, and fitter for secretion. But this is always determined according to their strength; in proportion to which, they will sooner or later come to their full perfection as well as decay; for, when ale or beer is kept till its particles are broken and comminated as far as they are capable, then it is that they are best; and, beyond this, they will be continually on the decay, till the finer spirits are entirely escaped, and the remainder becomes vapid and sour. **Malt-Distillery.** This is an extensive article of trade; and by which very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fortunes are made. The art is to convert fermented malt liquors into a clear inflammable spirit, which may be either sold for use in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> state of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> strength, that is, the same strength with French brandy; or is rectified into that purer spirit usually sold under the name of *spirit of wine*; or made into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> cordial waters, by being distilled again from herbs and other ingredients. See **Brewing** and **Wash.** To brew with malt in the most advantageous manner, it is necessary, 1. That the subject be well prepared; 2. That the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> be suitable and duly applied; and, 3. That some certain additions be used, or alterations made, according to the season of the year, and the intention of the operator; and by a proper regulation in these respects, all the fermentable parts of the subject will thus be brought into the tincture, and become fit for fermentation. The due preparation of the subject consists in its being judiciously malted and well ground. When the grain is not sufficiently malted, it is apt to prove hard, so that the water can have but very little power to dissolve its substance; and if it be too much malted, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the fermentable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is lost in that operation. The harder and more limity the malt is, the finer it ought to be ground; and in all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, when intended for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>, it is advisable to reduce it to a kind of finer or coarser <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>. When the malt is thus ground, it is found by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> that great part of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, trouble, and expense of the brewing is saved by it, and yet as large a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of spirit will be produced; for thus the whole substance of the malt may remain mixed among the tincture, and be fermented and distilled among it. This is a particular that very well deserves the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the malt distiller as that trade is at present carried on; for the dispatch of the business, and the quantity of spirit procured, is more attended to than the purity or perfection of it. The secret of this matter depends upon the thoroughly mixing or briskly agitating and throwing the meal about, first in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and then in hot water; and repeating this agitation after the fermentation is over, when the thick turbid wash being immediately committed to the still already hot and dewy with working, there is no danger of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>, unless by accident, even without the farther trouble of stirring, which in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is found needless, though the quantity be ever so large, provided that requisite care and cleanliness be used; and thus the business of brewing and fermenting may very commodiously be performed together, and reduced to one single operation. Whatever water is made choice of, it must stand in a hot state upon the prepared malt, especially if a clear tincture be desired; but a known and very great inconvenience attends its being applied too hot, or too near to Malt to a state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>; or even scalding with regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. To <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> time in this case, and to prevent the malt running into lumps and clods, the best way is to put a certain measured quantity of cold water to the malt first; the malt is then to be stirred very well with this, so as to form a sort of thin uniform paste or pudding; after which the remaining quantity of water required may be added in a state of boiling, without the least danger of making what, in the distiller's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is called a puddin'. In this manner the due and necessary degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> in the water, for the extracting all the virtues of the malt, may be <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> upon very expeditiously, and with a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of exactness, as the heat of boiling water is a fixed standard which may be let <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to any degree by a proportionate mixture of cold water, due allowances being made for the season of the year, and for the temperature of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. This little obvious improvement, added to the method <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> above hinted for the reducing brewing and fermentation to one operation, will render it practicable to very considerable advantages, and the spirit improved in quality as well as quantity. A much more profitable method than that usually practised for the fermenting malt for distillation, in order to get its spirit, is the following: Take ten pounds of malt reduced to a fine meal, and three pounds of common wheat meal; add to these two gallons of cold water, and stir them well together; then add five gallons of water, boiling hot, and stir altogether again. Let the whole stand two hours, and then stir it again; and when grown cold, add to it two ounces of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> yeast, and set it by loosely covered in a warmish <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to ferment. This is the Dutch method of preparing what they call the wash for malt spirit, whereby they save much trouble and procure a large quantity of spirit; thus commodiously reducing the two benefits of brewing and fermenting to one single operation. In England the method is to draw and malt for spirit as they ordinarily do for beer, only instead of boiling the wort, they <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a> it into large coolers, and afterwards run it into their fermenting backs, to be there fermented with yeast. Thus they below twice as much labour as is necessary, and lose a large quantity of their spirit by leaving the grofs bottoms out of the still for fear of burning. All simple spirits may be considered in the three different states of low wines, proof spirit, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCOHOL">alcohol</a>, the intermediate degrees of strength being of less general use; and they are to be judged of only according as they approach to or recede from these. Low wines at a medium contain a fifth part of pure inflammable spirit, five times as much water as spirit necessarily arising in the operation with a boiling heat. Proof goods contain about one half of the same totally inflammable spirit; and alcohol entirely consists of it. Malt low wines, prepared in the common way, are exceeding nauseous; they have, however, a natural vinosity or pungent agreeable acidity, which would render the spirit agreeable to the palate were it not for the large quantity of the grofs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of the malt that abounds in it. When this oil is detained in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> from mixing itself among the low wines, by the stretching a coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a> over the neck of the still or at the orifice of the worm, the spirit becomes much purer in all respects; it is less fulsome to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, less offensive to the smell, and less milky to the eye. When these low wines, in the rectification into proof spirits, are distilled gently, they leave a considerable quantity of this grofs fetid oil behind them in the still along with the phlegm; but if the fire be made fierce, this oil is again raised and brought over with the spirit; and being now broken somewhat more fine, it impregnates it in a more nauseous manner than at first. This is the common fault both of the malt distiller and of the rectifier: the latter, instead of separating the spirit from this nasty oil, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> intent of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, attends only to the leaving the phlegm in such quantity behind, that the spirit may be of a due strength as proof or marketable goods, and brings over the oil in a worse state than before. To this inattention to the proper business of the process, it is owing, that the spirit, after its several rectifications, as they are miscalled, is often found more stinking than when delivered out of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the malt distiller. All this may be prevented by the taking more time in the subsequent distillations, and keeping the fire low and regular; the sudden stirring of the fire, and the hasty way of throwing on the fresh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, being the general occasion of throwing up the oil by spurts, where the fire in general, during the process, has not been so large as to do that mischief. The use of a balneum mariae, instead of the common still, would effectually prevent all this mischief, and give a purer spirit in one rectification than can otherwise be procured in ten, or indeed according to the common methods at all. Malt low wine, when brought to the standard of proof spirit, loses its milky colour, and is perfectly clear and bright, no more oil being contained in it than is perfectly dissolved by the alcohol, and rendered miscible with that proportion of phlegm, which is about one half the liquor: its taste also is cleaner, though not more pleasant; there being less of the thick oil to hang on the tongue than its own form; which is not the case in the low wines, where the oil being undissolved, adheres to the mouth in its own form, and does not pass lightly over it. When proof spirit of malt is distilled over again, in order to be rectified into alcohol, or, as we usually call it, spirits of wine, if the fire be raised at the time when the faints begin to fall off, a very considerable quantity of oil will be raised by it, and will run in the visible form of oil from the nose of the worm. This is not peculiar to malt spirit; but the French brandy shows the same phenomenon, and that in so great a degree, that half an ounce of this oil may be obtained from a single piece of brandy. Malt spirit, more than any other kind, requires to be brought into the form of alcohol, before it can be used internally, especially as it is now <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> made up in the proof flate, with as much of this nauseous and viscous oil as will give it a good <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of bubbles. For this reason it ought to be reduced to an alcohol, or totally inflammable spirit, before it is admitted into any of the medicinal compositions. If it be used without this previous caution, the taste of the malt oil will be be distinguished among all the other flavours of the ingredients. A pure spirit being thus procured, should be kept carefully in vessels of glass or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, well stopped, to prevent the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> of any of its volatile parts. If preserved in casks, it is apt to impregnate itself very strongly with the wood. The quantity of pure alcohol obtainable from a certain quantity of malt, differs according to the goodness of the subject, the manner of the operation, the season of the year, and the skillfulness of the workmen; according to which variations, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of malt will afford from eight or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> to 13 or 14 gallons of alcohol. This should encourage the malt distiller to be careful and diligent in his business, as so very large a part of his profit depends wholly on the well-conducting his processes. After every operation in this business, there remains a quantity of faints, which in their own coarse state ought never to be admitted into the pure spirit; these are to be saved together, and large quantities of them at once wrought into alcohol. It is easy to reduce these to such a state that they will serve for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a>-spirits. Their disagreeable flavour being corrected by the adding of aromatics during the distillations, the reducing them into a perfect and pure alcohol is practicable, but not without such difficulties as render it scarcely worth the trader's while. One way of doing it is by distilling them from water into water, and that with a very slow fire. By this means a pure alcohol may be made out of the foulest faints. The malt distiller always gives his spirit a single rectification per se, in order to purify it a little, and make it up proof; but in this state it is not to be reckoned fit for internal uses, but serves to be distilled into <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">geneva</a> and other ordinary compound strong waters for the vulgar. The Dutch who carry on a great trade with malt spirit, never give it any farther rectification than this; and it is on this account that the malt spirit of England is in general so much more in esteem. The Dutch method is only to distil the wort into low wines, and then to full proof spirit; they then directly make it into geneva, or else send it as it is to Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, and the East Indies, for the Dutch have little notion of our rectification. Their spirit is by this means rendered very foul and coarse, and is rendered yet more nauseous by the immoderate use they make of rye meal. Malt spirit, in its unrectified state, is usually found to have the common bubble proof, as the malt distiller knows that it will not be marketable without it. The whole matter requisite to this is, that it have a considerable portion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> oil of the malt well broke and mixed along with it; this gives the rectifier a great deal of trouble if he will have the spirit fine; but in the general run of the business, the rectifier does not take out this oil, but breaks it finer, and mixes it faster in by alkaline salts, and disguises its taste by the addition of certain flavouring ingredients. The spirit loses in these processes the vinosity it had when it came out of the hands of the malt distiller, and is in all respects worse, except in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> of a mixed flavour. The alkaline salts used by the rectifier destroying the natural vinosity of the spirit, it is necessary to add an extraneous acid in order to give it a new one. The acid they generally use is the Spiritus nitri dulcis; and the common way of using it is the mixing it to the taste with the rectified spirit: this gives our malt spirit, when well rectified, a flavour somewhat like that of French brandy, but this soon flies off; and the better method is to add a proper quantity of Glauber's strong spirit of nitre to the spirit in the still. The liquor in this case comes over impregnated with it, and the acid being more intimately mixed, the flavour is retained. **Malt-Bruising, or Bruising-mill.** It has been found by repeated experiments, that bruising malt is a more advantageous method than the old one of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> and flouring. By bruising, there is not only less waste, but the malt is also better fitted for giving out all its virtues. It has therefore become a practice to squeeze malt between rollers, by means of a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a>, of which various contrivances have been invented. One of the best contrivances of this sort is said to be the bruising-mill of Mr Winlaw, which consists of a frame, a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROLLER">roller</a>, a small roller, a hopper, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a>, a frame to support the hopper, a fly wheel, and a windlass. To use this engine, it is directed to screw the large roller up to the small one, and not to feed too fast from the shoe, which is regulated by pins that have strings fixed to them. It is evident, that when two smooth surfaces are opposed to each other at a distance which can be regulated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, neither grain nor any other similar substance can pass between them without being bruised. This being the principle on which the bruising-mill acts, the mealy substance, which is the essential part of malt, is entirely removed from the skin or husk which contains it, and all the virtues of the malt are with ease extracted by the water in a manner superior to what is effected when the grain is only cut by grinding. The operation is at the same time so expeditiously performed, that two men can with ease bruise a bushel of malt in a minute. By the same engine may also be bruised oats and beans for horses. A great part of the corn given these animals, it is well known, is swallowed whole, and often passes through them in the same state; in which case, they cannot receive any nourishment from the grains that are unbroken; but when bruised in this engine, it eases mastication; and every grain being prepared for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUTRITION">nutrition</a>, a much less quantity will of course be found to be sufficient. For bruising beans, the two regulating screws must be unscrewed a little; and the fly-wheel requires to be then set in motion with the hand, on account that the rollers are then a little space apart, and will not turn each other before the beans come between them. **Malt-Tax,** is the sum of £50,000l. raised every year by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> since 1697, by a duty of 6d. on the bushel of malt, and a proportionable sum on certain liquors, such as cider and perry, which might otherwise prevent the consumption of malt. This is under the management of the commissioners of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a>; and is indeed itself no other than the annual excise. In 1760, an additional perpetual excise of 3d. per bushel was laid upon malt; and in 1763, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> excise was laid upon cider and perry, but new-modelled in 1766. See Excise. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALTA">MALTA</a>,** a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Mediterranean, situated... Malta situated between the 15th and 16th degrees of east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and between the 35th and 36th degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. It is about 19 or 20 miles in length, nine or ten in breadth, and 60 in circumference. Anciently it was called Melita; and is supposed by Cluverius, from its situation and other particulars, to be the Hyperia mentioned by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, whence the Phœaces were afterwards driven by the Phoenicians, and retired into Scheria and the island of Corfu; which is the more probable, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poet places the mountain Melita in that island. He has likewise brought some probable arguments to prove, that Melita or Malta is the ancient Ogygia; in which the famed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a> Calypso, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the Ocean and Thetis, received the shipwrecked Ulysses, and detained him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years. The most ancient possessors of Malta, of whom we have any certain account, were the Carthaginians; from whom it was taken by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; and yet during the whole time that it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> under the power of these polite nations it was almost entirely barren. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> was partly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> and partly rocky, having scarcely any depth of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; and withal so stony, that it was hardly capable of producing corn or any other grain except cummin, and some seeds of a similar nature. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> products were figs, melons, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, cotton, and some few other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and commodities, which the inhabitants exchanged for corn; and in this barren state it seems to have continued till it came into the possession of the Maltese knights. It laboured also under great scarcity of water and fuel: upon all which accounts it was till that time but thinly inhabited, there being only about 30 or 40 boroughs or other villages scattered about, and no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> except the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, called also Malta, and the town and fort of St Angelo, which defended the harbour: so that the whole <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of its inhabitants did not exceed 12,000, including women and children; the greatest part of whom were very indigent. According to an ancient <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, Malta was first possessed by an African <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> named Battus, an enemy to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Dido; from whom it was taken by the Carthaginians; from the Carthaginians it passed to the Romans, who made themselves masters of it when they subdued the island of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. These were driven out by the Arabs in the year 828; who were driven out in their turn by Roger the Norman, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Sicily, who took possession of it in 1190: from which time it continued under the dominion of the Sicilian princes till the time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V, when it fell under his power, along with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> and Sicily. To cover the island of Sicily from the Turks, Charles gave the island to the knights of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, since that time called knights of Malta, whose origin and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is given under the article Knights of Malta and Rhodes. At the first landing of the Maltese knights, they found themselves obliged to lodge in a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> town at the foot of the hill on which stands the castle of St Angelo, and where their only habitations were fishermen's huts. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, with the principal knights, took possession of the castle, where the accommodations were somewhat better; though these too were very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>, and out of repair. Three days after, he took possession of the city, which was formerly called Malta, but since that time hath taken the name of the Notable City; and after that, of the whole island of Malta, and the neighbouring one of Gozo. The first care of the knights, after having settled their authority through the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, was to provide some better accommodation for the present, and to choose a proper place where to fix their habitation. But as the island had no other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> than the old castle of St Angelo, and was so much exposed on all sides, that it would have required greater sums than their exhausted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> could spare to put it in a proper state of defence; the grand master was obliged to content himself with surrounding the borough above mentioned, wherein he had ordered new buildings to be reared for the present habitation of his knights, with a stout wall, to prevent its being surprised by the Turkish and Barbary corsairs. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, indeed, at this time, was not to have fixed the abode of the knights in the bare and defenseless island of Malta, but to stay in it only till he had got a sufficient force to attempt the conquest of Modon, a town of the Morea, and which was not only a populous and tempting opulent place, but lay very convenient for making an attempt on the island of Rhodes, their ancient habitation, and to which they were naturally attached. This success however, did not hinder his taking all proper <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> for securing Malta as well as Gozo, and laying out a proper <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> for securing them from attacks, in case the design on Modon should fail. In the mean time, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> was then universally prevalent, the grand master, among other precious relics which they had brought from Rhodes, caused the arm of St Catherine to be carried in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>. Whilst they were on their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, one of the centinels gave them notice, that a large Turkish merchantman was wrecked on their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. The grand master immediately despatched some of his knights and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> thither; who finding <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of the ship, a native of Modon, and one Mauritifalata Nocher, an excellent engineer, they were retained in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the order, and the latter was immediately employed in fortifying the island. The knights were hardly settled in Malta, when the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, and other European potentates, endeavoured to engage them in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the inhabitants of Barbary, as the city of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIPOLI">Tripoli</a>, then held by Charles, was in great danger of falling into the hands of the infidels. The attempt on Modon, however, was first made; but it proved unsuccessful, through the base avarice of the Maltese forces: for they having been admitted into the city, during the night began to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> and plunder the inhabitants, without waiting for the arrival of the galleys which were coming to their assistance. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> was, that the inhabitants armed, and a desperate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> began; in which the Maltese, notwithstanding the utmost efforts, were obliged to retire, but not till they had loaded themselves with plunder, and carried away 800 women captive. The grand master, looking upon this disappointment as a sign that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> had ordained Malta to be the residence of the knights, did not renew his attempts against the Turks; but, in 1532, joined with the emperor against the Turks, and sent a great number of his galleys to join the confederate fleet under the celebrated Andrew Doria. In consequence of this aid, the undertaking proved successful; and in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> the conquest of Modon would have been accomplished, had not the follyery, discouraged by the bad success of the last attempt, openly refused to proceed, and obliged the emperor to proceed to Corone, another town belonging to the Turks. Through the valor of the Maltese knights, this place was soon obliged to capitulate; and in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> expedition in 1533, the knights again distinguished themselves in a most eminent manner. They were quickly recalled, however, by the grand master to the defense of the island, which was now threatened with an invasion by Barbarossa the celebrated Turkish corsair, who scoured those seas at the head of above four hundred galleys. This invasion, however, did not take place; and in 1534 the grand master Villiers de l'<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> died, and was succeeded by Perino de Ponte, a native of the town of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTI">Asti</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. The new grand master, who received intelligence of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> at St Euphemia in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, very soon after received another express, giving an account of the wars which at that time reigned in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>, and the danger that Tripoli as well as Malta was in from Barbarossa, who was by this time become master both of Algiers and Tunis; upon which he made all the haste he could to his new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. His first care was to send a strong reinforcement to Italy; after which, he despatched an embassy to the emperor, intreating him to equip a powerful fleet against Barbarossa, without which it would be impossible for Tripoli to hold out much longer. By this embassy from De Ponte, and another to the same purpose from Muley Hassen, the defeated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Tunis, Charles was easily prevailed on to carry his arms into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>; in which he was assisted by a great number of the bravest knights, together with 18 brigantines of different sizes, four of the best Maltese galleys, and their vessel called the great carrack, of itself almost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to a squadron. In this expedition the knights distinguished themselves in a most eminent manner. At the siege of Goletta, one of the knights, named Conversa, an excellent engineer, by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARCA">barca</a> lunga, got almost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the great tower, which he furiously battered with large cannon, while the great carrack, which was behind all the rest of the vessels, and by reason of its height could fire over them, did prodigious execution. A <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> was soon made; and hardly was it wide enough to be sealed, when the Maltese knights jumped out of the galleys into their long boats; and thence into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, with their swords in their hands, and waded through the water above their girdles, it being too shallow for boats to approach the shore. The standard-bearer of the order was the first that jumped into the water, and led the rest to the attack; they claiming everywhere the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. They marched with the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> through the most terrible firing and showers of all kinds of missile weapons; and, having gained the shore, quickly ascended the breach, on the top of which they planted their great standard. A great number lost their lives, and fearlessly came off unwounded; but the emperor did them the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> to own, that the taking the place was chiefly owing to the valor of the Maltese knights. The city of Tunis was soon taken after the fortress of Goletta; on the surrender of which, the emperor, desirous to return into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, took his last dinner on board the great carrack; where he was magnificently entertained, and bellowed on the surviving knights the greatest eulogiums, and marks of his esteem and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> to the owner. There he accompanied with privileges considerable presents and with two new grants. By the first, they were allowed to import corn and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> from Sicily, without paying duty; and by the second, the emperor engaged, that none of the order should enjoy any of the estates or revenues, due to Maltese knights, throughout all his dominions, unless they were lawfully authorized by the grand master and his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>; or till the originals had been examined and registered by himself, or such ministers as he should appoint for that purpose. The fleet then set sail for Malta; where, on their arrival, they received the news of the grand master's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, who was succeeded by Didier de Tolon de St Jalle, a native of Provence, and then grand <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> of Thoulouse, where he resided at the time of his election. The present grand master was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of great conduct and bravery, which he had formerly shown at the siege of Rhodes; and the situation of affairs at this time required a person of experience. The Turkish corsairs, quite tired out with the dreadful havoc made among them by Botigella, grand prior of Pifa, who unsuccessful quitted the sea, and never failed out without attempting sinking some of them, or making considerable prizes on Tripoli, had agreed to enter into a strong confederacy, either to surprise the city of Tripoli where his retreat was, or, if that failed, to lay siege to it by sea and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>; in either of which attempts, they were sure of all the assistance of Barbarossa and Hayradin, then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of Tangiers. This last had undertaken the command and conduct of the whole enterprise; but the governor being informed of the design, prepared to give him a warm reception. Hayradin came thither with his whole force in the dead of the night, and began to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> the walls in those places where he reckoned them to be most defenceless. They no sooner appeared at the foot of them, than the garrison, which had been kept up in arms, poured down such streams of wildfire, boiling oil, melted lead, &c., and threw such volleys of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, while the great and small guns so annoyed those that stood farther off, that great numbers of them were destroyed. They persisted in the attack, however, with great fury and vigour, till Hayradin, who was foremost in one of the escalades, was knocked down by a musket-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> from the top of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LADDER">ladder</a>. He fell into the ditch, and was taken up almost dead; upon which his troops instantly dispersed themselves, and abandoned the enterprise. The governor of Tripoli, however, judging that this would not be the last visit of the kind which in all probability he would receive, immediately despatched an express to Malta, with proposals for fortifying the city, and demolishing a strong tower on that coast named <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCAID">Alcaid</a>, which was held by a Turkish corsair. His advice being approved of, the commander Botigella, now general of the galleys, was immediately despatched with a sufficient force; who, having landed his men at Tripoli, immediately marched with them and a body of Arab mercenaries towards Alcaid; and without staying to open the trenches, or any other covering than his gabions, levelled his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> against it. Hayradin being informed of this, came. came with his Turks to its defence; but was intercepted by a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> of Maltese knights at the head of the hired Arabs, and repulsed with loss; so that all he could do was to convey about 50 or 60 Turks into the place, and to annoy the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> with some slight skirmishes. Botigella, perceiving that his cannon did not make such quick dispatch as he wished, sent some of his galleys under the shelter of which he quickly sprung a mine, which brought down part of the wall, and buried most of the corsairs under it; upon which the rest, seeing the Maltese knights mount the breach <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>-in-hand, immediately threw down their arms. The tower was then razed to the ground; after which Botigella marched to a town called Adalat, whence he drove Hayradin, who had entrenched himself in it, and gave the plunder to the Arabs. In his return he attacked and took a large Turkish galley, the cargo of which was valued at 160,000 crowns, and had on board 200 persons; so that he landed in triumph, and was received with the loud acclamations of the whole order, who came to meet him on his arrival. Soon after the grand master fell sick and died, and was succeeded by John de Homedes. Fresh complaints having in 1564 been made to Soliman, he proposed, in a grand council where most of his officers attended, to extirpate the knights altogether. This design was strenuously opposed by Hali, one of Dragut's most experienced captains, who offered the most solid reasons against it; but being overruled by the rest, an expedition against Malta was resolved upon. One of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a>'s first cares was to send some spies, in the disguise of fishermen, to take a full view of the island, who found means to bring him an exact plan of it, with all its fortifications, havens, strength, the number of its inhabitants, &c., whilst he was halting his armaments against it. By this time, as the Maltese had very little reason to doubt that the Turkish armaments were designed against their island, the viceroy of Sicily, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a> Garcia, was ordered by his master to take it in his way to the castle of Golella, in order to consult with the grand master about the necessary means for opposing such a formidable power. The grand master acquainted him, that, in case of an attack upon Malta, he should want both men and corn: upon which the viceroy engaged to supply him with both on his return to Sicily; in pledge of which he left one of his sons with him, who was afterwards admitted into the order. He was no sooner departed, than the grand master summoned all the knights of the order, dispersed through several parts of Europe, to repair to him. Those that were in Italy raised a body of 2000 foot, to which the viceroy of Sicily added two companies of Spanish forces. All the galleys of the order were employed in transporting these troops, together with all manner of provisions and ammunition, into the island; and the knights that were in it, in distributing, disciplining, and exercising their new levies, as well as the Maltese <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, against the siege. Thus the grand master <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> himself strengthened by the arrival of 600 knights, all of whom brought with them retinues of stout good servants, fit to assist in the defence of the island; whilst those, who by reason of age, sickness, or other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-IMPEDIMENTS">impediments</a>, could not repair to him, sold their most valuable effects in order to assist him with their purses. The pope, on his part, contented himself with sending a supply of 10,000 Malta-crowns; and the king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> ordered his viceroy Don Garcia to raise an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of 20,000 men, to be ready to fall thither as soon as called for. The grand master employed the remainder of his time in visiting all the forts, magazines, arsenals, &c., and affixing to each tongue their several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, and making all necessary preparations, till the Ottoman fleet appeared in sight on the 18th of May 1565. It consisted of 150 large galleys and galleons, carrying on board 30,000 common forces, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANIZARIES">janizaries</a> and pashis, besides the slaves at the oar, accompanied by a considerable number of other vessels, laden with artillery, ammunition, and other necessaries for a siege. The whole armament was commanded by Mustapha Batha, an old experienced officer, aged about 85 years, and an old favourite and confidant of the sultan; of a haughty cruel temper, who made it a merit to violate his word, and to use all manner of violence against the Christians, especially against the Maltese. This formidable army landed at some distance from Il <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORGO">Borgo</a>, and soon afterwards spread themselves over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; setting fire to the villages, putting the peasants to the sword, and carrying off such of the cattle as, notwithstanding the orders of the grand master, had not been secured within the forts and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. While the Turks were thus employed, La Valette (the grand master) sent out De Copier, marshal of the order, with 200 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and 600 foot, to watch their motions. De Copier, an officer of great experience, executed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> with so much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and vigour, that, by falling unexpectedly on detached parties, he cut off 1500 Turks, with the loss only of 80 men. The Turkish general held a council of war as soon as all his troops were landed, to assist him in resolving where he should begin his attack. Piali, the Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, agreeably to what he understood to have been the sultan's instructions, was of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that they ought not to enter upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> till Dragut should arrive. But Multapha having received information of the king of Spain's preparations, thought something ought to be done instantly for the safety of the fleet; which lay at present in a creek, where it was exposed to the violence of the east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, and might be attacked with great advantage by the Spaniards. On this account he was of opinion, that they should immediately lay siege to a fort called St Elmo, which stood on a neck of land near Il Borgo, having the principal harbour on one side of it, and on the other another harbour large enough to contain the whole fleet in safety. This proposal was approved by a majority of the council, and Multapha proceeded without delay to carry it into execution. La Valette did not expect that a place which was desperate neither strong nor large enough to admit a numerous defence of garrison, could be defended long against so great a force as was employed to reduce it; but he thought it necessary that the siege of this fort should be prolonged as much as possible, in order to give the viceroy of Sicily time to come to his relief. With this view, he resolved to throw himself into St Elmo, with a select body of troops; and he was preparing to set out, when the whole body of knights remonstrated with such <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> importunity against his leaving the town. town, that he at last consented to suffer the reinforcement, which he had prepared, to be conducted to the fort by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> called De Medran, upon whose conduct and intrepidity he could rely with the most assured confidence. Not long after De Medran's arrival in the fort, the garrison made a vigorous sally, in which they drove the enemy from their intrenchments, and put a number of them to the sword. But the rest soon recovered from their surprize; and having returned to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, they compelled the Christians to retire. In this rencounter, the vigorous efforts of the janizaries were favoured by the wind, which blew the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of the guns upon the fort, and covered the besieged with a thick cloud, through which it was impossible to discern the operations of the enemy. This incident the Turks had the presence of mind to improve to very great advantage. They feigned, unperceived, upon the counterescarp; made a lodgment there with beams, woollocks, and gabions; and raised a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> upon it with incredible expedition. After the smoke was dispersed, the besieged beheld what had been done with much astonishment: and they were the more disquieted, as the fortification which the Turks had raised upon their counterescarp overtopped a ravelin which lay near it, in which the besieged could no longer appear with safety. They resolved, however, to defend this ravelin as long as possible, whatever it should cost them. In the mean time Dragut, and another noted corsair named Uluchiali, arrived with 20 galleys; having, besides slaves and seamen, 2500 troops on board. This reinforcement, and the presence of Dragut, added fresh vigour to the operations of the siege. This gallant corsair exposed himself, on all occasions, with the utmost intrepidity; spent whole days in the trenches; and as, besides his other extraordinary talents, he was particularly skilful in the management of artillery, he caused some new batteries to be raised in more advantageous situations than had hitherto been made choice of; and kept up a continual fire both on the ravelin above mentioned, and a cavalier that covered the fort and was one of its principal defences. This cavalier soon became the only defence which could prevent the besiegers from coming up to the very foot of the wall. Some Turkish engineers having approached the ravelin at daybreak, to observe the effects of their artillery, they perceived a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-port so low, that one of them, when mounted on the shoulders of another, looked into it, and saw the Christian soldiers lying on the ground asleep. Of this they gave immediate information to the troops; who, advancing as quickly and silently as possible, and clapping ladders to the gun-hole, got up into the ravelin, and cut most of the Christians to pieces. Between this ravelin and the cavalier lay the ditch, over which the besieged had thrown a temporary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of planks leading up to the cavalier. The Turks, perceiving this, leaped instantly upon the bridge, and attempted to make themselves masters of the cavalier, as they already were of the ravelin. But the garrison was now alarmed; the bravest of the knights hastened from different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> to the post of danger; and after an obstinate engagement, they compelled the Turks to retire into the ravelin. There, observing another way of reaching the cavalier by a path from the bottom of the ditch, they threw themselves down without dread or hesitation; and having ascended by this path to the other side, they renewed their attack with greater fury than ever. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> lasted from sunrise till noon, when the knights at last proved victorious. About 20 knights and 100 soldiers were killed; and near 3000 of the enemy. As the ravelin was open on the side towards the fort, the besieged pointed some cannon against it, and made great havoc among the infidels. But Mustapha, sensible of the value of the acquisition he had made, poured in fresh soldiers without number, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIONEERS">pioneers</a> coming forward with woollocks, planks, and gabions, put the troops, at length in safety, and made a lodgment in the ravelin, of which the garrison were never afterwards able to dispossess them. The grand master's concern on account of this disaster was greatly augmented, by considering, that it could not have happened so soon without some negligence on the part of the garrison. He sent them, however, an immediate reinforcement; and both the siege and the defence were carried on with the same vigour as before. But the situation of the besieged was now become much more dangerous than formerly. The Turks applied with unremitting diligence to heighten the ravelin till it overtopped the wall of the fort; and after this the garrison could no longer appear upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> with safety. Many were killed by the enemy's artillery, several breaches were made in the wall, and the hearts of the bravest knights began to fail within them. They agreed therefore, though with much reluctance, to apply to the grand master for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to quit the fort; and they made choice of the Chevalier de Medran for their messenger. He represented that the fort was in reality no longer tenable; and that, to continue in it, though only for a few days, would infallibly occasion the destruction of the garrison. Most of the knights in council thought that this request of the garrison ought to be immediately granted. But La Valette was of a contrary opinion.—This he represented to the Chevalier de Medran; and sent him back with instructions to remind the knights of the vows which they took at their entrance into the order, of sacrificing their lives for its defence. He likewise bade him assure them, in his name, that he would not fail to send them such reinforcements as they should stand in need of; and was determined, as soon as it should be necessary, to come himself to their assistance, with a fixed unalterable purpose to lay down his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> sooner than deliver the fort into the hands of the infidels. This answer had the desired effect on several of the knights, and particularly on those whose principles of honour and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the order were confirmed by years. But the greater part of them were much dissatisfied. They thought the grand master's treatment of them harsh and cruel; and wrote him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, subscribed by 53; in which they informed him, that if he did not, on the next night, send boats to carry them to the town, they were determined to fall out into the Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, where they might fall honourably by the sword, instead of suffering such an ignominious death. death as they had reason to expect if the fort was taken by storm. To this letter La Valette replied, "That they were much mistaken if they expected to satisfy their honour by throwing away their lives; since it was no less their duty to submit to his authority than to sacrifice their lives in defence of the order: that the preservation of the whole depended on their present obedience to his commands: that no aid was to be expected from Spain if the fort were given up. And that if he should yield to their request, and bring them to the town, the town itself would then be immediately invested; and they, as well as the fort, soon afterwards reduced to a situation more desperate than that from which they were so solicitous to escape, by deserting an important post which they had undertaken to defend." Besides this letter, he sent three commissioners to examine the state of the fortifications; intending by this measure either to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> time or to prevent the garrison from sinking into despair. These commissioners differed very widely in the accounts which they delivered at their return. Two of them thought it impossible to defend the fort much longer. But the third, named Constantine Caftriot, a Greek prince, descended from the famous Albanian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCANDERBEG">Scanderbeg</a>, whether from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> or a consciousness of greater resources in his native courage than the other two possessed, maintained that the garrison was far from being reduced to the last extremity; and to give a proof how firmly he was persuaded of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of what he said, he offered to enter the fort himself, and to undertake the defence of it with such troops as should be willing to accompany him. The grand master, strongly impressed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of protracting the siege, immediately accepted this offer, and bestowed the highest encouragements on Caftriot's zeal and resolution. Nor did Caftriot find any difficulty in persuading a sufficient number to attend him, who were no less zealous and resolute than himself. The soldiers crowded to his standard, and were emulous to have their names enrolled for that dangerous service in which he had engaged.
