Manca and mancufa are promiscuously used in the old books for the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>.

MANCHA

Pages 187-187

a territory of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of New Castle, lying between the river Guadiana and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>. It is a mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and it was here that the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a> Quixote was supposed to perform his exploits.

MANCHESTER

Pages 187-189

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a> in England, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 42. N. Lat. 53. 27. Mr Whittaker conjectures, that the station was first occupied by the Britons about 500 years B.C. but that it did not receive anything like the form of a town till 450 years after, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 50 years B.C. when the Britons of Cheshire made an irruption into the territories of their southern neighbours, and of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> alarmed the Settuntii, or inhabitants of Lancashire, so much, that they began to build fortresses, in order to defend their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Its British name was Mancenion, that is, "a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of tents;" it was changed, however, into Mancunium by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who conquered it under Agricola in the memorable year of the Christian era 79. It appears also to have been called Mandue-fundum, Manduefudum, Manuctum, and Maneufire; from which last it seems most evident that the present name has been derived. It is distant from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> 182 miles, and from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, 214; standing near the conflux of the Irk and the Irwell, about three miles from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERSEY">Mersey</a>. Manchester was accounted a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and populous town even 50 years ago; but since that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it is supposed to have increased in more than a triple proportion, both in respect to buildings and inhabitants. The houses amount to a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> not far short of 12,000; and perhaps it may not be an overrate to reckon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> persons to each, when it is considered, that, of the houses occupied by working people of various descriptions, many have two, three, and sometimes more, families in each. For though many hundred houses have been built in the course of a few late years, yet are they constantly engaged as soon as possible; the avidity for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> increasing with every new accession of inhabitants, and rents rising to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> scarcely known in other places. The progress of this increase may be partly estimated by the price of building, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and materials: a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">guinea</a> per <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> yard, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> rent, having been refused for some central plots; and bricks selling at 2s. per 1000, which about four years since were not more than half the price. Such, however, has been the happy concurrence of ingenuity and industry, and such the astonishing improvements daily making in its numerous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, together with the encouragement these afford to skilful artists in various branches, that streets must extend in proportion: yet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> appears to have increased more rapidly than buildings; hence competitions naturally arise, and hence a temporary advance of rents. The manufactures of this town and neighbourhood, from humble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> beginnings about two centuries ago, have now, after progressive improvements, acquired such celebrity, both in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of ornament and utility, as to spread in ten thousand forms and colours, not only in these kingdoms, but over all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and even into the distant continents; being at once most precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of well-earned private wealth, and important contributors to the necessary public <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> of the state. Its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST_OFFICE"><a class="x</a>ref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>-office alone may afford an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of its extensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. The population of the town may be further calculated from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> number of cotton factories within the boundaries of the town, wherein it is thought that 20,000 men, women, and children, are employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> branches of preparing warp and weft. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> to these be added the many <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> applied to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a> &c. &c. &c. beside all the more general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, as well as householders, domestic servants, &c. Manchester may be ranked as the most populous market-town in Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. The marriages in Manchester and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALFORD">Salford</a>, from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1791 to January 1792, were 1332, the christenings 2960, and the burials 2286. Hence, should it be computed that one in every 30 persons died, the number of inhabitants would amount to 68,580, which is thought to be much under the sum of an actual enumeration. The streets are about 600, many of them spacious and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a>, great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the old buildings being removed, and the new streets allowed a convenient breadth. The town is lighted every night by 2000 lamps, and guarded by nearly 200 watchmen. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> was founded in 1422 by Thomas Weft <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELAWARE">Delaware</a>; and consisted of a warden, eight fellows, four clerks, and five choristers. About the same time the present collegiate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> was built (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> only having been used for the former church). This church is a fine structure of what is termed the Gothic system, and is much enriched with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>. The collegiate body consists of a warden, four fellows, two chaplains, two clerks (one of whom, by a very late regulation, is to be at least bachelor of arts and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>'s orders), four choristers, and four singing men. Before the collegiate church, there are also the following. St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>'s, a handsome church, begun in 1709 and finished in 1723: it is in the gift of the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>. St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s, built by the clergy of the collegiate church, and consecrated upwards of 30 years ago, is a neat and indeed an elegant edifice; as is St John's, which was built about 20 years since by the late Edward Byrom, Esq. The next presentation thereof is, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, vested in his heirs, afterwards devolving to the warden and fellows of the collegiate church. St Paul's church was erected upwards of 12 years ago; and is a handsome spacious building, chiefly brick; to which has been added, within the last two years, a lofty and substantial <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> tower. St James's Manchester church has been finished within the last ten years: it is a large well-lighted building of brick and stone, with a small stone steeple. St Michael's is also of brick and stone, with a square tower. It was built by the late Rev. Humphrey Owen (one of the chaplains of the collegiate church, and rector of St Mary's), in whose heirs the presentation is vested for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of 65 years, and thenceforward in the warden and fellows of the college. To these may be added, St Thomas's, Ardwick Green, and Trinity church, Salford; for though the Irwell intervenes between Manchester and Salford, and each is governed by its respective constables; yet, being connected by three bridges, by mutual friendship, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pursuit of universally useful manufactures and commerce, the two places are generally considered under the name of Manchester, as the borough of Southwark is not improperly deemed a part of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>. In Salford there is likewise a Methodist chapel nearly finished. A new church is also about to be built and dedicated to St Stephen.—In Manchester a new church is lately finished, and called St George's; but divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> has not yet been performed therein. St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s church, at the end of Mosley-street, was begun about three years since: when finished, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be a strong and elegant stone structure with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> spire; at present the body only is completed, and lighted, in a manner not very common, by six semicircular windows. The foundation of another church, to be called St Clement's, has also been laid, within the present year 1792, in Stephenson's square lately planned; and also one called the New <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> Church, nearly finished. Besides the 14 churches above enumerated, there are, a Catholic chapel, a large Methodist chapel, a chapel for the people called <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>, and 5 chapels for dissenters of other denominations. Cheetham's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the College, because it was originally the place of residence of the warden and fellows, is deserving of particular notice. Humphrey Cheetham of Clayton near Manchester, Esq.; having been remarkably successful in trade in the middle of the last century, bought the college, and liberally endowed it for the maintenance and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of 40 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> boys, admissible between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 6 and 10 years. By an improvement of the funds of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, the numbers of boys was increased to 60; and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> such till the Easter meeting of the feoffees in 1780, when another augmentation took place, and the number has since been constantly 80. The townships, pointed out by the founder for objects of his charity, are the following, together with the respective numbers admitted from each: Manchester, original number 14, now 28; Salford 6, now 12; Droyden 3, now 6; Crumpsall 2, now 4; Bolton-le-moors 10, now 20; Turton 5, now 10. So that 80 persons are now annually provided for by this liberal benefactor; including for the hospital a governor, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and five women servants, a school-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>; and, on the library establishment, a librarian. (See an authentic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> in the Gent. Mag. for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1792, p. 521.) The boys of this hospital are comfortably provided for till the age of 14, when they are further clothed, and with a premium placed apprentices to useful trades; and, in order to incite early habits of industry, to make them good servants, and at length good masters, it has been suggested to Manchester furnish some kind of easy employment for a small part of their time not engaged at school. The Library, which occupies an extensive gallery of the same building, owes its foundation and increasing importance to the same benevolent source. The annual value of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> originally bequeathed for the purchase of books and for a librarian's salary was £161; but by recent improvements of the estate, the income is more than thrice that sum. The books at this time amount to 10,000 volumes, of which a catalogue handsomely printed in 2 volumes 8vo has been published by the present librarian, the Rev. John Radcliffe, A.M. At stated hours on all days, except Sundays and other holidays, the studious may have free access to read, in the library, any book it contains; and in order to render it comfortable during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> season of the year, several stoves are kept heated at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> hours. This college and a large inclosed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> are situated upon a high perpendicular rock, bounded by the Irk <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to its confluence with the Irwell; and is thought by Mr Whitaker to be included, as well as the collegiate church, within the boundaries of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman praetorium; the whole of which site towards the Irwell, as on the side of the Irk, is considerably elevated above the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and the opposite land of Salford. The free-school, higher up on the same side of the Irk, almost joining to the college, is supported by the rents of three <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>; one of which is for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> malt, another for corn, and the third is employed as a snuff mill. These rents are now increased to £600 per annum, from which salaries are paid to three masters and two assistants. The scholars educated here have certain exhibitions allowed at the university; and such of them as are entered at Brazen-nose college <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> have a chance of obtaining some valuable exhibitions arising from lands in Manchester bequeathed by Mr Hulme. The deserved reputation of this school is a powerful recommendation of its scholars entering at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>. The Academy is a large and commodious building, raised by the subscriptions of several respectable dissenters, and placed under the care of able tutors. Here youth above 14 years of age are admitted and instructed in the various branches of liberal knowledge, preparatory to trade or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a>. The Literary and Philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of Manchester was instituted in the beginning of the year 1781, and is well known by its <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a>, of which three volumes 8vo have been published; these have been translated into the German <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. A fourth volume is now in the press, and in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> will be published in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of 1793. A society was established here in November 1789, under the name of the Lancashire Humane Society, for the encouragement of all who may attempt the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of persons apparently drowned. The Infirmary, Dispensary, Lunatic <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">Asylum</a>, and public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">Baths</a>, are all situated on one large airy plot of land, in the most elevated and agreeable part of the town; a pleasant grass-plot and gravel-walk extending the whole length of the buildings; a canal intervening between them and the public street, next to which it is guarded by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> palisades. The Lying-in hospital is situated in Salford, at the end of the old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. A new <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">Work</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is nearly completed; and for such a purpose a happier spot could not be found. in any town than that whereon it is erected, being on an equal eminence with the college on the opposite side of the Irk, and promising the greatest polite comforts to such as may be necessitated to become its inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">Exchange</a> was a strong good building; but since the late act of parliament obtained for farther improvements of the town, it has been sold and taken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and its site formed into a convenient area, to the great advantage of the surrounding houses. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">Theatre</a> is a neat building, wherein the boxes are placed in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a> opposite to the stage. The Gentlemen's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCERT">Concert</a>-room is an elegant building, capacious enough to accommodate 1200 persons. The concerts are supported by annual subscriptions: but strangers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> gentlemen have free admission to the private concerts; as also to the public concerts, with a subscriber's ticket. The new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">Assembly</a>-rooms are large and commodious. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CIRCUS">Circus</a> is almost finished. Here are two Market-places, the old and the new; which are well supplied with everything in season, though at high <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a>. There are several charity-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> belonging to different churches and chapels, where children are furnished with clothes and taught to read. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>-schools are numerous, and afford instruction to upwards of 5000 children. Over the Irwell are three bridges, uniting the town with Salford: the old bridge is very high at the Manchester end, whence it slopes into Salford. The middle bridge, four feet wide, raised upon timber and flagged, is only for the accommodation of foot-passengers, who from the Manchester side must descend to it by nearly forty steps. The lower bridge is a handsome stone building of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>; this bridge affords a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> for two or three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> abreast. It was undertaken and finished by the private subscription of a few gentlemen; and a small toll is taken for all passing, which toll is now annually let by auction, and pays the proprietors remarkably well.—From Manchester there are likewise the same number of bridges over the Irk; only one, however, is adapted for the passage of carriages. The Irwell, having at a great expense been rendered navigable for vessels of 20 or 30 tons burden, there is a constant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a>, Manchester, and the intermediate places on the Irwell and Mersey, to the great advantage of the proprietors and the country at large. This <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, and more especially the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Bridgewater's canal, opening a passage from Manchester to the Mersey at 30 miles distance, have, together, greatly contributed to the present highly flourishing state of the town. Advantages still greater, because more widely diffusive, may result from the intended union of the Humber and the Mersey by means of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>. Indeed, every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> of canal would benefit many miles of land; and such would be the reciprocity of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, that it would undoubtedly extend and be felt far beyond the visible measurement of the navigation." The News Room and Library in Manchester is an elegant building, and an ornament to the town; and as it comprehends in it a news room, circulating library, and reading room, must be productive of general utility. The proposal of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> met with much opposition at first; but it was finally carried by the unrestrained exertions of a Mr Robinson, a man whose Manchester character was universally loved and admired. We must not omit to notice the new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENITENTIARY">penitentiary</a> house, called the New Bailey, for separate confinement of various criminals. Over the entrance is a large session room, with adjoining rooms for the magistrates, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, jurors, &c. Beyond this, in the centre of a very large area inclosed by very high walls, stands the Prison, an extensive building, forming a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> three stories high; and the four wards of each story may in an instant be seen by any person in its centre. This prison is kept surprisingly neat and healthy; and such as can work at any trade, and are not confined for crimes of the greatest magnitude, are employed in a variety of branches; so that one may be seen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> and cleansing cotton, another carding it, another roving, and a fourth <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a>. In the next place may be observed a man or a woman busy at the loom; and in another, one or more engaged in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> and raising the velvet pile. Hence industry is not suffered to flounder in the solitary <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a>, nor to quit it under the acquired impressions of that torpor which formerly accompanied the emancipated prisoner from his dungeon; rendering him, perhaps, totally unfit for the duties of honest society, though well qualified, in all probability, to lord it with gamblers, and be then, if not before, initiated into their pernicious <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a>.—At Kerel-moor, three miles distant, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-races are annually permitted. The banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and various brooks about the town afford excellent situations for the numerous dye-houses employed for a multitude of fabrics. Among other things, the manufacture and finishing of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a> is carried on to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of great importance.—The general market is here on Saturdays. Tuesday's market is chiefly for transacting business between the traders and manufacturers of the town and circumjacent country. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> are on Whit-Monday, October 1st, and November 17th. Manchester is a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> with courts leet and baron. It sends no members to parliament, but gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to a duke. The annual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> is here about 42 inches; though from January 1791 to January 1792 it was 44 inches. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> in 1791 was 76°, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 17. MANCHINEEL. See Hippomane, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MANCIPATIO

Pages 189-189

was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of in the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and may be thus explained; every father had such a regal authority over his son, that before the son could be released from his subjection and made free, he must be three times over sold and bought, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> father being the vender. The vendee was called pater fiduciarus. After this fictitious bargain, the pater fiduciarus sold him again to the natural father, who could then, but not till then, manumit <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> make him free. The imaginary <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> was called mancipatio; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of giving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> or setting him free after this was called emancipatio.

MANCIPATIO ALSO

Pages 189-189

o also signifies the selling <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> alienating of certain lands by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> paid by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, and five witnesses. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of alienation took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> only amongst Roman citizens, and that only in respect to certain estates situated in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, which were called mancipia.

MANCIPLE

Pages 189-190

MANCIPLE (maneops), a clerk of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> caterer. An officer in the inner temple was anciently so called, who is now the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> there; of whom Chaucer, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> English poet, some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> a student of that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, thus writes: A manciple there was within the temple, Of which all caterers might take ensample. This officer still remains in colleges in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>.

MANCUNIUM

Pages 190-190

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Brigantines in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. Now <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>. See MANCHESTER.

MANCUS

Pages 190-190

in antiquity, an Anglo-Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, equal in value to 2½ folds, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 30 pence; and in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> to 55 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a> grains. The first account of this coin that occurs in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, is about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the 8th century, in an embassy of Cenwulf <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Mercia to Leo III., requesting the restoration of the jurisdiction of the see of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>: this embassy was enforced by a present of 120 mancuses. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETHELWOLF">Ethelwolf</a> also sent yearly to Rome 300 mancuses; and these coins are said to have <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in some form or other till towards the conclusion of the Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. The heriots of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> are chiefly estimated by this standard in Canute's laws. It came originally from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where it was called ducat: and is supposed to have been the same with the drachma or miliarenis current in the Byzantine empire.

MANDAMUS

Pages 190-190

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a writ that issues out of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, sent to a corporation, commanding them to admit <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> refuse a person to his office. This writ also lies where justices of the peace refuse to admit a person to take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> in order to qualify himself for enjoying any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> or office; or where a bishop or archdeacon refuses to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> a probate of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, to admit an executor to prove it, or to swear a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-warden, &c.

MANDANES

Pages 190-190

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, who for the renown of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> was invited by the ambassadors of Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> to the banquet of the son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. A reward was promised him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he obeyed, but he was threatened with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of a refusal. Unmoved by promises and threatenings, the philosopher dismissed them with observing, that though Alexander ruled over a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the universe, he was not the son of Jupiter; and that he gave himself no trouble about the pretensions of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who possessed not wherewithal to content himself. "I despise his threats (added he): if I live, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> is sufficient for my subsistence; and to me <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> has no terrors, for it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> only be an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> of old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> and infirmity for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of a better <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>."

MANDARINS

Pages 190-190

a name given to the magistrates and governors of provinces in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, who are chosen out of the most learned men, and whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> is always at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of their birth. Mandarin is also a name given by the Chinese to the learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; for besides the language peculiar to every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, there is one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to all the learned in the empire, which is in China what Latin is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; this is called the mandarin tongue, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the language of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>.

MANDATE

Pages 190-190

in the canon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a rescript of the pope commanding an ordinary collator to put the person therein named in possession of the first vacant benefice in his collation.

MANDATUM

Pages 190-190

was a fee <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> retainer given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to the procuratores and advocati. The mandatum was a necessary condition, without which they had not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of pleading. Thus the legal eloquence of Rome, like that of our own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, could not be unlocked without a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a>.

MANDERSCHETT

Pages 190-190

a town of Germany in the circle of the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIER">Trier</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name, between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Trier and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Juliers. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 32. N. Lat. 50. 20.

MANDEVILLE

Pages 190-190

Sir John, a physician, celebrated on account of his travels, was born at St Albans, about the beginning of the 14th century. He had a liberal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of physic; but being at length seized with an invincible desire of seeing distant parts of the globe, he left England in 1332, and did not return till 34 years after. His friends, who had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> supposed him dead, did not know him when he appeared. He had traveled through almost all the east, and made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of languages. He particularly visited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCYTHIA">Scythia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a> the Greater and Lesser, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, Media, Mesopotamia, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, Chaldea, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, &c. His rambling disposition did not suffer him to rest; for he left his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and died at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a> in 1732. He wrote An Itinerary, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> an Account of his Travels, in English, French, and Latin. Mandeville, Bernard de, an eminent writer in the 18th century, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, where he studied physic, and took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>. He afterwards came over into England, and in 1714 published a poem, entitled "The Grumbling Hive, or Knaves turned Honest;" upon which he afterwards wrote remarks, and published the whole at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, 1723, in 8vo, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">Fable</a> of the Bees, or Private Vices made public Benefits; with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">Charity</a> and Charity-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, and a Search into the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>." This book was presented by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> the same year, and severely animadverted upon in "A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">Honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> C." printed in the London Journal of Saturday July 27, 1723. Our author published a Vindication. His book was attacked by several writers. He published other pieces, and died in 1724.

MANDING

Pages 190-191

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> state in the interior of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, situated in N. Lat. 12. 40. and W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 40. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, according to Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">Park</a>, seems to be a kind of republic, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather an oligarchy. Many <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of edible roots are found here; but the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a>, coffee, and the cocoa tree, appear to be unknown to the inhabitants. The Mandingoes are reputed a very gentle <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of people, cheerful in their dispositions, inquisitive, credulous, simple, and fond of flattery. The men, in general, are about the middle size, well-shaped, strong, and capable of enduring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> labour; the women are good- Manding, good-natured, sprightly, and agreeable. Both sexes dress in cotton cloth of their own manufacture, and both seem irresistibly inclined to commit depredations on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of unprotected strangers; yet, strange as it may appear, they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> contribute to the personal safety of the very people whom they are bent upon plundering. Parental and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILIAL">filial</a> affection is very strong between the mother and her child, but not so between the father and his children, which must originate from that divided <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> which never fails to be an attendant on polygamy. The care of the mother extends to the cultivation of the mind; and one of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> in which they instruct their offspring, is the practice of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. To fuckle their children three years is an ordinary occurrence, during which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the husband devotes all his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to his other wives. When a young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> intends to marry a young girl, he first addresses the parents, as her consent is not deemed necessary. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the parents are agreeable, she must either accept of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of her lover, or continue unmarried all her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> long. The Mandingoes practise circumcision both on males and females, which is a very painful operation, but not performed by them from any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a>, for they have a superstitious notion that it contributes to render the married state prolific. Mr Park affirms us, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of one God, and a future state of rewards and punishments, is universal among them, but that the management of all sublunary concerns is committed to certain subordinate or tutelary agents, whose wrath they deprecate by every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> in their power. These people seldom arrive at old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, being gray-headed and covered with wrinkles about 40, and few reach the age of 60, although their diseases are few, being confined almost to fevers, fluxes, elephantiasis, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEPROSY">leprosy</a> of the worst kind, together with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> worm. Their feelings, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of a relation, are manifested by loud and dismal howlings; and the body is interred, when rolled up in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> cotton with a mat above it, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of its decease. The men cultivate the ground, and the women manufacture cotton cloth, viz. the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a> of it, for it is wove by the men in looms of about four inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. Here also there are manufactories of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAN">tan</a> and dress leather with great expedition, and are said to be acquainted with the melting of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, which they convert into a great variety of ornaments, executed with much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and ingenuity. Their notions of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a> are rather puerile, as they conceive the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> to be an extended <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>, the termination of which no eye has as yet discovered, it being, according to them, overhung with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> and darkness. They suppose the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to be a large river of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, on the farther shore of which is situated a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> called Tobanabdoa, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of the white people; at a distance from which they describe another country, which they believe to be inhabited by cannibals of a gigantic size, called Koomi. As to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of property, they consider the lands in native woods to belong to government. When any individual of free condition has the means of cultivating more land than he actually possesses, he applies to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> man of the district, who allows him an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of territory, on condition of forfeiture, if the lands are not brought into cultivation by a given <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. The condition being fulfilled, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> becomes vested in the possessor, and in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> descends to his heirs. MANDRAGORA. See Atropa, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. MANDRAKE. See Atropa and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSA">Musa</a>, Botany Index.

MANDREL

Pages 191-191

a kind of wooden pulley, making a member of the turner's lathe. Of these there are several kinds; as Flat Mandrels, which have three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more little pegs or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> near the verge, and are used for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> flat boards on. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">Pin</a> Mandrels, which have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> wooden thank to fit into a round hole made in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> to be turned. Hollow Mandrels, which are hollow of themselves, and used for turning hollow work. Screw Mandrels, for turning screws, &c.

MANEGE

Pages 191-191
or MANAGE, the exercise of riding the great horse; or the ground set apart for that purpose; which is sometimes covered, for continuing the exercise in bad weather; and sometimes open, in order to give more liberty and freedom both to the horsemanship and horse. See Horsemanship. The word is borrowed from the French manage, and that from the Italian maneggio; or, as some will have it, à manu agendo, "acting with the hand."

MANES

Pages 191-191

a poetical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, signifying the shades <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> souls of the deceased. The heathens used a variety of ceremonies and sacrifices to appease the manes of those who were deprived of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>. See Lemures and Lemuria. Dii Manes, were the same with inferi, or the infernal gods, who tormented men; and to these the heathens offered sacrifices to assuage their indignation. The heathen <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> is a little obscure with regard to these gods manes. Some hold, that they were the souls of the dead; others, that they were the genii of men; which last <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> suits best with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> of the word. The heathens, it is pretty evident, used the word manes in several senses; so that it sometimes signified the ghosts of the departed, and sometimes the infernal or subterraneous deities, and in general all divinities that presided over tombs. The invocation of the manes of the dead seems to have been very frequent among the Thessalians; but it was expressly prohibited by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARES">Lares</a>. Manes the founder of the Manichean system. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANICHEES">Manichees</a>.

MANETHO

Pages 191-191

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Egyptian historian, who pretended to take all his accounts from the sacred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> on the pillars of Hermes Trismegistus. He was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELIOPOLIS">Heliopolis</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILADELPHUS">Philadelphus</a>, at whose request he wrote his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> in Greek; beginning from their gods, and continuing it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to near the time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> Codomannus who was conquered by Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>. His history of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> is a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, that is often quoted by Josephus and other ancient authors. Julius Africanus gave an abridgement of it in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>. Manetho's work is however lost; and there only

MANFREDONIA

Pages 191-192

a port town of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, which arose on the ruins of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Sipontum; (see the article Sipontum). It received its name from its founder Manfred; who transplanted hither the few inhabitants that remained at Sipontum, and attracted other settlers to it by various privileges and exemptions. In order to found it under the most favourable auspices, he called together all the famous professors of astrology (a science in which both he and his father placed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> confidence), and caused them to calculate the happiest <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> and minute for laying the first <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. He himself drew the plans, traced the walls and streets, superintended the works, and by his presence and largesse animated the workmen to finish them in a very short space of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The port was secured from storms by a pier; the ramparts were built of the most <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> materials; and in the great tower was placed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a> of so considerable a volume as to be heard over all the plain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPITANATA">Capitanata</a>, in order to alarm the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of an invasion. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> of Anjou afterwards removed the bell to Barri, and offered it at the shrine of St Nicholas, as a thanksgiving for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of one of his children. In spite of all the precautions taken by Manfred to secure a brilliant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a> to his new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, neither his pains, nor the horoscopes of his wizards, have been able to render it opulent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> powerful. At present, Mr Swinburne informs us, it fears me multos 6000 inhabitants, though most of the corn exported from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> is shipped off here, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> trade carried on with Venice and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, for which reason there is a lazaretto established; but from some late instances we may gather, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Naples has for many years past remained free from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, it is more owing to good luck, and the very trifling <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, than to the vigilance or incorruptibility of the officers of this port. In 1620, the Turks landed and pillaged Manfredonia. All sorts of vegetables abound here, for flavour and succulence infinitely superior to those raised by continual waterings in the cinerious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of Naples. Lettuce in particular is delicious, and fish plentiful and cheap.

MANGANESE

Pages 192-192
or MAGNESIA NIGRA, a metallic substance, the oxide of which has been long known by the name of glas-makers soap, from its property of rendering glas colourless. See CHEMISTRY and MINERALOGY Index.

MANGEART

Pages 192-192

Dom Thomas, a Benedictine of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of St Vanne and St Hidulph, whose knowledge was an ornament to his order. It gained him also the titles of antiquarian, librarian, and counsellor, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Lorraine. He was preparing a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> when he died, A.D. 1763, before he had put his last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to his book, which was published by Abbé Jacquin. This production appeared in 1763, in folio, with this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>: Introduction à la science des Médailles, pour servir à la connaissance des Dieux, de la <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a>, des Sciences, des Arts, et de tout ce qui appartient à l'Histoire ancienne, avec les preuves tirées des Médailleurs. The elementary treatises on the numismatic science were not sufficiently extensive, and the particular dissertations were by far too tedious and prolix. This learned Benedictine has collected into a single volume all the principles contained in the former, and all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> which are to be found scattered through the latter. His work may serve as a supplement to Montfaucon's Antiquity explained. From Mangeart likewise have a volume of sermons; and a treatise on Purgatory; <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NANCY">Nancy</a>, 1739, 2 vols 12mo. MANGEL wurzel. See Beta, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> Index.

MANGER

Pages 192-192

a small apartment, extending athwart the lower deck of a ship of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, immediately within the haufe-holes, and fenced on the after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> by a partition, which separates it from the other part of the deck behind it. This partition serves as a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> to interrupt the passage of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which occasionally gushes in at the haufe-holes, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> falls from the wet cable whilst it is heaved in by the capstern. The water, thus prevented from running aft, is immediately returned into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> by several small channels, called scuppers, cut through the ship's side within the manger. The manger is therefore particularly useful in giving a contrary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> to the water that enters at the haufe-holes, which would otherwise run aft in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> streams upon the lower deck, and render it extremely wet and uncomfortable, particularly in tempestuous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, to the men who mess and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> in different parts thereof.

MANGET

Pages 192-192

John-James, an eminent physician, born at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a> in 1652. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a> made him his first physician in 1699; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened at Geneva in 1742. He wrote many works; the most known of which are, 1. A collection of several Pharmacopoeias, in folio. 2. Bibliotheca Pharmaceutico-medica. 3. Bibliotheca Anatomica. 4. Bibliotheca Chymica. 5. Bibliotheca Chirurgica. 6. A Bibliotheca of all the authors who have written on medicine, in 4 vols folio. All these works are in Latin. Daniel le Clerc, the author of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Physic, assisted him in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> them.

MANGIFERA

Pages 192-192

the mango-tree; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MANGOSTAN

Pages 192-192
or Mangosteen. See Garcinia, Botany Index. MANGROVE. See Rhizophora, Botany Index.

MANHEIM

Pages 192-192

a town of Germany, in the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">Palatinate</a>, with a very strong citadel, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> Palatine often resides. It is seated at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Neckar and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 33. N. Lat. 49. 25. It surrendered to the French in September 1795; but it was retaken by the Austrians in November following.

MANHOOD

Pages 192-192

that stage of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> which succeeds puberty <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADOLESCENCE">adolescence</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">MAN</a>.

MANICHEES

Pages 192-194

Manichees, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Manicheans (Manichæi), a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> heretics, who affected two principles; so called from their author Manes or Manicheus, a Persian by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and educated among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGI">Magi</a>, being himself one of that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> before he embraced Christianity. This hereby had its first rise about the year 277, and spread itself principally in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. St. Epiphanius, who treats of it at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, observes that the true name of this heresiarch was Cubricus; and that he changed it for Manes, which in the Persian or Babylonian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> signifies vessel. A rich widow, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> he had been, dying without issue, left him store of wealth; after which he assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> or envoy of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ. Manes was not contented with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of apostle of Jesus Christ, but he also assumed that of the Paraclete, whom Christ had promised to send; which Augustine explains, by saying that Manes endeavoured to persuade men, that the Holy Ghost did personally dwell in him with full authority. He left several disciples, and among others, Addas, Thomas, and Hermas. These he sent in his lifetime into several provinces to preach his doctrine. Manes, having undertaken to cure the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>'s son, and not succeeding, was put in prison upon the young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, whence he made his escape; but he was apprehended soon after, and hanged alive. However, the oriental writers, cited by D'Herbelot and Hyde, tells us, that Manes, after having been protected in a singular manner by Hormizdas, who succeeded Sapor in the Persian throne, but who was not able to defend him, at length, against the united hatred of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, the Magi, the Jews, and the Pagans, was shut up in a strong castle, to serve him as a refuge against those who persecuted him on account of his doctrine. They add, that after the death of Hormizdas, Varanes I. his successor, first protected Manes, but afterwards gave him up to the fury of the Magi, whose resentment against him was due to his having adopted the Sadducean principles, as some say; while others <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> it to his having mingled the tenets of the Magi with the doctrines of Christianity. However, it is certain that the Manicheans celebrated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s death. It has been a subject of much controversy whether Manes was an impostor. The learned Dr. Lardner has examined the arguments on both sides; and though he does not choose to deny that he was an impostor, he does not discover evident proofs of it. He acknowledges, that he was an arrogant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> schemer; but whether he was an impostor, he cannot certainly say. He was too fond of philosophical notions, which he endeavoured to bring into <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, for which he is to be blamed; nevertheless, he observes, that every bold dogmatizer is not an impostor. The doctrine of Manes was a motley mixture of the tenets of Christianity with the ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> of the Persians, in which he had been instructed during his youth. He combined these two systems, and applied and accommodated to Jesus Christ the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> and actions which the Persians attributed to the god <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MITHRAS">Mithras</a>. He established two principles, viz. a good and an evil one: the first a most pure and subtle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, which he called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, did nothing but good; and the Manicheans, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> and corrupt substance, which he called darkness, nothing but evil. This philosophy is very ancient; and Plutarch treats of it at large in his Isis and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>. Manes borrowed many things from the ancient Gnostics; on which account many authors consider the Manicheans as a branch of the Gnostics. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, the Manichean doctrine was a system of philosophy rather than of religion. They made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of amulets, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASILIDIANS">Basilidians</a>; and are said to have made profession of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> and astrology. They denied that Jesus Christ, who was only God, assumed a true <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body, and maintained it was only imaginary; and therefore they denied his incarnation, death, &c. They pretended that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of Moses did not come from God, or the good principle, but from the evil one; and that for this reason it was abrogated. They rejected almost all the sacred books in which Christians look for the sublime truths of their holy religion. They affirmed, that the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> was not the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of God, but of the prince of darkness, who was substituted by the Jews in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the true God. They abstained entirely from eating the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of any animal; following herein the doctrine of the ancient Pythagoreans; they also condemned <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. The rest of their errors may be seen in St. Epiphanius and St. Augustine; which last, having been of their feet, may be presumed to have been thoroughly acquainted with them. Though the Manichees professed to receive the books of the New Testament, yet in effect they only took so much of them as suited with their own opinions. They first formed to themselves a certain idea or scheme of Christianity; and to this adjusted the writings of the apostles, pretending that whatever was inconsistent with this had been foisted into the New Testament by later writers, who were half Jews. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, they made fables and apocryphal books <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for apostolical writings; and even are suspected to have forged several others, the better to maintain their errors. St. Epiphanius gives a catalogue of several pieces published by Manes, and adds extracts out of some of them. These are the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">Mysteries</a>, Chapters, Gospel, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">Treasury</a>. The rule of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and manners which Manes prescribed to his followers was most extravagantly rigorous and severe. However, he divided his disciples into two classes; one of which comprehended the perfect Christians, under the name of the elect; and the other the imperfect and feeble, under the title of auditors or hearers. The elect were obliged to a rigorous and entire <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> from flesh, eggs, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, fish, wine, all intoxicating drink, wedlock, and all amorous gratifications; and to live in a state of the severest penury, nourishing their emaciated bodies with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, herbs, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, and melons, and depriving themselves of all the comforts that arise from the moderate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> passions, and also from a variety of innocent and agreeable pursuits. The auditors were allowed to possess houses, lands, and wealth, to feed on flesh, to enter into the bonds of conjugal tenderness; but this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> was granted them with many limitations, and under the strictest conditions of moderation and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>. The general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the Manicheans was headed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, president, who represented Jesus Christ. There were joined to him 12 rulers or matters, who were deigned to represent the 12 apostles, and these were followed by 72 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, the images of the 72 disciples of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>. These bishops had prebendaries or deacons under them, and all the members of these <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> orders were chosen out of the class of the elect. Their worship was simple and plain; and consisted of prayers, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> the scriptures, and hearing public discourses, at which both the auditors and elect were allowed to be present. They also observed the Christian appointment of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> and the eucharist. They kept the Lord's day, observing it as a fast; and they likewise kept Easter and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENTECOST">Pentecost</a>. Towards the 4th century, the Manicheans concealed themselves under various names, which they successively adopted, and changed in proportion as they were discovered by them. Thus they assumed the names of Encratites, Apocatastas, Saccophori, Hydroparastates, Solitaries, and several others, under which they lay concealed for a certain <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, but could not however <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> escape the vigilance of their enemies. About the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the 6th century, this sect gained a very considerable influence, particularly among the Persians. Toward the middle of the 12th century, the sect of Manicheans took a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>, on occasion of one Constantine, an Armenian, and an adherer to it; who took upon him to suppress the reading of all other books besides the Evangelists and the Epistles of St Paul, which he explained in such a manner as to make them contain a new system of Manicheism. He entirely discarded all the writings of his predecessors; rejecting the chimeras of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALENTINIANS">Valentinians</a>, and their 30 aeons; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of Manes, with regard to the origin of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a>; but still retained the impurities of Bahaïdes. In this manner he reformed Manicheism, in such a manner that his followers made no scruple of anathematizing Scythian, Buddhas, called also Aedas and Terebinth, the contemporaries and disciples, as some say, and, according to others, the predecessors and masters of Manes, and even Manes himself; Constantine being now their great apostle. After he had seduced an infinite number of people, he was at last stoned by order of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>. This sect prevailed in Bosnia and the adjacent provinces about the close of the 15th century; propagated their doctrines with confidence, and held their religious assemblies with impunity.

MANICORDON

Pages 194-194
or MANICHORD, a musical instrument in form of a spinet; the strings of which, like those of the clavichord, are covered with little pieces of cloth, to deaden as well as to soften their sound, whence it is also called the dumb spinet. MANIFESTO; a public declaration made by a prince in writing, showing his intentions to begin a war or other enterprise, with the motives that induce him to it, and the reasons on which he founds his rights and pretensions.

MANILLA

Pages 194-195

LUZONIA, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Luzon, the name of the largest of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIPPINE_ISLANDS">Philippine <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the East Indies, subject to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. It had the name of Luzon from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> that prevailed among the natives of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> or bruising their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> in wooden mortars, before they boil or bake it; luzon in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, signifying "a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>." As to situation, it is remarkably happy, lying between the eastern and western continents, and having <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, at the distance of about 65 leagues; the islands of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a> on the north-east, at the distance of about 250 leagues from the nearest of them; the ocean on the east; the other islands on the south; and on the west <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALACCA">Malacca</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATNA">Patna</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBODIA">Cambodia</a>, Cochin-China, and other provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, the nearest at the distance of 320 leagues. The middle of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> is in latitude 15° north; the east point in 13° 38', and the most northern point in 19°. The shape of it is said to resemble that of an arm bent; the whole length being about 160 Spanish leagues, the greatest breadth between 30 and 40, and the circumference about 350. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTS">charts</a> differ, some making the middle of the island to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> 113° east from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and others 106°. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is hot and moist. One thing is held very extraordinary, that in stormy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> there is much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, and that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> is seldom heard till this is over. During the months of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, August, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of September, the west and south winds blow, which they call vendavals, bringing such rains and storms, that the fields are all overflowed, and they are forced to have little boats to go from one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to another. From October till the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, the north <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> prevails; and from that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> till May, the east and south-east; which winds are there called breezes. Thus there are two seasons in those seas, by the Portuguese called monzeens; whence our word monsoons, that is, the breezes half the year, with a serene dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>; and the vendavals the other half, wet and stormy. It is further to be observed, that in this climate no vermine breed upon Europeans, though they wear dirty shirts, whereas it is otherwise with the Indians. The days here being always of an equal length, and the weather never <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, neither their clothes, nor the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of dining, supping, doing business, studying, or praying, are ever changed; nor is cloth worn, but only against the rain. The air here being, as has been observed, very hot and moist, is not wholesome, but is worse for young men that come from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> than for the old. As for the natives, without using many precautions, they live very <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> to fourscore or 100. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is so rich, that rice grows even on the tops of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> without being watered; and this makes it so plentiful, that the Indians value <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> so little as not to pick it up, though it lies almost everywhere under their feet.
