Among the disadvantages of the island, besides frequent and terrible earthquakes, here are several <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> mountains. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the island, however, is far from being disfigured by them, or by the consequences of their explosions. The mountaineers, called Tingiani, have no particular place of abode, but always live under the shelter of trees, which serve them instead of houses, and furnish them with food; and when the fruit is eaten up, they remove where there is a fresh <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>. Here are 40 different sorts of palm-trees, the most excellent cocoas, wild <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>, wild nutmegs, and some say wild cloves also; ebony; <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANDAL">sandal</a> wood; the best. best cassia, and in such plenty, that they feed their hogs with its fruit; all kinds of cattle, and prodigious quantities of gold, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBERGRIS">ambergris</a>. There are several sorts of people in this island besides the Spaniards, as the Tagalians or Tagaleze, the Pintadores or painted <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>, the Ilayas or Tinglianos, and the Negrellos. The Tagalians, who are thought to be Malayans by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, are a modest, tractable, and well-disposed people. The Pintadores, or painted negroes, are tall, straight, strong, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, and of an excellent disposition. The Tinglianos, whom some suppose to be descended from the Japanese, are very brave, yet very courteous and humane. They live entirely on the gifts of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; and never <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> under any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> than that of the trees or a cave. The Negrellos, who are held to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABORIGINES">aborigines</a> of the island, are barbarous and brutal to the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. When they kill a Spaniard, they make a cup of his skull, and drink out of it. This island is divided into several provinces, containing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of which are Manilla, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CACERES">Caceres</a>, New Segovia, Bondo, Palacca, Ibalon, Bulaw, Serfocon or Bagatoo, Lampoon, Fernandina, Bolinao, Playahonda, <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol6.html#article-CAVITE">Cavite</a>, Mindora, Caleyea, and Bayan. Manilla, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of an island of the same name in the East Indies, on the south-east side of the island, where a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> river falls into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and forms a noble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> 30 leagues in compass, to which the Spaniards have given the name of Bahia, because the river runs out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> lake Bahi, which lies at the distance of six leagues behind it. In compass it is two miles, in length one-third of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a>; the shape <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, being narrow at both ends, and wide in the middle. On the south it is washed by the sea, and on the north and east by the river; being also strongly fortified with walls, battions, forts, and batteries.—Manilla contains about 30,000 souls, who are a very motley <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, distinguished by several strange names, and produced by the conjunction of Spaniards, Chinese, Malabars, Blacks, and others inhabiting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> and islands depending on it. Without the walls are large suburbs, particularly that inhabited by the Chinese <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, called Sangleyes. In proportion to the size of the place, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of churches and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses is very great. Only small vessels can come up to Manilla; but three leagues south of it is the town and port of Cavite, defended by the castle of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, and capable of receiving the largest ships. Here stands the arsenal where the galleons are built, for which there are from 300 to 600 or 800 men constantly employed, who are relieved every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, and while upon duty are maintained at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s expense. By an earthquake which happened here in 1645, a third part of the city of Manilla was destroyed, and no less than 3000 people perished in the ruins. Spain having entered into engagements with France, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the family-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURBON">Bourbon</a>, it was found expedient by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> to declare <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> also against Spain. Whereupon a force was sent out from our East India settlements, particularly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MADRAS">Madras</a>, for the conquest of the Philippine islands, under General Draper and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Cornish; who, after a siege of 12 days, took Manilla on the 6th of October 1762 by storm; but to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> so fine a city from destruction, agreed to accept a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a>, amounting to a million <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>, a part of which, it is said, was never paid. The Spanish viceroy resides in this city, and lives like a sovereign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> is said to be one of the best in the gift of the king of Spain. When the city was taken, as above, the archbishop, who is a kind of pope in this part of the world, was also viceroy. Five large ships, loaded with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of the East, as diamonds from Golconda, cinnamon from Ceylon, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>, cloves and nutmegs from the Moluccas and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BANDA_ISLANDS">Banda islands</a>, camphire from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORNEO">Borneo</a>, benjamin and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> from Cambodia, silks, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a>, and china-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a> from China, &c., sail yearly from hence to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACAPULCO">Acapulco</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, and return freighted with silver, making 400 per cent. profit. The city of Manilla is governed by two alcaldes; the rest of the cities and great towns have each an alcalde; and in every village there is a corregidor. Appeals from their sentences are made to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> at Manilla, in which there are four judges, and a fiscal or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTORNEY_GENERAL">attorney-general</a>; each of these judges has a salary of 3300 pieces of eight per annum. The viceroy is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>; and in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> has an income of 4000 pieces of eight, but he has no vote; yet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the judges are equally divided, the president names a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, who, in virtue of his appointment, has a decisive vote. The attorney-general, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of his office, is protector of the Chinese, in consideration of which he receives 600 pieces of eight every year. As for the Indians that are in subjection, they pay tribute in the following proportions: Young men from 18, and from thence, if they continue single, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 60, pay five rials of plate by way of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>; as single women likewise do from 24 to 50; married men pay ten rials. It is computed that there are within the compass of this government 250,000 Indians subject to his Catholic majesty, of whom two-fifths hold immediately from the king, and the rest from lords or proprietors, who pay two rials each for maintenance of the forces, and the like sum for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>. The royal revenue is computed at about half a million of pieces of eight, exclusive of casualties. In regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> establishment, the garrison of Manilla consists of about 800 or 1000 men, and there are about 3000 more in the Philippines. The viceroy is by his office <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>-general, with a salary of about 4000 pieces of eight. Manilius, Marcus, a Latin poet, whose poem had the ill luck to lie buried in some German <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>, and was not heard of in the world, until Poggius, about two centuries ago, published him from some old <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> he found there. There is no account to be found of him but what can be drawn from his poem, which is called Astronomicon; and contains a system of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> and astrology, together with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> of the Stoics. It consists of five books; though there was a sixth, which has not been recovered. From the style, and no mention of the author being found in ancient writers, it is probable he died young. It is collected, however, that he was a Roman of illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>, and lived under the reign of Augustus, whom he invokes, though not by name, yet by circumstances and character that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> no other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>.

MANILLES

Pages 195-196

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> brafs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> in the form of a bracelet, either plain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> engraven, flat or round. Manilles are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> commodities which the Europeans carry to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> with the natives for slaves. These people wear them as ornaments on the small of the leg, and on the thick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the arm above the elbow. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men wear manilles of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver; but these are made in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> by the natives themselves.

MANIPULUS

Pages 196-196

MANIPULE, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, was a little body of infantry, which in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> consisted of 100 men; and in the time of the consuls, and first Caesars, of 200.

MANIS

Pages 196-196

the SCALY LIZARD, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> belonging to the order of bruta. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">MAMMALIA</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MANLEY

Pages 196-196

Mrs., the celebrated writer of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIS">Atlantis</a>, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sir Roger Manley, the reputed author of the first volume of the Turkilh S. y. She lost her parents very early; and after having been deluded into a false <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> by her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a>, who was her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a>, and afterwards deserted her, she was patronized by the duchess of Cleveland, mistress of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. But the duchess, being a woman of a very fickle temper, grew tired of Mrs Manley in six months <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and discharged her upon a pretence, whether groundless <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not is uncertain, that the intrigued with her son. After this she wrote her first tragedy, called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Mischief, which was acted with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause in 1696; and her apartment being frequented by men of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and gaiety, she soon engaged in amours, and was taken into keeping. Her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> now grew as licentious as her conduct: for, in her retired hours, she wrote four volumes, called <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the New Atlantis; in which she was not only very free in her wanton tales of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> adventures, but satirized the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of many distinguished personages, especially those who had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> concern in the Revolution. A prosecution was commenced against her for this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; but whether those in power were ashamed to bring a woman to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> for a few amorous trifles; or whether the laws could not reach her disfigured <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, she was discharged; and a total change of the ministry ensuing, Mrs Manley lived in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> reputation and gaiety, amusing herself with the conversation of wits, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> plays, poems, and letters. She died in 1724.

MANLIUS CAPITOLINUS

Pages 196-196

the renowned Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> and general, who saved the capitol when it was attacked by the Gauls in the night: he was alarmed by the cries of geese, which were ever after held sacred. But being afterwards accused of aspiring at the sovereignty, he was thrown from the Tarpeian rock. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">GAUL</a> and ROME. MANLIUS Torquatus, a celebrated consul and Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>; had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, but a difficulty in expressing himself, which induced Manlius Imperiosus, his father, to keep him almost by force in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Pompey, tribune of the people, enraged at this instance of severity, formed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of accusing Manlius the father before the judges; but Torquatus being informed of it, went to that tribune, and, with a poniard in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, made him swear, that he would not proceed in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> against him to whom he owed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. At length Torquatus was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> tribune, and killed a soldier of the Gauls in single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, from whom he took a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> chain that he wore about his neck. From this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> he obtained the name of Torquatus. He was consul in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against the Latins; when he ordered his own son to be beheaded for fighting contrary to his orders, though he had gained the victory. He conquered the enemies of the republic, and was several times made consul; but at last refused the consulship, saying, That it was no more possible for him to bear with the vices of the people, than it was for the people to bear with his severity.

MANNA

Pages 196-197

in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, the juice of certain Manna, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAIN">tain</a> trees of the ath kind, either naturally concreted on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> exsiccated and purified by art. See Materia Medica <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Manna, is also a Scripture <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, signifying a miraculous kind of food which fell from heaven for the support of the Israelites in their passage through the wilderness, being in form of coriander seeds, its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> like that of beldiium, and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. The Scripture gives to manna the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> of heaven, and the food of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>, Psalm lxxviii. 25; whether it would intimate to us, that the angels sent and prepared this food, or that angels themselves, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had need of any food, could not have any that was more agreeable than manna was. The author of the Book of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">Wisdom</a> says, xvi. 20, 21, that manna so accommodated itself to every one's taste, that every one found it pleasing to him; and that it included everything that was agreeable to the palate and fit for good nourishment; which expressions some have taken in the literal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, though others understand them figuratively. The critics are divided about the original of the word manna. Some think that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is put instead of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> word mah, which signifies "What is this?" and that the Hebrews, then first seeing that new food which God had sent them, cried to one another, man-hu, instead of mah-hu, "What is this?" Others maintain, that the Hebrews very well knew before what manna was; and that, seeing it in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance about their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, they said one to another, Man-hu, "This is manna." Mr Saumaise and some other moderns are of this last <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. They imagine, that the manna which God sent the Israelites was nothing else but that fat and thick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a> which still falls in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, which presently condensed, and served for food to the people; that this is the same thing as the wild honey, mentioned Matth. iii. 4, wherewith John the Baptist was fed; and that the miracle of Moses did not consist in the production of any new substance, but in the exact and uniform manner in which the manna was dispensed by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> for the maintenance of such a great multitude. On the contrary, the Hebrews and Orientals believe, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the manna was wholly miraculous. The Arabians call it the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-plums of the Almighty; and the Jews are so jealous of this miracle, that they pronounce a curse against all such as presume to deny the interposition of a miraculous power. Our translation, and some others, make Moses fall into a plain <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> in relating this story of the manna, which they render thus: "And when the children of Israel <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> it, they said one to another, It is manna; for they wist not what it was." Exodus xvi. 15. Whereas the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a>, and several authors both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, have translated the text according to the original, "The Israelites seeing this, said one to another, What is this? for they knew not what it was." For we must observe, that the word by which they asked, what is this? was in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> man, which signifies likewise meat readily provided; and therefore it was always afterwards called man or manna. Whether this manna had those extraordinary qualities in it or not, which some imagine, it must be allowed to be truly miraculous, upon the following accounts. 1. That it fell but six days in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>. 2. That it fell in such a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, as it alarmed almost three millions of souls. 3. That there fell a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> quantity every Friday, to serve them for the next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, which was their Sabbath. 4. That what was gathered on the first five days (thouk and bred <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>) kept above one day; but that which was gathered on Friday kept sweet for two days. And, lastly, That it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> falling while the Israelites abode in the wilderness, but ceased as soon as they came out of it and had got corn to eat in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a>. Manna-Tree, is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the ash, and a native of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. See Fraxinus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index, and Materia Medica Index.

MANNER

Pages 197-197

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, a habitude that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> acquires in the three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> parts of painting, the management of colours, lights, and shadows; which is either good <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bad according as the painter has practised more or less after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, with judgement and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. But the best painter is he who has no manner at all. The good or bad choice he makes is called goote.

MANNERS

Pages 197-199

the plural noun, has various significations; as the general way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, the morals, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the habits, of any person or people; also ceremonious behaviour, or studied civility. See the next article. Good Manners, according to Swift, is the art of making those people easy with whom we <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a>. Whoever makes the fewest persons uneasy, is the best bred in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. As the best <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> is founded upon reason, so are the best manners. And as some lawyers have introduced unreasonable things into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law; so likewise many teachers have introduced absurd things into common good manners. One <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> point of this art is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> our behaviour to the three several degrees of men; our superiors, our equals, and those below us. For instance, to press either of the two former to eat or drink is a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of manners; but a tradesman or a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> must be thus treated, or else it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be difficult to persuade them that they are welcome. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">Pride</a>, ill <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, are the three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> sources of ill manners; without some one of these defects, no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> will behave himself ill for want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>; or of what, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of fools, is called knowing the world. "I defy (proceeds our author), any one to assign an incident wherein reason will not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> us what we are to say or do in company, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we are not misled by pride or ill nature. Therefore, I insist that good sense is the principal foundation of good manners; but because the former is a gift which very few among mankind are possessed of, therefore all the civilized nations of the world have agreed upon fixing some rules for common behaviour, best suited to their general customs, or fancies, as a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> good sense to supply the defects of reason. Without which, the gentlemanly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of dunces would be perpetually at cuffs, as they seldom fail when they happen to be drunk, or engaged in squabbles about women or play. And, God be thanked, there hardly happeneth a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUEL">duel</a> in a year, which may not be imputed to one of those three motives. Upon which account, I should be exceedingly sorry to find the legislature make any new laws again." against the practice of dwelling; because the methods are easy, and many, for a wise man to avoid a quarrel with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, or engage in it with innocence. And I can discover no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> evil, in suffering bullies, sharpers, and rakes, to rid the world of each other by a method of their own, where the law hath not been able to find an expedient. As the common forms of good manners were intended for regulating the conduct of those who have weak understandings; so they have been corrupted by the persons for whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> they were contrived. For these people have fallen into a needless and endless way of multiplying ceremonies, which have been extremely troublesome to those who practise them, and inapposite to every body else; insomuch that wise men are often more uneasy at the over civility of these refiners, than they could possibly be in the conversations of peasants or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>. The importunities of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONIAL">ceremonial</a> behaviour are nowhere better seen than at those tables, where ladies preside who value themselves upon account of their good breeding; where a man must reckon upon passing an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> without doing any one thing he hath a mind to, unless he will be so hardy as to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> through all the settled <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECORUM">decorum</a> of the family. She determines what he loveth best, and how much he shall eat; and if the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> happeneth to be of the same disposition, he proceedeth in the same tyrannical manner to prescribe in the drinking part: at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> you are under the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of answering a thousand apologies for your entertainment. And although a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of this humour is pretty well worn off among many people of the best fashion, yet too much of it still remaineth, especially in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; where an honest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> assured me, that having been kept four days against his will at a friend's house, with all the circumstances of hiding his boots, locking up the stable, and other contrivances of the like nature, he could not remember, from the moment he came into the house to the moment he left it, any one thing wherein his inclination was not directly contradicted; as if the whole family had entered into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> to torment him. But, besides all this, it would be endless to recount the many foolish and ridiculous accidents I have observed among these unfortunate protelytes to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>. I have seen a duchess fairly knocked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by the precipitancy of an officious coxcomb running to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> her the trouble of opening a door. I remember, upon a birthday at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, a great lady was rendered utterly disconsolate, by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISH">dish</a> of sauce let <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> by a page directly upon her head-dress and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROCADE">brocade</a>, while she gave a sudden turn to her elbow upon some point of ceremony with the person who sat next her. Monsieur Buys, the Dutch envoy, whose politics and manners were much of a size, brought a son with him about 13 years old to a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> at court. The boy and his father, whatever they put on their plates, they first offered round in order, to every person in the company; so that we could not get a minute's quiet during the whole dinner. At last their two plates happened to encounter, and with so much violence, that being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">china</a>, they broke in twenty pieces, and stained half the company with wet sweetmeats and cream. There is a pedantry in manners as in all arts and sciences, and sometimes in trades. Pedantry is properly the overrating any kind of knowledge we pretend to. And if that kind of knowledge be a trifle in itself, the pedantry is the greater. For which reason I look upon fiddlers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>-masters, heralds, masters of the ceremony, &c., to be greater pedants than Lipsius, or the elder Scaliger. With these kind of pedants, the court, while I knew it, was always plentifully stocked: I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> from the gentleman-usher (at least) inclusive, downward to the gentleman-porter; who are, generally speaking, the most insignificant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of people that this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> can afford, and with the smallest tincture of good manners, which is the only trade they profess. For being wholly illiterate, conversing chiefly with each other, they reduce the whole system of breeding within the forms and circles of their several offices: and as they are below the notice of ministers, they live and die in court under all revolutions, with great obsequiousness to those who are in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> or favour, and with rudeness and insolence to every body else. From whence I have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> concluded, that good manners are not a plant of the court growth; for if they were, those people who have understandings directly of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> for such acquirements, and who have served such long apprenticeships to nothing else, would certainly have picked them up. For as to the great officers who attend the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>'s person or councils, or preside in his family, they are a transient body, who have no better a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to good manners than their neighbours, nor will probably have recourse to gentlemen-ushers for instruction. So that I know little to be learned at court on this head, except in the material circumstance of dress; wherein the authority of the maids of honour must indeed be allowed to be almost equal to that of a favourite's. I remember a passage my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Bolingbroke told me: That going to receive Prince Eugene of Savoy at his landing, in order to conduct him immediately to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, the prince said he was much concerned that he could not see her majesty that night; for Monsieur Hoffman (who was then by) had assured his highness, that he could not be admitted into her presence with a tied-up periwig; that his equipage was not arrived; and that he had endeavoured in vain to borrow a long one among all his valets and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a>. My lord turned the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to a jest, and brought the prince to her majesty: for which he was highly censured by the whole tribe of gentlemen ushers; among whom Monsieur Hoffman, an old dull resident of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s, had picked up this material point of ceremony; and which, I believe, was the best lesson he had learned in 25 years residence. I make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between good manners and good breeding; although, in order to vary my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, I am sometimes forced to confound them. By the first, I only understand the art of remembering, and applying, certain settled forms of general behaviour. But good breeding is of a much larger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>: for besides an uncommon degree of literature sufficient to qualify a gentleman for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> a play, or a political pamphlet, it taketh in a great compass of knowledge; no less than that of dancing, fighting, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a>, making the circle of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, riding the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and speaking French; not to mention some other secondary or subaltern accomplishments, which are more easily Manners, fily acquired. So that the difference between good breeding and good manners lieth in this, That the former cannot be attained by the best understandings without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> and labour; whereas a tolerable degree of reason will instruct us in every part of good manners without other affluence. "I can think of nothing more useful upon this subject, than to point out some particulars wherein the very essentials of good manners are concerned, the neglect or perverting of which doth very much disturb the good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of the world, by introducing a traffic of a mutual uneasiness in most companies. "First, A necessary part of good manners is a punctual observance of time at our own dwellings or those of others, or at third places; whether upon matters of civility, business, or diversion; which rule, though it be a plain dictate of common reason, yet the greatest minister I ever knew, was the greatest trespasser against it; by which all his business doubled upon him, and placed him in a continual arrear. Upon which I often used to rally him as deficient in point of good manners. I have known more than one <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>, and secretary of state, with a very moderate portion of intellects, execute their offices with great success and applause, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> force of exactness and regularity. If you duly observe time for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of another, it doubles the obligation; if upon your own account, it would be manifest folly, as well as ingratitude, to neglect it; if both are concerned, to make your equal or inferior attend on you to his own disadvantage, is pride and injustice. "<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">Ignorance</a> of forms cannot properly be styled ill manners: because forms are subject to frequent changes; and consequently, being not founded upon reason, are beneath a wife man's regard. Besides, they vary in every country; and after a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of time vary frequently in the same: so that a man who travelleth must needs be at first a stranger to them in every court through which he passeth; and, perhaps, at his return, as much a stranger in his own; and, after all, they are easier to be remembered or forgotten than faces or names. "Indeed, among the many imperfections that superficial young men bring with them from abroad, this bigotry of forms is one of the principal, and more predominant than the rest: who look upon them not only as if they were matters capable of admitting of choice, but even as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of importance; and therefore are zealous upon all occasions to introduce and propagate the new forms and fashions they have brought back with them: so that, usefully speaking, the worst bred person in the company is a young traveller <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> arrived from abroad."

MANNORY

Pages 199-199
Lewis, advocate of the parliament of Paris, where he was born in 1696, and died in 1777. From him we have 18 vols. 12mo of Pleadings and Memoirs. A great number of singular cases occur in this collection, and the author has the talent of rendering them more striking by the agreeable manner in which they are stated. He was Tronvill's counsel in his process against Voltaire, and was very satirical against that poet. The latter took revenge by describing him as a mercenary babblet, who sold his pen and his abuse to the highest bidder. Whatever may be the case, Mannory would certainly have been more esteem- ed, both as an advocate and as a writer, if he had paid more attention to his style, and had been less prolix; if he had thought more deeply, and been more sparing of his pleasantness in cases where nothing was required but knowledge and sound reasoning. He published also a translation into French of Father Paree's funeral Oration on Louis XIV. and very judicious Observations on the Semiramis of Voltaire.

MANOEUVRE

Pages 199-199

in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, consists solely in distributing equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> to every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a body of troops, to enable the whole to form, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> change their position, in the most expeditious and best method, to answer the purposes required of a battalion, brigade, or line of cavalry, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, or infantry. It has always been lamented, that men have been brought on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> without being informed of the uses of the different manoeuvres they have been practising; and, having no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of anything but the uniformity of the parade, instantly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into disorder and confusion when they lose the step, or see a deviation from the straight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> they have been accustomed to at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>. It is a pity to see so much <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> given to show, and so little to instruct the troops in what may be of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to them in real service. No manoeuvre should be executed in presence of the enemy, unless protected by some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the troops.

MANOMETER

Pages 200-200

for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>. This is a small glass tube about two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, hermetically sealed at one end, and open at the other, being divided regularly into inches and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. It is used for ascertaining the rarefaction of the air produced by working an air pump. The tube previously filled with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, is placed in the receiver of an air pump. As the piston is worked, the mercury gradually sinks in the tube, and the expansion is estimated by its height; for the smaller the height at which the mercury in the tube stands above the mercury in the basin, the greater is the expansion.

MANOR

Pages 200-201

MANERIUM (à manere), because the usual residence of the owner), seems to have been a district of ground held by lords <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> personages; who kept in their own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> so much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> as was necessary for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of their families, which were called terrae dominicales, or demesne lands; being occupied by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, as dominus manerii, and his servants. The other, or tenemental lands, they distributed among their tenants; which, from the different modes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a>, were called and distinguished by two different names.—First, book-land, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> land, which was held by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> under certain rents and free services, and in effect differed nothing from free socage lands: and from hence have arisen most of the freehold tenants who hold of particular manors, and owe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the same. The other <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> was called folk-land, which was held by no assurance in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, but distributed among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> folk or people at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of the lord, and refused at his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>; being indeed land held in villenage. See VILLENAGE. The residue of the manor, being uncultivated, was termed the lord's waste, and served for public <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, and for common of pasture to the lord and his tenants. Manors were formerly called baronies, as they still are lordships; and each lord or baron was empowered to hold a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, called the court baron, for redressing misdemeanors and nuisances within the manor, and for settling disputes of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> among the tenants. This court is an inseparable ingredient of every manor; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of suitors should fail, as not to leave sufficient to make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a> or homage, that is, two tenants at the least, the manor itself is lost. In the early times of our legal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s greater barons, who had a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of territory held under the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, granted out frequently smaller manors to inferior persons to be held of themselves; which do therefore now continue to be held under a superior lord, who is called in such <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the lord paramount over all the manors; and his feignory is frequently termed an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, not a manor; especially if it hath belonged to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> feudal baron, or hath been at any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the hands of the crown. In <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> whereof, these inferior lords began to carve out and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> to others still more minute estates to be held as of themselves, and were so proceeding downwards in infinitum, till the superior lords observed, that, by this method of subinfeudation, they lost all their feudal profits of wardships, marriages, and elcheats, Mans cheats, which fell into the hands of these mesne or middle lords, who were the immediate superiors of the terre tenant, or him who occupied the land; and also that the mesne lords themselves were so impoverished thereby, that they were disabled from performing their services to their own superiors. This occasioned, first, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> in the 33rd <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNA_CHARTA">magna <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTA">charta</a>, 9 Hen. III. (which is not to be found in the first chapter granted by that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, nor in the great charter of King John), that no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> should either give or sell his land without reserving sufficient to answer the demands of his lord; and, afterwards, the statute of Westm. 3. or quia emptores, 18 Edw. I. c. 1, which directs, that, upon all sales, or encroachments of land, the feoffee shall hold the same, not of his immediate seofor, but of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> lord of the fee, of whom such seofor himself held it. But these provisions not extending to the king's own tenants in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPITE">capite</a>, the like <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> concerning them is declared by the statutes of prerogativa regis, 17 Edward II. c. 6. and of 34 Edw. III. c. 15, by which last all subinfeudations, previous to the reign of King Edward I. were confirmed; but all subsequent to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> were left open to the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>. And from hence it is clear, that all manors existing at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, must have existed as early as King Edward the First: for it is essential to a manor, that there be tenants who hold of the lord; and, by the operation of these statutes, no tenant in capite since the accession of that prince, and no tenant of a common lord since the statute of quia emptores, could create any new tenant to hold of himself. See VILLENAGE.

MANSE

Pages 201-201

Mansus, Manfa, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Manfum; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>-books, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, or habitation, either with or without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>. See HOUSE and MANSION. The word is formed à manendo, "abiding;" as being the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of dwelling or residence. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">Capital</a> Manses, (Manfum Capitale), denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>-house, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">MANOR</a>. Mansus Presbyteri, is a parsonage or vicarage house for the incumbent to reside in. This was originally, and still remains, an essential <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the endowment of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, together with the glebe and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a>. It is sometimes called Presbyterium. See PRESBYTERY.

MANSFELD

Pages 201-202

Ernst de, the illegitimate son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Ernest by a lady of Malines, was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>, in the principles of the Roman Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, by his godfather Ernest archduke of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. He was employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> in the Low Countries, and in that of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, together with his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Mansfeld. He was legitimated on account of his bravery by the emperor Rudolphus II.; but his father's plots and possessions in the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a> having been refused him, contrary to promises which he had received, he, in 1610, joined the party of the Protestant princes. Being now become one of the most dangerous enemies of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Austria, who called him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTILA">Attila</a> of Christianity, he let himself, in 1618, at the head of the rebels in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, and got possession of Pilsen in 1619. Though his troops were defeated in several battles, he was able to penetrate into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a>. He there took several places, ravaged <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALSACE">Alsace</a>, made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Haguenau, and defeated the Bavarians. At length he was totally defeated by Wallstein, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Dalsou, which happened in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of April 1626. He gave over his remaining troops to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WEIMAR">Weimar</a>, and intended to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> into the Venetian states; but fell sick in a village between Zerz and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPALATRO">Spalatro</a>, and there expired, A.D. 1626, aged 46. The procurator Nani thus describes him: "He was bold, intrepid in danger, and the most skilful negotiator of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which he lived. He possessed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> eloquence, and well knew how to infuse himself into the hearts of those whom he wished to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a>. He was greedy of others' wealth, and prodigal of his own.—He was full of vast projects and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> hopes, and yet possessed neither lands nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>." He did not wish to die in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>; but dressed himself in his finest robes, put on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, sat up, leaning upon two domestics, and in this position, highly becoming a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a>, breathed his last. But of all the actions Manfield editors of this great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> and singular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, the following is without doubt the most extraordinary: Having got the most certain information that Cazel, in whom of all his officers he placed the greatest confidence, had communicated his plans to the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, he showed neither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> nor resentment at his treachery, but gave him 300 rix-dollars, and sent him to Count Buquoy, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> expressing in these words: "Cazel being attached to you and not to me, I send him to you, that you may have the benefit of his services." The opinions of men were divided about this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and it was as much censured as applauded. Be this as it may, Ernest is deservedly esteemed one of the greatest generals of his age. There never was a leader more patient, more indefatigable, more inured to toil and hardship, to watchings, to colds and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>. He raised armies, and ravaged the enemy's territories with an incredible celerity. The Hollanders said of him, that he was bonus in auxilio, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARUS">carus</a> in pretio; that is, that he rendered great services to those who employed him, but that he made them pay well for it.

MANSFIELD

Pages 202-202

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAMSHIRE">Nottinghamshire</a>, in England, seated in the forest of Sherwood, 140 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It was anciently a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> demesne. It has a market on Thursdays, and two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>. By an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>, the heirs were declared of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> as soon as born. It is a well-built town, and has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade in malt. Its market is well stocked with corn, cattle, &c. Here is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> school for 36 boys.

MANSIO

Pages 202-202
or Mansus, was sometimes also used in the same sense with hide; that is, for as much land as one plough could till in a year. See HIDE.

MANSION

Pages 202-202

MANSIO, a dwelling <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> habitation, especially in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. See MANSE. MANSION is more particularly used for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> dwelling house within his fee; otherwise called the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> messuage or manse, or chief <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. See MANOR.

MANSLAUGHTER

Pages 202-203

the unlawful killing of another, without malice either express <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> implied: Which may be either voluntary, upon a sudden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>; or involuntarily, but in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of some unlawful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>. These were called, in the Gothic constitutions, homicidia vulgaria; que aut cafu, aut etiam fronte committuntur, sed in jubitanco quodam iracundia calore et impetu. And hence it follows, that in manslaughter there can be no accessories before the fact; because it must be done without premeditation. 1. As to the first, or voluntary branch: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> upon a sudden quarrel two persons fight, and one of them kills the other, this is manslaughter; and so it is, if they upon such an occasion go out and fight in a field; for this is one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> act of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> pays that regard to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> frailty, as not to put a hasty and deliberate act upon the same footing with regard to guilt. So also if a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> be greatly provoked, as by pulling his nose, or other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> indignity, and immediately kills the aggressor; though this is not excusable se defendendo, since there is no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> for doing it to preserve himself; yet neither is it <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, for there is no previous malice; but it is manslaughter. But in this, and in every other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMICIDE">homicide</a> upon provocation; if there be a sufficient cooling-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> for passion to subside and reason to interpose, and the person provoked afterwards kills the other, this is deliberate <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, and not heat of blood; and accordingly amounts to murder. So if a man takes another in the act of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a> with his wife, and kills him directly upon the spot; though this was allowed by the law of Solon, as likewise by the Roman civil law (if the adulterer was found in the husband's own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>), and also among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>; yet in England it is not absolutely ranked in the class of justifiable homicide, as in case of a forcible <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a>, but it is manslaughter. It is, however, the lowest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of it; and therefore in such a case the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> directed the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to be gently inflicted, because there could not be a greater provocation. Manlaughter, therefore, on a sudden provocation, differs from excusable homicide se defendendo in this: That in the one case there is apparent necessity, for self-preservation, to kill the aggressor; in the other no necessity at all, being only a sudden act of revenge. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> branch, or involuntary manslaughter, differs also from homicide excusable by misadventure, in this: That misadventure always happens in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a lawful act, but this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of manslaughter in consequence of an unlawful one. As if two persons play at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> and buckler, unless by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s command, and one of them kills the other; this is manslaughter, because the original act was unlawful; but it is not murder, for the one had no intent to do the other any personal mischief. So where a person does an act, lawful in itself, but in an unlawful manner, and without due caution and circumvention; as when a workman flings <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> into the street, and kills a man; this may be either misadventure, manslaughter, or murder according to the circumstances under which the original act was done. If it were in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> village, where few passengers are, and he calls out to all people to have a care, it is misadventure only: but if it were in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, or other populous <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, where people are continually passing, it is manslaughter, though he gives loud warning; and murder, if he knows of their passing and gives no warning at all, for then it is malice against mankind. And, in general, when an involuntary killing happens in consequence of an unlawful act, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be either murder or manslaughter according to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the act which occasioned it. If it be in prosecution of a felonious intent, or in its consequences naturally tending to bloodshed, it will be murder; but if no more was intended than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> civil trespass, it will only amount to manslaughter. 3. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of this degree of homicide: The crime of manslaughter amounts to felony, but within the benefit of clergy; and the offender shall be burnt in the hand, and forfeit all his goods and chattels. But there is one species of manslaughter, which is punished as murder, the benefit of clergy being taken away from it by statute; namely, the offence of mor- tally stabbing another, though done upon sudden provocation. See STABBING.

MANTA

Pages 203-203

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a>; a flat fish mentioned by Ulloa and others, as exceedingly hurtful to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a>-fishers, and which seems to be the same with that which Pliny has described under the name of nubes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> nebulosa: Ipsa ferunt (Urinatores) et nubem quandom crepitescere super capita, planorum piscium fumissem, promentem eos, ardentemque a reciprocando, et ob filos praecutos lineis annexos habere se; quia nisi perfusae ita, non refedant caliginis et pavoris, ut arbitratur, opere. Nubem enim five nebulam (cuius nomine id malum appellunt) inter anima- tia haud ullam repertit quisquam. (Plin. Hist. lib. ix. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 46.) The account given of this cloud by those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> is much the same with that which the divers in the American seas give of the manta; and the name of the cloud is perfectly applicable to it, as it really seems to be a cloud to those who are in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> below it: the swimmers likewise carry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> knives, or sharp sticks, for the purpose of dispersing this animal. It is not improbable, that this fish has made its way into those seas from those of the old world, in the same manner as some others appear to have done. The strength of this fish is so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, that it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not only strangle a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> whom it embraces or winds itself about, but it has even been seen to take the cable of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> and move it from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it had been <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a>. It has been called manta, because, when it lies stretched upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, as it frequently does, it seems like a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEECE">fleece</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> floating upon the water.

MANTE

Pages 203-203

a considerable town of France, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Mantois, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 45. N. Lat. 48. 58.

MANTEGAR

Pages 203-203
or MAN-TIGER, as it is sometimes written, is the tufted ape, a species of simia. See MAMMALIA Index.

MANTEGNA

Pages 203-203

Andrew, was born in a village near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a> in 1431, and at first employed in keeping sheep. It was observed, that instead of watching over his flock, he amused himself with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>; and he was placed with a painter who, being delighted with his ease and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and with his gentle and agreeable conduct in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, adopted him for his son, and made him his heir. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 17, Mantegna was employed to paint the altar of St Sophia in Padua, and the four evangelists. James Bellini, who admired his talents, gave him his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. Mantegna painted, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, the Triumph of Caesar, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> d'oeuvre of this painter, and has been engraved in claro-obscuro, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> plates. From respect to his extraordinary merit, the duke made him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of his order. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of engraving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> with the graver is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> ascribed to Mantegna, who died at Mantua in 1517.

MANTELETS

Pages 203-203

in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, a kind of moveable parapets, made of planks about three inches thick, nailed one over another, to the height of almost six feet, generally cased with tin, and set upon little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, so that in a siege they may be driven before the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIONEERS">pioneers</a>, and serve as <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol2.html#article-BLINDS">blinds</a> to shelter them from the enemy's small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>.

MANTICHOARA

Pages 203-203

a name given by the Roman authors to a fierce and terrible creature, which they describe from the Greeks, who call it sometimes also mantichora, martichora, and martiora. We have formed the name <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>-tiger on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of the Roman Mantinea name, though expelling a very different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>; and our authors of the histories of animals, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> to us under this name a terrible creature, partly from the accounts of Pliny exaggerated, and partly from their own imagination, with three rows of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and with such a shape as no animal ever possessed. See MANTEGAR.

MANTINEA

Pages 203-203

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town situated in the south of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>, on the confines of Laco- nia (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); called afterwards Antigonea, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Antigonus. It is memorable for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought in its neighbourhood between the Thebans and Spartans, in which fell the celebrated commander Epaminondas. See THEBES.

MANTIS

Pages 203-203

a genus of insects belonging to the order of hemiptera. See ENTOMOLOGY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MANTLE

Pages 203-203
or Mantling, in Heraldry, that appearance of folding of cloth, flourishing, or drapery, which in any achievement is drawn about a coat of arms. See HERALDRY, sect. v.

MANTO

Pages 203-203

in poetical <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Tire- sias, and like her father strongly inspired with prophecy. She was in so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem, that when the Argives pillaged Thebes, they thought they could not acquit their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOW">vow</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, of consecrating to him the most precious thing in their plunder, without offering him this young woman. She was therefore sent to the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>. But this did not engage her in any vow of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINENCE">continence</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it did, she observed it very ill: for she bore a son called Amphilocheus to Alcmeon, who had been <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERALISSIMO">generalissimo</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> which took Thebes; and a daughter to the same, named Tisiphone. These children were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMOUR">amour</a> carried on during the madness which had seized Alcmeon, after he had put his mother to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> transports her into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, nor for the sake of securing her virginity, but to produce a son of her who built <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>.

MANTUA

Pages 203-207

anciently a town of the Transpadana in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, situated on the Mincio, a river running from the Lacus Benacus. It is said to have been founded about 300 years before Rome by Bianor <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Ocnum, the son of Manto; and was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Etruria. When <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREMONA">Cremona</a>, which had followed the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Brutus, was given to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> of Octavius, Mantua also, which was in the neighbourhood, shared the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> calamity, and many of the inhabitants were tyrannically deprived of their possessions. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, who was among them, and a native of the town, applied for redress to Augustus, and obtained it by means of his poetical talents. It is still called MANTUA, and is the capital of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of that name. It is now a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, having eight gates and about 16,000 inhabitants. The streets are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and straight, and the houses well built. It is very strong by situation as well as by art; lying in the middle of a lake, or rather morass, formed by the river Mincio. There is no access to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> but by two causeways which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> this morass, and which are strongly fortified: so that the city is looked upon to be one of the most considerable fortresses of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and the allies in 1745, though their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> was in the duchy, did not undertake the siege. It was greatly noted for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, which are now much decayed. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> is very unwholesome. The celebrated poet Virgil was born at a village near this city. It was besieged by the French for above six months, in 1796, and surrendered to them on February 2d, 1797. On the recommencement of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, it was attacked by the Austrian and Russian army, to which it surrendered on the 30th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, 1799, after a short siege; and finally, not only this city, but the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, was subdued by the arms of Bonaparte, one of whose brothers is now styled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Italy. F. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 10. 47. N. Lat. 45. 10. Mantua, the duchy of, a country of Italy, lying along the river Po, which divides it into two parts. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Veronese; on the south by the duchies of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGGIO">Reggio</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRANDOLA">Mirandola</a>; on the east by the Ferrarese; and on the west by the Cremonese. It is about 50 miles in length, and 25 in breadth; is fruitful in corn, pastures, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and excellent wine. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> IV., the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Mantua, being a vassal of the empire, took <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> with the French in the dispute relating to the succession of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; for which reason he was put under the ban of the empire, and died at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in 1708.
