He having no heirs, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> kept the Mantuan in his own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and the duke of Savoy had Montferrat, which were confirmed to them by subsequent treaties. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the emperor in 1742, his eldest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, now empress <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, kept possession of the Mantuan; and the governor of the Milanese had the administration of affairs. The Mantuan comprehends the duchies of Mantua, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUASTALLA">Guastalla</a>, and Sabbieta; the principalities of Calliglione, Solforino, and Bofolo; likewise the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Novellara. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Po, the Oglio, and the Mincio; and the principal town is Mantua. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUAL">Manual</a>, a word signifying anything performed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Manual (manualis), in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies what is employed or used by the hand, and whereof a present profit may be made; as such a thing in the manual occupation of one, is where it is actually used or employed by him. Manual is the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> book used in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, containing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>, directions to the priests, and prayers used in the administration of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> and other sacraments; the form of blessing holy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and the whole service used in processions. Manual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">Exercise</a>, in the army, consists in the observance of certain words of command appointed for this purpose. When a regiment is drawn up, or paraded for exercise, the men are placed three deep, either by companies, or divided into platoons, with the grenadiers on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>. When soldiers are drawn up for exercise, the ranks and files should be exactly even; and each soldier should be instructed to carry his arms well, to keep his firelock steady and even upon his shoulder, with the right hand hanging <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and the whole body without constraint. The distances between the files must be equal, and the ranks eight feet distant from each other. Every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> should be performed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and the greatest exactness observed in all firings, wheelings, and marching; and therefore a regiment should never be under arms longer than two hours. The following is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of the words of command at the manual exercise, with their explanations: 1. Poise your firelock: i.e. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">Seize</a> the firelock with your right hand, and turn the lock outwards, keeping the firelock perpendicular; then bring up the firelock with a quick motion from the shoulder, and seize it with the left hand, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> above the lock, so that the fingers may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> upon the stock, with the elbows down, and the thumb upon the stock; the firelock must not be held too far from the body, and the left hand must be of an equal height with the eyes. 2. Cock your firelock: i.e. Turn the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> opposite to your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>, and place your thumb upon the cock, raising your elbow <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> at this motion; then cock your firelock, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> your elbow down, placing your right thumb on the breech <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a>, and the fingers under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>. 3. Present: i.e. Step back about six inches to the rear with the right foot, bringing the left toe to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a>; at the same time the butt-end of the firelock must be brought to an equal height with the shoulder, placing the left hand on the swell, and the forefinger of the right hand before the trigger, finking the muzzle a little. 4. Fire: i.e. Pull the trigger briskly, and immediately after, bringing up the right foot to the inside of the left, come to the priming position, with the lock opposite to the right <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, the muzzle to the height of the hat, keeping it firm and steady; and at the same time seize the cock with the forefinger and thumb of the right hand, the back of the hand being turned up. 5. Half-cock your firelock: i.e. Half-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> the cock briskly with a draw-back of the right elbow, bringing it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the butt of the firelock. 6. Handle your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARTRIDGE">cartridge</a>: i.e. Bring your right hand with a short round to your pouch, flapping it hard; seize the cartridge, and bring it with a quick motion to your mouth; bite the top well off, and bring the hand as low as the chin, with the elbow down. 7. Prime: i.e. Shake the powder into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">pan</a>, placing the three last fingers behind the rammer, with the elbow up. 8. Shut your pan: i.e. Shut your pan briskly, drawing your right arm at this motion towards your body, holding the cartridge fast in your hand as before; then turn the piece nimbly round to the loading position, with the lock to the front, and the muzzle to the height of the chin, bringing the right hand behind the muzzle, with both feet kept fast in this motion. 9. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">Charge</a> with cartridge: i.e. Turn up your hand, and put the cartridge into the muzzle, shaking the powder into the barrel; place your hand, clofed, with a quick and strong motion, upon the rammer. 10. Draw your rammer: i.e. Draw the rammer with a quick motion half out, seizing it at the muzzle back-handed; draw it quite out, turn it, and enter it into the muzzle. 11. Ram down your charge: i.e. Ram the cartridge well down in the barrel, instantly recovering and seizing the rammer back-handed at the centre, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> it, and entering it as far as the lower pipe, placing at the same time the edge of the hand on the butt end of the rammer, with fingers extended. 12. Return your rammer: i.e. Return the rammer, bringing up the piece with the left hand to the shoulder, seizing it with the right hand under Manual under the cock, keeping the left hand fast at the swell, turning the body square to the front. 13. Shoulder your firelock: i.e. Quit the left hand, and place it strong upon the butt; quit the right hand, and throw it down the right side. 14. Rest your firelock: i.e. Seize the firelock with the right hand, turning the lock outwards; raise the firelock from the shoulder, and place your left hand with a quick motion above the lock, holding the piece right up and down in both hands before you, and your left hand even with your eyes; step briskly back with your right foot, placing it a hand's breadth distance from your left heel, and at the same time bring down your firelock as quick as possible to the rest, sinking it as far down before your left hand as your right hand <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> permit without constraint; your left hand being at the feather <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, and your right, with fingers extended, held under the guard, taking care to draw in the muzzle well towards your body, and to dress in a line with the butt-end. 15. Order your firelock: i.e. Place your firelock nimbly with your left hand against your right shoulder; quit the firelock with the right hand, sinking it at the same time with your left; seize it at the muzzle, which must be of an equal height with your chin, and hold it close against your right side; lift up your right foot, and place it by your left; at the same time throw back your left hand by your left side; and with your right bring down the butt-end strong upon the ground, placing it even with the toe of your right foot; the thumb of your right hand lying along the barrel, and the muzzle kept at a little distance from your body. 16. Ground your firelock: i.e. Half face to the right upon your heels, and at the same time turn the firelock, so that the lock may point to the rear, and the flat of the butt-end lie against the inside of your foot; at the same time clipping the right foot behind the butt of the firelock; the right toe pointing to the right, and the left to the front: step directly forward with your left foot, about as far as the swell of the firelock, and lay it upon the ground, your left hand hanging down by your left leg, and your right kept fast, with the butt end against it; raise yourself up again nimbly, bringing back your left foot to its former position, keeping your body faced to the right; face again to the left upon your heels, and come to your proper front, letting your hands hang down without motion. 17. Take up your firelock: i.e. Face to the right upon both heels; sink your body down, and come to the position described in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> motion of grounding; raise yourself and firelock, bringing it close to your right side; come to your proper front, seizing your firelock at the muzzle, as in explanation 15. 18. Rest your firelock: i.e. Bring your right hand as far as the swell; raise the firelock <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> up in a perpendicular line from the ground with your right hand, and seize it with your left above the firing, the cock being at the height of the waist-belt; step back with your right foot, placing it behind your left heel, and come to the rest. 19. Shoulder your firelock: i.e. Lift up your right foot, and place it by your left; bring the firelock at the same time to your left shoulder, and seize the butt-end with the left hand, keeping it in the same position as above described; throw your right hand briskly back. 20. Secure your firelock: i.e. Bring the right hand briskly up, and place it under the cock, keeping the firelock steady in the same position; quit the butt with the left hand, and seize the firelock with it at the swell, bringing the elbow close down upon the lock; the right hand being kept fast in this motion, and the piece still upright; quit the right hand, and bring it down your right side, bringing the firelock nimbly down to the secure; the left hand in a line with the waist belt. 21. Shoulder your firelock: i.e. Bring the firelock up to a perpendicular line, seizing it with the right hand under the cock; quit the left hand, and place it strong upon the butt, quit the right hand, and bring it smartly down the right side. 22. Fix your bayonet: i.e. First and second motions, as in the two first of the secure; quit the right hand, and bring the firelock smartly down to the left side with the left hand, as far as it will admit without constraint, seizing the bayonet at the same time with the right hand, and fixing it, placing that hand just below the brafs, with the piece kept close to the hollow of the shoulder. 23. Shoulder your firelock: i.e. Quit the right hand, and bring up the firelock with the left; seize it again under the cock with your right, as in the second motion of the secure; quit the left hand, and place it strong upon the butt; quit the right hand, and bring it down the right side. 24. Present your arms: i.e. as explained in the three motions of the 14th word of command. 25. To the right face: i.e. Bring up the firelock with a quick motion high before you, till your left hand comes even with your eyes, both the fingers of that hand extended along the stock, just above the feather spring; the right foot to be brought close up to the left heel in this motion; face to the right, taking care in facing to hold the firelock right up and down, and steady in your hands; step back with your right foot, and come down to your present, as in the foregoing explanation. 26. To the right face: i.e. as in the foregoing explanation, facing to the right. 27. To the right about face: i.e. as in the 25th explanation, only coming to the right about instead of to the right. 28. To the left face: i.e. Bring the right foot briskly to the hollow of your left, with the firelock in the same position as in the first motion of facing to the right; face to the left; come down to the present, as before. 29. To the left face: i.e. as in the foregoing explanation. 30. To the left about face: i.e. as before, coming to the left about instead of to the left. 31. Shoulder your firelock: i.e. as in the two motions of the 19th explanation. 32. Charge your bayonets: i.e. as in the first explanation: bring the swell of the firelock down strong upon the palm of the hand, grasping the piece at the small, behind the lock, and as high as the waist-belt; the firelock upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the barrel upwards. 33. Shoulder your firelock: i.e. Bring up the firelock to the shoulder, place the left hand upon the butt, bringing the feet square to the front; quit the right hand, and throw it down the right side. 34. Advance your arms: i.e. first and second motions, as in the first explanation; bring the firelock down the right side, with the right hand as low as it will admit without constraint, flipping up the left hand at the same time to the swell, the guard between the thumb and forefinger of the right hand, the three last fingers under the cock, with the barrel to the rear; quit the left hand. 35. Shoulder your firelock: i.e. Bring up the left hand, and fixe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">MAN</a> it at the swell; come smartly up to the poise; shoulder. 36. Prime and load: i.e. Come smartly to the recover, by springing the firelock straight up with the left hand, turning the barrel inwards to the proper height of the recover; at the same time that the left hand <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> the firelock, the right hand is raised briskly from the right side, and seizes the firelock across the breast: as it rises below the cock, the left hand comes with a quick motion from the butt, and seizes the firelock strong above the lock, the little finger of the left hand at the spring of the lock, the left hand at an equal height with the face, the butt close to the body, but not pressed, the firelock, perpendicular opposite the left side of the face: bring the firelock down with a brisk motion to the priming position, the left hand holding the firelock, as in priming; the thumb of the right hand placed against the face of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, the fingers clinched, and the elbow a little turned out, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WRIST">wrist</a> may be clear of the cock; open the pan, by throwing up the steel with a strong motion of the right arm, turning the elbow in, and keeping the firelock steady in the left hand; handle your cartridge, prime, shut your pan, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> about, load, draw rammers, ram down the cartridge, return the rammers, shoulder. N.B. The motion of recover, and coming down to the priming position and opening pans, are to be done in the usual time. The motions of handling cartridge to shutting the pans, are to be done as quick as possible: when the pans are shut, a small pause is to be made, and then cast about together; then the loading motions are to be done as quick as possible; but before the rammer is returned, another small pause is to be made, counting 1, 2, between each motion, till the firelock is shouldered.—Front <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> make ready: i.e. Spring the firelock briskly to the recover, keeping the left foot fast in this motion: as soon as the firelock is at the recover, without any flop, sink the body briskly without slopping forward, with a quick motion down upon the right knee; the butt-end of the firelock at the same time falls upon the ground, the front part of the butt being in a line with the heel of the left foot. As soon as the butt comes to the ground, the firelock is to be cocked, immediately seizing the cock and steel in the right hand; the firelock to be held firm in the left hand, about the middle of that part of the firelock between the lock and the swell of the stock; the point of the left thumb to be close to the swell, pointing upwards. As the body is sinking, the right knee is to be thrown as far back as the left leg may be right up and down; the right foot to be thrown a little to the right; the body to be kept straight; the head up, looking to the right along the rank, the same as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> shouldered; the firelock to be upright; and the butt about four inches to the right of the inside of the left foot. Present: i.e. Bring the firelock briskly down to the present, by extending the left arm to the full length with a strong motion; at the same time spring up the butt by the cock with the right hand, and raise the butt so high upon the right shoulder, that you may not be obliged to stoop too much with the head; the right cheek to be close to the butt, and the left eye shut, and look along the barrel with the right eye from the breech-pin to the muzzle; kept the left elbow down in an easy position, and stand as steady as possible; the thumb of the right hand to remain in the position as described in the third explanation of the manual. Fire: i.e. Pull the trigger as directed in the manual; and as soon as the piece is fired, give yourself a strong spring upon your left leg, raising your body briskly, and straight up, keeping your left foot fast, and bringing the right heel to the inside of the left; at the same time the firelock is to be brought up to the priming position, and half-cocked immediately: a short pause is to be made; then handle cartridge, and go on with the loading motions described in the explanation of prime and load.—Centre rank, make ready: i.e. Spring the firelock briskly to the recover; so soon as the left hand seizes the firelock above the lock, the right elbow is to be nimbly raised a little, placing the thumb of that hand upon the cock; the fingers open by the plate of the lock, and as quick as possible force the piece to the cock, by dropping the elbow, and forcing down the cock with the thumb, stepping at the same time a moderate pace to the right, keeping the left foot fast; as the firelock is cocked, the thumb is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> below the cock, the right hand seizing the firelock close under the cock firmly, the forefinger not to be before the trigger; the piece to be held in this position perpendicular, opposite the left side of the face, the butt close to the left breast, but not pressed; the body to be straight, and as full to the front as possible; the head kept up, looking to the right of the rank, that the body and the firelock may not slope forward, nor lean much out of the rank. Present: i.e. Spring the firelock from the body to the arm's length with a quick motion, pressing down the muzzle with the left hand, and spring up the butt with the right hand, as in the foregoing explanation of the front rank. Fire: As in explanation 4, in the manual, with this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that the left foot is to be brought up to the right, at the same time that the firelock is brought down to the priming position. The loading motions as in the explanations of priming and loading; and at the last motion of shouldering, to spring to the left again, and cover the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILE">file</a>-leader.—Rear rank, make ready: i.e. Recover the firelock, and cock as before directed for the centre rank; as the firelock is recovered and cocked, step briskly straight to the right, with the right foot, a full pace; bring the left heel about six inches before the right foot; the body straight, and as square to the front as possible, as in the explanation of the centre rank. Present: As in explanation present, before. Fire: As in explanation of the centre rank; and as the firelock is coming down to the priming position, the left is to be brought back to the right; and at the last motion of shouldering, to spring to the left again, and cover the file-leader (A). (A) The manual exercise now described is not precisely the same that it is at present (1807). The difference indeed is not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>; but depending partly on the peculiar views of commanding officers, it is subject to change that it would be useless to detail it in its present form. There are some peculiar words of command at the manual exercise of the grenadiers, when apart from the battalion; and also for the cavalry and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>.

MANTULUS

Pages 196-196

among physicians, is used to signify a handful of herbs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> leaves, or so much as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> can grasp in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> at once; which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> is frequently denoted by the abbreviation, M, or m.

MANUDUCTOR

Pages 207-207

a name given to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> officer in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; who, from the middle of the choir, where he was placed, gave the signal for the choristers to sing, and marked the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and regulated the music. The Greeks called him *me-fachoros*, because seated in the middle of the choir; but in the Latin church he was called *manuductor*; from *manus* and *duco*, "I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>;" because he led and guided the choir by the motions and gesticulation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>.

MANUFACTURE

Pages 207-207

a commodity produced from raw <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> materials, either by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> or by machinery.

MANUFACTURER

Pages 207-207

one who works up a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> product into an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> commodity.

MANUMISSION

Pages 207-207

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> whereby a slave <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> villain is set at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, or let out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a>. The word comes from the Latin *manus* "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>," and *mittere*, "to send"; *quaia servus mittatur extra manum seu postglatium domini fuit*. Some authors define manumission an act by which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> enfranchises his tenants, who till that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> had been his vassals, and in a state of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> inconsistent with the sanctity of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, the manumission of slaves was performed three several ways. 1. When, with his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s consent, a slave had his name entered in the census or public <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of the citizens. 2. When the slave was led before the praetor, and that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> laid his wand called *vindicta* on his head. 3. When the master gave the slave his freedom by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a>. Servius Tullius is said to have set on foot the first manner; and P. Valerius Publicola the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. A particular account is given of the third in the Institutes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>. It was not necessary that the praetor should be on his tribunal to perform the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of manumission: he did it anywhere indifferently, in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, in the street, in going to bathe, &c. He laid the rod on the slave's head, pronouncing these words, *Dico eum liberum effe move Quiritum*, "I declare him a freeman, after the manner of the Romans." This done, he gave the rod to the lictor, who struck the slave with it on the head, and afterwards with his hand on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> and back; and the notary or scribe entered the name of the new freedman in the register, with the reasons of his manumission. The slave had likewise his head shaved, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> given him by his master as a token of freedom. Tertullian adds, that he had then also a third name given him: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> this were so, three names were not a token of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, but of freedom. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Constantine ordered the manumissions at Rome to be performed in the churches. Of manumission there have also been various forms in England. In the time of the Conqueror, villains were manumitted, by the master's delivering them by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> hand to the vicount, in full <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, showing them the door, giving them a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCE">lance</a> and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and proclaiming them free. Others were manumitted by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>. There was also an implicit manumission: as when the lord made an obligation for payment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONDMAN">bondman</a> at a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, or sued him where he might enter without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, and the like.

MANURE

Pages 207-207

anything used for fattening and improving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MANUSCRIPT

Pages 207-207

a book <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> written with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; by which it stands opposed to a printed book or paper. A manuscript is usually denoted by the two letters MS. and in the plural by MSS. What makes public <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> valuable, is the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> reposed in them; see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIAN">Alexandrian</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, Clermont, Cottonian, Harleian, Vatican, &c.

MANUTIUS

Pages 207-207

Aldus**, the first of those celebrated Venetian printers who were as illustrious for their learning as for uncommon skill in their profession. He was born at Baffano in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> about the middle of the 15th century; and hence is sometimes called Baffianus, though generally better known by the name of Aldus. He was the first who printed Greek neatly and correctly; and acquired so much reputation by it, that whatever was finely printed was proverbially said to have "come from the press of Aldus." We have a kind of Greek <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> of his; with Notes upon <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, Horace, &c. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, where he exercised his profession, in 1516. **Manutius, Paulus**, son of the former, was brought up to his father's profession. He was more learned than he; and he acquired, by continual <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> of Tully, such a purity in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> Latin, as even Scaliger allows a Roman could not exceed. Pope Pius IV. placed him at the head of the apostolical press, and gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the Vatican library. His Epistles are infinitely laboured, and very correct; but, as may be said of most of the Ciceronians, they contain scarcely any thing but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> words. This constant reading of Tully, however, together with his profound knowledge of antiquity, qualified him extremely well for an editor of Tully; whose works he accordingly published, with Commentaries on them, in 4 vols folio, at Venice in 1523. He died in 1574. **Manutius, Aldus**, the Younger, the son of Paulus, and the grandson of Aldus, was esteemed one of the greatest geniuses and most learned men of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Clement VIII. gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the Vatican <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; but probably the profits of that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> were very small, since Manutius was obliged, for his subsistence, to accept of a professor of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, and to sell the excellent library that was in his family, which his father, his uncle, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>-uncle, had collected with extraordinary care, and which it is said contained 80,000 volumes. He died at Rome in 1597, without any other recompense than the praises due to his merit. He wrote, 1. Commentaries on Cicero. 2. A Treatise on Orthography. 3. Three books of Epistles; and other works in Latin and Italian, which are esteemed.

MAOUNA

Pages 207-208

one of the Navigator's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the south <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific ocean</a>. Here M. de la Perouse, commander of the French ships the Bouffole and Astrolabe, met with his first fatal accident in 1787; M. de Langle, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of the Astrolabe, with 11 officers and sailors, sailors, were massacred by the natives. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 169. S. Lat. 14.19.

MAPPARIUS

Pages 208-208

in Roman antiquity, the officer who gave the signal to the gladiators to begin fighting; which he did by throwing an handkerchief that he had received from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>.

MARACANDA

Pages 208-208

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Sogdiana. Now thought to be <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARCAND">Samarcand</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Ulbec <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAMERLANE">Tamerlane</a>. See Samarcand.

MARACAYBO

Pages 208-208

a lake in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, 200 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 100 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, which discharges itself by a river into the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It is well defended by strong forts; which, however, did not hinder Sir Henry Morgan, a bucanier, from entering it, and plundering several Spanish <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, after defeating a squadron sent out against him.

MARAGNAN

Pages 208-208

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a> in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, which comprehends a fertile populous <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, 112 miles in circumference. The French settled here in 1612, and built a town; but they were soon driven from thence by the Portuguese, who have possessed it ever since. The town is little, but strong; and has a cattle, a harbour, and a bishop's see. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is very agreeable and wholesome, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> produces plenty of all the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 54. 35. S. Lat. 2. 0.

MARALDI

Pages 208-208

James <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, a learned mathematician and astronomer, of the Academy of Sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, was born in 1665. He was the son of Francis Maraldi and Angela Catharine Caffini, the sister of the famous astronomer of that name. His uncle made him go to France in 1687, where he acquired <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation on account of his learning and observations. He made a catalogue of the fixed stars, which is more particular and exact than Bayer's; and has given a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of curious and interesting observations in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of the academy; in particular, those on bees and petrifications have been universally applauded. He died in 1729.

MARANA

Pages 208-208

John Paul, an ingenious writer of the 17th century, was of a distinguished family, and born at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>; where he received an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> suitable to his birth, and made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of polite literature and the sciences. Having been engaged in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> of Raphael della Terra, to deliver up Genoa to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy, he was in 1674, when 28 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, imprisoned in the tower of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and remained there four years. Being at length set at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, he was ordered to write the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of that conspiracy; but, when finished, it was seized and prevented from being published. When the republic of Genoa was at variance with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of France, Marana, who had always an inclination for that court, was afraid of being imprisoned a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and retired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONACO">Monaco</a>, where he again wrote the history of the conspiracy in Italian; and, in 1682, went to Lyons to get it printed. From Lyons he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where his merit soon acquired him powerful protectors. He spent the rest of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in a happy and tranquil mediocrity, devoted to study and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of men of learning; and died in 1693. His history of the conspiracy contains many curious and interesting anecdotes, which are nowhere else to be found. He also wrote several other works; the most known of which is the Turkish Spy, in 6 vols 12mo, which was in 1742 augmented, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>. Of this ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> we have an excellent English translation.

MARANO

Pages 208-208

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Friuli, with a strong citadel; seated in a marsh at the bottom of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Venice, which renders it difficult of access.

MARANS

Pages 208-208

a rich town of France, in the territory of Aunis and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a>, seated among <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> marshes, near the river Sevre, three miles from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It carries on a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade in corn; and is seated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 55. N. Lat. 46. 20.

MARANTA

Pages 208-208
Indian Arrow-root, a genus of plants belonging to the monandra class; and in the natural method ranking under the eighth order Scitaminea. See Botany Index.

MARASMUS

Pages 208-208

among physicians, denotes an atrophy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> consumption in its last and most deplorable stage.

MARATHON

Pages 208-210

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, one of the demi <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hamlets of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>; about 10 miles to the northeast of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, towards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>, near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It still retains its ancient name (Dr Chandler informs us); but is very inconsiderable, consisting only of a few houses and gardens. The plain of Marathon, famous for Miltiades's victory over the Persians, by which the liberties of Athens and other cities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> were saved, is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and narrow, but consisting chiefly of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> ground, and therefore admitting the operations of cavalry, which formed the main strength of the barbarian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and with which the Greeks were very poorly provided. Here the Persians, under the command of Datis, pitched their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, by the advice of Hippias the banished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Athens, whose solicitations and intrigues had promoted the expedition, and whose perfect knowledge of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and intimate acquaintance with the affairs of Greece, rendered his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> on all occasions respectable. The Persian army is said to have consisted of 100,000 infantry, and 10,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>.—Athens was in the utmost consternation and dismay. She had, upon the first Marathon: first appearance of the Persian fleet, sent to implore <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> from the other nations of Greece; but some had submitted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a>, and others trembled at the very name of the Medes and Persians. The Lacedaemonians alone promised troops; but various obstacles did not allow them immediately to form a junction with those of Athens. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> therefore could only rely on its own strength; and happily at this moment there appeared three men destined to give new energy to the state. These were Miltiades, Ariftides, and Themistocles; whose example and harangues kindled the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> of the noblest heroism in the minds of the Athenians. Levies were immediately made. Each of the ten tribes furnished 1000 foot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> with a commander at their head. To complete this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> it was necessary to enrol the slaves (A). No sooner were the troops assembled than they marched out of the city into the plain of Marathon, where the inhabitants of Platea in Boeotia sent them a reinforcement of 1000 infantry. Scarcely were the two armies in sight of each other, before Miltiades proposed to attack the enemy. Ariftides and several of the commanders warmly supported this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>; but the rest, terrified at the excessive disproportion of the armies, were delirious of waiting for the succours from Lacedaemon. Opinions being divided, they had recourse to that of the polemarch, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, who was consulted on such occasions, to put an end to the equality of suffrages. Miltiades addressed himself to him, with the ardour of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> deeply impressed with the importance of present circumstances: "Athens (said he to him) is on the point of experiencing the greatest of vicissitudes. Ready to become the first power of Greece, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> of the tyranny and fury of Hippas, from you alone, Callimachus, the now awaits her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we suffer the ardour of the troops to cool, they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> shamefully bow beneath the Persian yoke; but if we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> them on to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, the gods and victory will favour us. A word from your mouth must now precipitate your country into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> or prefer her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>." Callimachus gave his suffrage, and the battle was resolved. To ensure success, Ariftides, and the other generals after his example, yielded to Miltiades the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the command which belonged to them in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a>; but, to secure them from every hazard, he preferred waiting for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> which of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> placed him at the head of the army. When that day arrived, Miltiades drew up his troops at the foot of a mountain, on a spot of ground scattered over with trees to impede the Persian cavalry. The Plateans were placed on the left wing; Callimachus commanded the right; Ariftides and Themistocles were in the centre of the battle, and Miltiades everywhere. An <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of nearly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> separated the Grecian army from that of the Persians. At the first signal the Greeks advanced over this space running. The Persians, astonished at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of attack so <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVEL">novel</a> to both nations, for a moment remained motionless; but to the impetuous fury of the enemy Marathon, they soon opposed a more sedate and not less formidable fury. After an obstinate conflict of some hours, victory began to declare herself in the two wings of the Grecian army. The right dispersed the enemy in the plain, while the left drove them back on a morass that had the appearance of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a>, in which they stuck fast and were lost. Both these bodies of troops now flew to the succour of Ariftides and Themistocles, ready to give way before the flower of the Persian troops placed by Datis in the centre of his battle. From this moment the rout became general. The Persians, repulsed on all sides, found their only <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> in the fleet which had approached the shore. The conquerors pursued them with fire and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and took, burnt, or sunk the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of their vessels; the rest escaped by dint of rowing. The Persian army lost about 6,000 men; that of the Athenians 192. Miltiades was wounded; Hippas was left dead on the field, as were Steleus and Callimachus, two of the Athenian generals. Scarcely was the battle over, when a soldier, worn out with fatigue forms the project of carrying the first news of so signal a success to the magistrates of Athens, and without quitting his arms, he runs, flies, arrives, announces the victory, and falls dead at their feet. This battle was fought on the 6th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOEDROMION">Boedromion</a>, in the third year of the 72nd Olympiad (or 29th September anno 490 B.C.). The next day 2000 Spartans arrived. In three days and nights they had marched 1200 stadia. Though informed of the defeat of the Persians, they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> to Marathon, nor did they enviously turn to behold those fields where a rival <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> had signalized itself by so heroic an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>: they there beheld the tents of the Persians still standing, the plain strewn over with dead, and covered with costly spoils: they there found Ariftides, who with his tribe was guarding the prisoners and booty; and did not retire until they had bestowed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> applause on the victors. The Athenians neglected nothing to eternalize the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of those who fell in the battle. It had been usual to inter the citizens who perished in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> at the public expense, in the Ceramicus without the city; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of these was deemed uncommonly meritorious. They were buried, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARROW">barrow</a> was made for them, where their bravery had been manifested. Their names were engraven on half columns erected on the plain of Marathon. These monuments, not excepting those of the generals Callimachus and Steleus, were in a style of the greatest simplicity. In the intervals between them were erected trophies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the arms of the Persians. An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> of eminence had painted all the circumstances of the battle in one of the most frequented porticoes of the city: Miltiades was there represented at the head of the generals, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of exhorting the troops to fight for their country. Paulanias examined the field of battle about 600 years (A) Travels of Anacharsis; authority, Pauson. i. 79. But Dr Gillies seems to think that the armed slaves were not included in the 10,000; but amounted of themselves to a greater number, and which formed the centre of the battle. years after this event. His account of it is as follows: The barrow of the Athenians is in the plain, and on it are pillars containing the names of the dead under those of the tribes to which they belonged; and there is another for the Plateans and slaves; and a distinct monument of Miltiades the commander, who survived this exploit. There may be perceived nightly the neighing of horses and the clashing of arms. No person has derived any good from walking on purpose to behold the spectres; but their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> does not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on any one who happens to see them without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. The Marathonians worship those who were slain in the battle, calling them heroes.—A trophy also of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble has been erected. The Athenians say the Medes were buried, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> requiring that the corpse of a man be covered with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; though I was not able to find any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of sepulture, for there is no barrow or other sign visible; but they threw them promiscuously into a pit.—Above the lake are the marble mangers of the horses of Artaphernes, with marks of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENT">tent</a> on the rocks." Many centuries have elapsed since the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of Pausanias; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> barrow, it is likely that of the gallant Athenians, still towers above the level of the plain. It is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> fine earth, and has a bush or two growing on it. Dr Chandler informs us, that he enjoyed a pleasing and satisfactory view from the summit; and looked, but in vain, for the pillars on which the names were recorded, lamenting that such memorials should ever be removed. At a small distance northward is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> basement of white marble, perhaps part of the trophy. A Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> has stood near it; and some <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> and rubbish, disposed so as to form an open place of worship, remain. MARATTA. See MARATTAS.

MARATTI

Pages 210-210

CARLO, a celebrated painter, was born at Camorano, near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a>, in 1625. He came a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> boy to Rome, when only 11 years old; and at 12 recommended himself so effectually to Andrea Sacchi, by his drawings after Raphael in the Vatican, that he took him into his school, where he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> 25 years till his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. His graceful and beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> occasioned his being generally employed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> madonas and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> saints. No <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> ever performed in a better style, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> with a greater elegance. From the finest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> and pictures, he made himself master of the most perfect forms, and the most charming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRS">airs</a> of heads, which he sketched with equal ease and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>. He has produced a noble variety of draperies, more artfully managed, more richly ornamented, and with greater propriety, than even the best of the moderns. He was inimitable in adorning the heads, in the disposal of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and the elegance of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and feet, which are equal to those of Raphael; and he particularly excelled in gracefulness. In his younger days he etched a few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a>, as well as his own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> as after others, with equal spirit and correctness. It would be endless to recount the celebrated paintings done by this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> man. Yet he executed nothing slightly, often changed his designs, and almost always for the better, whence his pictures were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. By the example of his master, he made several admirable portraits of popes, cardinals, and other people of distinction, from whom he received the highest testimonies of esteem, as he likewise did from almost all the monarchs and princes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Inno-Marzalini XI. appointed him keeper of the paintings in his chapel and the Vatican. Maratti erected two noble monuments for Raphael and A. Caracci, at his own expense, in the Pantheon. How well he maintained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of his profession, appears by his answer to a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, who complaining of the excessive price of his pictures, he told him there was a vast debt due from the world to the famous artists his predecessors, and that he, as their rightful successor, was come to claim those arrears. His abilities in painting were accompanied with many virtues, and particularly with an extensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>. This great painter died at Rome in 1713, in the 88th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>.

MARAUDING

Pages 210-210

in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, means a party of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, who, without any order, go into the neighbouring houses and villages, when the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> is either in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> garrison, to plunder and destroy, &c. Marauders are a disgrace to the camp, to the military profession, and deserve no better <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> from their officers than they give to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> peasants, &c.

MARAVEDI

Pages 210-210

a little Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, worth somewhat more than a French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENIER">denier</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> half a farthing English. The Spaniards always <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> by maravedis, both in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> and in their finances, though the coin itself is no longer current among them. Sixty-three maravedis are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to a rial of silver; so that the piastra, or piece of eight reals, contains 504; and the pito of four pieces of eight, 2016 maravedis. This smallness of the coin produces vast numbers in the Spanish accounts and calculations; inasmuch that a stranger correspondent would think himself indebted several millions for a commodity that cost but a few pounds. In the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, we meet with several kinds of maravedis; Alphonsine maravedis, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> maravedis, maravedis of good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, maravedis Combreños, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> maravedis, and old maravedis. When we find maravedis alone, and without any addition, it is to be understood of those mentioned above. The rest are different in value, fineness of metal, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, &c. Mariana affirms, that this coin is older than the Moors; that it came from the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>; that it was anciently equal to a third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the rial, and consequently of 12 times the value of the present maravedi. Under Alphonsus XI. the maravedi was 17 times, under Henry II. ten times, under Henry III. five times, and under John II. two times and a half, the value of the present maravedi.

MARBELLA

Pages 210-210

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, situated at the mouth of the Rio Verde, 30 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of Gibraltar, and 28 south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALAGA">Malaga</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 25. N. 30. 25.

MARBLE

Pages 210-212

a calcareous <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, of which there are many beautiful varieties. The word comes from the French marbre, and from the Latin marmor, of the Greek μάρμαρος to "shine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> glitter." See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">MINERALOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">Artificial</a> Marbles. The stucco, of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, busts, bas-reliefs, and other ornaments of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> are made, ought to be marble pulverized, mixed in a certain proportion with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>; the whole well fitted, worked up with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and used like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> plaster. See STUCCO. There is also a kind of artificial marble made of the flaky selenites, or a transparent stone resembling plaster; which Marble, which becomes very hard, receives a tolerable polish, and may deceive a good eye. This kind of selenite resembles Mulcovy talc. There is another sort of artificial marble formed by corrosive tinctures, which, penetrating into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble to the depth of a line or more, imitate the various colours of other dearer marbles. There is also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of brimstone in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of marble. To do this, you must provide yourself with a flat and smooth piece of marble; on this make a border or wall, to encompass either a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> or oval <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, which may be done either with wax or clay. Then having several sorts of colours, as white <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, vermillion, lake, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORPIMENT">orpiment</a>, mastic, malm, Prussian blue, &c.; melt on a slow fire some brimstone in several glazed pipkins; put one particular sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> into each, and stir it well together; then having before oiled the marble all over within the wall, with one colour quickly drop spots upon it of larger and lesser size; after this, take another colour and do as before, and so on till the stone is covered with spots of all the colours you <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. When this is done, you are next to consider what colour the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> or ground of your table is to be; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> of a gray colour, then take fine fitted ashes, and mix it up with melted brimstone; or if <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, with English red ochre; if white, with white lead; if <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> black. Your brimstone for the ground must be pretty hot, that the colour dropped on the stone may unite and incorporate with it. When the ground is poured even all over, you are next, if judged necessary, to put a thin wainscot board upon it; this must be done while the brimstone is hot, making also the board hot, which ought to be thoroughly dry, in order to cause the brimstone to stick the better to it. When the whole is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, take it up, and polish it with a cloth and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> look very beautiful. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">Elastic</a> Marble, an extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of fossil which has surprised all the naturalists who have seen it. There are several tables of it preserved in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Borghese at Rome, and shown to the curious. F. Jacquer, a celebrated mathematician, has given a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> in the Literary Gazette of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, but the naturalists cannot be contented with it. If permission was given to make the requisite experiments, this curious phenomenon might be better illustrated. There are five or six tables of that marble; their length is about two feet and a half, the breadth about ten inches, and the thickness a little less than three. They were dug up, as the Abbé Fortis was told, in the field of Mondragon; the grain is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRARA">Carrara</a> marble, or perhaps of the finest Greek. They seem to have suffered some attack of fire; though the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of pulverization observable in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, can, perhaps, scarcely be called that of imperfect calcination. They are very dry, do not yield to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>, resound to the hammer, like other generous marble, and are perhaps susceptible of a polish. Being set on end, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> oscillating backward and forward; when laid horizontally, and raised at one end, they form a curve, beginning towards the middle; if placed on a table, and a piece of wood or any thing else is laid under them, they make a salient curve, and touch the table with both ends. Notwith- standing this flexibility, they are liable to be broken if indifferently handled; and therefore one table only, and that not the best, is shown to the curious. Formerly they were all together in the prince's apartment on the ground <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>. Colouring of Marble. This is a nice art; and in order to succeed in it, the pieces of marble on which the experiments are tried, must be well polished, and free from the least spot or vein. The harder the marble is, the better will it bear the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> necessary in the operation; therefore alabaster and the common soft white marble are very improper for performing these operations upon. Heat is always necessary for opening the pores of marble, so as to render it fit to receive the colours; but the marble must never be made red-hot; for then the texture of it is injured, and the colours are burnt, and lose their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. Too small a degree of heat is as bad as one too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>; for, in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, though the marble receives the colour, it will not be fixed in it, nor strike deep enough. Some colours will strike even cold; but they are never so well sunk in as when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> degree of heat is used. The proper degree is that which, without making the marble red, will make the liquor boil upon its surface. The menstruums used to strike in the colours must be varied according to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the colour to be used. A lixivium made with horses or dogs urine, with four parts of quicklime and one of potashes, is excellent for some colours; common ley of wood-ashes is very good for others; for some, spirit of wine is best; and lastly, for others, oily liquors, or common white wine. The colours which have been found to succeed best with the peculiar menstruums, are these: Stone blue dissolved in five times the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of spirit of wine, or of the urinous lixivium, and that colour which the painters call luteum, dissolved in common ley of wood-ashes. An extract of saffron, and that colour made of buckthorn berries, and called by painters sap green, both succeed well when dissolved in urine and quicklime; and tolerably well when dissolved in spirit of wine. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMILION">Vermilion</a>, and a very fine powder of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COCHINEAL">cochineal</a>, also succeed very well in the same liquors. Dragon's blood succeeds in spirit of wine, as does also a tincture of logwood in the same spirit. Alkanet-root gives a fine colour; but the only menstruum to be used for it is oil of turpentine; for neither spirit of wine, nor any lixivium, will do with it. There is another kind of fangus draconis, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called dragon's blood in tears, which, mixed with urine, gives a very elegant colour. Besides these mixtures of colours and menstruums, there are other colours which must be laid on dry and unmixed. These are, dragon's blood of the purest kind, for a red; gamboge for a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>; green wax, for a green; common brimstone, pitch, and turpentine, for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> colour. The marble for these experiments must be made considerably hot, and then the colours are to be rubbed on dry in the lump. Some of these colours, when once given, remain immutable, others are easily changed or destroyed. Thus, the red colour given by dragon's blood, or by a decoction of logwood, will be wholly taken away by oil of tartar, and the polish of the marble not hurt by it. A fine <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> colour is given in the following manner: Take crude sal ammoniac, vitriol, and verdigris, of each equal quantities. White vitriol succeeds best; and all must be thoroughly mixed in fine powder. The staining of marble to all the degrees of red or yellow, by solutions of dragon's blood or gamboge, may be done by reducing these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a> to powder, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> them with the spirit of wine in a glass <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>. But, for smaller attempts, no method is so good as the mixing a little of either of those powders with spirit of wine in a silver spoon, and holding it over <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>. By this means a fine tincture will be extracted; and, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> dipped in this, the finest traces may be made on the marble while cold; which, on the heating of it afterwards, either on sand, or in a baker's oven, will all sink very deep, and remain perfectly distinct on the stone. It is very easy to make the ground colour of the marble red or yellow by this means, and leave white veins in it. This is to be done by covering the places where the whites are to remain with some white paint, or even with two or three doubles only of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>; either of which will prevent the colour from penetrating. All the degrees of red are to be given to marble by this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> alone; a slight tincture of it, without the affluence of heat to the marble, gives only a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> colour; but the stronger tinctures give it yet deeper; to this the affluence of heat adds greatly; and finally, the addition of a little pitch to the tincture, gives it a tendency to blackness, or any degree of deep red that may be desired. A blue colour may be given also to marble by dissolving turpentine in lye, lime and urine, or in the volatile spirit of urine; but this has always a tendency to purple, whether made by the one or the other of these ways. A better blue, and used in an easier manner, is furnished by the Canary turpentine, a substance well known among the dyers. This needs only to be dissolved in water, and drawn on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> with a pencil; it penetrates very deeply into the marble; and the colour may be increased, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> the pencil wetted afresh several times over the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. This colour is subject to spread and diffuse itself irregularly; but it may be kept in regular bounds, by circumscribing its lines with beds of wax, or any such substance. It is also to be observed, that this colour should always be laid on cold, and no heat given even afterwards to the marble; and one great advantage of this colour is, that it is therefore easily added to marbles already stained with other colours, is a very beautiful tinge, and lasts a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARUNDEL">Arundel</a> Marbles, marbles with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONICLE">chronicle</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> on them (as was supposed) many years before our Saviour's birth; presented to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> by Thomas <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Arundel, whence the name. See Arundelian Marble.

MARBLED

Pages 212-212

something veined <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> clouded, resembling marble. See MARBLING. Marbled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, a name given by many to a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> or china-ware, which seems to be full of cemented flaws. It is called by the Chinese, who are very fond of it, you tchi. It is generally plain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, sometimes blue, and has exactly the appearance of a piece of china which had been first broken, and then had all the pieces cemented in their places again, and covered with the original <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>. The manner of preparing it is easy, and might be imitated with us. Instead of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> varnish of the china-ware, which is made of what they call <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> and oil of fern mixed together, they cover this with a simple thing made only of a sort of coarse agates, calcined to a white powder, and separated from the groser parts by means of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> in mortars. When the powder has been thus prepared, it is left moist, or in form of a sort of cream, with the last water that is suffered to remain in it, and this is used as the varnish. Our crystal would serve full as well as those coarse agates, and the method of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> is perfectly easy. The occasion of the singular appearance of this sort of porcelain is, that the varnish never spreads evenly, but runs into ridges and veins. These often run naturally into a sort of mosaic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which can scarcely be taken for the effect of chance. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the marbled china be desired blue, they first give it a general coat of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> the vessel into a blue varnish; and when this is thoroughly dry, they add another coat of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGATE">agate</a> oil. Playing Marbles, are mostly imported from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; where it is said they are made by breaking the stone alabaster, or other substance, into pieces or chips, of a suitable size; these are put into an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> mill which turns by water: there are several partitions with raps within, cut float-wise, not with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, which turn constantly round with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> swiftness; the friction against the raps makes them round, and as they are formed, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> out of different holes, into which size or chance throws them. They are brought from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and from thence dispersed over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>.

MARBLING

Pages 212-213

the method of preparing and colouring the marbled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>. There are several kinds of marbled paper; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of them lies in the forms in which the colours are laid on the ground; some being disposed in whirls <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> circumvolutions; some in jagged lengths; and others only in spots of a roundish or oval <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. The general manner of managing each kind is, nevertheless, the same; being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> the paper, in a solution of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-tragacanth, or, as it is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called, gum dragon; over which the colours, previously prepared with ox-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALL">gall</a> and spirit of wine, are first spread. The peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> necessary for this purpose, is a trough for containing the gum tragacanth and the colours; a comb for disposing them in the figure usually chosen; and a burnishing <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> for polishing the paper. The trough may be of any kind of wood; and must be somewhat larger than the sheets of paper for marbling which it is to be employed; but the sides of it need only rise about two inches above the bottom; for by making it thus shallow, the less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the solution of the gum <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> serve to fill it. The comb may be also of wood, and five inches in length; but should have bristles, which may be about two inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and placed at about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an inch distance from each other.
