The burnishing stone may be of jasper or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGATE">agate</a>; but as those <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> are very dear when of sufficient largeness, marble or glass may be used, provided their surface be polished to a greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of smoothness. Marbling. These implements being prepared, the solution of gum-tragacanth must be made, by putting a sufficient proportion of the gum, which should be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and clear from all foulness, into clean <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and letting it remain there a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> or two, frequently breaking the lumps and stirring it till the whole shall appear dissolved and equally mixed with the water. The consistence of the solution should be nearly that of strong gum-water used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it appear thicker, water must be added; or if thinner, more of the gum. When the solution is thus brought to a due state, it must be passed through a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth; and being then put into the trough, it will be ready to receive the colours. The colours employed for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> are carmine, lake, rose-pink, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMILION">vermilion</a>; but the two last are too hard and glaring, unless they be mixed with rose-pink or lake, to bring them to a softer <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a>; and with respect to the carmine and lake, they are too dear for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> purposes; for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, Dutch pink and yellow ochre may be employed;—for blue, Prussian blue and verditer may be used;—for green, verdigris, a mixture of Dutch pink and Prussian blue or verditer, in different proportions;—for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>, the orange lake, or a mixture of vermilion, or red <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, with Dutch pink; for purple, rose-pink and Prussian blue. These several colours should be ground with spirit of wine till they be of a proper fineness; and then, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of using them, a little flint-gall, or in default of it the gall of a beast, should be added, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> them over again with it. The proper proportion of the gall must be found by trying them; for there must be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> so much as will suffer the spots of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, when sprinkled on the solution of the gum-tragacanth, to join together, without intermixing or running into each other. When every thing is thus prepared, the solution of the gum-tragacanth must be poured into the trough; and the colours, being in a separate pot, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> appropriated to each, must be sprinkled on the surface of the solution, by shaking the pencil, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with its proper colour over it; and this must be done with the several kinds of colour desired, till the surface be wholly covered. When the marbling is proposed to be in spots of a simple form, nothing more is necessary; but where the whirls or snail-shell figures are wanted, they must be made by means of a quill; which must be put among the spots to turn them about, till the effect be produced. The jagged lengths must be made by means of the comb above described, which must be passed through the colours from one end of the trough to the other; and will give them that appearance: but if they be desired to be pointed both ways, the comb must be again passed through the trough in a contrary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>; or if some of the whirls or snail-shell figures be required to be added, they may be yet made by the means before directed. The paper should be previously prepared for receiving the colours, by dipping it over-night in water; and laying the sheets on each other with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> over them. The whole being thus ready, the paper must be held by two corners, and laid in the most gentle and even manner on the solution covered with the colours; and there softly pressed with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, Marbling that it may bear everywhere on the solution. After which it must be raised and taken off with the same care, and then hung to dry across a proper <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, subtended near at hand for that purpose; and in that state it must continue till it be perfectly dry. It then remains only to give the paper a proper polish; in order to which, it is first rubbed with a little <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>; and then must be thoroughly smoothed by the glass polishers, such as are used for linen, and called the calender glasser. After which it should be again rubbed by a burnisher of jasper or agate; or, in default of them, of glass ground to the highest polish; for on the perfect polish of the paper depends in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and value. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> or silver powders may be used, where desired, along with the colour; and require only the same treatment as them, except that they must be first tempered with gum-water. Marbling of books or paper is performed thus: Dissolve four ounces of gum-arabic in two quarts of fair water; then provide several colours mixed with water in pots or shells; and, with pencils peculiar to each colour, sprinkle them by way of intermixture upon the gum-water, which must be put into a trough or some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> vessel; then with a stick curl them, or draw them out in streaks, to as much variety as may be done. Having done this, hold your book or books <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> together, and only dip the edges in, on the top of the water and colours, very lightly; which done, take them off, and the plain <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of the colours in mixture will be upon the leaves; doing as well the ends as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the book in the like manner. Marbling a book on the covers is performed by forming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a>-fortis or spirit of vitriol mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a>, and afterwards glazing the covers. See Book Binding. MARCA ANTONIO. See Raimondi. MARCA-ITÉ, an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">mineralogy</a>, given indifferently to ores, pyrites, and to semi-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>. But more lately confined to pyrites, and to such pyrites as are regularly formed. See Pyrites, Mineralogy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MARCELLIANISM

Pages 213-213

the doctrines and opinions of the Marcellians, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> heretics, towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century, so called from Marcellus of Ancyra, their leader, who was accused of reviving the errors of Sabellius. Some, however, are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that Marcellus was orthodox, and that they were his enemies the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>, who fathered their errors upon him. St Epiphanius observes, that there was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of dispute with regard to the real tenets of Marcellus; but that, as to his followers, it is evident they did not own the three hypostases: for Marcellus considered the Son and Holy Ghost as two emanations from the divine <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, which, after performing their respective offices, were to return again into the subsistence of the Father; and this opinion is altogether incompatible with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of three distinct persons in the Godhead.

MARCELLUS

Pages 213-214

Marcus Claudius, a famous Roman general, who, after the first Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, had the management of an expedition against the Gauls. Here Marcellus he obtained the *spolia opima*, by killing with his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> Viridomarus the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the enemy. Such success rendered him popular, and soon after he was intrusted to oppose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. He was the first Roman who obtained some advantage over this celebrated Carthaginian, and showed his countrymen that Hannibal was not invincible. The troubles which were raised in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> by the Carthaginians at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Hieronymus, alarmed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; and Marcellus, in his third consulship, was sent with a powerful force against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>. He attacked it by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>; but his operations proved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> ineffectual, and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> and industry of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHIMEDES">Archimedes</a> were able to baffle all the efforts, and to destroy all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and stupendous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> engines of the Romans, during three successive years. The perseverance of Marcellus at last obtained the victory. After this conquest, Marcellus was called upon by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to oppose Hannibal. In this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> he behaved with greater vigour than before; the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of the Samnites, which had revolted, were recovered by force of arms, and 3000 of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> of Hannibal made prisoners. Some time after, in an engagement with the Carthaginian general, Marcellus had the disadvantage; but on the morrow a more successful skirmish vindicated his military character and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the Roman soldiers. Marcellus, however, was not sufficiently vigilant against the snares of his adversary. He imprudently separated himself from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, and was killed in an ambuscade, in the 65th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, in his 5th consulship, A.U.C. 544. His body was honoured by the conqueror with a magnificent funeral, and his ashes were conveyed in a silver urn to his son. Marcellus claims our commendation for his private as well as public virtues; and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> of a general <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> ever be remembered, who, at the surrender of Syracuse, wept on the thought that many were going to be exposed to the avarice and rapaciousness of an incensed soldiery, which the policy of Rome and the laws of war rendered inevitable.

MARCGRAVE

Pages 214-214
or **MARGRAVE**, a kind of dignity in Germany, answering to our marquis; (see Marquis). The word is derived from the German Marche, or Marcke, which signifies "a frontier;" and Graffe, "count, governor;" Maregraves being originally governors of cities lying on the frontiers of a country or state.

MARCH

Pages 214-215

(Martius), the third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the year, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> way of computing. See Month, and Year. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, March was the first month; and in some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> computations, that order is still preferred; as particularly reckoning the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of years from the incarnation of our Saviour; that is, from the 25th of March. It was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> who divided the year into months; to the first of which he gave the name of his supposed father <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>. Ovid, however, observes, that the people of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> had the month of March before Romulus's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but that they placed it very differently, some making it the third, some the fourth, some the fifth, and others the tenth month of the year. In this month it was that the Romans sacrificed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNA">Anna</a> Perenna; that they began their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMITIA">comitia</a>; that they adjudged their public farms and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEASES">leases</a>; that the Marchmistresses served the slaves and servants at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, as the matters did in the Saturnalia; and that the vestals renewed the sacred fire. The month of March was always under the protection of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, and always consisted of 31 days.—The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> held it an unhappy month for <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, as well as the month of May. March, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, is the moving of a body of men from one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to another. Nothing is laid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> particularly concerning the marches of the Jewish armies; only thus much we may collect, that they made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of trumpets, to the different sounds of which they prepared themselves by packing up their baggage, putting themselves in readines, and attending at the standards, to wait the signal for marching. We are told that the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of the Israelites marched in general no more than one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> and a half; but this appears to hold good only of their progress through difficult <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>: For <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLLARD">Pollard</a> says they might, in an open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, march four leagues in a day <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more. The Rabbins suppose that the Israelites marched in the same order they were placed in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. The Greeks, let the posture of their affairs be what it would, never marched against their enemies till favourable omens encouraged the enterprise. An eclipse of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, or any untoward accident, or the intervening of what they esteemed an unlucky day, entirely prevented their march. But of all the Greeks the Lacedemonians were the most nice and scrupulous. The heavenly bodies directed all their motions; and it was an invariable maxim with them never to march before the full moon. The Greeks are particularly remarked by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> for marching in good order and profound silence; whereas the Barbarian forces were all noise, clamour, and confusion. It is needless to say anything concerning the marches of the Roman armies, more than that they were performed with the greatest order and despatch, infomuch that their unexpected presence frequently damped the spirits of their enemies. The Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> were inured to the military pace, that is, to walk 20 miles in five hours, though at the same time they carried burdens of 60 pounds <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. Of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> parts of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times, none is more essential than that of marching. It may be justly called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a> which leads to all sublime motions and manoeuvres of an army; for they depend entirely on this point. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> can be attacked in four different ways; in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, on both flanks, and in the rear: but he can defend himself, and annoy the enemy, only when placed with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> towards him. Hence it follows, that the general object of marching is reduced to three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> only; to march forwards, and on both sides, because it is impossible to do it for any time backwards, and by that means face the enemy wherever he presents himself.—The different steps to be made use of are three: slow, fast, and oblique. The first is proper in advancing, when at a considerable distance from the enemy, and when the ground is unequal, that the line may not be broke, and a regular fire kept up without intermission. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is chiefly necessary when you want to anticipate the enemy in occupying some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>, in passing a defile, and, above all, in attacking an intrenchment, March, to avoid being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> while exposed to the fire of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> and small arms, &c. The third step is of infinite <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, both in the infantry and cavalry; columns may be opened and formed into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, and vice versa, lines into columns, by this kind of step, in a lesser space, and consequently in less time, than by any other method whatsoever. In coming out of a defile, you may instantly form the line without presenting the flank to the enemy. The line may be formed, though ever so near to the enemy, with safety; because you face him, and can with ease and safety protect and cover the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the troops, while they are coming out of the defiles, and forming. The same thing may be equally executed, when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> is to be formed in order to advance or retreat; which is a point of infinite consequence, and should be established as an <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-AXIOM">axiom</a>. The order of march of the troops must be so disposed, that each should arrive at their rendezvous, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> possible, on the same day. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> general, or his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>, with an able engineer, should sufficiently reconnoitre the country, to obtain a perfect knowledge of it and the enemy, before he forms his routes. Before a march, the army generally receives several days' <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. The quarter-masters, camp colourmen, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIONEERS">pioneers</a>, parade according to orders, and march immediately after, commanded by the quarter-master-general or his deputy. They are to clear the roads, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> the ways, make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> for the march of the army, &c. The general, for instance, beats at two, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> at three, and the army to march in 20 minutes after. Upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> the general, the village, and general officer's guards, quarter and rear guards, join their respective corps; and the army pack up their baggage. Upon beating the assembly, the tents are to be struck, and sent with the baggage to the place appointed, &c. The companies draw up in their several streets, and the rolls are called. At the time appointed, the drummers are to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> a march, and fifers play at the head of the line, upon which the companies march out from their several streets, form battalions, as they advance to the head of line, and then halt. The several battalions <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be formed into columns by the adjutant-general, and the order of march, &c., be given to the general officers who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> the columns. The cavalry generally march by regiments or squadrons. The heavy artillery always keeps the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> roads in the centre of the columns, escorted by a strong party of infantry and cavalry. The field pieces march with the columns. Each soldier generally marches with 36 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROUNDS">rounds</a> of powder and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>, and two good flints; one of which is to be fixed in the cock of his firelock. The routes must be formed so that no columns <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> one another on the march.

MARCHAND

Pages 215-215

Professor, was from his youth brought up at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in the profession of a bookseller, and in the knowledge of books. He kept a regular correspondence with several learned men, among whom was Bernard the continuator of the Nouvelles de la République des Lettres, and furnished this writer with the literary anecdotes of France. Marchand, having embraced the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, went to join Bernard in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, where he might be at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to profess Marchand his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> opinions. He <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the trade of bookseller for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but afterwards quitted it, that he might dedicate himself wholly to the pursuits of literature. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of France, together with a knowledge of books and authors, was always his favourite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. In the latter he was so eminently distinguished, that he was consulted from all parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. He was also one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> authors of the Journal Littéraire, one of the best periodical works which have appeared in Holland; and he furnished excellent extracts for the other journals. This valuable and learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> died at an advanced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, the 14th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1756; and left the little fortune which he had to a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> instituted at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> and instruction of a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people. His library, which was excellently chosen for literary history, together with his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, was left by his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>. From him we have, 1. The History of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">Printing</a>, a new edition of which has been promised by one of his friends. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which is full of notes and critical discussions, appeared in 1749 at the Hague, in 4to. There is such a prodigious display of erudition, and remarks and quotations are heaped together in such confusion, that when you get to the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a>, you know not what conclusion to form concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> which have been discussed. Abbé Mercier, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of Saint Leger de <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOISSONS">Soissons</a>, gave in 1775, 4to, a supplement to this history, which is equally curious and accurate. 2. An Historical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> Critical and Literary, printed at the Hague in 1758, in two small volumes, folio. In this work we meet with historical singularities, literary anecdotes, and a discussion of points of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BIBLIOGRAPHY">bibliography</a>; but too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> minuteness prevails in it, the style is deficient in point of purity, and the author is too much carried away by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and eagerness of his character. More erudition could not well be collected; especially upon subjects which, at least to the generality of readers, are so uninteresting. 3. A new edition of Bayle's Dictionary, and Letters of the Cymbalum mundi, &c.

MARCHANTIA

Pages 215-215

a genus of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order of algae, belonging to the cryptogamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MARCHE

Pages 215-215

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of France, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Berry, on the east by Auvergne, on the west by Argoatmois, and on the south by Limosin. It is about 55 miles in length, and 25 in breadth, and is pretty fertile in corn and wine.

MARCHENA

Pages 215-215

a handsome, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, and considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>, and a suburb as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as the town, seated in the middle of a plain, particularly fertile in olives, though very defective of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 20'. N. Lat. 37° 20'.

MARCHERS

Pages 215-215
or LORDS MARCHERS, were those noblemen that lived on the marches of Wales or Scotland; who, in times past, according to Camden, had their laws, and potestatem vitae, &c. like petty kings, which are abolished by the stat. 27 Hen. VIII. c. 26. and 1 Edw. VI. c. 10. In old records the lords marchers of Wales were styled Marchianae de Marchia Walliae. See 1 et 2 P. et M. c. 15.

MARCHES

Pages 215-216

from the German <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>. Marchet i.e. fines, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> from the French marque, viz. signum (being the notorious distinction between two countries or territories), are the limits between England and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, or between England and Scotland, which last are divided into well and middle marches, 4 Hen. V. c. 7 22 Ed. IV. c. 8. 24 Hen. VIII c. 9. And there was formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> called the court of the marches of Wales, where pleas of debt or damages, not above the value of 50 pounds, were tried and determined; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of the marches held <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> for debts above that sum, &c., a prohibition might be awarded. Hill. 14 Car. I. Cro. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">Act</a>. 38.

MARCHET

Pages 216-216
or MARCHETTA, a pecuniary fine, anciently paid by the tenant to his lord, for the marriage of one of the tenant's daughters. This custom obtained, with some difference, throughout all England and Wales, as also in Scotland; and it still continues to obtain in some places. According to the custom of the manor of Dinover in Caernarvonshire, every tenant at the marriage of his daughter pays ten shillings to the lord; which, in the British language, is called equal-r-merched, i.e. maid's fee. In Scotland, and the north parts of England, the custom was, for the lord to lie the first night with the bride of his tenant; but this usage was abrogated by King Malcolm III. at the instance of his queen; and, instead thereof, a mark was paid by the bridegroom to the lord; whence it was called marchetta mulieris. See Borough English. MARCIA Silva, in Ancient Geography, a forest situated between the Rauraci and the Danube, before it comes to be navigable; a part of the Hercynia. Now Schwartzwald, or Black Forest, in the south-west of Swabia, near the rise of the Danube and Neckar.

MARCIANITES

Pages 216-216
or MARCIONISTS, Marcionites, a very ancient and popular sect of heretics, who, in the time of St Epiphanius, were spread over Italy, Egypt, Palestine, Syria, Arabia, Persia, and other countries: they were thus denominated from their author Marcion. Marcion was of Pontus, the son of a bishop, and at first made profession of the monastic life; but he was excommunicated by his own father, who would never admit him again into the communion of the church, not even on his repentance. On this he abandoned his own country, and retired to Rome, where he began to broach his doctrines. He laid down two principles, the one good, the other evil: between these he imagined an intermediate kind of deity of a mixed nature, who was the creator of this inferior world, and the god and legislator of the Jewish nation; the other nations, who worshipped a variety of gods, were supposed to be under the empire of the evil principle. These two conflicting powers exercise oppressions upon rational and immortal souls; and therefore the supreme God, to deliver them from bondage, sent to the Jews a being more like unto himself, even his son Jesus Christ, clothed with a certain shadowy resemblance of a body: this celestial messenger was attacked by the prince of darkness, and by the god of the Jews, but without effect. Those who follow the directions of this celestial conductor, mortify the body by fasting and austerities, and renounce the precepts of the god of the Jews and of the prince of darkness, shall after death ascend to the mansions of felicity and perfection. The rule of manners which Marcion prescribed to his followers was excessively austere, containing an express prohibition of wedlock, wine, flesh, and all the external comforts of life. Marcion denied the real birth, incarnation, and passion of Jesus Christ, and held them to be all apparent only. He denied the resurrection of the body; and allowed none to be baptized but those who preserved their continence; but these, he granted, might be baptized three times. In many things he followed the sentiments of the heretic Cerdon, and rejected the law and the prophets. He pretended the gospel had been corrupted by false prophets, and allowed none of the evangelists but St Luke, whom also he altered in many places as well as the epistles of St Paul, a great many things in which he threw out. In his own copy of St Luke he threw out the two first chapters entire.

MARCIANUS

Pages 216-216

a native of Thrace, born of an obscure family. After he had for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> served in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> soldier, he was made private secretary to one of the officers of Theodosius. His winning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> and uncommon talents raised him to higher stations; and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Theodosius II. A.D. 450, he was invested with the imperial purple in the east. The subjects of the Roman empire had reason to be satisfied with their choice. Marcianus showed himself <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and resolute; and when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTILA">Attila</a>, the barbarous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Huns, asked the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> the annual tribute, which the indolence and cowardice of his predecessors had regularly paid, the successor of Theodosius firmly said, that he kept his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> for his friends, but that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> was the metal which he had prepared for his enemies. In the midst of universal popularity, Marcianus died, after a reign of six years, in the 69th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, as he was making warlike preparations against the barbarians that had invaded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. His death was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> lamented; and indeed his merit was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, since his reign has been distinguished by the appellation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">Golden</a> Age. Marcianus married Pulcheria the sister of his predecessor. It is said, that in the years of his obscurity he found a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who had been murdered, and that he had the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> to give him a private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>; for which circumstance he was accused of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMICIDE">homicide</a>, and imprisoned. He was condemned to lose his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> would have been executed, had not the real murderer been discovered, and convinced the world of the innocence of Marcianus. Another emperor of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARCIONITES">Marcionites</a> east, A.D. 479, &c.

MARCITES

Pages 216-216

Marcites, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of heretics in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century, who also called themselves the perfecti, and made profession of doing everything with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> and without any fear. This doctrine they borrowed from Simon Magus, who however was not their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>; for they were called Marcites from one Marcus, who conferred the priesthood, and the administration of the sacraments, on women.

MARCOMANNI

Pages 216-217

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> people of Germany, who seem to have taken their name from their situation on the limits <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> marches, to the east of the Higher <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the Danube. Chaucer allots to them the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Wurtemburg, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Marcosians the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> between the Rhine and the Necker, the Brigau, and a part of Suabia, lying between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of the Danube and the river Bregenz; they afterwards removed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Boii, whom they expelled and forced to withdraw more to the east, occupying what is now called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>. (Strabo, Velleius.)

MARCOSIANS

Pages 217-217
or COLOBARIANS, an ancient sect in the church, making a branch of the VALENTINIANES. St Irenaeus speaks at large of the leader of this sect, Marcus, who it seems was reputed a great magician. The Marcosians had a great number of apocryphal books which they held for canonical, and of the same authority with ours. Out of these they picked several idle fables touching the infancy of Jesus Christ, which they put off for true histories. Many of these fables are still in use and credit among the Greek monks.

MARCULUS

Pages 217-217

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, a knocker <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> to knock at doors with. MARCUS AURELIUS ANTONINUS. See ANTONINUS.

MARDIKERS

Pages 217-217
or TOPASSES, a mixed breed of Dutch, Portuguese, Indians, and other nations, incorporated with the Dutch at Batavia, in the East Indies.

MAREOTIS

Pages 217-217

a lake in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>. Its neighbourhood was famous for wine, though according to some the Mareoticum vinum is the produce of Epirus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>, called also Mareotis, near Egypt.

MARETS

Pages 217-217

Samuel de, one of the most celebrated divines of the reformed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, was born in Picardy, in 1599. In 1620, he was settled in the church of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAON">Laon</a>; but, in 1624, accepted a call to that of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEDAN">Sedan</a>, to succeed James Cappel in the office of pastor and professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. Having soon after obtained leave of absence from his flock, he visited <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, where he was admitted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of divinity at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, in 1625. From Holland he took a voyage to England, and after a short stay in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> he returned to Sedan, where he commenced his labours in the divinity <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>. There he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years with reputation to himself, but not without being sometimes involved in troubles, which he bore with a commendable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>. In 1631 he was made chaplain to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> de Bouillon in Holland; but that nobleman having married a Roman Catholic lady, M. de Marets advised him to adhere steadfastly to the protestant <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, on which account he incurred the displeasure of the duchess. Thus circumstanced, he received in 1636, an invitation to become pastor to the church of Boisduval, with which he complied, and in the following year he was appointed professor of the schola illuftris of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. The duties of this office he discharged with such diligence and success, that in 1640, the curators of the university of Franeker sent him the offer of a professorship, which he declined; but two years after he accepted a similar offer from the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRONINGEN">Groningen</a>, to which his services were devoted for upwards of thirty years. In 1652 he was made sole minister of the Walloon church at Groningen, where till that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he had gratuitously preached once every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>, to assist the pastor. Influenced by the fame of his extraordinary merits, the magistrates of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERNE">Berne</a> in 1661 offered him the chair of professor of divinity at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAUSANNE">Lausanne</a>, with considerable emoluments, but he declined this offer; and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> happened before he took possession of a similar <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> at Leyden, of which he had accepted. His System of Divinity was found to be so methodical, that it was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of at other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a>; and at the end of it may be found a chronological <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of all his works. Their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> is prodigious; and their variety shows the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of his genius. He was moreover engaged in many disputes and controversies, and died in 1673.

MARGARET

Pages 217-219

St., a celebrated virgin, who, as is supposed, received the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of martyrdom at Antioch in the year 275; the manner of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> is not known. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> martyrologists make no mention of her name, and she did not become famous till the 11th century. There is no more foundation for what is said concerning her relics and girdle than for the stories which are told of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. A festival, however, is still held in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of her <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> on the 20th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>: See Baillet's Lives of the Saints, for that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. "Her actions (says this authority) have been so falsified and altered, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> even of Metaphrastus, that the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> have not thought proper to infest any of them into their breviary. The Orientals pay reverence to her by the name of Saint Pelagia <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Saint Marina, and the western church by that of Saint Gerusa or Saint Margaret." Margaret, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> and heiress of Florent <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, who is famous on account of a story repeated by a hundred compilers even of the 18th century. Having refused <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> to a woman whom she at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> accused of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a>, she was, a Margaret, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> from God, brought to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> (A.D. 1276), of 365 children, partly boys and partly girls. The boys, it is added, were all named John, and the girls <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. This story is represented in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> in a village not far from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>; and by the side of the painting are seen two large balcons of bras, on which it is pretended the 365 children were presented to be baptized. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> is a sufficient authority for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of any thing, it is impossible to tell how many fables would be fully attested. It has been remarked, that the most ancient annals are altogether silent concerning this fact; and that it is related only by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> writers, who besides do not agree with one another concerning either the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> of time, or the life of the countess, or the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the children; and in short, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a>, who was at that time bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, was called John, and not Gui, as the chronicles declare. Several learned men have endeavoured to trace the cause which could have given rise to a relation so extraordinary. M. Struik fixed upon the epitaphs of the mother and son, which appeared to him worthy of some <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>; and, in conformity to the dates which they bear, he supposed that the countess was brought to bed on Good Friday 1276, which was the 26th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>. Now, as the year then began on the 25th of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, there were only two days of the year elapsed when the countess was brought to bed, which circumstance caused it to be said that she had brought into the world as many children as there were days in the year. In fact only two children are mentioned in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, John and Elizabeth. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> thus explained is only a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> event, wherein there is nothing of the marvellous, but in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> meaning in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>. Later writers, who have not examined this circumstance, have ascribed 365 children to the countess. Margaret, Countess of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHMOND">Richmond</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a>, the learned and pious mother of Henry VII., was born at Bethloe in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEDFORDSHIRE">Bedfordshire</a>, in 1441; and was the sole heiress of John <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUFORT">Beaufort</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Somerset, grandson to John of Gaunt. Her mother was the heiress of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Beauchamp of Powick. Whilst yet very young, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> duke of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, minister to Henry VI., or rather to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Margaret, fought her in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> to his son; and she was at the same time solicited by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> for his half-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Edmund <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Richmond. To the latter she gave her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Henry VII. was the sole fruit of this marriage, his father dying when he was but 15 weeks old. Her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> husband was Sir Henry <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORD">Stafford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>, second son to the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a>; by whom she had no issue. Soon after his death, which happened in the year 1482, she sought consolation in a third husband, Thomas Lord Stanley, who, in the first year of her son's reign, was created earl of Derby. He died in the year 1504, without issue, being then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a> of England. She survived her lord not quite five years, dying at Westminster in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1509, in the 60th year of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. She was buried in Henry VII.'s chapel; on the south side of which was erected to her memory an altar-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> marble, with her statue of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>. From her funeral sermon preached by her confessor Margaret Bishop Fisher, who says Ballard, knew the very secrets of her <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, we learn, "that the poesyfied almost all things that were commendable in a woman, either in mind or body." She understood the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> perfectly, and had some knowledge of the Latin. She was devout even to austerity, in humility romantic, profuse in the encouragement of learning, and singularly chaste; but this last virtue became conspicuous only towards the latter end of a third marriage. "In her last husband's days (says Baker), she obtained a licence of him to live chaste, whereupon she took upon her the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOW">vow</a> of celibacy." A boon (says Mr Walpole), as seldom requested, I believe of a third husband, as it probably would be easily granted. Her life, from the turbulence of the times, and vicissitude of her son's fortune, must necessarily have been subject to infinite disquiet, which however she is said to have supported with singular fortitude. She wrote, 1. The Mirroure of Golde for the sinfull soule, translated from a French translation of a book called Speculum aureum peccatorum. Emprynted at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, in Fleet-street, at the signe of St George, by Richard Pynson, quarto, with cuts on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VELLUM">vellum</a>. 2. Translation of the fourth book of Dr Gerfen's Treatise of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">Imitation</a> and following the blest Life of our most merciful Saviour Christ. Printed at the end of Dr William Atkinson's English translation of the three first books, 1504. 3. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the king: in Howard's collection. 4. By her son's order and authority, she also made the orders for great estates of ladies and noble women, for their precedence, and wearing of barbes at funerals, over the chin and under the same. Margaret, the daughter of Woldemar III., king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, styled the Semiramis of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a>; she succeeded her father in the throne of Denmark, her husband in that of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>; and the crown of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> was given her as a recompense for delivering the Swedes from the tyranny of Albert their king. Thus possessed of the three kingdoms, she formed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of a perpetual union, which she accomplished, pro tempore only, by the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> styled the union of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALMAR">Calmar</a>. She died in 1412, aged 59. Margaret of Anjou, daughter of René d'Anjou, king of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and wife of Henry VI., king of England: an ambitious, enterprising, courageous woman. Intrepid in the field, she signalized herself by heading her troops in several battles against the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>; and if she had not been the author of her husband's misfortunes, by putting to death the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a> his uncle, her name would have been immortalized for the fortitude, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, and policy with which she supported the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of her husband and son, till the fatal defeat at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEWKESBURY">Tewkesbury</a>, which put an end to all her enterprises, the king being taken prisoner, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Edward their only son barely murdered by Richard duke of York. Margaret was ransomed by her father, and died in Anjou in 1482. See ENGLAND, No 201—226. Margaret, Duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>. See CAVENDISH. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARGARITA">Margarita</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEARL">Pearl</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, an island of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, the middle of which is seated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. MARGARITA Long. 64° 2' N. Lat. 11° 30'. It was discovered by Columbus, and is about 35 leagues in compass. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is very fertile in maize and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and abounds in pasture and verdant groves; yet is totally destitute of fresh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which the inhabitants are obliged to bring from the continent. When the Spaniards first landed here, they found the natives busy in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> for oysters. Columbus ordered some of the savages aboard his ship, who were so far from being terrified, that they very soon became familiar with the Spaniards. The latter at first imagined that the oysters served them for food; but on opening the shells, they found they contained valuable pearls. Upon this discovery they immediately landed, and found the natives ready to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> with their pearls for the merest trifles. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time the Spaniards built a castle, called Monopadre, and employed prodigious numbers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGOLA">Angola</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> in the pearl fishery; cruelly forcing them to tear up the oysters from the rocks to which they stuck, during which time many of them were destroyed by the sharks and other voracious fishes. In 1620, this island was invaded by the Dutch, who demolished the castle upon it; since which time it has been in a manner abandoned by the Spaniards; and is now principally inhabited by the natives, to whom some particular indulgences were granted by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, on account of their ready submission to Columbus.

MARGARITINI

Pages 219-219

are glass ornaments, made at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, of small glass tubes of different colours, which are blown at Murano, and which the women of the lower class wear about their arms and necks. The largest are used for making rosaries. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is performed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> dispatch, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> taking a whole handful of these tubes at once, and breaking them off one after another with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> tool. These short cylinders are mixed with a kind of ashes, and put over the fire in an iron <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">pan</a>; and when the two ends begin to melt, by stirring them about with an iron wire, they are brought to a round <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; but care is taken not to leave them too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> over the fire, lest the hole through which they are to be strung should be entirely closed by the melting of the glass. There are several streets at Francesco de Vigna entirely inhabited by people whose sole occupation is to make and string these margaritini.

MARGATE

Pages 219-219

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Thanet, near the North Foreland. It is noted for shipping vast quantities of corn (most, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not all, the product of that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>) for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; and has a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> bath at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, which has performed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> cures in nervous and paralytic <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, and numbness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>. It lies in St John's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>, which is a member of the port of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a>, at the distance of 14 miles, 12 from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, and 72 from London; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> season is frequented for sea-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a>, having become one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> watering places for the idle, the opulent, and the invalid, where they meet with every requisite accommodation; and the adjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> abounds with most extensive prospects and pleasant rides. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 30'. N. Lat. 51° 24'.

MARHATTAS

Pages 219-221

Merhattais, Marattas, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Mahattas; a people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, and by far the most Mahattas considerable of all the Hindoo powers. The Marhattas boast a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> antiquity; they profess the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of Brahma; speak a dialect of the Sanscrit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, in which they have introduced all the technical terms of Mogul administration; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> a character of their own in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, though not very different from some of the other tribes around them; and are divided into four castes or classes of people, with the various subdivisions of professional distinction found over the rest of Hindoostan; but with this remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that among the Marhattas every individual may, as in fact he occasionally does, follow the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of a soldier. As a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> inhabiting immemorially the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> properly denominated Marhat or Merhat, and comprehending the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Paithwa's present dominions in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECCAN">Deccan</a>, they were completely subjugated, and afterwards for many centuries deprived, first by the Patans, then by the Mogul conquerors of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a>. At length, towards the end of Alamgir's reign, they united, rebelled, and under the famous Seva-jeer or Seva-jeer, a leader of their own tribe, laid the foundations of their present vast empire, which has risen gradually on the ruins of the Mohamedan power, as related under the article Hindostan. Seva-jeer was succeeded by his son Rajah Sahou, who considerably extended the Marhatta dominions. When Rajah Sahou grew old and infirm, and the fatigues of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> began to press heavy upon him, he appointed Biffonat Balajee, a Brahman born at Gokum, and leader of about 25,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, to the office of Paithwa or vicegerent. Rajah Sahou died without issue, but left nephews by his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>. The courage and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of Balajee had gained him, during the latter years of the old rajah, the affection and esteem of all the nation. But, under an appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> and self-denial, his prevailing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> was ambition; and the sentiments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> and loyalty were absorbed in the desire to command. He made use of the influence he had acquired under his benefactor to firmly establish his own power, that he not only retained the high office of Paithwa during his life, but transmitted it to his posterity. The Marhattas, gradually forgetting a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> they knew nothing of, became accustomed to obey his vicegerent only; yet a certain respect for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, or the dread of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of violating the strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> which the nation still retains in favour of the family of its founder, have served perhaps to preserve it; and the descendants of Rajah Sahou's nephews yet exist, but are kept in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at Sattarah. The eldest is styled Ram Rajah, or sovereign; his name is on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> of the Marhatta state; but his person is unknown, except to those who immediately surround him. He resides in his splendid prison, encompassed with the appendages of eastern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, but deprived of all power, and kept totally ignorant of business. The seat of government was transferred from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> royal residence of Sattarah to Poonah; and the usurper, as well as his successors, seem still to have acted under the supposed authority of the deposed prince, by their assuming no other <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> or character than that Marhattas of Paithwa or prime minister. From this change, the empire of the Ram Rajah has been distinguished only by the appellation of the Pai/ba/ship, or otherwise the Government of Poonah, from the name of its present <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. Biflonat Balajee was succeeded as Paithwa by his eldest son Balajee Row (called also Nana Saheb, or Nanah Row), who left three sons, the eldest of whom, Balajee Pundit, sometimes called Nanah Pundit, succeeded him. The two others were Rogobah or Ragornat Row, and Shamheer Row. Balajee Pundit left two sons; Mahadava Row, who was Paithwa twelve years; and Narrain Row, who succeeded him. During the latter part of the life of Mahadava Row, his uncle Rogobah was confined to the palace at Poonah, for reasons with which we are not acquainted. Mahadava Row died without issue; and upon the accession of Narrain his brother, a youth of about 19 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, Rogobah in vain applied to be released from his confinement. He is therefore suspected of having entered into a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> with two officers in his nephew's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, Somair Jing and Yuluph Gardie, in order to procure that by force which he could not obtain by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>. The correspondence between the conspirators was carried on with so much secrecy, that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> had not the least intimation or suspicion of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, till every avenue leading to the palace had been secured, and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> surrounded by the troops under the command of those two officers. It is said, that on the first alarm, Narrain Row, supposing his uncle, ran to his apartment, threw himself at his feet, and implored his protection: "You are my uncle (said he), spare the blood of your own family, and take possession of a government which I am willing to resign to you." Somair and Yuluph entered the room whilst the young Paithwa was in this suppliant posture. Rogobah, with apparent surprise and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a>, ordered them to withdraw; but as they either knew him not to be sincere, or thought they had proceeded too far to retreat, they stabbed Narrain with their poniards whilst he clung to his uncle's <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>. The office of Paithwa being now vacant, the chiefs of the nation then at Poonah were assembled, and Rogobah being the only survivor of the family of Biflonat Balajee, to whose <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> the Marhattas in those parts are enthusiastically attached, he was named to fill it. Being naturally of a warlike temper, he resolved to undertake some foreign expedition; for besides gratifying his passion for the field, he probably hoped, by the splendour of his exploits, to draw off the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the public from inquiring into the late catastrophe. A pretence for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> was not difficult to be found. He renewed the claim of his nation to the chout, and marched his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> towards Hydrabad, the capital of the Nizam. The vigour of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> procured him an accommodation of his demand; and he was proceeding to enforce a similar one upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARNATIC">Carnatic</a>, when he received intelligence which obliged him to return hastily to Poonah. Although the Marhatta chiefs had acknowledged Rogobah as Paithwa, yet they and the people in general were much dissatisfied with his conduct. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDERERS">murderers</a> of Narrain Row had not only escaped <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, but, as was reported, had been rewarded. The crime was unexampled, and the perpetrators were beheld with uncommon horror and detestation. The Paithwa had hitherto so fully possessed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of the people, that, till then, guards were considered as unnecessary about the person of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> whose character rendered him inviolable. Every one therefore had free access to his palace, and he relied with confidence for his safety upon the affections of those who approached him. These reflections operated powerfully upon the minds of the Marhattas; but perhaps no violent consequences would have ensued, had it not been discovered, soon after the departure of Rogobah from Poonah, that the widow of Narrain Row, Ganga Baee, was pregnant. This determined their wavering resolutions. Frequent consultations were held among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> men then in the capital; and it was finally resolved to abjure the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> they had sworn to Rogobah, and declare the child, yet unborn, to be the legal successor of the late paithwa. A <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of regency was immediately appointed to govern the country until the child should become of age; and it was agreed to reserve their deliberations, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it should prove a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> or die, till the event should render them necessary. They who principally conducted these measures, and whose names <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> on that account be remembered, were Sackharam Baboo and Balajee Pundit, called also Nanah Pher Nevees from his having been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> the principal secretary of the Marhatta state. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">Nine</a> other Marhatta leaders approved of these measures, and swore to maintain them. As the first step towards the execution of their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, the widow of Narrain Row was conveyed to Poorendher, a fort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strength, situated on a high mountain, about 25 miles from Poonah. As soon as Rogobah received intimation of this revolution, he marched back towards the capital. But discontent had already infected his troops; some of the chiefs retired to their estates, and others joined the standard of the regents. He however risked a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> with an army of the revolters commanded by Trimbec Row, in which the latter was slain; but though he obtained a victory, the strength of the confederates daily increased, while his own troops were diminished by continual defections. He therefore found it necessary to retire to Ugein, and to solicit the affluence of the Marhatta chiefs Scindia and Holkar; but meeting with a refusal, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURAT">Surat</a>, and applied for succours to the English. Rogobah's success in this application was the cause of two wars with the Marhatta state; which, after much waste of blood and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, we were obliged to conclude by relinquishing his claim, and acknowledging as legal paithwa the son of Narrain Row, who was born about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> months after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father. See INDIA and HINDOSTAN. The Marhatta dominions, as already observed, are governed by a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of separate chiefs, all of whom acknowledge the Ram Rajah as their sovereign; and all except Moodajee Boonfalal, own the paithwa as his vicegerent. The country immediately subject to the paithwa, including all the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> territories that were left by the Rajah Sahou to the Ram Rajah, Mookajee Boonsaiah, rajah of Berar, possessed, besides Berar, the greatest part of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORISSA">Orissa</a>. This prince being descended from the line of the Ram Rajah, eyes the power of the peshwa, by whom a branch of his family is kept in ignominious confinement, with ill will; has often refused to support his measures; and, on some occasions, has even seemed inclined to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> against him. Next to Mookajee, in point of importance, must be ranked Madajee Scindia, a bold and aspiring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, who possesses the greatest part of the extensive feudatory or government of Malwa, together with part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Candith. The remainder is under the dominion of Holkar. Both he and Scindia pretend to be descended from the ancient kings of Malva. Scindia resides chiefly at Ugein, near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Mandu, once the capital of these kings; and Holkar at Indore, a town little more than 30 miles west of it. The dominions of these, and of some chiefs of less consequence, extend as far as the river Jumna. The measures pursued by the Marhattas for some years left little room to doubt that they aspired at the sovereignty of all Hindostan, or at least at the expulsion of the Mohammedan princes: And in this last design they appear to have succeeded*, and to have gained a great accession of territory, through the arms of Scindia, both by the capture of the cities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGRA">Agra</a> and Delhi, with their territorial dependencies, and the consequent captivity of the unfortunate monarch who ruled there as the last imperial representative of the great Mogul race of Timur. "The whole of the dominion thus newly established is of vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, stretching near 1200 miles along the frontiers of Tippoo and the Nizam in a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, from Goa on the Malabar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> to Balafere in Orissa adjoining to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>; and from thence north-westly 1200 miles more, touching the confines of the British and allied states, on the borders of the Ganges and Jumna, to the territory of the Seiks at Paniput," rendered famous in 1761 for the last memorable defeat sustained by the Marhattas in their ambitious contest for empire with the united declining power of the Mohammedans. From this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in a southerly course, with great encroachment on the old eastern boundary of the Rajapoot country of Ajmere, it runs about 260 miles to the little Hindoo principality of Kotta, and thence south-westly 540 miles further to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> point of the foubah of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUJERAT">Gujerat</a> at Duarka, including the whole of that fertile province; from whence, along the seacoast of Cambay and Malabar to Goa, the distance may be reckoned 800 miles.
