Thus the overgrown empire of the Marhattas may be said to extend east 19 degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> of 22 degrees north latitude, from the mouths of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDUS">Indus</a> to those of the Ganges; and about 13 degrees of latitude north, from the Kishnagh to Paniput; comprehending at least an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of 400,000 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> geographical miles, being considerably more than a third part of Hindostan, including the Decan, and equal perhaps in dimensions to all the British and allied states in India, with those of Golconda and Mylore, taken together. Such was the state of affairs in India so far as the Marhattas were concerned a few years ago. By consulting the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of India, the reader will observe, that the power and dominion of these enterprising chiefs have been since greatly abridged by the successful progress of the British arms. See INDIA.

MARIA

Pages 221-221
or Sancta Maria, an island of the Indian ocean, lying about five miles east from Madagascar. It is about 27 miles long and five broad; well watered, and surrounded by rocks. The air is extremely moist, for it rains almost every day. It is inhabited by 500 or 600 negroes, but seldom visited by ships. Maria, St., a considerable town of South America, in the audience of Panama, built by the Spaniards after they had discovered the gold mines near it, and soon after taken by the English. It is seated at the bottom of the gulf of St Michael, at the mouth of a river of the same name; which is navigable, and the largest that falls into the gulf. The Spaniards come here every year in the dry season, which continues three months, to gather the gold dust out of the sands of the neighbouring streams; and carry away great quantities. W. Long. 148°. N. Lat. 7°. Maria, St., a handsome and considerable town of Spain, in Andalusia, with a small castle. It was taken by the English and Dutch in 1702, for the archduke of Austria. It is seated on the Guadalata, at the mouth of which is a tower and a cloister. W. Long. 5°. 33'. N. Lat. 36°. 35'. MARIAN ISLANDS. See Ladrones Islands.

MARIANA

Pages 221-221

John, a learned Spanish historian, born at Talavera in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>. He entered among the Jesuits in 1554, at 17 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and became one of the most learned men of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> divine, a good humanist, and profoundly versed in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> as well as profane <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. He taught at Rome, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; and died at Toledo in 1624. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are: 1. An excellent history of Spain in 30 books; which he himself translated from the Latin into Spanish, without fervently following his own Latin edition. 2. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SCHOLIUM">Scholium</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> short notes on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>. 3. A treatise on the changes the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> has undergone in Spain; for which he was thrown into prison by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Lerma, the Spanish minister. 4. A famous treatise De regis et regiae institutione, which made much noise, and was condemned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of Paris to be burnt by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> hangman, for his asserting in that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, that it is lawful to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> tyrants. 5. A work on the faults of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of Jesuits, which has been translated into Spanish, Latin, Italian, French, &c.

MARIANUS SCOTUS

Pages 221-221

an Irish monk, was related to the venerable Bede, and wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONICLE">chronicle</a> which is esteemed. He died in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FULDA">Fulda</a> in 1086, aged 38.

MARIBONE

Pages 221-222
or St Mary le Bone, or rather Borne, from the neighbouring brook, a parish of Middlesex, on the north-west side of London. The manor appears to have belonged anciently to the bishop of London. London. The houses in this parish are very numerous, comprising several extensive streets and squares, which are every year increasing. The Paddington road from Illington passes through this parish, which gives it communication with the eastern part of London without passing through the streets. Here were three conduits erected about the year 1238, for supplying the city of London with water; but anno 1753, when it was plentifully served by the New River, the citizens let them out at £100 a-year for 43 years. There were two for receiving its water at the north-east corner of the bridge on the river Tyburn, and over them stood the lord mayor's banqueting house, to which (the use of coaches being not then known) his lordship and the aldermen used to ride on horseback, as their ladies did in waggons. This banqueting house, after being many years neglected, was taken down in 1737, and the cisterns arched over. This village, if it may be called by that name, is joined by new buildings to London. The old church, which was a mean edifice, was pulled down, and a new one erected in 1741. Besides which it has a great number of chapels of every sect and persuasion, and an extensive workhouse for the poor.

MARIDUNUM

Pages 222-222

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Demetae in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. Now Caer Mardin, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CAERMARTHEN">Caermarthen</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAERMARTHENSHIRE">Caermarthenshire</a>.

MARIGALANTE

Pages 222-222

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and one of the least of the Caribbees, lies in N. Lat. 16° 32' and W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 61° 5', from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, at the distance of four leagues from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUADALOUPE">Guadaloupe</a>, to the south. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, produce, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, are pretty much the same as the other Caribbees. Columbus discovered it in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> American voyage in 1493, and called it by the name of his ship <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> Galanta, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Gallant <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>. It is about six leagues long, and between three and four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. Viewed at a distance from on board a ship, it appears like a floating island, because, as it is for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> flat, the trees seem to swim; but a nearer prospect shows it to be intersected by some rising grounds, which give a fine variety to the landscape. The French settled here in 1648; and it was taken by the English in 1691, but the French soon got possession of it again. It was again taken by the British in 1759, but afterwards restored at the peace 1763.—This island was thought, on its first discovery, to want <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; but a charming running stream has in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> been discovered, no less convenient than refreshing and wholesome, on the banks of which are some wealthy planters, and excellent plantations of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. A little village in a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the island, and here the commandant resides. The whole island is very capable of improvement; the soil being almost equally good, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> rising nowhere too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> affords many little bays, and safe anchorage and shelter to ships.

MARINE

Pages 222-222

a general name for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> state; as also the whole economy of naval affairs; or whatever respects the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, rigging, arming, equipping, navigating, and fighting ships. It comprehends also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of naval armaments, and the state of all the persons employed therein, whether civil or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the marine affairs of any one state is a very comprehensive subject, much more that of all nations. Those who would be informed of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> affairs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> it has made at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> in all ages, may find abundance of curious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in Selden's Mare Clavigera; and from his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to ours, we may trace a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of facts in Ledward's and Burchet's Naval History; but above all in the Lives of the Admirals, by the accurate and judicious Dr Campbell.

MARINES

Pages 222-225
or Marine Forces, a body of soldiers raised for the sea service, and trained to fight either in a naval engagement or in an action ashore. The great service of this useful corps was manifested frequently in the course of the war before last, particularly at the siege of Belleisle, where they acquired a great character, although lately raised and hardly exercised in military discipline. At sea they are incorporated with the ship's crew, of which they make a part; and many of them learn in a short time to be excellent seamen, to which their officers are ordered by the admiralty to encourage them, although no sea officer is to order them to go aloft against their inclination. In a sea fight their small arms are of very great advantage in securing the decks of the enemy; and when they have been long enough at sea to stand firm when the ship rocks, they must be infinitely preferable to seamen if the enemy attempts to board, by raising a battalion with their fixed bayonets to oppose him. The sole direction of the corps of marines is vested in the lords commissioners of the admiralty; and in the admiralty is a distinct apartment for this purpose. The secretary to the admiralty is likewise secretary to the marines, for which he has a salary of £300 a-year; and he has under him several clerks for the management of this department. The marine forces of Great Britain in the time of peace are stationed in three divisions; one of which is quartered at Chatham, one at Portsmouth, and another at Plymouth. By a late regulation, they are ordered to do duty at the several dock-yards of those ports, to prevent embezzlement of the king's stores, for which a captain's guard mounts every day; which certainly requires great vigilance, as so many abuses of this kind have been committed, that many of the inhabitants, who have been long used to an infamous traffic of this kind, expect these conveyances at certain periods as their due, and of course resent this regulation in the highest degree as an infringement of their liberties as British subjects. The marine corps are under the command of their own field officers, who discipline them, and regulate their different duties. His late majesty in 1760 formed a new establishment of marine officers, entitled, the general, lieutenant-general, and three colonels of marines (one for each division), to be taken from officers in the royal navy. The two first are always enjoyed by flag officers, the last by post captains only. This establishment was formed to reward such officers who distinguished themselves in the service of their country. Marine Discipline, is the training up soldiers for sea service, in such exercises as the various positions of the firelock and body, and teaching them every manoeuvre that can be performed on board ships of war at sea. See Exercise. Marine Chair, a machine invented by Mr Irwin for viewing the satellites of Jupiter at sea, and of course course determining the longitude by their eclipses. An account of it is given in the Journal Etranger for March 1768. An account of its accuracy was published the year following by M. de l'Isle astronomer in the Imperial academy of Petersburg; but notwithstanding the encomiums bestowed upon it by this gentleman, it hath never come into general use; and therefore we may conclude, that it is much inferior to the inventions of Mr Harrison for the same purpose. See Harrison and Longitude. Marine Surveyor, is the name of a machine contrived by Mr H. de Saunarez for measuring the way of a ship in the sea. This machine is in the form of the letter Y, and is made of iron, or any other metal. At each end of the lines which constitute the angle or upper part of that letter, are two pallets, not much unlike the figure of the log; one of which falls in the same proportion as the other rises. The falling or pendant pallet meeting a resistance from the water, as the ship moves, has by that means a circular motion under water, which is faster or slower according as the vessel moves. This motion is communicated to a dial within the ship, by means of a rope fastened to the tail of the Y, and carried to the dial. The motion being thus communicated to the dial, which has a bell in it, it strikes exactly the number of geometrical paces, miles, or leagues, which the ship has run. Thus the ship's distance is ascertained; and the forces of tides and currents may also be discovered by this instrument: which, however, has been very little used. Marine Acid, an old name given to muriatic acid, which see in Chemistry Index. Mariner, the same with a sailor or seaman. See these articles. Method of preserving the health of Mariners. See Seamen. Mariner's Compass. See Compass. St Marino, a small town and republic of Italy, situated in E. Long. 13° 44'. N. Lat. 44° 21'. This small republic consists only of a mountain, and a few hillocks, that lie scattered about the bottom of it. The number of the inhabitants is about 5000. The mountain yields good wine, but they have no other than rain or snow water. The founder of the republic was a Dalmatian, and a man, who upwards of 1300 years ago turned hermit, and retired to this mountain. Here his devotion and austerity, and, in consequence of that, his reputation for sanctity, were such, that the princes of the country made him a present of the mountain; on which many, out of veneration for the saint, soon after took up their abode. Thus was the foundation laid of the town and republic, which still bears the name of the saint. The town stands on the top of the mountain, and there is only one way by which it can be come at. In the whole territory are only three villages, three convents, and five churches. The largest of the churches is dedicated to the saint, and contains his ashes and his statue. He is looked upon as the greatest saint, next to the blessed Virgin; and to speak disrespectfully of him is accounted blasphemy, and punished as such. The republic is under the protection of the pope. All that are capable of bearing arms are exercised, and ready at a minute's call. In the ordinary course of government, the administration is in the hands of the council of 60, which, notwithstanding its name, consists only of 40; one-half of the members of which are of the noble families, and the other of the plebeian: on extraordinary occasions, however, the arengo, in which every house has its representative, is called together. The two principal officers are the capitaneos, who are chosen every half year; and next to them is the commissary, who judges in civil and criminal matters, and is joined in commission with the capitaneos; both he and the physician must be foreigners, and both have their salaries out of the public stock. When any person, after due summons, neglects to assist at the council according to their statute book, he is to be fined in about a penny English; and when an ambassador is to be sent to any foreign state, he is to be allowed about 1s. a-day. Marino, John Baptist, a celebrated Italian poet, born at Naples in 1569. His father, who was an able civilian, obliged him to study the law; at which being disgusted, he left his parents, and retired to the house of the Sieur Manzi, who was a friend to all persons of wit. He at length became secretary to Matthew of Capua, great admiral of the kingdom of Naples, and contracted a friendship with Talio. A short time after, he went to Rome; and entered into the service of Cardinal Aldobrandini, nephew to Pope Clement VIII. who took him with him to Savoy. Marino was in great favour with the court of Turin; but afterwards created himself many enemies there, the most furious of whom was the poet Gasparo Murtola, who, attempting to shoot him with a pistol, wounded one of the duke of Savoy's favourites. Marino being obliged to leave Turin, went to Paris at the desire of Queen Mary de Medicis, and published there his poem on Adonis. He afterwards went to Rome, where he was made prince of the academy of the humorists; from thence to Naples, where he died while he was preparing to return home. He had a very lively imagination, but little judgement; and, giving way to the points and conceits then in vogue, his authority, far from correcting the false taste of the Italians, served rather to keep it farther from reformation. His works, which are numerous, have been often printed. Marinus, an engraver, who flourished about the year 1630, and resided principally at Antwerp. His plates, Mr Strutt observes, are executed in a very singular style, with the graver only: The strokes are very fine and delicate, and crossed over each other in a lozenge-like form, which he filled up with thin long dots. His prints, though generally very neat, want the style of the matter in the determination of the folds of the draperies and the outline of the human figure; the extremities of which are heavy, and not marked with precision. Fine impressions from his best plates are, however, much sought after by collectors; those especially after Rubens and Jordans are held in high estimation. Marionis, in Ancient Geography, a town of Germany: now Hamburg, a famous trading city on the Elbe, in Lower Saxony, in the duchy of Holstein. Another Marionis (Ptolemy), thought to be Wismar, a town of Lower Saxony, in the duchy of Mecklenburgh. Marjoram. See Origanum, Botany Index. Maritagium. In the feudal custom, maritagium glia. This prohibited all ships of foreign nations from trading with any English plantations, without license from the council of state. In 1651, the prohibition was extended also to the mother country; and no goods were suffered to be imported into England, or any of its dependencies, in any other than English bottoms; or in the ships of that European nation of which the merchandise imported was the genuine growth or manufacture. At the Restoration, the former provisions were continued, by stat. 12 Car. II. c. 18, with this very material improvement, that the master and three-fourths of the mariners shall also be English subjects. Many laws have been made for the supply of the royal navy with seamen; for their regulation when on board; and to confer privileges and rewards on them during and after their service. 1. For their supply. The principal, but the most odious, though often necessary method for this purpose, is by impressing; see IMPRESSING. But there are other ways that tend to the increase of seamen, and manning the royal navy. Parishes may bind out poor boys apprentices to the masters of merchantmen, who shall be protected from impressing for the first three years; and if they are impressed afterwards, the masters shall be allowed their wages: great advantages in point of wages are given to volunteer seamen, in order to induce them to enter into his majesty's service: and every foreign seaman, who, during a war shall serve two years in any man of war, merchantman, or privateer, is naturalized ipso facto. About the middle of King William's reign, a scheme was set on foot for a register of seamen to the number of 30,000 for a constant and regular supply of the king's fleet; with great privileges to the registered men; and, on the other hand, heavy penalties in case of their non-appearance when called for; but this registry, being judged to be rather a badge of slavery, was abolished by stat. 9 Ann. c. 21. 2. The method of ordering seamen in the royal fleet, and keeping up a regular discipline there, is directed by certain express rules, articles, and orders, first enacted by the authority of parliament soon after the Restoration; but since new modelled and altered, after the peace of Aix-la-Chapelle, to remedy some defects which were of fatal consequences in conducting the preceding war. In these articles of the navy almost every possible offence is set down, and the punishment thereof annexed: in which respect the seamen have much the advantage over their brethren in the land service; whose articles of war are not enacted by parliament, but framed from time to time at the pleasure of the crown. Yet from whence this distinction arose, and why the executive power, which is limited to properly with regard to the navy, should be so extensive with regard to the army, it is hard to assign a reason: unless it proceeded from the perpetual establishment of the navy, which rendered a permanent law for their regulation expedient, and the temporary duration of the army, which subsisted only from year to year, and might therefore with less danger be subjected to discretionary government. But, whatever was apprehended at the first formation of the mutiny act, the regular renewal of our standing force at the entrance of every year has made this distinction idle. For, For, if from experience past, we may judge of future events, the army is now lattingly ingratiated into the British constitution; with this singularly fortunate circumstance, that any branch of the legislature may annually put an end to its legal existence, by refusing to concur in its continuance. 3. The privileges conferred on sailors, are pretty much the same with those conferred on soldiers, with regard to relief, when maimed, or wounded, or superannuated, either by county-rates, or the royal hospital at Greenwich; with regard also to the exercise of trades, and the power of making nuncupative testaments; and farther, no seaman aboard his majesty's ships can be arrested for any debt, unless the same be sworn to amount at least to twenty pounds; though, by the annual mutiny acts, a soldier may be arrested for a debt which extends to half that value, but not to a less amount.

MARIUS

Pages 225-226

the famous Roman general, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> times <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, who fulfilled his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> reputation by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> barbarities. He was born at Arpinum, of obscure and illiterate parents. He forsook the meaner occupations of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>; and dignified himself under Scipio, at the siege of Numantia. The Roman general <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the courage and intrepidity of young Marius, and foretold the era of his future greatness. By his seditions and intrigues at Rome, while he exercised the inferior offices of the state, he rendered himself known; and his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with Julia, who was of the family of the Caesars, contributed in some manner to raise him to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. He passed into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> to the consul Metellus against Jugurtha; and after he had there ingratiated himself with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, and raised enemies to his friend and benefactor, he returned to Rome and canvassed for the consulship. The extravagant promises he made to the people, and his malevolent intimations about the conduct of Metellus, proved successful. He was elected and appointed to finish the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against Jugurtha. He showed himself capable in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> to succeed to Metellus. Jugurtha was defeated, and afterwards betrayed into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> by the perfidy of Bocchus. No sooner was Jugurtha conquered, than new honours and fresh trophies awaited Marius. The provinces of Rome were suddenly invaded by an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of 300,000 barbarians, and Marius was the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> and boldness could resist so powerful an enemy. He was elected consul, and sent against the Teutones. The war was prolonged, and Marius was a third and fourth <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> invested with the consulship. At last two engagements were fought, and not less than 200,000 of the barbarian forces of the Ambrones and Teutones were slain in the field of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, and 90,000 made prisoners. The following year, A.U.C. 651, was also marked by a total overthrow of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CIMBRI">Cimbri</a>, another horde of barbarians; in which 140,000 were slaughtered by the Romans, and 60,000 taken prisoners. After such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> victories, Marius with his colleague Catullus entered Rome in triumph; and for his eminent services he received the appellation of the third founder of Rome. He was elected consul a fifth time; and as his intrepidity had delivered his country from its foreign enemies, he sought employment at home, and his restless ambition began to raise seditions, and to oppose the power of Sylla. This was the foundation of a civil war. Sylla refused to deliver up the command of his forces, with which he was empowered to prosecute the Mithridatic war; and he resolved to oppose in person the authors of a demand which he considered as arbitrary and improper. He advanced to Rome, and Marius was obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> by flight. The unfavourable winds prevented him from seeking a safer retreat in Africa, and he was left on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Campania, where the emissaries of his enemy soon discovered him in a marsh, where he had plunged himself in the mud, and left only his mouth above the surface for respiration. He was violently dragged to the neighbouring town of Minturnae; and the magistrates, all devoted to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Sylla, passed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of immediate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> on their magnanimous prisoner. A <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a> was commanded to cut off his head in the dungeon; but the stern countenance of Marius disarmed the courage of the executioner; and when he heard the exclamation of Tune, homo, audes occidere Caenum Marium? the dagger dropped from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Such an uncommon adventure moved the compassion of the inhabitants of Minturnae. They released Marius from prison; and favoured his escape to Africa, where he joined his son Marius, who had been arming the princes of that country in his cause. Marius landed near the walls of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, and he received no small consolation at the sight of the venerable ruins of a once powerful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, which like himself had been exposed to calamity, and felt the cruel vicissitude of fortune. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his retreat was soon known; and the governor of Africa, to conciliate the favour of Sylla, compelled Marius to fly to a neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. He soon after learned that Cinna had embraced his cause at Rome, when the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> had stripped him of his consular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and bestowed it upon one of his enemies. This intelligence animated Marius; he set sail to assist his friend only at the head of 1000 men. His army, however, was soon increased, and he entered Rome like a conqueror. His enemies were inhumanly sacrificed to his fury; Rome was filled with blood; and he, who once had been called the father of his country, marched through the streets of the city, attended by a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of assassins, who immediately slaughtered all those whose salutations were not answered by their leader. Such were the signals for bloodshed. When Marius and Cinna had sufficiently gratified their resentment, they made themselves consuls; but Marius, already worn out with old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> and infirmities, died sixteen days after he had been honoured with the consular dignity for the seventh time, A.U.C. 666. Such was the end of Marius, who rendered himself conspicuous by his victories and by his cruelty. As he was brought up in poverty and among peasants, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not appear wonderful that he always betrayed rudeness in his behaviour, and despised in others those polished manners and that studied <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> had denied him. He hated the conversation of the learned only because he was illiterate; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he appeared an example of sobriety and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>, he owed these advantages to the years of obscurity which he passed at Arpinum. His countenance was stern, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> firm and imperious, and his disposition untractable. He was in the 70th year of his age when he died; and Rome seemed to rejoice at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of a man whose ambition had proved so fatal to many of her citizens. His only qualifications were those of a great general; and with these he rendered himself the most illustrious and powerful of the Romans, because he was the only one whose ferocity seemed capable to oppose the barbarians of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. Marius, C., the son of the great Marius, was as cruel as his father, and shared his good and his adverse fortune. He made himself consul in the 25th year of his age, and murdered all the senators who opposed his ambitious views. He was defeated by Sylla, and fled to Praeneste, where he killed himself. Marius, M. Aurelius, a native of Gaul; who, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> employment of a blacksmith, became one of the generals of Gallienus, and at last caused himself to be saluted <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>. Three days after this elevation, a man who had shared his poverty without partaking of his more prosperous fortune, publicly assassinated him, and he was killed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> which he himself had made in the time of his obscurity. Marius has been often celebrated for his great strength; and it is confidently reported, that he could flop, with one of his fingers only, the wheel of a chariot in its most rapid course. Marius, Maximus, a Latin writer, who published an account of the Roman emperors from Trajan to Alexander, now lost. His compositions were entertaining, and executed with great exactness and fidelity. Some have accused him of inattention, and complain that his writings abounded with many fabulous and insignificant stories.

MARIVAX

Pages 226-226
Peter Carlet de, a French writer in the dramatic way and in romance, was born of a good family at Paris in 1688. A fine understanding, well improved by education, distinguished him early. His first object was the theatre, where he met with the highest success in comic productions; and these, with the merit of his other works, procured him a place in the French academy. The great characteristic of both his comedies and romances was, to convey an useful moral under the veil of wit and sentiment: "My only object (says he) is to make men more just and more humane;" and he was as amiable in his life and conversation as he was in his writings. He died at Paris in 1763, aged 75. His works consist of: 1. Pieces de Theatre, 4 vols. 12mo. 2. Homere travesti, 12mo; which is not supposed to have done much honour to his tale. 3. Le Spectateur Francais, 2 vols. 12mo. 4. Le Philosophe Indigent, 12mo. 5. Vie de Marianne, 2 vols. 12mo; one of the best romances in the French language. 6. Le Payson Parvenu, 12mo. 7. Pharsamon; inferior to the former.

MARK

Pages 226-227

Sr., was by birth a Jew, and descended of the tribe of Levi. He was converted by some of the apostles, probably by St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>; to whom he was a constant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> in all his travels, supplying the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of an amanuensis and interpreter. He was by St Peter sent into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, fixing his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> residence at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, and the places thereabout: where he was so successful in his ministry, that he converted multitudes both of men and women. He afterwards removed westwards, towards the parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>, going through the countries of Marmarica, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTAPOLIS">Pentapolis</a>, and others thereabouts; where, notwithstanding the barbarity and idolatry of the inhabitants, he planted the gospel. Upon his return to Alexandria, he ordered the affairs of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and there suffered martyrdom in the following manner. About Easter, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the solemnities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERAPIS">Serapis</a> were celebrated, the idolatrous people, being excited to vindicate the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of their deity, broke in upon St Mark, while he was performing divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and, binding him with cords, dragged him through the streets, and thrust him into prison, where in the night he had the comfort of a divine vision. Next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> the enraged multitude used him in the same manner, till his spirits failing, he expired under their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. Some add, that they burnt his body, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> decently interred his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> and ashes near the place where he used to preach. This happened in the year of Christ 68. Some writers assert, that the remains of St Mark were afterwards, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pomp, translated from Alexandria to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. However, he is the tutelar saint and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of that republic, and has a very rich and stately church erected to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> is author of one of the four gospels <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> with his name. See the following article. St Mark's Gospel, a canonical book of the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, being one of the four gospels. St Mark wrote his gospel at Rome, where he accompanied St Peter in the year of Christ 44. Tertullian and others pretend, that St Mark was no more than an amanuensis to St Peter, who dictated this gospel to him; others affirm, that he wrote it after St Peter's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Nor are the learned less divided as to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> it was written in; some affirming that it was composed in Greek, others in Latin. Several of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> heretics received only the gospel of St Mark; others, among the Catholics, rejected the 12 last verses of this gospel. The gospel of St Mark is properly an abridgement of that of St Matthew. St Mark the Evangelist's Day, a festival of the Christian church, observed April 25. Canons of St Mark, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of regular canons founded at Manua, by Albert Spinola, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, towards the end of the 12th century. Spinola made a rule for them, which was approved, corrected, and confirmed by several succeeding popes. About the year 1450 they were reformed, and followed only the rule of St Augustine. This congregation having flourished for the space of 400 years, declined by little and little, and is now become extinct. Knights of St Mark, an order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a> in the republic of Venice, under the protection of St Mark the evangelist. The arms of the order are, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULES">gules</a>, a lion winged <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>; with this device, Pax tibi Marge Evangelista. This order is never conferred but on those who have done signal service to the commonwealth. Mark, or Marc, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> used in several states of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and for several commodities, especially <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver. In France, the mark is divided into eight ounces, 64 drachms, 192 deniers or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>-weights, 160 écuflins, 300 muids, 642 félins, or 4668 grains. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, the mark weight is also called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>-weight, and is equal to that of France. When gold and silver are sold by the mark, it is divided into 25 carats. MARK is also used among us for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> of account, and in some other countries for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>. See Money-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">Table</a>. The English mark is two thirds of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>, or 13s. 4d., and the Scotch mark is of equal value in Scots money of account, viz. 13½d.

MARKET

Pages 227-227

a public <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> town, in which live cattle, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, or other goods, are set to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>; and also a privilege, either by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, by which a town is enabled to keep a market. Courts of the Clerk of the Market, is incident to every fair and market in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, to punish misdemeanors therein; and a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of pie powdr is to determine all disputes relating to private or civil <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. The object of this jurisdiction (see Stat. 17 Car. II. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 10.; 22 Car. II. cap. 8.; 23 Car. II. cap. 12.) is principally the cognizance of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WEIGHTS_AND_MEASURES">weights and <a class</a>="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> to try whether they be according to the true standard thereof or not; which standard was anciently committed to the custody of the bishop, who appointed some clerk under him to inspect the abuse of them more narrowly; and hence this officer, though now usually a layman, is called the clerk of the market.—<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> they be not according to the standard, then, beside the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of the party by fine, the weights and measures themselves ought to be burnt. This is the lowest court of criminal jurisdiction in the kingdom.

MARKLAND

Pages 227-227

JEREMIAH, one of the most learned scholars and penetrating critics of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was born in 1692, and received his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in Christ's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>. He became first publicly known by his Epistle Critica, addressed to Bishop Hare. In this he gave many proofs of extensive erudition and critical facility. He afterwards published an edition of Statius, and some plays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a>; and assisted Dr Taylor in his editions of Lytias and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEMOSTHENES">Demosthenes</a>, by the notes which he communicated to him. He has also very happily elucidated some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, which may be found in Mr Bowyer's edition of it; and was author of a very valuable volume of remarks on the epistles of Cicero to Brutus, and of an excellent little treatise under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Quæstio Grammatica. He died in 1775, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DORKING">Dorking</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>; and was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> not more valued for his universal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> than beloved for the excellency of his heart and primitive simplicity of his manners.

MARLBOROUGH

Pages 227-227
Duke of. See Churchill. MARLBOROUGH-Fort, an English factory on the west coast of the island of Sumatra in Asia; seated three miles west of the town of Bencoolen. E. Long. 101° 12'. S. Lat. 4° 21'.

MARLE

Pages 227-227

a mixture of calcareous with siliceous and argillaceous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, very much used in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> as a manure. See Agriculture and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MARLINE

Pages 227-227

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> affairs, are tarred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> skains, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> wreaths or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of untwisted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, dipped in pitch or tar, with which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a> or other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> are wrapped round, to prevent their fretting or rubbing in the blocks or pulleys through which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>. The same serves in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> upon ropes used for rigging guns, usually put up in small parcels called skains.

MARLOE

Pages 227-227

CHRISTOPHER, an English dramatic author, was a student in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; but afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> player, he trode the same stage with the inimitable Shakespeare. He was accounted an excellent poet even by Ben Johnson himself. He wrote six tragedies, one of which called Lucretilis Domination, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Lascivious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>, has been altered by Mrs Behn, and acted under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Abdelazar, or the Moor's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">Revenge</a>. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he had made a considerable progress in an excellent poem entitled <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">Hero</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEANDER">Leander</a>: which was afterwards finished by George Chapman, who is said to have fallen short of the spirit and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> discovered by Marloe. Mr Anthony Wood represents him as a freethinker, in the worst <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the word; and gives the following account of his death. Falling deeply in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with a low girl, and having for his rival a fellow in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a>, Marloe, imagining that his mistress granted him favours, was fired with jealousy, and rushed upon him in order to stab him with his dagger; but the footman avoided the stroke, and, seizing his writ, stabbed him with his own weapon; of which wound he died, in the year 1593.

MARLOW

Pages 227-228

a town of Buckinghamshire, in England, 31 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, lies under the Chiltern hills, in a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLY">marly</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. It is a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> borough, though not incorporated, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, not far from its confluence with Wycomb, and has a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and town-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>. It first sent members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> in the reign of Edward II. Bone <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACE">lace</a> is its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> manufacture. The Thames brings goods hither from the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, especially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> and malt from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> Wycomb, and beech from several parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, which abounds with this wood more than any in England. In the neighbourhood are frequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-races; and here are several corn and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, particularly... MAR on the river Loddon, between this town and High Wycomb. There are, besides, the Temple-mills, for making thimbles, and another for prelling <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> seeds. At Great Marlow there is an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> supported by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of young men destined for the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. The pupils are entirely under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, and are instructed by able professors in the various branches of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, &c., connected with military <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TACTICS">tactics</a>.

MARLY

Pages 228-229

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of France, between <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a> and St. Germain; seated in a valley, near a village and forest of the same name. It is noted for its fine gardens and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER_WORKS"><a class="x</a>ref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-works, there being a curious machine on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, which not only supplies them with water, but also those of Versailles. It is 10 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 11. N. Lat. 48. 52. Marly, Machine at. When <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> had fixed upon a favourite situation in the forest of Marly, where he intended to erect a splendid castle, he found that it wanted nothing either in point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> convenience but a fountain of water; and he immediately determined to supply by the affluence of art what <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> had denied it. An ingenious and self-taught carpenter from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a>, named Ramequin, undertook to conduct from the Seine a copious supply of water, and for this purpose contrived and erected the celebrated and complicated machine which we are now to describe. The machinery is driven by 14 underhot water <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> of 36 feet diameter, reckoning from the ends of the floatboards, disposed in three rows. In the first row there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> wheels, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> six, and in the third only one. By these wheels the water is raised through pumps into the first reservoir about 160 feet above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the river, then to a second reservoir 346 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and from this to the summit of a tower about 533 feet above the Seine. The two extremities of the axle of each wheel extend beyond the gudgeons on which they rest, and are bent into a crank so as to form a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVER">lever</a> two feet long. The crank which is towards the mountain drives the water of the river into the first reservoir, and the other crank gives <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> to the balances. An engine of eight pumps is wrought by one of the cranks of each of the five wheels in the first row. These engines consist of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a>, at each end of which hangs a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> piece of wood that supports and directs four pistons. This balance is moved by a beam in the form of a T, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of which is connected at one end with the balance by the intervention of a vertical regulator or beam, and at the other with the crank of the wheel by means of a horizontal <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> rod. One of the cranks of each of the five wheels of the first row, (excepting that which is next the mountain), and two of the cranks of the 14th wheel, or that in the last row, give motion to the pumps in the river and carry the water into the first reservoir. This motion is communicated from the cranks by means of an iron rod which is fixed to the lower end of a vertical balance. A horizontal regulator or beam is fixed to each end of this balance, and to these regulators are fastened chains which follow the declivity of the mountain till they reach the superior reservoirs. When the wheel is revolving, therefore, one of these chains <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> Marly be dragged towards the river, and the other towards the mountain. In order to produce this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> motion, the chains are supported and kept at equal distances by a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of vertical balances, placed along the mountain at every three todes, and moving upon a centre supported by a frame lying between the two chains and equidistant from them. When these chains reach the first reservoir they are fixed to vertical regulators, which carry frames, to which are adapted the pistons of the sucking pumps. These regulators therefore will be drawn one after another by their corresponding chains; and when one regulator is drawn by its chain, the piston of the pumps which it carries will be raised, and the water will follow them: At the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the pistons of the other regulators are descending to form a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a>; and these in their turn ascend with their load of water when the others are in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of descending. In the pumps formerly mentioned which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in the river, an effect is produced upon the pistons both when they ascend and descend, because they are moved by stiff iron rods; but in the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the pistons descend merely by their own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, as the motion is transmitted only by a chain. By these pumps the water is conveyed to the upper reservoir by two conduit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> of eight inches and three others of six inches diameter. The fifth wheel of the first row, which is the first towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a>, moves a long chain which works the pumps of one of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> of the upper reservoir. The seventh wheel gives motion to a chain which goes to the first cistern. By means similar to these already described, the six wheels of the second row move by each of their cranks a chain that goes to the second reservoir, and eight of these chains work 16 pumps behind it, to bring back into the reservoir the water which is lost out of the six pipes that go to the tower. These chains go over one of the first cisterns, and five of them at the same time give motion to the pistons of thirty pumps, whilst the other chains go on straight to the great reservoir. These 30 pumps convey their water through two pipes of 8 inches diameter into the upper reservoir. The five chains, after working these 30 pumps, give motion to the pistons of 82 pumps in the second reservoir which raise the water from it to the tower. The base of the tower which receives the water raised from the river is 610 fathoms distant from it; and the water runs from this basin along an aqueduct of 36 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> by its own weight. From this aqueduct the water is distributed into great reservoirs, from which it is conveyed to the gardens and fountains around the castle. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water raised by this machine amounts at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> rate to 30,000 or 40,000 gallons per <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>; though in favourable circumstances it raises more than 60,000 gallons per hour. But while the Seine either overflows its banks, or is frozen, or when the water is very low, the machine is scarcely capable of performing any work. The yearly expense of the machine at Marly including the salaries of the superintendents and the expenses of repairs, amounts to about 3300l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>, or 9l. per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, which makes the expense of 90 gallons of water one farthing. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we take into the account the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. Marly interest of £33,000. The original expense of the machine, 90 gallons will cost three halfpence, or 15 gallons one farthing. Notwithstanding the magnificence of this great machine, and the ingenuity which is displayed in its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, every person who examines it with care, will perceive innumerable defects, whether he examines it as a whole, or attends to the parts of which it is composed. In several positions the moving forces act with great obliquity, and therefore occasion an immense waste of power; and in order to give an alternate motion to a number of chains of balances extending to a distance of 380 feet, more than <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>-tenths of the impelling power are destroyed. By a few changes upon the construction of the machine, the water might have been raised from the river to the tower without any intermediate reservoirs. This appears from two experiments made upon the machine in 1738 and 1775. In 1738 M. Camus attempted to raise the water to the tower at once. He was able, however, only to bring it to the bottom of the tower which was considerably higher than the second reservoir. By this experiment the machine was so much strained that several parts required chains to secure it. In 1775 the water was elevated to the second reservoir at one jet at different times, but from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> and infirmity of the pipes several of them burst during the experiment. Hence it is obvious that if the pipes had been made stronger, the first reservoir and the machinery connected with it might have been dispensed with; and it is very probable that if the machine had been constructed with more judgement, the water might have been conducted at once from the river to the tower.

MARMADE

Pages 229-229

a town of France, in the department of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT_AND_GARONNE"><a class="xref"</a> href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a> and Garonne. It carries on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade in corn and wine, and is seated on the river Garonne, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0° 15'. N. Lat. 44° 20'. MARMOR. See MARBLE.

MARMALADE

Pages 229-229

a confection of plums, apricots, quinces, &c. boiled up to a consistence with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. In Scotland, it is made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a> oranges and sugar only.

MARMORA

Pages 229-229

the name of four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of the same name. The largest is about 30 miles in circumference; and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of them all produces corn, wine, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. The sea of Marmora is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>, which communicates both with the Archipelago and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> sea by that of Constantinople, being 120 miles in length and 50 in breadth; and all ships must <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through it that sail to Constantinople from the Mediterranean. It was anciently the Propontis.

MARMORICA

Pages 229-229

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> anciently inhabited by the Libyans. It was bounded on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRENAICA">Cyrenaica</a>, on the south by Sahara, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a> Interior, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Mediterranean; and was reckoned a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Egypt. There is no distinct <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the country.

MAROBUDUN

Pages 229-229

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence of Marobaudas, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Marcomanni; and hence the appellation. Now thought to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>.

MAROLLES

Pages 229-229

Michel de, born in 1600, was the son of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CLAUDE">Claude</a> de Marolles, whom French <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>. Michel, however, was of a different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. He entered early into the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> state, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of his father obtained two abbeys. He was formed with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> ardour for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, which never abated all his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; for, from 1619 when he published a translation of Lucan, to 1681 the year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he was constantly employed in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>. He attached himself unfortunately to the translating of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Latin writers: but, being devoid of all classical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and spirit, they sunk miserably under his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, the poets especially. He was certainly, however, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning, and discovered all his life a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> for the arts. He was one of the first who paid any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a>; and collected about 100,000, which make at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> one of the ornaments of the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a>'s cabinet. He composed memoirs of his own life, which were published by the abbé Goujet, 1755, in 3 vols. They contain, like such sort of things, some interesting facts, but an infinity of minute and insipid nothing.

MARONITES

Pages 229-230

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of eastern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, who follow the Syrian rite, and are subject to the pope; their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> habitation being on Mount Lebanon. Motheim informs us, that the doctrine of the Monothelites, condemned and exploded by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Constantinople, found a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of refuge among the Mardaites, a people who inhabited the mounts Libanus and Antilibanus, and who, about the conclusion of the seventh century, were called Maronites, after Maro their first bishop; a name which they still retain. None (he says) of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers give any certain account of the first person who instructed these mountaineers in the doctrine of the Monothelites: it is probable, however, from several circumstances, that it was John Maro, whose name they had adopted; and that this ecclesiastic received the name of Maro from his having lived in the character of a monk in the famous convent of St Maro, upon the borders of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORONTES">Orontes</a>, before his settlement among the Mardaites of Mount Lebanon. One thing is certain, from the testimony of Tyrius and other unexceptionable witnesses, as also from the most authentic records, viz., that the Maronites retained the opinions of the Monothelites until the 12th century, when, abandoning and renouncing the doctrine of one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> in Christ, they were readmitted in the year 1182 to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The most learned of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Maronites have left no method unemployed to defend their church against this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a>; they have laboured to prove, by a variety of testimonies, that their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> always persevered in the Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, in their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the Roman pontiff, without ever adopting the doctrine of the Monophysites, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Monothelites. But all their efforts are insufficient to prove the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of these assertions to such as have any acquaintance with the history of the church and the records of ancient times; for to all such the testimonies they allege will appear absolutely fictitious and destitute of authority. Paulus Nairon, a Maronite settled at Rome, has published an apology for Maro and the rest of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. His tenet is, that they really took their name from the Maro who lived about the year 450, and of whom mention is made in Chrysostom, Theodore, and Maronites, and the Menologium of the Greeks. He adds, that the disciples of this Maro spread themselves throughout all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>; that they built several monasteries, and among others, one that bore the name of their leader; that all the Syrians who were not tainted with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> took refuge among them; and that for this reason the heretics of those times called them Maronites. Mofheim observes, that the subjection of the Maronites to the spiritual jurisdiction of the Roman pontiff was agreed to with this express condition, that neither the popes nor their emissaries should pretend to change or abolish any thing that related to the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>, moral precepts, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> opinions, of this people: so that in reality there is nothing to be found among the Maronites that favours of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">popery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we except their attachment to the Roman pontiff, who is obliged to pay very dear for their friendship. For, as the Maronites live in the utmost distress of poverty, under the tyrannical yoke of the Mahometans, the bishop of Rome is under the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of furnishing them with such subsidies as may appease their oppressors, procure a subsistence for their bishop and clergy, provide all things requisite for the support of their churches, and the uninterrupted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of public worship, and contribute in general to lessen their misery. It is certain that there are Maronites in Syria who still behold the church of Rome with the greatest aversion and abhorrence; nay, what is still more remarkable, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of that nation residing in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, even under the eye of the pontiff, opposed his authority during the last century, and threw the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Rome into great perplexity. One body of these nonconforming Maronites retired into the valleys of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, where they joined the Waldenses; another, above 600 in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, with a bishop and several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> at their head, fled into Corsica, and implored the protection of the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a> against the violence of the inquisitors. The Maronites have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>, who resides in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of Cannubin, on Mount Libanon, and assumes the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of patriarch of Antioch, and the name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, as if he seemed desirous of being considered as the successor of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a>. He is elected by the clergy and the people, according to the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>; but, since their reunion with the church of Rome, he is obliged to have a bull of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> from the pope. He keeps a perpetual celibacy, as well as the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> his suffragans: as to the rest of the ecclesiastics, they are allowed to marry before ordination; and yet the monastic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> is in great esteem among them. Their monks are of the order of St Anthony, and live in the most obscure places in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, far from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of the world. As to their faith, they agree in the main with the rest of the eastern church. Their priests do not say <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> singly; but all say it together, standing round the altar. They communicate in unleavened <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a> have hitherto partaken in both kinds, though the practice of communicating in one has of late been getting footing, having been introduced by little and little. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">Lent</a> they eat nothing, unless it be two or three hours before sunrise; their other fastings are very numerous. To MAROON, to put one or more sailors ashore upon a desolate <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, under pretence of their having committed some great crime. This detestable expedient has been too often practised by some inhuman commanders of ships.

MAROT

Pages 230-230

CLEMENT, the best French poet of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAHORS">Cahors</a> in 1495; and was the son of John Marot, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALET">valet</a> de chambre to Francis I. and poet to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> of Brittany. He enjoyed his father's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of valet de chambre to Francis I. and was page to Margaret of France wife to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Alençon. In 1521 he followed that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and was wounded and taken prisoner at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>; but at his return to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> was accused of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>, and thrown into prison, from whence he was delivered by the protection of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Francis I. He at length retired to the queen of Navarre, then to the duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a>, and in 1536 returned to Paris; but declaring openly for the Calvinists, he was obliged to fly to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>; which he at length left, and retiring to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, died at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a> in 1544, aged 50. His verses are agreeably filled with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> beauties. La Fontaine acknowledged himself his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a>, and contributed greatly to restore to vogue the works of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poet. Marot, besides his other works, has translated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Psalms into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, which was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> by Beza, and are still sung in the Protestant churches abroad.—Michael Marot, his son, was also the author of some verses; but they are not comparable to those of John, and much less to those of Clement Marot.—The works of the three Marots were collected and printed together at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a> in 1731, in 3 vols. 4to, and in 6 vols. 12mo.

MARPURG

Pages 230-230

a handsome town of Germany, in Lower Styria, seated on the river Drave, 25 miles south-west of Grazt, and 60 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of Laubach. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16° 10'. N. Lat. 46° 42'.

MARQUARD

Pages 230-230

FRIER, an eminent German civilian, born at Augsburg in 1565.
