But there is no <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> to deprive religion of this triumph, or philosophy of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> which conviction and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENITENCE">penitence</a> must confer on it. "The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of a great genius (says Bayle, who is entitled to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> on this subject), is not totally extinguished: It is like a spark under the ashes. Reflection and the prospect of danger call forth its exertions. There are certain situations in which philosophers are as full of anxiety and remorse as other men." Whatever were the last sentiments of Du Marfaïs, it cannot be denied that in the vigour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> he furnished several examples of irreverence, and to these have been added many absurd stories. The superiority of Du Marfaïs's talents consisted in exactness and perspicuity. His <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the world, and of the customs of mankind, together with the greatest latitude in expressing whatever he thought, gave him that frank and unguarded simplicity which is often the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> ingredient of genuine humour. Fontenelle used to say of him, "that he was the most lively simpleton, and as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> the most simple he ever knew." He was the Fontaine of philosophers. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this character, he was a nice judge of what was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> in every production, and a great enemy to all kind of affectation. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are, 1. Exposition de la doctrine de l'Eglise Gallicane par rapports aux pretentions de la Cour de Rome, 12mo. This accurate work was begun at the desire of the pre- Marsais fident de Maisons, and did not appear till after the death of the author. 2. Exposition d'une méthode rai- sonnée pour apprendre la langue Latine, 1722, rare. This method appears conformable to the natural unfold- ing of the powers of the mind, and on that account ren- ders the acquisition of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> less difficult; but it was liable to two great objections to vulgar and un- enlightened understandings, namely, its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a>, and the censure which it conveyed against the former meth- od. 3. Traité des tropes, 1739, 8vo; again printed in 1771, 12mo. This work is intended to explain the different significations of the same word. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>- piece of logic, of accuracy, of perspicuity, and preci- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SION">sion</a>. The observations and the rules are illustrated by striking examples calculated to show both the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and the abuse of the rhetorical figures. It is wonderful at the same time that this excellent book had very little fame, and is scarcely known. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> who want- ed to compliment the author on this extraordinary per- formance, told him that he had heard a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of his Histoire des Tropes, and begged to know in what particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the world the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> flourished. 4. Les veritable Principes de la Grammaire raisonnée pour apprendre la langue Latine, 1729, 4to. There was only the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> of this work published, in which he introduced the greatest part of his méthode raisonnée. 5. L'abégie de la <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> du Père Jouvenel, arranged after the manner of the original <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, 1731, 12mo. 6. Une réponse manuscrite à la Critique de l'Histoire des <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">Oracles</a> par le Père Balus. There are only imperfect frag- ments of these papers to be found. 7. Logique, ou re- flexions sur les operations de l'Esprit. This is a short tract, which nevertheless contains every thing necessary to be known on the art of reasoning. It was reprinted at Paris in two parts, together with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> which he had furnished for the Encyclopédie, 1762.

MARSAL

Pages 241-241

a town of France, in Lorraine, remark- able for its <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> works; seated in a marth on the river Selle, of difficult access, which, together with the for- tifications, render it an important <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 43. N. Lat. 48. 46.

MARSALA

Pages 241-241

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, in the valley of Mazara. It is well peopled, and built on the ruins of the ancient Lilybaeum. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12. 27. N. Lat. 37. 52.

MARSAN

Pages 241-241
or MOUNT MARSAN, a town of France, in Gascony, and capital of a small territory of the same name, fertile in wine; seated on the river Midule, in W. Long. o. 39. N. Lat. 44. o.

MARSEILLES

Pages 241-241

a strong <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port, and the richest town of Provence, in France. Here is a good har- bour, where the French galleys are stationed; for it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not admit <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The entrance of the harbour, which is extremely narrow and surround- ed by lofty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, protects and shelters vessels dur- ing the most violent storms. The port itself forms a delightful walk even in the middle of winter, as it is open to the southern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and crowded with vast num- bers of people, not only of all the European nations, Marceilles but of Turks, Greeks, and natives of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">Bar</a>- bary. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> is one of the most agreeable that can be imagined, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the chains of the galley slaves heard among the hum of business did not taint it with the hateful idea of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. The galleys them- selves, useless and neglected, rot peaceably in their re- spective stations: and it is said that no others will ever be constructed to supply their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, as they have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> ceased to be of any utility to the state, and are scarcely even navigable in severe <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. Marceilles pretends to the most remote antiquity; a colony of Phocians, in ages unknown, having given it birth. It is divided into the Old Town and the New; which are separated by a street, bordered with trees on each side. The Old Town is one of the worst built of any in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The New has sprung up since the commencement of the 18th century, and has all that regularity, elegance, and convenience, which distinguish the present times. It is said to contain 100,000 inhabitants, and is one of the most trading <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in France. Without the walls is the castle of Notre-Dame, which is very well fortifi- ed. It is a bishop's see, and there is a French aca- demy; it having been noted at all times for men of learning. In 1660, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. built the citadel and Fort St John to keep the inhabitants in awe, because they pretended to be free. The Jesuits had a very fine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a> here; and in the arsenal, built not long ago, there are arms for 40,000 men. In the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">Discipline</a> they weave <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> brocades. The drugs are brought thither from all parts of the world. It is seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> shore of the Mediter- ranean, in E. Long. 4. 27. N. Lat. 43. 18. The sur- rounding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is rocky and barren, but covered for several miles on all sides with villas and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> houses, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> has erected.

MARSH

Pages 241-241

signifies a piece of ground flowed with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, yet so that the grass and other vegetables rise above the surface of the water, and, by their decaying, give rise to putrid effluvia, which are very pernicious to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body.

MARSHAL

Pages 241-242
or MARESCHAL, (marescallus), pri- marily Marshall denotes an officer who has the care or the command of horses. Nicod derives the word from *polemarchos*, "master of the camp;" Matthew Paris from *Maris senescallus*. In the old Gaulish language, *marc* signified "horse;" whence *marvelet* might signify "him who commanded the cavalry." Other derivations have been given by different authors; and the name itself has been applied to officers of very different employments. **Marshal of France**, the highest dignity of preferment in the French armies under the old government. The dignity of marshal came to be for life, though at its first institution it was otherwise. They were then only the king's first ecuyers under the constable; but in time they became the constable's lieutenants in the command of the army, the constable himself being then become captain-general. At first they were but two in number; and their allowance was but 500 livres per annum in time of war, and nothing in time of peace; but in the reign of Francis I, a third was added; Henry II created a fourth. Since, it has been various; Louis XIV increased it to 20. Their office at first was, to marshal the army under the constable, and to command in his absence. They did then what the marshals de camp do now; to which last they have given their title, and the least considerable part of their authority. **Earl Marshal of Scotland.** His office was to command the cavalry, whereas the Constable commanded the whole army. They seem, however, to have had a sort of joint command, as of old all orders were addressed "to our constable and marshal." The office of earl marshal has never been out of the noble family of Keith. It was reserved at the Union; and when the heritable jurisdictions were bought, it was in the crown, being forfeited by the rebellion of Geo. Keith, earl marshal, in 1715. **Earl Marshal of England** is the eighth great officer of state. This office, until it was made hereditary, always passed by grant from the king, and never was held by tenure or ferjeantry (by any subject), as the offices of lord high steward and lord high constable were sometimes held. The title is personal, the office honorary and officiary. They were formerly styled lord marshal only, until King Richard II, June 20, 1397, granted letters patent to Thomas Mowbray, earl of Nottingham, and to the heirs male of his body lawfully begotten, by the name and style of earl marshal; and further, gave them power to bear in their hand a gold truncheon, enamelled with black at each end; having at the upper end of it the king's arms engraven thereon, and at the lower end his own arms. King James I was pleased, by letters patent, dated August 29th 1622, to constitute Thomas Howard, earl of Arundel and Surrey, earl marshal for life; and the next year, the same king granted (with the advice of the privy s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council, letters-patent, wherein it was declared, that during the vacancy of the office of lord high constable of England, the earl marshal had the like jurisdiction in the court of chivalry, as both constable and marshal jointly ever exercised. See CHIVALRY, Court of. On the 19th of October 1672, King Charles II was pleased to grant to Henry Lord Howard, and the heirs male of his body lawfully begotten, the office and dignity of earl marshal of England, with power to execute the same by deputy or deputies, in as full and ample a manner as the same was heretofore executed by Henry Howard, Lord Maltravers, late earl of Arundel, Surrey, and Norfolk, grandfather to the said Henry Lord Howard; or by Thomas Howard, late duke of Norfolk, grandfather to the said Thomas Howard, late earl of Arundel, Surrey, and Norfolk; or by Thomas Howard duke of Norfolk, grandfather of the said Thomas Howard duke of Norfolk; or by John Mowbray duke of Norfolk, or any other earl marshal of England; with a pension of 20l. each year, payable out of the hanaper office in chancery; and on default of the issue-male of the said Henry Lord Howard, with limitation to the heirs male lawfully begotten of the body of the said Thomas Howard earl of Arundel, &c.; and, on the default of such issue, to descend in like manner to the heirs male of Thomas late earl of Suffolk; and, on default of his issue male, to the heirs male of Lord William Howard, late of Naworth in the county of Cumberland, youngest son to Henry Howard late duke of Norfolk; and, on default of his issue male, to Charles Howard earl of Nottingham, and the heirs male of his body lawfully begotten. **Field-Marshal**, an officer of high rank in the European armies. It is now, however, divided in the British army; Lord Tyrawley was the last, appointed in 1763. **Knight-Marshal**, or Marshal of the King's House, an English officer, whose business, according to Fleta, is to execute the commands and decrees of the lord steward, and to have the custody of prisoners committed by the court of verge. Under him are six marshal's men, who are properly the king's bailiffs, and arrest in the verge of the court, when a warrant is backed by the board of green-cloth. The court where causes of this kind, between man and man, are tried, is called the Marshalsea, and is under the knight-marshal. See MARSHALSEA. This is also the name of the prison in Southwark; the reason of which may probably be, that the marshal of the king's house was wont to sit there in judgement, or keep his prison. **Marshal of the King's Bench**, an officer who has custody of the prison called the King's Bench in Southwark. He gives attendance upon the court, and takes into his custody all prisoners committed by the court; he is finable for his absence, and non-attendance incurs a forfeiture of his office. The power of appointing the marshal of the king's bench is in the crown. In Fleta, mention is also made of a marshal of the exchequer, to whom the court commits the custody of the king's debtors, &c. **MARSHALLING a Coat**, in Heraldry, is the disposal of several coats of arms belonging to distinct families in one and the same escutcheon or shield, together with their ornaments, parts, and appurtenances. See HERALDRY, chap. vi. p. 466.

MARSHALSEA

Pages 242-243

the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">Court</a> of, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">Palace</a> Court at Westminster, though two distinct courts, are frequently confounded together. The former was originally holden before the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> and marshal of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSHFIELD">Marshfield</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and was instituted to administer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> between the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> servants, that they might not be drawn into other courts, and thereby the king lose their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. It was formerly held in, though not a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of, the aula regis; and, when that was subdivided, remained a distinct jurisdiction: holding <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> of all trespasses committed within the verge of the court, where only one of the parties is in the king's domestic service (in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the inquest shall be taken by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>); and of all debts, contracts, and covenants, where both of the contracting parties belong to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>; and then the inquest shall be composed of men of the household only. By the statute of 13 Rich. II. stat. 1. c. 3. (in affirmance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>), the verge of the court in this respect extends for 12 miles round the king's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of residence. And, as this tribunal was never subject to the jurisdiction of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> jurist, no writ of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> lay from it (though a court of record) to the king's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, but only to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, till the statutes of 5 Edw. III. c. 2. and 10 Edw. III. stat. 2. c. 3. which allowed such writ of error before the king in his place. But this court being ambulatory, and obliged to follow the king in all his progresses, so that by the removal of the household actions were frequently discontinued, and doubts having arisen as to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of its jurisdiction, King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. in the fifth year of his reign, by his letters patent, erected a new court of record, called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CURIA">curia</a> palatii, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> palace court, to be held before the steward of the household and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>-marshal, and the steward of the court, or his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>; with jurisdiction to hold plea of all manner of personal actions whatsoever, which shall arise between any parties within 12 miles of his majesty's palace at Whitehall. The court is now held once a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, together with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> court of marshall, in the borough of Southwark: and a writ of error lies from thence to the court of king's bench. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the cause is of any considerable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, it is usually removed on its first commencement, together with the custody of the defendant, either into the king's bench or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS">common pleas</a>, by a writ of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABEAS_CORPUS">habeas corpus</a> cum causa: and the inferior business of the court hath of late years been much reduced, by the new courts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> erected in the environs of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; in consideration of which the four counsel belonging to these courts had salaries granted them for their lives by the stat. 23 Geo. II. c. 27.

MARSHFIELD

Pages 243-243

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles from Bath, 12 from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIPPING_SODBURY">Chipping-Sodbury</a>, 12½ from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, 35 from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>, and 104 from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to Bristol, and on the very borders of Wilts. It is a considerable clothing-town, drives a good trade in malt, and is famous for cakes. It consists chiefly of one street of old buildings near a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; and is governed by a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a>. It has a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, with a well endowed alms <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and a chapel to it for eight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> school; and it has a weekly market and two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>.

MARSHLAND

Pages 243-243

a marthy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, opposite to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a>'s Lynn, almost surrounded with the Ouse and other navigable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and an arm of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It seems formerly to have been recovered out of the ocean, from whose inundations it could never be altogether defended; and in Sir Henry Spelman's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it suffered two general ones, viz. one from the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, the other from the freshes; by the last Marshal, of which the inhabitants suffered 42,000l. damage. It contains about 30,000 acres, which turn to more profit by grazing than ploughing. It is about 10 miles in the widest <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and has no less than 111 brick bridges. The commonage of it belongs to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> villages that surround it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is so unhealthy, that an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGUE">ague</a> is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the Marshland <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a>. MARSHMALLOW. See ALTHEA, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MARSI

Pages 243-243

a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of Germany, who afterwards came to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where they occupied the territory in the environs of the Fucine lake. They at first proved very inimical to Rome, but in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they became its firmest supporters. They were allowed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to be the most intrepid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> of their legions when in friendship, and the most formidable of their enemies when at variance; and it was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> saying, that Rome could neither triumph over the Marsi nor without them. They are particularly celebrated for the civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> in which they were engaged, and which from them has received the name of the Marian war. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> contributions they made to support the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Rome, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of men which they continually supplied to the republic, rendered them bold and aspiring; and they claimed, with the rest of the Italian states, a share of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and privileges which were enjoyed by the citizens of Rome. This petition, though supported by the interest, the eloquence, and the integrity of the tribune Drufus, was received with contempt by the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>; upon which, in the 662d year of Rome, the Marsi put themselves at the head of the Social war, one of the most obstinate and dangerous oppositions ever made to the progress of the Roman power. They obtained several victories; but they were at last defeated; though the war was not terminated but by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of those privileges for which they contended.

MARSICO NUOVO

Pages 243-243

a small, rich, and handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and in the Hither Principato, with a bishop's see. It is seated at the foot of the Apennines, near the river Agri, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15° 49'. N. Lat. 28° 42'.

MARSIGLI

Pages 243-243
LEWIS FERDINAND, COUNT, an Italian, famous for letters as well as arms, was descended from an ancient and noble family, and born at Bologna in 1658. He acquired a great knowledge in the art of war and fortification; served under the emperor Leopold II. against the Turks, by whom he was taken prisoner in 1683, but redeemed, after a year's captivity. In the Spanish succession war, Marsigli, then advanced to the rank of marshal, being in the fortress of Brifac, which surrendered to the duke of Burgundy in 1703, when the place was deemed capable of holding out much longer, was stripped of all his commissions, and had his sword broken over him; and the count d'Arco who commanded was beheaded. Marsigli now fought for consolation in the sciences; as, amidst all the hurry and fatigue of war, he had made all the advantages the most philosophic man could do, who had travelled purely in quest of knowledge. He had a rich collection of every thing proper to the advancement of natural knowledge, instruments astronomical and chemical, plans of fortifications, models of machines,

MARSQUIVER

Pages 241-241
or MARSAQUIVER, a strong and ancient town of Africa, on the coast of Barbary, and in the province of Beni Arax, in the kingdom of Tremefen, with one of the best harbours in Africa. It was taken by the Spaniards in 1732. It is seated on a rock near a bay of the sea, in W. Long. o. 10. N. Lat. 35. 40.

MARSTON

Pages 244-244

JOHN, an English dramatic writer, who lived in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of James I. Wood says he was a student in Corpus Christi <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; but neither his family nor the time of his birth is known. He produced eight plays for the stage, which were all acted at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACKFRIARS">Blackfriars</a> with applause; and one of them, called the Dutch Courtesan, was once revived since the Restoration, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">Revenge</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">Match</a> in Newgate. There is no account when he died; but we find his works were published after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by Shakespeare, and may thence reasonably conclude that it happened about the year 1614. He was a chaste and pure writer; avoiding all that obscenity, ribaldry, and scurrility, which too many of the playwrights of that time, and indeed much more so in some periods since, have made the basis of their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> disgrace and scandal of the stage.

MARSYAS

Pages 244-244

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a celebrated musician of Celene in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, son of Olympus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of Hyagnis, or Oenagrus. He was so skilful in playing on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>, that he is generally deemed the inventor of it. According to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of some, he found it when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> had thrown it aside on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTORTION">distortion</a> of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> when she played upon it. Marsyas was enamoured of Cybele, and he travelled with her as far as Nysa, where he had the imprudence to challenge <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of his skill as a musician. The god accepted the challenge, and it was mutually agreed that he who was defeated should be flayed alive by the conqueror. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>, or (according to Diodorus) the inhabitants of Nysa, were appointed umpires. Each exerted his utmost skill, and the victory, with much difficulty, was adjudged to Apollo. The god upon this tied his antagonist to a tree, and flayed him alive: (See APOLLO). The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Marsyas was universally lamented; the Fauns, Satyrs, and Dryads, wept at his fate; and from their abundant tears arose a river of Phrygia, well known by the name of Marsyas. The unfortunate Marsyas is often represented on monuments, as tied with his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> behind his back to a tree, while Apollo stands before him with his lyre in his hands. In independent cities, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, the statue of Marsyas was generally erected in the forum, to represent the intimacy which subsisted between <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a> and Marsyas as the emblems of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. At Celene, the skin of Marsyas was shown to travellers for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. It was suspended in the public <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, in the form of a bladder or a foot <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>. The sources of the Marsyas were near those of the Meander, and those two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> had their confluence a little below the town of Celene.

MART

Pages 244-244

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fair held every year for buying and selling goods. Public marts, on places of buying and selling, such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, with the tolls thereunto belonging, can only be set up by virtue of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and immemorial usage and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, which presupposes such a grant. The limitation of these public resorts, to such <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> as may be most convenient for the neighbourhood, forms a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of economics, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> policy; which, considering the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> family, and the king as the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of it, he has clearly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to dispose of and order as he pleases.

MARTABAN

Pages 244-244

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEGU">Pegu</a>, lying in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> that produces <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> and all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> proper to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. It has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of several sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, and carries on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town, which is of the same name, is rich, handsome, and very populous, with a good harbour. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 97° 50'. N. Lat. 15° 35'.

MARTEAU

Pages 244-244

the name given by French naturalists to a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of oysters, called allo mollus by others, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of which is that of a hammer, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather of a pickaxe. See OSTREA, <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">CONCHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MARTHA

Pages 244-244

Sr., <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Sierra Nevada, a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain in New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. Some say it is 100 miles in circumference at the bottom, and five miles in height. The top is always covered with snow in the hottest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; and the French affirm, that they can perceive it from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of St Domingo, which is 370 miles distant. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 74° 35'. N. Lat. 8° 0'. MARTHA's Vineyard, an island of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of New England, 80 miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOSTON">Boston</a>. The inhabitants apply themselves chiefly to their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>, in which they have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success. W. Long. 70° 35'. N. Lat. 41° 0'.

MARTIAL

Pages 244-245

is sometimes used to express preparations of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> such as are impregnated therewith; as the martial regulus of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, &c. Martial <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">Court</a>. See COURT Martial. Martial <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is the law of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> that depends upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> but arbitrary <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, or his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>: for though the king doth not make any laws but by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> consent in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, yet, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of war, by reason of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of it to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> against But the martial law (according to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">Chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">Justice</a> Hale), is in reality not a law, but something indulged rather than allowed as a law; and it relates only to members of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, being never intended to be executed on others, who ought to be ordered and governed by the laws to which they are subject, though it be a time of war. And the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of martial law, whereby any person might lose his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, or member, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, may not be permitted in time of peace, when the king's courts are open for all persons to receive justice.

MARTIALIS

Pages 245-245

MARCUS VALERIUS, a famous Latin poet, born at Bilbilis, now called Bubiera, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Arragon in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, was of the order of knights. He went to Rome at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 21, and laid there 35 years, under the reign of Galba and the succeeding emperors, till that of Trajan; and having acquired the esteem of Titus and Domitian, he was created tribune. At length, finding that he was neglected by Trajan, he returned to his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> Bilbilis, where he married a wife, and had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> to live with her several years. He admires and commends her much, telling her that she alone was sufficient to supply the want of everything he enjoyed at Rome. "Romam tu mihi sola facis," says he, in the 21st epigram of the 12th book. She appears like-wife to have been a lady of a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fortune; for, in the 31st epigram of the same book, he extols the magnificence of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and gardens he had received from her, and says that she had made him a little kind of monarch." There are still extant 14 books of his epigrams, filled with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, a play upon words, and obscenities. The style is affected. However, some of his epigrams are excellent; many of them are of the middling kind; but the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of them are bad: so that Martial never spoke a greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, than when he said of his own works, Sunt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONA">bona</a>, sunt quaedam mediocra, sunt mala plura. There is also attributed to him a book on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECTACLES">spectacles</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>; but the most learned critics think that this last <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was not written by Martial. The best editions of Martial are, that in Ufum Delphini, 4to, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1617, and that cum Notis Variis.

MARTIGUES

Pages 245-245

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of France, in Provence, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a principality; seated near a lake 12 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, which is navigable throughout, and from whence they get excellent <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. E. Long. 4° 20'. N. Lat. 43° 38'.

MARTIN

Pages 245-249

St., was born at Sabaria in Pannonia, (at present Szent in Lower <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>), in the beginning of the fourth century. His father was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> tribune; and he himself was obliged to carry arms, although peace and solitude were much more agreeable to his inclination. He was remarkable for every virtue, in a profession which is generally considered to give a sanction to vice. He divided his coat with a naked wretch whom he met at the gate of Amiens; Martin, and it is reported, that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ appeared to him on the night following, clothed in this half of his coat. Martin was then a catechumen; but he soon afterwards received <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, and renounced the military profession for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a>. After passing many years in solitude, St Hilary bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POITIERS">Poitiers</a> gave him the power to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> out devils. On his return to Pannonia, he persuaded his mother to embrace Christianity; and with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> zeal and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> opposed the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>, who governed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in Illyria. When he was publicly whipt for giving testimony to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> of Christ, he bore the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> of the first martyrs. This illustrious champion for Christianity, when he heard that St Hilary was returned from banishment, went and settled in the neighbourhood of Poitiers. In this retirement, a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of monks placed themselves under his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. His virtues became every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> more splendid and remarkable, till he was drawn from his solitude, and with the general approbation of the clergy and people elected bishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOURS">Tours</a> in the year 374. To the zeal and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> of a bishop, he joined the humility and poverty of an anchorite. That he might detach himself more from the world, he built the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARMOUTIER">Marmoutier</a>, which still remains, and which is believed to be the oldest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> in France. It is situated near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Tours, betwixt the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a> and a steep rock. In this situation, together with 80 monks, St Martin displayed the most exemplary fidelity and mortification; nor were there any monks better disciplined than those of Marmoutier. After he had converted his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> to the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, he became the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> of all <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>. He diffused the doctrines of Christianity among the heathens, destroyed their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, and (according to the writers of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>), confirmed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> by an infinite number of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALENTINIAN">Valentinian</a>, at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in Gaul, received him with every mark of respect and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> Maximus, who had revolted against the emperor Gratian, and seized on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, England, and Gaul, received him in a manner no less distinguished. The holy bishop attended him at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREVES">Treves</a> in the year 383, to solicit some favours. Maximus made him sit at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> with the most illustrious persons of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and placed him at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. In drinking, the usurper commanded his servants to give him a cup, that he might again receive it from him; but this extraordinary prelate gave it to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> who accompanied him on his journey. This holy boldness, far from displeasing them, gained him the favour of the emperor and of his court. Martin, who was an enemy to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>, but a friend of mankind, employed his influence with this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> to preserve the Priscillianists, who were persecuted by Ithace and by Idace, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of Spain. The bishop of Tours would hold no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> with men whose principles of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> inclined them to shed the blood of mankind; and he obtained the life of those whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> they had solicited. On his return to Tours, he prepared himself for the reward of his labours in another world. He died at Candes the 8th of November 397, but according to others on the 11th of November 400. His name is given to a particular <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> concerning the mystery. Martin, mystery of the holy Trinity. St Martin is the first of the saints confessors to whom the Latin church offered public prayers. His life is written in elegant Latin by Fortunatus, and Sulpicius Severus one of his disciples. Paul of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIGUEUX">Perigueux</a> and Fortunatus of Poitiers have given us Sulpicius's life of Martin in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; but they have debased the admirable prose of the author by a wretched poetical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>. Nicolas Gervais wrote also the life of St Martin, full of many curious and entertaining facts, published at Tours in 1699, in 4to. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> at Amiens is, that St Martin performed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of charity which rendered him so famous, near an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> gate of the city, of which the ruins are still visible. The following Latin verses, which do more honour to the saint than to the poet, are <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> on one of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>: Hic quondam vefem Martiauus demiavil; Ut faceremus idem, nobis exemplificavit. Martin, Benjamin, one of the most eminent artists and mathematicians of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was born in 1704. After publishing a variety of ingenious treatises, and particularly a Scientific <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a> under his own name, and carrying on for many years a very extensive trade as an optician and globe-maker in Fleet-street, the growing infirmities of age compelled him to withdraw from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of business. Trusting too fatally to what he thought the integrity of others, he unfortunately, though with a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> more than sufficient to pay all his debts, became a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKRUPT">bankrupt</a>. The unhappy old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, in a moment of desperation from this unexpected stroke, attempted to destroy himself; and the wound, though not immediately mortal, hastened his death, which happened February 9th 1782, in his 78th year. He had a valuable collection of fossils and curiosities of almost every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; which, after his death, were almost given away by public auction. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> publications, as far as they have occurred to recollection, are, The Philosophic <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>; being a view of the present state of experimental physiology, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, 1735, 8vo. A new, complete, and universal System or Body of Decimal <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a>, 1735, 8vo. The young Students Memorial Book, or Patent Library, 1735, 8vo. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">Description</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">Use</a> of both the Globes, the Armillary Sphere and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORRERY">Orrery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIGONOMETRY">Trigonometry</a>, 1736, 2 vols 8vo. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the Academy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1740, 5 vols. System of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEWTONIAN_PHILOSOPHY">Newtonian Philosophy</a>, 1759, 3 vols. New Elements of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, 1759. Mathematical Institutions, viz. Arithmetic, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUXIONS">Fluxions</a>, 1759. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">Natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of England, with a Map of each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">County</a>, 1759, 2 vols. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PHILOLOGY">Philology</a>, and Philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, 1759. Mathematical Institutions, 1764, 2 vols. Lives of Philosophers, their Inventions, &c. 1764. Introduction to the Newtonian Philosophy, 1765. Institutions of Astronomical Calculations, 2 parts, 1765. Description and Use of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">Air</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">Pump</a>, 1766. Description of the Torricellian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAROMETER">Barometer</a>, 1766. Appendix to the Description and Use of the Globes, 1766. Philosphia Britannica, 1778, 3 vols. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a> and Lady's Philosophy, 3 vols. Miscellaneous Correspondence, 4 vols. System of Philology. Philosophical Geography. Magazine complete, 14 vols. Principles of Pump-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">Theory</a> of the Hydrometer. Doctrine of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOGARITHMS">Logarithms</a>. Martin, Sr., a small but strong town of France in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Rhée, with a harbour and a strong citadel, fortified after the manner of Vauban. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> lies near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Poitou. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1°. N. Lat. 45°. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Martin, a promontory of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a> in Spain, near a town called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DENIA">Denia</a>, and separates the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Valencia from that of Alicant. Martin, St., an island of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and one of the Caribbees, lying on the gulf of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of St Bartholomew, and to the south-west of Anguilla. It is 42 miles in circumference; has neither harbour nor river, but several <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> pits. After various revolutions, it is at length in possession of the French and Dutch, who possess it conjointly. W. Long. 62°. 35'. N. Lat. 13°. 15'. Martin. See Hirundo. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>, and Muscida, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> Index. Free Martin, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, is a name given in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to a cow calf cast at the same time with a bull calf, which is a kind of hermaphrodite that is never known to breed nor to discover the least inclination for the bull, nor does the bull ever take the least notice of it. See Hermaphrodite. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARTINGALE">Martingale</a>, in the manege, a thong of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, fastened to one end of the girths under a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s belly, and at the other end to the muffs-roll, to keep him from rearing. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARTINICO">Martinico</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the French <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, the middle of which is situated in W. Long. 61°. N. Lat. 14°. 30'. This island was first settled by M. Dehambuc a Frenchman, in the year 1635, with only 100 men from St Christopher's. He chose rather to have it peopled from thence than from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; as he foresaw, that men, tired with the fatigue of such a long voyage, would mostly perish soon after their arrival, either from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, or from the hardships incident to most emigrations. They completed their first settlement without any difficulty. The natives, intimidated by their fire-arms, or seduced by promises, gave up the western and southern parts of the island to the newcomers. In a short time, however, perceiving the number of these enterprising strangers daily increasing, they resolved to extirpate them, and therefore called in the savages of the neighbouring islands to assist them. They fell jointly upon a little fort that had been hastily erected; but were repulsed, with the loss of 700 or 800 of their best warriors, who were left dead on the spot. After this check, the savages for a long time disappeared entirely; but at last they returned, bringing with them presents to the French, and making excuses for what had happened. They were received in a friendly manner, and the reconciliation sealed with pots of brandy. This peaceable state of affairs, however, was of no long continuance; the French took such undue advantages of their superiority over the savages, that they soon rekindled in the others that hatred which had never been entirely subdued. The savages, whose manner of life requires a vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, finding themselves daily more and more irritated, had recourse to stratagem, in order to destroy their Martinico became famous all over Europe. In 1736, Martinico there were on the island 447 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> works; 11,953,232 coffee trees, 103,870 of cocoa; 2,068,480 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of cotton, 39,400 of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, 6750 of annatto. The supplies for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> consisted of 4,806,142 banana trees, 34,483,000 trenches of caffava; and 247 plots of potatoes and yams. The number of blacks amounted to 72,000 men, women, and children. Their labour had improved the plantations as far as was consistent with the consumption then made in Europe of American productions; and the annual exports from the island amounted to about 700,000l. The connexions of Martinico with the other islands entitled her to the profits of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, and the charges of transport; as she alone was in the possession of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>. This profit might be rated at the tenth of the produce; and the sum total must have amounted to near 765,000l. This standing debt was seldom called in, and left for the improvement of their plantations. It was increased by advances in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, slaves, and other necessary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>; so that Martinico became daily more and more a creditor to the other islands, and thus kept them in constant dependence; while they all enriched themselves by her assistance. The connexions of this island with Cape Breton, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUISIANA">Louisiana</a>, procured a market for the ordinary sugars, the inferior coffee, the molasses, and rum, which would not sell in France. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> the inhabitants received salt fish, dried vegetables, deals, and some flour. In the clandestine trade on the coasts of Spanish America, consisting wholly of goods manufactured by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, she <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> made a profit of 90 per cent. on the value of about 175,000l. sent yearly to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARACCAS">caraccas</a>, or neighbouring colonies. So many prosperous engagements brought immense sums into Martinico. Upwards of 787,000l. were constantly circulated in that island with great rapidity; and this is perhaps the only country in the world where the specie has been so considerable as to make it a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of indifference to them whether they dealt in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, or commodities. This extensive trade brought into the ports of Martinico annually 220 ships from France; 14 or 15 fitted out by the mother country for the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, 60 from Canada, 10 or 12 from the islands of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARGARITA">Margarita</a> and Trinidad; besides the English and Dutch ships that came to carry on a smuggling trade. The private <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> from the island to the northern colonies, to the Spanish continent, and to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDWARD">windward</a> islands, employed 120 vessels from 20 to 30 tons burden. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of 1744 put a stop to this prosperity. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">Note</a> that the fault was in Martinico itself; its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, constantly exercised, and accustomed to frequent engagements, which the carrying on a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRABAND">contraband</a> trade required, was prepared for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. In less than six months, 40 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIVATEERS">privateers</a>, fitted out at St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s, spread themselves about the latitude of the Caribbee islands. They signalized themselves in a manner worthy of the ancient freebooters; returning confidently in triumph, laden with an immense booty. Yet, in the midst of these successes, an entire stop was put to the navigation of the colony, both to the Spanish coast and to Canada, and they were constantly disturbed even on their own coasts. The few ships that came from France, Martinique, France, in order to compensate the hazards they were exposed to by the loss of their commodities, sold them at a very advanced price, and bought them at a very low one. By this means the produce decreased in value, the lands were ill cultivated, the works neglected, and the slaves perishing for want. When everything thus seemed tending to decay, the peace at last restored the freedom of trade, and with it the hopes of recovering the ancient prosperity of the island. The event, however, did not answer the pains that were taken to attain it. Two years had not elapsed after the cessation of hostilities, when the colony lost the contraband trade she carried on with the American Spaniards. This was owing to the substitution of regular ships to the fleets; and thus were the attempts of the smugglers confined within very narrow bounds. In the new system, the number of ships was determined, and the time of their arrival uncertain; which occasioned a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> in the price of commodities unknown before; and from that time the smuggler, who only engaged in this trade from the certainty of a fixed and constant profit, would no longer pursue it, when it did not secure him an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to the risks he ran. But this loss was not so sensibly felt by the colony, as the hardships brought upon them by the mother country. An unskilful administration clogged the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> and necessary connexion between the islands and North America with so many formalities, that in 1755 Martinique sent but four vessels to Canada. The direction of the colonies, now committed to the care of ignorant and avaricious clerks, soon lost its importance, sunk into contempt, and was prostituted to venality. The debts which had been contracted, during a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of calamities, had not yet been paid off, when the war broke out afresh. After a series of misfortunes and defeats, the island fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the British. It was restored, however, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1763, 16 months after it had been conquered; but deprived of all the necessary means of prosperity, that had made it of so much importance. For some years past, the contraband trade carried on to the Spanish coasts was almost entirely lost. The cession of Canada had precluded all hopes of opening again a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a>, which had only been interrupted by temporary mistakes. The productions of the Grenades, St Vincent, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMINICA">Dominica</a>, which were now become British dominions, could no longer be brought into their harbours; and a new regulation of the mother country, which forbade her having any intercourse with Guadeloupe, left her no hopes from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. The colony, thus deprived of every thing as it were, and destitute, nevertheless contained, at the last survey, which was taken on the 1st of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1770, in the compass of 28 parishes, 12,450 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> people of all ages and of both sexes; 1814 free blacks or mulattoes; 79,553 slaves, and 443 fugitive <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>. The number of births in 1766, was in the proportion of one in 30 among the white people, and of one in 25 among the blacks. From this observation, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it were constant, it should seem that the climate of America is much more favourable to the propagation of the Africans than of the Europeans: since the former multiply still more in the labours and hardships of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>, than the latter in the midst of plenty and freedom. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> must be, that in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time the Martinico increase of blacks in America <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> surpass that of the white men; and, perhaps, at last avenge this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of victims on the descendants of the oppressors. The cattle of the colony consists of 8283 horses or mules; 12,376 head of horned cattle; 975 hogs; and 13,544 sheep or goats. Their provisions are, 17,920,596 trenches of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASSAVA">cassava</a>; 3,509,048 banana trees, and 400 squares and a half of yams and potatoes. Their plantations contain 11,444 squares of land, planted with sugar; 6,638,957 coffee trees; 871,043 cocoa trees; 1,764,807 cotton plants; 59,966 trees of eucalyptus, and 61 of arnotto. The meadows or savannahs take up 10,072 squares of land; there are 11,966 in wood, and 8448 uncultivated or forsaken. The plantations which produce coffee, cotton, cocoa, and other things of less importance, are 1515 in number. There are but 286 for sugar. They employ 116 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, 12 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>-mills, and 184 turned by oxen. Before the hurricane of the 13th of August 1766, there were 302 small habitations and 15 sugar-works more. In 1760, France imported from Martinico, upon 202 trading vessels, 177,116 quintals of fine sugar; 12,579 quintals of raw sugar; 68,518 quintals of coffee; 11,731 quintals of cocoa; 60,48 quintals of cotton; 2518 quintals of cassia; 783 casks of rum; 307 hogheads of molasses; 150 pounds of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>; 2147 pounds of preserved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>; 47 pounds of chocolate; 282 pounds of raised tobacco; 494 pounds of rope-yarn; 334 chests of liqueurs; 234 hogheads of molasses, &c.; 451 quintals of wood for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>; and 12,108 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. All these productions together have been bought in the colony itself, for £56,631l. 9s. 10d. It is true, that the colony has received from the mother country to the amount of £88,412l. 16s. 6d. of merchandise; but part of this has been sent away to the Spanish coasts, and another part has been conveyed to the English settlements. The island is 16 leagues in length and 45 in circumference, leaving out the capes, some of which extend two or three leagues into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It is very uneven, and intersected in all parts by a number of hillocks; which are mostly of a conical form. Three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> rise above these smaller eminences. The highest bears the indelible marks of a volcano. The woods with which it is covered continually attract the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, which occasions noxious damps, and contributes to make it horrid and inaccessible; while the two others are in most parts cultivated. From these mountains issue the many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> that water the island. These waters, which flow in gentle streams, are changed into torrents on the slightest storm. Their qualities are derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> over which they flow. In some places they are excellent; in others so bad, that the inhabitants are obliged to drink the water they have collected during the rainy season. Of all the French settlements in the West Indies, Martinico is the most happily situated with regard to the winds which prevail in those seas. Its harbours possess the inestimable advantage of affording a certain shelter from the hurricanes which annoy these latitudes. The harbour of Fort <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> is one of the best in all the Martinico the windward islands; and so celebrated for its safety, that, when it was open to the Dutch, their shipmasters had orders from the republic to take shelter there in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, July, and August, the three months in which the hurricanes are most frequent. The lands of the Lamentin, which are but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> distant, are the richest and most fertile in the whole island. The numerous streams which water this fruitful country, convey loaded canoes to a considerable distance from the sea. The protection of the fortifications secured the peaceable enjoyment of so many advantages; which, however, were balanced by a swampy and unwholesome soil. This capital of Martinico was also the rendezvous of the men of war; which branch of the navy has always oppressed the merchantmen. On this account, Port Royal was an improper <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to become the centre of trade, which was therefore removed to St Peter's. This little town, notwithstanding the fires that have four times reduced it to ashes, still contains 1700 houses. It is situated on the western coast of the island, on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, or inlet, which is almost circular. One part of it is built on the strand along the sea side, which is called the anchorage; and is the place destined for ships and warehouses. The other part of the town stands upon a low hill; it is called the Fort, from a small fortification that was built there in 1665, to check the seditions of the inhabitants against the tyranny of monopoly; but it now serves to protect the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from foreign enemies. These two parts of the town are separated by a rivulet. The anchorage is at the back of a pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and steep hill. Shut up as it were by this hill, which intercepts the easterly winds, the most constant and most salubrious in these parts; exposed, without any refreshing breezes, to the scorching beams of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, reflected from the hill, from the sea, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> sand on the beach; this place is extremely hot, and always unwholesome. Besides, there is no harbour; and the ships which cannot winter safely upon this coast are obliged to take shelter at Fort Royal. But these disadvantages are compensated by the convenience of the road of St Peter's, for loading and unloading of goods; and by its situation, which is such that ships can freely go in and out at all times, and with all winds. Martinico again fell into the hands of the British in 1794; but was restored to France by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of peace in 1801.

MARTLETS

Pages 249-249

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, little birds represented without feet; and used as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mark of distinction for younger brothers, to put them in mind that they are to trust to the wings of virtue and merit, in order to raise themselves, and not to their feet, they having little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> to set their foot on. See Heraldry.

MARTON

Pages 243-244
machines, &c., all which he presented to the senate of Bologna by an authentic act in 1712, forming at the same time out of them what he called the Institute of the arts and sciences at Bologna. He also founded a printing house, and furnished it with the best types for Latin, Greek, Hebrew, and Arabic, which he presented in 1728 to the Dominicans at Bologna, on condition of their printing all the writings of the Institute at prime cost; this was called the printing house of St Thomas Aquinas. His writings on philosophical subjects are numerous and valuable, in Latin, Italian, and French. He died in 1730.

MARTYNIA

Pages 249-249

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the didynamia clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 10th order, Perforatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MARTYR

Pages 249-251

is one who lays <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> suffers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, for the sake of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. The word is Greek, μαρτυρικός, and properly signifies "a witness." It is applied, by way of eminence, to those who suffer in witness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the gospel. The Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> has abounded in martyrs, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is filled with surprising accounts of their singular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a> and fortitude under the cruellest torments <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> was capable of suffering. The primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> were accused by their enemies of paying a Martyr fort of divine worship to the martyrs. Of this we have an instance in the answer of the church of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a> to the suggestion of the Jews, who at the martyrdom of Polycarp, desired the heathen judge not to suffer the Christians to carry off his body, lest they should leave their crucified <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and worship him in his stead. To which they answered, "We can neither forsake Christ, nor worship any other: for we worship him as the Son of God; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> the martyrs as the disciples and followers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> affection they have shown to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> and Master." A like answer was given at the martyrdom of Fructuosus in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. For when the judge asked Eulogius, his deacon, Whether he would not worship Fructuosus? as thinking, that, though he refused to worship the heathen idols, he might yet be inclined to worship a Christian martyr; Eulogius replied, "I do not worship Fructuosus, but him whom Fructuosus worships." The primitive Christians believed, that the martyrs enjoyed very singular privileges; that upon their death they were immediately admitted to the beatific vision, while other souls waited for the completion of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of judgement; and that God would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> chiefly to their prayers the hastening of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and shortening the times of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>. The churches built over the graves of the martyrs, and called by their names, in order to preserve the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of their sufferings, were distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> martyrium confessio, or memoria.
