The festivals of the martyrs are of very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> in the Christian church, and may be carried back at least till the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Polycarp, who suffered martyrdom about the year of Christ 168. On these days the Christians met at the graves of the martyrs, and offered prayers and thanksgivings to God for the examples they had afforded them: they celebrated the eucharist, and gave alms to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>; which, together with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> or sermon, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> the acts of the martyrs, were the spiritual exercises of these assemblies. Of the sayings, sufferings, and deaths of the martyrs, though preserved with great care for the above purpose, and to serve as models to future ages, we have but very little left, the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of them having been destroyed during that dreadful persecution which Diocletian carried on for ten years with fresh fury against the Christians; for a most diligent search was then made after all their books and papers; and all of them that were found were committed to the flames. Eusebius, indeed, composed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARTYROLOGY">martyrology</a>, but it never reached down to us; and those since compiled are extremely suspected. From the eighth century downwards, several Greek and Latin writers endeavoured to make up the loss, by compiling, with vast labour, accounts of the lives and actions of the ancient martyrs, but which consist of little else than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of fables: Nor are those records that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> under the name of Martyrology worthy of superior <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, since they bear the most evident marks both of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and falsehood. Martyr, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, a famous divine, born at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> in 1500. He studied <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and the languages at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, was a regular Augustine in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIESOLE">Fiesole</a>, and was counted one of the best best preachers in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Zuinglius and Bucer's writings gave him a good <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, and his conversation with Valdes confirmed it. He preached that doctrine at Rome in private; but, being impeached, fled to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and thence to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a>, where he brought over to the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> Emmanuel Tremellius, Celsus, Martinengas, Paul Laetius, and Jeremiah Zanchy. He was sent for to England by King Edward VI. and made professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> in 1549. In <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s reign he returned to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STRASBOURG">Strasbourg</a>, and was present at the conference of Poissy. His sentiments were not the same with Calvin's about Christ's presence in the eucharist. He wrote a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of works, and died in 1562. Martyrology, a catalogue or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of martyrs, including the history of their lives and sufferings for the sake of religion. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> comes from παράγω "to bring," and ἀπόστολος "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a>." The martyrologies draw their materials from the calendars of particular churches, in which the several festivals dedicated to them are marked; and which seem to be derived from the practice of the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who inserted the names of heroes and great men in their fasti or public registers. The martyrologies are very numerous, and contain many ridiculous and even contradictory narratives: which is easily accounted for, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we consider how many forged and spurious accounts of the lives of saints and martyrs appeared in the first ages of the church, which the legendary writers afterwards adopted without examining into the truth of them. However, some good critics, of late years, have gone a great way towards clearing the lives of the saints and martyrs from the monstrous heap of fiction they laboured under. See the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGEND">LEGEND</a>. The Martyrology of Eusebius of Cesarea was the most celebrated in the ancient church. It was translated into Latin by St Jerome; but the learned agree that it is not now extant. That attributed to Beda, in the eighth century, is of very doubtful authority; the names of several saints being there found who did not live till after the time of Beda. The ninth century was very fertile in martyrologies; then appeared that of Florus, subdeacon of the church at Lyons; who, however, only filled up the chasms in Beda. This was published about the year 830, and was followed by that of Waldenbertus, monk of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREVES">Treves</a>, written in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> about the year 844, and this by that of Ufuard, a French monk, and written by the command of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> the Bald in 875, which last is the martyrology now ordinarily used in the Roman church. That of Rabanus Maurus is an improvement on Beda, and Florus, written about the year 845; that of Notker, monk of St Gal, was written about the year 894. The martyrology of Ado, monk of Ferrières, in the diocese of Treves, afterwards archbishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VIENNE">Vienne</a>, is a descendant of the Roman, if we may so call it; for Du Sallier gives its genealogy thus: The martyrology of St Jerome is the great Roman martyrology; from this was made the little Roman one printed by Rofweyd; of this little Roman martyrology was formed that of Beda, augmented by Florus. Ado compiled his in the year 858. The martyrology of Nevelon, monk of Corbie, written about the year 1089, is little more than an abridgement of that of Ado; Father Kircher also makes mention of a Coptic martyrology preserved by the Maronites at Rome. We have also several protestant martyrologies, containing the sufferings of the reformed under the papists, viz. an English martyrology, by J. Fox; with others by Clark, Bray, &c. Martyrology is also used, in the Romish church, for a roll or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> kept in the vestry of each church, containing the names of all the saints and martyrs, both of the universal church and of the particular ones of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> or monastery. Martyrology is also applied to the painted or written catalogues in the Romish churches, containing the foundations, obits, prayers, and masses, to be said each day. Marvell, Andrew, an ingenious writer in the 17th century, was bred at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. He travelled through the most polite parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and was secretary to the embassy at Constantinople. His first appearance in public business at home was as assistant to Mr John <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, Latin secretary to the protector. A little before the restoration, he was chosen by his native town, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a> upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HULL">Hull</a>, to sit in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, which began at Westminster April 25th 1660; and is recorded as the last member of parliament who received the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a> or allowance anciently paid to representatives by their constituents. He seldom spoke in parliament, but he had great influence without doors upon the members of both houses; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Rupert had always the greatest regard for his advice. He made himself very obnoxious to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> by his actions and writings; notwithstanding which, King Charles II. took great delight in his conversation, and tried all means to win him over to his side, but in vain, nothing being ever able to shake his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>. There were many instances of his firmness in resisting the offers of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>; but he was <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> against all temptations. The king having one night entertained him, sent the lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> Danby the next morning to find out his lodgings; which were then up two <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of stairs in one of the little courts in the Strand. He was busy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, when the treasurer opened the door abruptly upon him. Surprised at the sight of so unexpected a visitor, Mr Marvell told his Lordship, "That he believed he had mistaken his way." Lord Danby replied, "Not, now I have found Mr Marvell;" telling him he came from his majesty, to know what he could do to serve him. Coming to a serious explanation, he told the lord treasurer, that he knew the nature of courts full well; that whoever is distinguished by a prince's favour, is certainly expected to vote in his interest. The Lord Danby told him, that his majesty had only a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of his merits, in regard to which he only desired to know if there was any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> at court he could be pleased with. These offers, though urged with the greatest earnestness, had no effect upon him. He told the lord treasurer, that he could not accept of them with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>; for he must be either ungrateful to the king in voting against him, or false to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in giving into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of the court. The only favour therefore he had to request of his majesty was, that he would esteem him as dutiful a subject as any he had, and more in his proper interest by refusing his offers than if he had embraced them. The Lord Danby finding no arguments Marvelments could prevail, told him, that the king had ordered a thousand pounds for him, which he hoped he would receive till he could think what farther to ask of his majesty. The last offer was rejected with the same steadfastness of mind as the first; though, as soon as the lord treasurer was gone, he was forced to send to a friend to borrow a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">guinea</a>. He died not without strong suspicions of his being poisoned, in 1678, in the 58th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. In 1683, the town of Kingston upon Hull contributed a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to erect a monument over him in the church of St Giles in the Fields, where he was interred, and an epitaph composed by an able <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; but the ministry of that church forbade both the inscription and monument to be placed there. He wrote many ingenious pieces; as, The Rehearsal transprosbed; A short Historical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> concerning General Councils, Creeds, and Impositions in matters of religion, &c.; also Poems and Letters.

MARVEL OF PERU

Pages 251-251

See MIRABILIS, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">INDEX</a>.

MARY

Pages 251-267

the mother of our Saviour <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, and a virgin at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that she conceived him; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Joachim and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNA">Anna</a>, of the tribe of Judah, and married to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> of the same tribe. The Scripture tells us nothing of her parents, not so much as their names, unless Heli mentioned by St Luke iii. 23. be the same with Joachim. All that is said concerning the birth of Mary and of her parents is only to be found in some apocryphal writings: which, however, are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>. Mary was of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, as was also her husband; "A virgin, espoused to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> whose name was Joseph, of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of David," says our translation of St Luke i. 27. which translation Mr <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITBY">Whitby</a> thinks might be better rendered thus: "A virgin of the house of David, espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, and the virgin's name was Mary;" because this agrees better with the words of the angel, "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> shall give him the throne of his father David," ver. 32. For since the angel had plainly told the virgin, that she should have this son without the knowledge of any man, it was not Joseph's but Mary's being of the house of David, that made David his father. Mary was akin to the race of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a>, since <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> the wife of Zacharias was her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> (ver. 36). Mary very early made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOW">vow</a> of chastity, and engaged herself to perpetual virginity. The Proto-evangelium of St James tells us, that she was consecrated to the Lord, and offered in the temple from her earliest youth; and that the priests gave her Joseph for a spouse, who was a holy and venerable old man, whom <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> appointed for his purpose by a miracle, the rod which he <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> carried having grown green and flourished as Aaron's did formerly. He espoused Mary, not to live with her in the ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, and to have children by her, but only that he might be the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> of her virginity. Though these circumstances are not to be relied on as certain, yet Mary's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of continency, even in a married state, cannot be called in question, since her virginity is attested by the gospel, and that herself speaking to the angel, who declared to her that she should become the mother of a son, told him that "she knew not a man" (ver. 34.), <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that she lived in continency with her husband: for which reason, when Joseph perceived her pregnancy, he was extremely surprized at it, knowing the mutual resolution they had agreed to of living in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINENCE">continence</a> though in a state of marriage. When Mary was ready to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in, an edict was published by Caesar Augustus, which decreed, that all the subjects of the empire should go to their own cities, there to have their names registered according to their families. Thus Joseph and Mary, who were both of the lineage of David, betook themselves to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Bethlehem, from whence was the original of their family. But while they were in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, the time being fulfilled in which Mary was to be delivered, she brought forth her first-born son. She wrapped him in swaddling-clothes, and laid him in the manger of the stable or cavern whither they had retired: for they could find no place in the public inn, because of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> concourse of people that were then at Bethlehem on the same occasion; or they were forced to withdraw into the stable of the inn, not being able to get a more convenient lodging, because of the multitude of people then at Bethlehem. At the same time the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> made it known to the shepherds who were in the fields near Bethlehem, and who came in the night to see Mary and Joseph and the child lying in the manger, and to pay him their tribute of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a>. Mary took notice of all these things, and laid them up in her heart, (Luke ii. 19. Matth. ii. 8, 9, 10, 11, &c.) A few days after, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGI">magi</a> or wise men came from the east, and brought to Jesus the mysterious presents of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, frankincense, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MYRRH">myrrh</a>; after which being warned by an angel that appeared to them in a dream, they returned into their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> by a way different from that by which they came. But the time of Mary's purification being come, that is forty days after the birth of Jesus, Mary went to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> (Luke ii. 21.), there to present her son in the temple, and there to offer the sacrifice appointed by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> for the purification of women after childbirth. There was then at Jerusalem an old man named Simeon, who was full of the Holy Ghost, and who had received a secret assurance that he should not die before he had seen Christ the Lord. He came then into the temple by the influence of the spirit of God, and taking the little Jesus within his arms, he blessed the Lord: and afterwards addressing himself to Mary, he told her, "That this child should be for the rising and falling of many in Israel, and for a sign which should be spoken against; even so far as that her own <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> should be pierced as with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, that the secret thoughts in the hearts of many might be discovered." Afterwards when Joseph and Mary were preparing to return to their own country of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAZARETH">Nazareth</a> (Matth. ii. 13, 14.), Joseph was warned in a dream to retire into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> with Mary and the child, because Herod had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to destroy Jesus. Joseph obeys the admonition, and they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in Egypt till after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Herod; upon which he and Mary returned to Nazareth, not daring to go to Bethlehem because it was in the jurisdiction of Archelaus the son and successor of Herod the Great. Here the holy family took up their residence, and remained till Jesus began his public ministry. We read of Mary being present at the marriage of Cana in Galilee, with her son Jesus and his disciples (John ii. On which occasion Jesus having turned <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> into wine, being the first public miracle that he performed, he went from thence to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPERNAUM">Capernaum</a> with his mother and his brethren, or his parents and disciples; and this seems to be the place where the holy virgin afterwards chiefly resided. However, St Epiphanius thinks she followed him everywhere during the whole time of his preaching; though we do not find the evangelists make any mention of her among the holy women that followed him and ministered to his necessities. The Virgin Mary was at Jerusalem at the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSOVER">passover</a> that our Saviour celebrated there; she <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> all that was transacted against him, followed him to Calvary, and stood at the foot of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a> worthy of the mother of God. There Jesus seeing his mother and his beloved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> near her, he said to his mother, "Woman, behold thy son;" and to the disciple, "Behold thy mother." And from that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> the disciple took her home to his own house. It is not to be doubted, but that our Saviour appeared to his mother immediately after his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a>; and that she was the first, or at least one of the first, to whom he vouchsafed this great consolation. She was with the apostles at his ascension, and continued with them at Jerusalem, expecting the coming of the Holy Ghost (Acts i. 14.). After this, she dwelt in the house of St John the Evangelist, who took care of her as of his own mother. It is thought that he took her along with him to Ephesus, where she died in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the ecumenical <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Ephesus, importing, that in the fifth century it was believed she was buried there. Yet this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> was not so universal, but that there are authors of the same age who think she died and was buried at Jerusalem. Mary Magdalen, who has been generally confounded with Mary the sister of Martha and Lazarus, but very improperly, was probably that sinner mentioned by St Luke, chap. vii. 36. 37. &c., whose name he does not tell us. There are some circumstances sufficient to convince us, that she is the same whom he calls Mary Magdalen in chap. viii. 2. and from whom he says Jesus drove out <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> devils. Jesus having healed the widow's son of Nain, entered into the city, and there was invited to eat by a Pharisee named Simon. While he was at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, a woman of a scandalous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> came into the house, having an alabaster box full of perfumed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and standing upright behind Jesus, and at his feet, for he was lying at table on a couch after the manner of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, she poured her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERFUME">perfume</a> on his feet, kissed them, watered them with her tears, and wiped them with her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. The Pharisee observing this, said within himself, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this man were a prophet, he would know who this woman is that touches him, that she is one of a wicked life. Then Jesus, who knew the bottom of his heart, illustrated her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> by a parable; and concluded with answering the woman, that her sins were forgiven her. In the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>, St Luke tells us, that Jesus, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with his apostles, preached the gospel from city to city; and that there were several women whom he had delivered from evil spirits, and had cured of their infirmities, among whom was Mary called Magdalen, out of whom went seven devils. This, it must be owned, is no positive <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that the sinner mentioned before was Mary Magdalen; however, it is all we have in support of this opinion: An opinion which has been able controverted by others. Mary Magdalen had her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a>, it is thought, from the town of Magdalia in Galilee. Lightfoot believes that this Mary is the same with Mary the sister of Lazarus. Magdalen is mentioned by the evangelists among the women that followed our Saviour, to minister to him according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the Jews. St Luke viii. 2. and St Mark xvi. 9. observe, that this woman had been delivered by Jesus Christ from seven devils. This some understand in the literal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>; but others take it figuratively, for the crimes and wickedness of her past life (supposing her to be the sinner first above mentioned), from which Christ had rescued her. Others maintain, that she had always lived in virginity; and consequently they make her a different person from the sinner mentioned by St Luke: and by the seven devils of which she was possessed, they understand no other than a real possession, which is not inconsistent with a holy life. This indeed is the most probable opinion, and that which has been best supported. In particular, the author of a "Letter to Jonas Hanway" on the subject of Magdalen House, published in 1758, has shown by a variety of learned remarks, and quotations both from the Scriptures and from the best commentators, that Mary Magdalen was not the sinner spoken of by St Luke, but on the contrary that she "was a woman of disfavour, and very easy in her worldly circumstances. For a while, she had laboured under some bodily indisposition, which our Lord miraculously healed, and for which benefit she was ever after very thankful. So far as we know, her conduct was always regular and free from censure; and we may reasonably believe, that after her acquaintance with our Saviour it was edifying and exemplary. I conceive of her (continues our author) as a woman of a fine understanding, and known virtue and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of behaviour becoming her age, her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, and her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> station: by all which, she was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to him whom she followed as her <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> and benefactor. She showed our Lord great respect in his life, at his death, and after it; and she was one of those to whom he first showed himself after his resurrection." Mary Magdalen followed Christ in the last journey that he made from Galilee to Jerusalem, and was at the foot of the cross with the holy virgin (John xix. 25. Mark xv. 47.) After which she returned to Jerusalem to buy and prepare the perfumes, that she might embalm him after the Sabbath was over which was then about to begin. All the Sabbath <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> she remained in the city; and the next day early in the morning she went to the sepulchre, along with Mary the mother of James and Salome (Mark xvi. 1, 2. Luke xxiv. 1, 2.) On the way, they inquired of one another, who should take away the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> from the mouth of the sepulchre, and were sensible of a great earthquake. This was the token of our Saviour's resurrection. Being come to his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, they saw two angels, who informed them that Jesus was risen. Upon this Mary Magdalen runs immediately to Jerusalem, and acquaints the apostles with this good news, returning herself Mary herself to the sepulchre. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> and John came also, and were witnesses that the body was no longer there. They returned; but Mary stayed, and stooping forward to examine the inside of the tomb, she there saw two angels sitting, one at the head and the other at the foot of the tomb; and immediately afterwards, upon <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> about, she beheld the Lord himself. She would have <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> herself at his feet to kiss him. But Jesus said to her, "Touch me not, for I am not yet ascended to my Father." As if he had said, "You shall have leisure to see me hereafter; go now to my brethren, my apostles, and tell them I am going to ascend to my God and to their God, to my Father and to their Father." Thus had Mary the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of first seeing our Saviour after his resurrection. (See Math. xxxviii. 5. &c. Mark xvi. 6. &c. John xx. 11, 17.) She returned then to Jerusalem and told the apostles that she had seen the Lord, that she had spoken to him, and told them what he had said to her. But at first they did not believe her, till her report was confirmed by many other testimonies.—This is what the gospel informs us concerning Mary Magdalen, different from Mary the sister of Martha, though she has been often called by this name. For, as to the pretended <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Mary Magdalen, which is said to have been written in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> by Marcella <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of Martha; this can only relate to Mary sister of Martha, and besides is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> piece of imposture. Mary, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of England, was eldest daughter of Henry VIII. by his first wife Catherine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> in February 1517. Her mother was very careful of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and provided her with tutors to teach her what was fitting. Her first preceptor was the famous Linacre, who drew up for her use the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">Rudiments</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, and afterwards De emendata structura Latini sermonis libri xv. Linacre dying when she was but six years old, Ludovicus Vives, a very learned man of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a> in Spain, was her next <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>; and he composed for her De ratione studii puerialis. Under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of these excellent men, she became so great a mistress of Latin, that Erasmus commends her for her epistles in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Towards the end of her father's reign, at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> solicitation of Queen Catharine Parr, she undertook to translate Erasmus's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPHRASE">Paraphrase</a> on the gospel of St John; but being cast into sickness, as Udall relates, partly by overmuch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, after she had made some progress therein, she left the rest to be done by Dr <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALLET">Mallet</a> her chaplain. This translation is printed in the first volume of Erasmus's Paraphrase upon the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, 1548, folio; and before it is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">Preface</a>, written by Udall, the famous master of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETON">Eton</a> school, and addressed to the queen dowager (A).—Had she been educated in Spain, however, and an inquisitor had been her preceptor, she could not have imbibed more strongly the bloody principles of Romanist <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>; and to the eternal disgrace of the English prelacy, though the reformation had taken root in both <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, she found English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> ready to carry her cruel designs to subvert it into effectual execution. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Edward her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> dying the 6th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1553, she was proclaimed queen the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, and crowned in October by Stephen Gardiner bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>. Upon her accession to the throne, she declared, in her speech to the council, that she would not persecute her Protestant subjects; but in the following month, she prohibited preaching without a special license; and before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of three months, the Protestant bishops were (A) As this preface contains many reflections which may very much edify the females of this age, we shall for their sakes here transcribe a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it. Mr Udall takes occasion in it to observe to her majesty, "The great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of noble women at that time in England, not only given to the study of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> sciences and strange tongues, but also so thoroughly expert in the Holy Scriptures, that they were able to compare with the best writers, as well in editing and penning of godly and fruitful treatises, to the instruction and edifying of realms in the knowledge of God, as also in translating good books out of Latin or Greek into English, for the use and commodity of such as are rude and ignorant of the said tongues. It was now (he said) no news in England to see young damsels in noble houses, and in the courts of princes, instead of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a> and other instruments of idle trifling, to have continually in their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> either psalms, homilies, and other devout meditations, or else Paul's epistles, or some book of holy scripture matters, and as familiarly both to read or reason thereof in Greek, Latin, French, or Italian, as in English. It was now a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> thing to see young virgins so trained in the study of good letters, that they willingly set all other vain pastimes at nought for learning's sake. It was now no news at all to see queens and ladies of most high estate and progeny, instead of courtly dalliance, to embrace virtuous exercises of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, and with most earnest study, both early and late, to apply themselves to the acquiring of knowledge, as well in all other liberal arts and disciplines, as also most especially of God and his holy word. And in this behalf (says he), like as to your highnesses, as well as for composing and setting forth many godly psalms, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> other contemplative meditations, as also for causing these paraphrases to be translated into our vulgar tongue, England can never be able to render thanks sufficient; so may it never be able, as her defects require, enough to praise and magnify the most noble, the most virtuous, the most witty, and the most studious Lady Mary's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, for taking such pain and travail in translating this Paraphrase of Erasmus upon the gospel of St John.—What could be a more plain <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of her most constant purpose to promote God's word, and the free grace of his gospel?" &c. Mr Udall was mistaken; she never meant any such thing: for soon after her accession to the throne, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> was issued for calling in and suppressing this very book, and all others that had the least tendency towards furthering the reformation. And Mr Walpole is of opinion, that the sickness which came upon her while she was translating St John, was all affected; "for (says he) she would not so easily have been cast into sickness, had she been employed on the Legends of St Teresa or St Catharine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIENNA">Sienna</a>." were excluded the house of lords, and all the statutes of Edward VI, repressing the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> were repealed. In July 1554 she was married to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Spain, eldest son of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V.; and now began that persecution against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> for which her reign is so justly infamous. Some have supposed, that the queen was herself of a compassionate and humane disposition; and that most of those barbarities were transacted by her bishops without her knowledge or privy. Without her knowledge and privy they could not be: it would be a better <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of her to say, that a strict adherence to a false religion, and a conscientious observance of its pernicious and cruel dictates, overruled and got the better of that goodness of temper which was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to her. But neither can this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> be reasonably admitted by any one, who considers her unkind and inhuman treatment of her sister the Lady Elizabeth; her admitting a council for the taking up and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of her father's body; her most ungrateful and perfidious <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a> men; her ungenerous and barbarous treatment of Judge Hales, who had strenuously defended her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of succession to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; and of Archbishop Cranmer, who in reality had saved her life. Shall we excuse all this by saying, "Tantum religio potuit suadere malorum?" Her obligations to Cranmer deserve to be more particularly set forth. Burnet says, "that her firm adherence to her mother's cause and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, and her backwardness in submitting to the king her father, were thought crimes of such a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> by his majesty, that he came to a resolution to put her openly to death; and that when all others were unwilling to run any risk in saving her, Cranmer alone ventured upon it." In his gentle way he told the king "that she was young and indiscreet, and therefore it was no wonder if she obstinately adhered to that which her mother and all about her had been insinuating into her for many years; but that it would appear strange, if he should for this cause so far forget the father, as to proceed to extremities with his own child; that if she was separated from her mother and her people, in a little time there might be ground gained on her; but that to take away her life, would raise horror through all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> against him;" by which means he preferred her. —Along with Archbishop Cranmer, who had thus saved her life, the bishops Ridley and Latimer were also condemned for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and afterwards burnt. In 1556, the persecution became general; and Protestants of all ranks and ages, and of both sexes, fell victims to papal fury. It is observable, likewise, that the same perfidious violation of promises and treaties prevailed in the queen's council, with respect to public affairs. By the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of marriage concluded between the queen and Philip, it was expressly stipulated that England should not be engaged in any wars with France on account of Spain; yet in 1557, Philip who had brought immense sums of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> into England, procured an offensive and defensive <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> against France, from the English administration, and 8000 of the queen's choicest troops were sent over to the assistance of the Spaniards in the Low Countries: the loss of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALAIS">Calais</a> to the French was the first fruit of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and some afflert, that upon this single occasion the queen showed a strong <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to her native country, lamenting this stroke so deeply, that it occasioned her death; but it is better authenticated that she was carried off by an epidemic fever, which raged so violently that it did not leave a sufficient number of men in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> to get in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>. She had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, however, been a prey, if not to remorse, yet to disappointment and chagrin, arising from various cross accidents, such as want of children, and the absence and unkindness of Philip consequent thereupon. Her death happened Nov. 7, 1558, in the 43d year of her age, after a reign of five years, four months, and eleven days. There are some things of her writing still extant. Strype has preserved three prayers or meditations of hers: the first, "Against the Assaults of Vice;" the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, "A Meditation touching Adversity;" the third, "A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">Prayer</a> to be read at the Hour of Death." In Fox's "Acts and Monuments" are printed eight of her letters to King Edward and the lords of the council, on her nonconformity, and on the imprisonment of her chaplain Dr Mallet. In the Sylloge epistolae are several more of her letters, extremely curious: one of her delicacy in never having written but to three men; one of affection for her sister; one after the death of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> Boleyn; and one very remarkable of Cromwell to her. In "Haynes's State Papers," are two in Spanish, to the emperor Char. V. There is also a French letter, printed by Strype from the Cottonian library, in answer to a haughty mandate from Philip, when he had a mind to marry the Lady Elizabeth to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy, against the queen's and prince's inclination: it is written in a most abject manner, and a wretched style. Mary of Medicis, wife of Henry IV, king of France, was declared sole regent of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> in 1610, during the conflagration which the affliction of that beloved king had occasioned. By her ambitious intrigues, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> lost all its influence abroad, and was torn to pieces at home by contending factions. After several vicissitudes of fortune, she was abandoned by her son <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIII., whose reign had been constantly disturbed by the civil commotions she had occasioned; and died in indigence at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a> in 1642, aged 68. She built the superb <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Luxembourg at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and embellished that city with <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-AQUEDUCTS">aqueducts</a> and other ornaments. Mary, queen of Scotland, daughter of James V., was born in the royal palace of Linlithgow on the 8th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1542. Her mother was Mary, the eldest daughter of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CLAUDE">Claude</a> duke of Guise, and widow of Louis duke of Longueville. Her father dying a few days after her birth, she scarcely existed before she was hailed queen. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of a queen was unknown in Scotland; and the government of an infant queen could not command much respect from martial and turbulent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>, who exercised a kind of sovereignty over their own vassals; who looked upon the most warlike of their monarchs in hardly any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> than as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the aristocracy; and who, upon the slightest disquiet, were ever ready to fly into rebellion, and to carry their arms to the foot of the throne. James had not even provided against the disorders of a minority, by committing to proper persons the care of his daughter's education, and the administration of affairs in her name. The former of these objects, however, Mary, however, was not neglected, though the regency of the kingdom was intrusted to very feeble hands. At six years of age Mary was conveyed to France, where she received her education in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Henry II. The opening powers of her mind, and her natural dispositions, afforded early hopes of capacity and merit. After being taught to work with her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, she was instructed in the Latin tongue; and she is said to have understood it with an accuracy, which is in this age very uncommon in persons of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a> and elevated <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, but which was not then surprising, when it was the fashion among great ladies to study the ancient languages. In the French, the Italian, and the Spanish tongues, her proficiency was still greater, and she spoke them with equal ease and propriety. She walked, danced, and rode with enchanting gracefulness; and she was qualified by nature, as well as by art, to attain to distinction in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and music. To accomplish the woman, was not, however, the sole object of her education. Either she was taught, or she very early discovered, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of acquiring such branches of knowledge as might enable her to discharge with dignity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> the duties of a sovereign; and much of her time was devoted to the study of history, in which she delighted to the end of her life. Whilst Mary resided in the court of Henry II., her personal charms made a deep <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on the mind of the Dauphin. It was in vain that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTMORENCY">Montmorency</a> opposed their marriage with all his influence. The importance of her kingdom to France, and the power of her uncles the princes of Lorraine, were more than sufficient to counteract his intrigues; and the Dauphin obtained the most beautiful princess in Christendom. Though this alliance placed the queen of Scotland in the most conspicuous point of view, in the politest court of Europe, and drew to her those attentions which are in the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> pleasing to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> mind in the gaiety of youth; it may yet be considered as having accidentally laid the foundation of the greatest part of her future misfortunes. Elizabeth, who now swayed the sceptre of England, had been declared illegitimate by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and though the English Protestants paid no regard to a declaration which was compelled by the tyranny of Henry VIII., and which he himself had indeed rendered null by calling his daughter to the throne after her brother and elder sister; yet the papists both at home and abroad had objections to the legitimacy of Elizabeth's birth, founded on principles which with them had greater <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> than the acts of any human legislature. Mary was unquestionably the next heir in regular succession to the English throne, if Elizabeth should die without legitimate issue; and upon her marriage to the Dauphin, she was induced by the persuasion of her uncles, by the authority of the French king, and no doubt partly by her own ambition, to assume the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> and arms of queen of England and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. These, indeed, she forebore as soon as she became her own mistress; but the having at all assumed them was an offence which Elizabeth could never forgive, and which rankling in her bosom made her many years afterwards pursue the unhappy queen of Scots to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>. Henry II., dying soon after the marriage of the Dauphin and Mary, they mounted the throne of France. In that elevated station, the queen did not fail to distinguish herself. The weakness of her husband served to exhibit her accomplishments to the greatest advantage; and in a court where gallantry to the sex, and the most profound respect for the person of the sovereign, were inseparable from the manners of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, she learned the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> of royalty. But this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of successful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and unmixed felicity was of short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. Her husband Francis died unexpectedly after a short reign of fifteen months. Regret for his death, her own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMILIATION">humiliation</a>, the disgrace of her uncles the princes of Lorraine, which instantly followed, and the coldness of Catharine of Medici, the queen mother, who governed her son Charles IX., plunged Mary into inexplicable sorrow. She was invited to return to her own kingdom, and she tried to reconcile herself to her fate. She was now to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> from a situation of elegance and splendour to the very reign of incivility and turbulence, where most of her accomplishments would be utterly lost. Among the Scots of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, elegance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> was little known. The generality of them were sunk in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and barbarism; and what they termed religion, dictated to all a petulant rudeness of speech and conduct to which the queen of France was wholly unaccustomed. During her minority and absence, the protestant religion had gained a kind of establishment in Scotland; obtained, indeed, by violence, and therefore liable to be overturned by an act of the sovereign and the three estates in parliament. The queen, too, was unhappily of a different opinion from the great body of her subjects, upon that one topic, which among them actuated almost every heart, and directed almost every tongue. She had been educated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, and was strongly attached to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>: Yet she had either moderation enough in her spirit, or discretion enough in her understanding, not to attempt any innovation in the prevailing <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of Protestantism. She allowed her subjects the full and free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of their new religion, and only challenged the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> for her own. She contrived to attach to her, whether from his heart or only in appearance, her natural brother, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> of St Andrew's; a man of strong and vigorous parts, who, though he had taken the usual oath of obedience to the pope, had thrown off his spiritual <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>, and placed himself at the head of the reformers. By his means she crushed an early and formidable rebellion; and in reward for his services conferred upon him a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> estate, and created him <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Murray. For two or three years her reign was prosperous, and her administration applauded by all her subjects except the Protestant preachers; and had she either remained unmarried, or bestowed her affections upon a more worthy object, it is probable that her name would have descended to posterity among those of the most fortunate and the most deserving of Scottish monarchs. But a queen, young, beautiful, and accomplished, an ancient and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> kingdom, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of a mightier inheritance, were objects to excite the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and ambition of the most illustrious personages. Mary, however, who kept her eye steadily fixed on the English succession, rejected every offer of a foreign alliance; and, swayed at first by prudential motives, Mary motives, and afterwards by love the most excessive, she gave her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to Henry Stuart lord Darnley, the son of the earl of Lennox. This nobleman was, after herself, the nearest heir to the crown of England; he was likewise the first in succession after the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARRAN">Arran</a> to the crown of Scotland; and it is known that James V. had intended to introduce into his kingdom the Salique law, and to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the crown upon Lenox in preference to his own daughter. These considerations made Mary solicitous for an interview with Darnley; and at that interview love stole into her heart, and effaced every favourable thought of all her other suitors. Nature had indeed been lavish to him of her kindness. He was tall of stature; his countenance and shapes were beautiful and regular; and, amidst the mists and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> with which his arrival was celebrated, he shone with uncommon lustre. But the bounty of nature extended not to his mind. His understanding was narrow; his ambition excessive; his obstinacy inflexible; and under the guidance of no fixed principle, he was inconsistent and capricious. He knew neither how to enjoy his prosperity nor how to ensure it. On the 29th of July 1565, this ill-fated <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> were married; and though the queen gave her husband every possible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of the most extravagant love; though she infringed the principles of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> to confer upon him the title of king; and though she was willing to share with him all the offices, honours, and dignities of royalty—he was not satisfied with his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>, but soon began to clamour for more power. He had not been married seven months, when he entered into a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> to deprive Mary of the government, and to seat himself on her throne. With this view he headed a band of factious nobles, who entered her chamber at night; and though she was then far advanced in her pregnancy, murdered her secretary in her presence, whilst one of the ruffians held a cocked pistol to her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>. Such an outrage, together with his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a> and frequent amours, could not fail to alienate the affections of a high spirited woman, and to open her eyes to those defects in his character which the ardors of love had hitherto prevented her from seeing. She fidgeted and wept over the precipitation of her marriage: but though it was no longer possible to love him, she still treated him with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and respect, and laboured to fashion him to the humour of her people. This was labour in vain. His preposterous vanity and aspiring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> roused the resentment and the scorn of the nobles; his follies and want of dignity made him little with the people. He deserted the conspirators with whom he had been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> in the assassination of the secretary; and he had the extreme imprudence to threaten publicly the earl of Murray, who, from his talents and his followers, possessed the greatest power of any man in the kingdom. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> was, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> was formed for the king's destruction; and, on the 10th day of February 1567, the house in which he then resided was early in the morning blown up with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, and his Mary dead and naked body, without any marks of violence, was found in an adjoining field. Such a daring and atrocious <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> filled every mind with horror and astonishment. The queen, who had been in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> reconciled to her husband, was overwhelmed with grief, and took every method in her power to discover the regicides; but for some days nothing appeared which could <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to the discovery. Papers indeed were posted on the most conspicuous places in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, accusing the earl of Bothwell of the crime; and rumours were industriously circulated that his horrid enterprise was encouraged by the queen. Conscious, it is to be presumed, of her own innocence, Mary was the less disposed to believe the guilt of Bothwell, who was accused as having only acted as her <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>; but when he was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with the murder by the earl of Lennox, she instantly ordered him on his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>. Through the management of the earl of Morton and others, who were afterwards discovered to have been partners in his guilt, Bothwell was acquitted of all share and knowledge of the king's murder; and what is absolutely astonishing, and shows the total want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> at that time in Scotland, this flagitious man procured, by means of the same treacherous friends, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> signed by the majority of the nobles, recommending him as a fit husband for the queen! Armed with this instrument of mischief, which he weakly thought sufficient to defend him from danger, Bothwell soon afterwards seized the person of his sovereign, and carried her a prisoner to his castle at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUNBAR">Dunbar</a>. It has indeed been alleged by the enemies of the queen, that no force was employed on the occasion; that she was seized with her own consent; and that she was even privy to the subscribing of the bond by the nobles. But it has been well observed by one of her ablest vindicators (A), that "her previous knowledge of the bond, and her acquiescence in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZURE">seizure</a> of her person, are two facts in apparent opposition to each other. Had the queen acted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> with Bothwell in obtaining the bond from the nobles, nothing remained, but, under the sanction of their unanimous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, to have proceeded directly to the marriage. Instead of which, can we suppose her to be weak as to reject that address, and rather choose that Bothwell should attempt to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> and carry her off by violence?—an attempt which many accidents might frustrate, and which at all events could not fail to render him or both of them odious to the whole nation. Common sense, then, as well as candour, must induce us to believe, that the scheme of seizing the queen was solely the contrivance of Bothwell and his associates, and that it was really by force that she was carried to Dunbar." Being there kept a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> prisoner for 12 days; having, as there is reason to believe, actually suffered violence on her person; perceiving no appearance of a release; and being shown the infamous bond of the nobles; Mary promised to receive her rather for a husband, as in her opinion the only refuge for (a) Tytler's Dissertation on the Marriage of Queen Mary with the earl of Bothwell: Transactions of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of Antiquaries of Scotland, vol. i. for her injured honour. Without condemning with alacrity this compliancy of the queen, it is impossible not to recollect the more dignified conduct which Richardson attributes in similar circumstances to his Clarissa; and every man who feels for the sufferings, and respects the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Mary, must regret that she had not fortitude to resist every attempt to force upon her as a husband the profligate and audacious villain who had offered her such an insult as no virtuous woman ought ever to forgive. This, however, is only to regret that she was not more than human; that she who possessed so many perfections, should have had them blended with one defect. "In the irrevocable situation of her affairs, let the most severe of her sex say what course was left for her to follow? Her first and most urgent concern was to regain her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. That probably she attained by promising to be directed by the advice of her council, where Bothwell had nothing to fear." The marriage, thus inauspiciously contracted, was solemnized on the 15th of May 1567; and it was the signal for revolt in Morton, Lethington, and many of the other nobles, by whose wicked and relentless policy it had been chiefly brought about, and who had bound themselves to employ their swords against all persons who should presume to disturb so desirable an event. As Bothwell was justly and universally detested, and as the rebels pretended that it was only against him and not against their sovereign that they had taken up arms, troops flocked to them from every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. The progress and issue of this rebellion <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be seen in our history of Scotland: suffice it to say here, that upon the faith of promises the most solemn, not only of personal safety to herself, but of receiving as much honour, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and obedience, as ever in any former period was paid by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> to the princes her predecessors, the unhappy queen delivered herself into the hands of her rebels, and persuaded her husband to fly from the danger which in her <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> threatened his life. These promises were instantly violated. The faithless nobles, after insulting their sovereign in the crudest manner, hurried her as a prisoner to a castle within a lake, where she was committed to the care of that very woman who was the mother of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a> brother; who, with the natural insolence of a whore's menials, says Mr Whitaker, affected the legitimacy of her own child and the illegitimacy of Mary; and who actually carried the natural vulgarity of a whore's impudence so far, as to strip her of all her royal ornaments, and to dress her like a mere child of fortune in a coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> caffo. In this distress the queen's fortitude and presence of mind did not forsake her: She contrived to make her escape from her prison, and soon found herself at the head of 6000 combatants. This <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, however, was defeated; and, in opposition to the advice and entreaties of all her friends, she hastily formed the resolution of taking refuge in England. The archbishop of St Andrew's in particular accompanied her to the border; and when she was about to quit her own kingdom, he laid hold of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDLE">bridle</a>, and on his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> conjured her to return: but Mary proceeded, with the utmost reliance on the friendship of Elizabeth, which had been offered to her when she was a prisoner, and of the sincerity of which she harboured not a doubt. That princess, however, who had not yet forgotten her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSUMPTION">assumption</a> of the title and arms of queen of England, was now taught to dread her talents, and to be envious of her charms. She therefore, under various pretences, and in violation not only of public faith, but even of the common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of hospitality, kept her a close prisoner for 19 years: encouraged her rebellious subjects to accuse her publicly of the murder of her husband: allowed her no opportunity of vindicating her honour: and even employed venal scribblers to blast her fame. Under this unparalleled load of complicated distresses, Mary preserved the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a> of a queen, and practised with sincerity the duties of a Christian. Her sufferings, her dignified affability, and her gentleness of disposition, gained her great popularity in England, especially among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>; and as she made many attempts to procure her liberty, and carried on a constant correspondence with foreign powers, Elizabeth became at last so much afraid of her intrigues, that she determined to cut her off, at whatever hazard. With this view she prevailed upon her servile parliament to pass an act which might make Mary answerable for the crimes of all who should call themselves her partizans; and upon that flagitious statute she was tried as a traitor concerned in the conspiracy of Babington: (See Scotland). Though the trial was conducted in a manner which would have been illegal even if she had been a subject of England, and though no certain proof appeared of her connexion with the conspirators, she was, to the amazement of Europe, condemned to suffer death. The fair heroine received her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> with great composure; saying to those by whom it was announced, "The news you bring cannot but be most welcome, since they announce the termination of my miseries. Nor do I account that soul to be deserving of the felicities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a>, which can shrink under the sufferings of the body, or scruple the stroke that sets it free." On the evening before her execution, for which, on the succeeding morn, she prepared herself with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> solemnity and perfect resignation, she ordered all her servants to appear before her, and drank to them. She even condescended to beg their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> for her omissions or neglects; and she recommended it to them to love <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, to avoid the unhappy passions of hatred and malice, and to preserve themselves steadfast in the faith of Christ. She then distributed among them her money, her jewels, and her clothes, according to their rank or merit. She wrote her will with her own hand, constituting the duke of Guise her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> executor; and to the king and queen of France she recommended her son, provided he should prove worthy of their esteem.—In the castle of Fotheringay she was beheaded on the 8th of February 1587, in the 45th year of her age; and her body, after being embalmed and committed to a leaden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>, was buried with royal pomp and splendour in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of Peterborough. Twenty years afterwards her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> were, by order of her son and only child King James I., removed to Westminster, and deposited in their proper place among the kings of England. The general character of Mary, which in the regular order of biography should now be laid before the reader, has furnished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of controversy for 200 years.—She is universally allowed to have had considerable talents, and a mind highly cultivated. By one party she is painted with more virtues and with fewer defects than almost any other woman of the age in which she lived. By another, she is represented as guilty of the grossest crimes which a woman can commit—<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a> and the murder of her husband. By all it is confessed, that, previous to her connexion with the earl of Bothwell, her life as a Christian was exemplary, and her administration as a queen equitable and mild; and it has never been denied that she bore her tedious sufferings with such resignation and fortitude as are seldom found united with conscious guilt. These are strong presumptions of her innocence. The moral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of men change by degrees; and it seems hardly consistent with the known principles of human nature, that any person should at once plunge deliberately from the summit of virtue to the depths of vice; or, when sunk so low, should by one effort recover his original state of elevation. But in this controversy presumptions must go for nothing. The positive evidences which were brought against the queen of Scots are so conclusive, that if they be genuine she must have been guilty; and if they be spurious there can be no doubt of her innocence. They consisted of a box with letters, contracts, and fonnets, said to be written by herself and sent to the earl of Bothwell. In addition to these, the supposed confessions of the criminals who had suffered for the king's murder were originally urged as proofs of her guilt; but those confessions are now admitted by all parties to be either wholly forged, or so grossly interpolated, that no stress whatever can be laid upon them; and during Mary's life it was affirmed by her friends, and not sufficiently contradicted by her enemies, that the persons who had accused Bothwell, and were doubtless his accomplices, instead of criminating the queen, had openly protested her innocence in their dying moments. This box then, with its contents, was the evidence upon which her accusers had the chief and indeed the only reliance; and it is upon this evidence, whatever it be, that the guilt or innocence of the Scottish princess must finally be determined. It is uniformly affirmed upon the part of the earl of Murray and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a>, that the casket with the letters and the fonnets had been left by Bothwell in the castle of Edinburgh; that this nobleman, before he fled from Scotland, sent a messenger to recover them; and that they were found in the possession of this person. The 20th day of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1567 is fixed as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> of this remarkable discovery. The governor of the castle at that time was Sir James Balfour. George Dalgleish, a servant of Bothwell's, is named as his messenger upon this errand. He was seized, it is said, by the domestics of the earl of Morton; and it was the earl of Morton himself who made the actual production of the casket and its contents. This story is unsupported by vouchers, contains improbabilities, and cannot be reconciled with history and events. There remains not any authentic or unsuspicious evidence that the queen had dishonoured the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of Lord Darnley; and there is the most satisfactory evidence*, that though Bothwell was intrusted with the defence of the borders on account of his tried courage and loyalty, he was privately disliked by Mary for his uncommon zeal in the cause of Protestantism. At the very time when the queen is said to have had the most violent love for that nobleman, and with him to have been carrying on the most criminal intercourse against her husband, we know both from Randolph and from Knox, that Bothwell refused to gratify her by the smallest compliance with the ceremonies of her religion, though many of the other Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> scrupled not to accompany her to the celebration of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>. That the villain who could deliberately commit murder, should be so ferociously conscientious with respect to modes of faith and worship, as to stand forward with a peculiar strain of bravery to oppose, in a favourite measure, the queen, who was then admitting him to her bed, and actually forming plans for raising him to her throne, is surely, to say the least of it, extremely improbable. But let us suppose this non-compliance on the part of Bothwell to have been a measure concerted between the queen and him to conceal more effectually from the eyes of the public the criminal intercourse in which they were engaged; is it not very surprising, that of such politicians, the one should have written those letters, and the other have left them in the power of their enemies? The earl of Bothwell was exposed to more than suspicions of a concern in the murder of the king. These papers contained manifest proofs of his guilt. It evidently was not his interest to preserve them; or admitting, that till his marriage was solemnized with the queen he might look upon them as his best security for the realizing of his ambitious hopes, yet, after that event, when all his former friends had deserted him, he must have felt the strongest inducements to destroy such a criminal correspondence; and Mary must have been ardently animated with the same wish. The castle of Edinburgh, where the box is said to have been lodged, was at this time entirely at their command; and Sir James Balfour, their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>, was the creature of Bothwell. If his enemies, who were now in arms against him, should possess themselves of this box and its contents, his destruction was inevitable. From his marriage till the 24th day of June, it was in his power to have destroyed the fatal papers; and if they had existed, it is not to be imagined that he would have neglected a step so expedient, not only for his own security and reputation, but also for those of the queen. During all this time, however, he made no effort to recover his box and letters: he had lodged them in the castle of Edinburgh; and there he chose to leave them in the custody of a man in whom he could not have one particle of affiance. This was excessively foolish; but his subsequent conduct was still more so.
