This invention is the more ingenious, as it presents the tedious parts of education, namely, reading, writing, and the elements of languages, to the youthful mind as a delightful entertainment; and many people in France, both in the capital and in the provinces, have adopted it with success. After he had conceived the idea of this invention, he made the first trial of it on the young Candiac, who was remarkable for his understanding in his earliest years. Du Mas conducted his pupil to Paris and the principal cities in France, where he was universally admired. This prodigy was carried off in the year 1726 before he was seven years of age, and his loss had nearly deprived Du Mas of his reason. A dangerous illness was the consequence of his vexation; and he would have died of want, if a gentleman had not taken him from his garret and entertained him in his own house. Du Mas afterwards retired with Madame de Vaujour within two leagues of Paris, and died.

MASAFUERO

Pages 269-269

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, lying in S. Lat. 33° 45', W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 82° 46'. It is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and mountainous, and at a distance seems to consist of one hill <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rock. It is of a triangular form, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight leagues in circumference. There is such plenty of fish, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> with a few hooks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> may very soon catch as many as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> serve 100 people. Here are coal-fish, cavilliers, cod, halibut, and cray-fish. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Carteret's crew caught a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>-fisher that weighed 87 pounds, and was five feet and a half long. The sharks were here so ravenous, that, in taking foundlings, one of them swallowed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, by which they hauled him above <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; but he regained his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> by disgorging his prey. Seals are so numerous here, that Captain Carteret says, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> many thousands were killed in a night, they would not be missed next morning. These animals yield excellent train <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>; and their hearts and plucks are very good food, having a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> something like those of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOG">hog</a>; their skins are covered with a very fine fur. There are many birds here, and some very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> hawks. Of the pintado <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> one ship caught 700 in one night. Commodore Byron landed here with difficulty in 1765, in order to take in wood and water, of both which he found plenty. He found also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of goats, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> tasted as well as venison in England.

MASCULINE

Pages 269-269

is more ordinarily used in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> to signify the first and worthiest of the genders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a>. See GENDER. The masculine gender is that which belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> kind, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> something analogous to it. Most substances are ranged under the heads of masculine or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMININE">feminine</a>.—This, in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, is done with a show of reason; but in others is merely arbitrary, and for that reason is found to vary according to the languages and even according to the words introduced from one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> into another.—Thus the names of trees are generally feminine in Latin and masculine in the French. Farther, the genders of the same word are sometimes varied in the same language. Thus alveus, according to Priscian, was anciently masculine, but is now become feminine. And navire, "a ship," in French, was anciently feminine, but is now masculine. MASCULINE <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHYME">Rhyme</a>, in the French <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, is that made with a word which has a strong, open, and accented <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a>; as all words have, excepting those which have an e feminine in their last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a>. For instance, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMOUR">amour</a> and jour, mort and fort, are masculine rhymes; and père and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a>, gloire and memoire, are feminine. Hence also verses ending with a masculine rhyme, are called masculine verses, and those ending with a feminine rhyme, feminine verses. It is now a rule established among the French poets never to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the above two masculine or two feminine verses successively, except in the looser kind of poetry. Marot was the first who introduced this mixture of masculine and feminine verses, and Ronsard was the first who practised it with success. The masculine verses should always have a syllable less than the feminine ones. MASCULINE Signs. Astrologers divide the signs into masculine and feminine; by reason of their qualities, which are either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, and hot or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, accounted masculine; or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a>, dry and moist, which are feminine.—On this principle they call the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, masculine; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">Moon</a> and Venus feminine. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, they suppose, partakes of the two. Among the signs, Aries, Libra, Gemini, Leo, Sagittarius, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUARIUS">Aquarius</a>, are masculine; Cancer, Capricornus, Taurus, Virgo, Scorpio, and Pisces, are feminine. MASCULUS FLOS. See Flos, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MASEOTHAEI

Pages 269-269
or MASEOETHAEI, the name of a sect, or rather of two sects; for Eusebius, or rather Hegesippus whom he cites, makes mention of two different sects of Mabuthaeans. The first was one of the seven sects that rose out of Judaism, and proved very troublesome to the church; the other was one of the seven Jewish sects before the coming of Jesus Christ. The word is derived from the Hebrew שָׁבַע, shabat, "to rest or repose," and signifies idle easy indolent people. Eusebius speaks of them as if they had been so called from Mabuthaeus their chief; but it is much more probable that their name is Hebrew, or at least Chaldaic, signifying the same thing with a Sabbatarian in our language; that is, one who makes profession of keeping Sabbath. Valentinus will not allow the two sects to be confounded together: the last being a sect of Jews before, or at least contemporary with Christ; and the former a sect of heretics descended from them. Rufinus distinguishes them in their names; the Jewish sect he calls Mabuthaei; and the heretics Mabuthaeani. The Mabuthaeans were a branch of the Simonians.

MASH

Pages 269-270

a drink given to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, made of half a peck of ground malt put into a pail, into which as much scalding hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is poured as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> wet it very well: when that is done, stir it about, till, by tasting, you find it as sweet as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>; and when it has stood till it is lukewarm, it is to be given to the horse. This liquor MASK. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASQUE">MASQUE</a>.

MASINISSA

Pages 270-270

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, who at first assisted the Carthaginians in their wars against Rome; but afterwards joined the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and became the firmest ally they ever had. See <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMIDIA">NUMIDIA</a>.

MASON

Pages 270-270

William, an English poet of distinction, born in 1725, was the son of a clergyman who held the living of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HULL">Hull</a>. He took his first degrees at St John's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a> in 1745, whence he removed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a> college, of which he was admitted a fellow in 1747. He was M.A. in 1749, a minister in 1754. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Holdernesse presented him to the valuable rectory of Aton in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, and procured for him the office of chaplain to his majesty. His ode on the installation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the university of Cambridge was the first specimen of his poetical talents, which gained him considerable reputation, although the subject was not popular. His monody to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Pope, and Isis, an elegy, added to his fame, which was still farther increased by his dramatic poem of Elfrida in 1752, and Caractacus in 1759. He did not succeed in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> tragedy as he did not compose for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> stage, but wished to revive the manner of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. He published a small collection of odes in 1756, intended as an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of his dear friend Gray. He gave the world some elegies in 1763, which in general are marked with the simplicity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> proper to this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, breathing noble sentiments of freedom and of virtue. In point of morality he may justly be considered as the purest of poets, and one of the warmest friends of civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> by which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> he lived in was distinguished. The first book of his English Garden made its appearance in 1772, a didactic poem in blank <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, of which the fourth and last book was printed in the year 1781. Some good critics consider this poem as rather stiff, and the dry minuteness of the preceptive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, prevented it from bringing the author any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of popularity. In 1775 he published the poems of Mr Gray, to which he prefixed <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and writings. His observations on the character and genius of his friend did <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and feelings, and of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> the volume was favourably received. At the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his residence he acted with the friends of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a>, and the enemies of such <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> as were deemed incompatible with the liberties of freemen. During the continuance of the American <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, he addressed an ode to the naval officers of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, on the acquittal of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Keppel in 1779, in which he decidedly execrated the war carrying on against the people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. When Mr Pitt rose to power in 1782, Mason addressed an ode to him, which contained patriotic and manly sentiments, but his lyric imagery did it considerable injury. He published in 1783 a poetical translation of Fresnay's Latin poem on the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, which unites great elegance of language and versification with a correct representation of a difficult original. Besides the living with which he was presented soon after taking orders, he obtained the preferments of precentor and canon residentary of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>. At that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> he preached an occasional discourse in 1788 on the subject of the slave-trade, full of animated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLAMATION">declamation</a> against the inhumanity of the traffic. The centenary commemoration of the revolution in that year produced his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> ode, which breathed his usual spirit of freedom. An additional volume of his poems was given to the world in 1797, consisting of miscellaneous pieces, the revised productions of his youth, and the effusions of his old age. In his Pindaric ode to Liberty we behold the change wrought in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> principles by the melancholy events of the French revolution. Mr Mason died in April 1797, at the age of 72, the consequence of a mortification by a hurt in his leg. He had married an amiable lady, who died of a consumption in 1767, and was buried at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a> cathedral, under a monument on which are <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> some very tender and beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> by her husband. The character of Mason in private life was exemplary for worth and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> benevolence. A tablet has been placed to his memory in Poets Corner in Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>. Some satirical pieces of merit have been ascribed to him, but some are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the internal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> is sufficient to decide against his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to them; yet it must be allowed that he could write with energy and simplicity, and the objects of satire in these pieces are such as it was extremely probable that he would fix upon.

MASONRY

Pages 270-300

in general, a branch of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, consisting in the art of hewing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> squaring <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> or perpendicular, for the uses of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; but, in a more limited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, masonry is the art of assembling and joining stones together with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>. Hence arise as many different kinds of masonry as there are different forms and manners for laying or joining stones. Vitruvius mentions several kinds of masonry used among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; three of hewed <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, viz. that in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>, that in binding, and that called the Greek masonry; and three of unhewn stones, viz. that of an equal course, that of an unequal course, and that filled up in the middle; and the seventh was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of all the rest. Net masonry, called by Vitruvius reticulatum, from its resemblance to the meshes of a net, consists of stones squared in their courses, and so disposed as that their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> Masonry joints go obliquely; and their diagonals are the one perpendicular and the other level. This is the most agreeable masonry to the eye, but it is very apt to crack. Bound masonry, is that in which the stones were placed one over another, like tiles; the joints of their beds being level, and the mounters perpendiculars, so that the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> that mounts and separates two stones always falls directly over the middle of the stone below. This is less beautiful than the net <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; but it is more <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> and durable. Greek masonry, according to Vitruvius, is that where after we have laid two stones, each of which makes a course, another is laid at the end, which makes two courses, and the same order is observed throughout the building; this may be called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> binding, in regard the binding is not only of stones of the same course with one another, but likewise of one course with another course. Masonry by equal courses, called by the ancients *isodomum*, differs in nothing from the bound masonry, but only in this, that its stones are not hewn. Masonry by unequal courses, called *pleudifodomum*, is also made of unhewn stones, and laid in bound work; but then they are not of the same thickness, nor is there any equality observed excepting in the several courses, the courses themselves being unequal to each other. Masonry filled up in the middle, is likewise made of unhewn stones, and by courses; but the stones are only set in order as to the courses. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">Compound</a> masonry is of Vitruvius's proposing, so called as being formed of all the rest. In this the courses are of hewed stone; and the middle being left void, is filled up with mortar and pebbles thrown in together; after this the stones of one course are bound to those of another course with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> cramps fastened with melted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>. All the kinds of masonry now in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> may be reduced to these five, viz. bound masonry; that of brick work, where the bodies and projectures of the stones enclose <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> spaces or pannels, &c. fet with bricks; that of masonry, or small work, where the courses are equal, well squared, and their edges or beds ruficated; that where the courses are unequal; and that filled up in the middle with little stones and mortar. Free Masonry, denotes the rules or system of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> and secrets peculiar to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of free and accepted masons. 1. When men are in a state of barbarity, and are scattered over the surface of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in small and independent tribes, their wants are as small in magnitude, as they are few in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. It is in the power, therefore, of every individual, to perform, for himself and his family, every work of labour which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> or comfort requires; and while, at one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, he equips himself for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHASE">chase</a> or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, at another, he is rearing a habitation for his offspring, or hollowing his canoe to surmount the dangers of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. But as soon as these tribes associate together, for the purposes of mutual protection and comfort, civilization advances apace; and, in the same proportion, the wants and desires of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> increase. In order to gratify these, the ingenuity of individuals is called forth; and those, who, from inability or indolence, cannot satisfy their own wants, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> immediately <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> to the superior skill of their neighbours. Those members of the community, who can execute their work with the greatest elegance and celerity, will be most frequently employed; and, from this circumstance, combined with the principle of emulation, and other causes, that distinction of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a> will arise, which is found only among nations considerably advanced in civilization and refinement. 2. One of the first objects of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, in a rude state, is reasons to screen himself and his family from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the tropic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, from the inclemency of the polar regions, or from the sudden changes of more temperate climates; been the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> he has arrived at such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of improvement, as first professed to live under the dominion of a superior, and under the influence of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, and the temple of his gods, will be reared in the most magnificent style which his skill can <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVISE">devise</a> and his industry accomplish, and decked with those false ornaments which naturally catch the eye of unpolished men. From that principle which impels the lower orders to imitate the magnificence and splendour of their superiors, a foundation will be laid for improvement in the art of building; and it is extremely probable, from the circumstances which have been mentioned, as well as from others which the slightest reflection will suggest, that architecture will be the first profession to which men will exclusively devote their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and for which they will be trained by an established course of preparatory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. 3. Nor is it from this ground only, that masonry de-Architectures its superiority as a separate profession. While ture super- many other arts administer to our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, other gratify only those temporary wants and unnatural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> defies which refinement has rendered necessary, the profession, art of building can lay claim to a higher object. The undertakings of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a>, not only furnish us with elegant and comfortable accommodation from the inclemency of the seasons, from the rapacity of wild beasts, and the still more dangerous rapacity of man; they contribute also to the ornament and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of nations, and it is to them that we are indebted for those fortresses of strength which defend us from the inroads of surrounding enemies. Nor can the works of the architect be ranked among those objects which furnish amusement and accommodation for a few years, or at most during the short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; they descend unimpaired from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> to generation; they acquire additional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and value from an increase of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and are the only specimens of human labour which, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, survive the revolutions of kingdoms, and the waste of time. The splendid remains of Egyptian, Grecian, and Roman architecture, which, in every age, have attracted the attention of the learned, and excited the astonishment of the vulgar, are standing monuments of the ingenuity and power of man; and, in ages yet to come, they will reflect a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> on the art of building, to which no other profession can arrogate the slightest claim. 4. But there is still another consideration, which entitles architecture to a decided pre-eminence among the other arts. It is itself the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> of many separate professions; and requires a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of talents, and an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of knowledge, for which other professions have not the smallest occasion. An acquaintance with the sciences sciences of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> and mechanical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, with the arts of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, and other admirable and elegant branches of knowledge, are indispensible requisites in the education of a good architect; and raise his art to a vast height above those professions, which practice alone can render familiar, and which consist in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> exertion of muscular force. It appears, then, from these considerations, that there is some foundation, in the very <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of architecture, for those extraordinary privileges to which masons have always laid claim, and which they have almost always possessed—privileges, which no other artists could have confidence to ask, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to enjoy; and there appears to be some foundation for that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and respectable order of free masons, whose <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> we are now to investigate. 5. But, that we may be enabled to discover free masonry under those various forms, which it has assumed in different countries, and at different times, before it received the name which it now bears, it will be necessary to give a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the nature of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, without developing those mysteries, or revealing those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONIAL">ceremonial</a> observances which are known only to the brethren of the order. 6. Free masonry is an ancient and respectable institution, embracing individuals of every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, of every <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and of every condition in life. In order to confirm this institution, and attain the ends for which it was originally formed, every candidate comes under a solemn engagement never to divulge the mysteries of the order, nor communicate to the uninitiated the secrets with which he may be entrusted, and the proceedings and plans in which the fraternity may be engaged. After the candidate has undergone the necessary ceremonies, and received the usual instructions, appropriate words and significant signs are imparted to him, that he may be enabled to distinguish his brethren of the order from the uninitiated vulgar, and convince others that he is entitled to the privileges of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, should he be visited by distress or want, in a distant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>. If the newly admitted member be found qualified for a higher degree, he is promoted, after due intervals of probation, till he has received that masonic knowledge, which enables him to hold the highest offices of trust to which the fraternity can raise its members. At regular and appointed seasons, convivial meetings of the fraternity are held in lodges constructed for this purpose: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>, and joy, characterize these mixed assemblies. All distinctions of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> seem to be laid aside, all differences in religious and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> sentiments are forgotten; and those petty quarrels which disturb the quiet of private life, cease to agitate the mind. Every one strives to give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> to his brother; and men seem to recollect, for once, that they are sprung from the same origin, that they are possessed of the same nature, and are destined for the same end. 7. Such are the prominent features of an institution, which has of late produced so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> in the opinions of the learned, respecting its origin and tendency. While a certain class of men (a), a little over-anxious for the dignity of their order, have represented it as coeval with the world; others, influenced by an opposite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a>, have maintained it to be the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of English Jesuits, to promote the views of that intriguing and dangerous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> (b). Some philosophers, among whom we may reckon the celebrated Chevalier Ramfay, have laboured to prove, that free masonry arose during the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRUSADES">crusades</a>; that it was a secondary order of chivalry; that its forms originated from that warlike institution, and were adapted to the peaceful habits of scientific men (c). Mr Clinch (d) has attempted, with considerable ingenuity and learning, to deduce its origin from the institution of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>. M. Barruel (e) supposes it to be a continuation of the society of knights <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEMPLARS">templars</a>; while others, with a degree of audacity and malice rarely to be found in the character of ingenious men, have imputed the origin of free masonry to secret associations, adverse to the interests of true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and pursuing the villainous and chimerical project of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVELLING">levelling</a> the distinctions of society, and freeing the human mind from the sacred obligations of religion and morality. 8. Without adopting any of these untenable opinions, or attempting to discover the precise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> when free masonry arose, it may be sufficient to establish its claim to an early origin, and to show that it has existed in different ages of the world under different forms and appellations (f). In the execution of this task, the true candid enquirer will be satisfied with strong and numerous resemblances, as the nature of the subject excludes the possibility of rigid demonstration. Every human institution is subject to great and numerous variations; the different aspects under which they appear, and the principles by which they are regulated, depend upon the progress of civilization, upon the nature of the governments by which they are protected, and on the peculiar opinions and habits of their members. If, therefore, in comparing free masonry with other ancient associations, we should find it coincide with them in every circumstance, there would be strong reasons for suspecting, that the imagination of the writer had counterfeited resemblances when destitute of authentic information; or that the order had adopted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> and ceremonies of antiquity, to cloak the recency of their origin. --- (a) Anderson's History and Constitutions of Free Masonry, p. i. Preston's Illustrations of Masonry, p. 6. tenth edition. (b) Manuscript of Bode of Germany, in the possession of M. Mounier. (c) <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRELIMINARY">Preliminary</a> Dissertation to the Complaint of Scotland, p. 67, 71. (d) Anthologia Hibernica, for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, April, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1794. (e) <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of Jacobinism, vol. ii. p. 377, 378; &c. (f) M. Mounier observes, that if the order of free masons existed among the ancients, it would have been mentioned by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> authors. This argument, however, for the recency of their origin, is far from being conclusive. For though it is allowed by all, that free masonry has existed in this country for at least 300 years, yet the association is never once mentioned in any of the histories of England. Masonry, origin, to command the veneration and excite the notice of the public. Against free masonry, however, this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> cannot be preferred: we shall have occasion to consider it when connected with the idolatry of the heathens, when devoted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, and when flourishing under the milder influence of the reformed religion. 9. As men, in the early ages of society, were destitute of those methods of diffusing knowledge which we now enjoy, and even of those which were used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> and Rome, when the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> was unknown; the few discoveries in art and science which were then made, must have been confined to a small number of individuals. In these ages, the pursuit of science must have been a secondary consideration, and those who did venture to explore the untried regions of knowledge, would overlook those unsubstantial speculations, which merely gratify the curiosity of philosophers; and would fix their attention on those only which terminate in public utility, and administer to the necessities of life. As architecture could only be preceded by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, it must have been in this science that the first efforts of human skill were tried; and in which man must have first experienced success in extending his dominion over the works of nature. The first architects, therefore, would be philosophers. They alone required the assistance of art; and they alone would endeavour to obtain it. The information which was acquired individually, would be imparted to others of the same profession; and an association would be formed for the mutual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> of knowledge, and the mutual improvement of its members. In order to preserve among themselves that information which they alone collected; in order to excite amongst others a higher degree of respect for their profession, and prevent the intrusion of those who were ignorant of architecture, and consequently, could not promote the object of the institution, appropriate words and signs would be communicated to its members; and significant ceremonies would be performed at their initiation, that their engagement to secrecy might be impressed upon their minds, and greater regard excited for the information they were to receive. Nor is this mere speculation; there exist at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, in the deserts of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, such monuments of architecture, as must have been reared in those early ages which precede the records of authentic history; and the erection of these stupendous fabrics, must have required an acquaintance with the mechanical arts, which is not in the possession of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> architects. It is an undoubted fact, also, that there existed, in these days, a particular association of men, to whom scientific knowledge was confined, and who resembled the society of free masons in every thing but the name. 10. In Egypt, and those countries of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> contiguous to that favoured <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, the arts and sciences were cultivated with success, while other nations were involved in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>: it is here, therefore, that free masonry would flourish, and here only can we discover marks of its existence in the remotest ages. It is extremely probable, that the first and the only object of the society of masons, was the mutual communication of knowledge connected with their profession; and that those only would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> admittance into their order, whose labours were subsidiary to those of the architect. But when the ambition or vanity of the Egyptian priests prompted them to erect huge and expensive fabrics, for celebrating the worship of their gods, or perpetuating the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of their kings, they would naturally desire to participate in that scientific knowledge, which was possessed by the architects they employed; and as the sacerdotal order seldom fail, among a superstitious people, to gain the objects of their ambition, they would, in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, succeed in their attempts, and be initiated into the mysteries, as well as instructed in the science of free masons. These remarks will not only assist us in discovering the source from which the Egyptian priests derived that knowledge for which they have been so highly celebrated; they will aid us also in accounting for those changes which were superinduced on the forms of free masonry, and for the admission of men into the order, whose professions had no connection with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> art. 11. When the Egyptian priests had, in this manner, procured admission into the society of free masons, they connected the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a> of their country, and their metaphysical speculations, concerning the nature of God and the condition of man, with an afflication formed for the exclusive purpose of scientific improvement, and produced that combination of science and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> which, in after ages, formed such a conspicuous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the principles of free masonry. 12. The knowledge of the Egyptians was carefully concealed from the vulgar; and when the priests did condescend to communicate it to the learned men of other nations, it was conferred in symbols and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a>, accompanied with particular rites and ceremonies, marking the value of the gift they bestowed. What those ceremonies were, which were performed at initiation into the Egyptian mysteries, we are unable, at this distance of time, to determine. But as the Eleusinian and other mysteries had their origin in Egypt, we may be able, perhaps, to discover the qualities of the fountain, by examining the nature of the stream. 13. The immense <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Egypt, conjoined with other causes, occasioned frequent emigrations from that enlightened country. In this manner it became the centre of civilization, and introduced into the most distant and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> climes the sublime mysteries of its Greece religion, and those inventions and discoveries which originated in the ingenuity of its inhabitants. The first colony of the Egyptians that arrived in Greece, was conducted by Inachus, about 1970 years before the Christian era; and about three centuries afterwards, he was followed by Cecrops, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADMUS">Cadmus</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANAUS">Danaus</a> (c). The savage inhabitants of Greece beheld with astonishment the magical tricks of the Egyptians; and regarded as gods those skilful adventurers, who communicated (c) Voyage du Jeune Anacharsis en Grece, 4to. tom. i. p. 2. Cecrops arrived in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a> in 1657 B.C. Cadmus came from Phenicia to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a> in 1593 B.C. and Danaus to Argolis in 1586 B.C. to them the arts and sciences of their native land (H). In this manner were sown those seeds of improvement, which, in future ages, exalted Greece to such pre-eminence among the nations. 14. After the Egyptian colonies had obtained a secure settlement in their new territories, and were freed from those uneasy apprehensions which generally trouble the invaders of a foreign land; they instituted, after the manner of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, particular festivals or mysteries, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of those who had benefited their country by arts or by arms. In the reign of Eriophonius, A.C. 1500, the mysteries of the Egyptian Isis were established at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELEUSIS">Eleusis</a> under the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELEUSINIA">Eleusinia</a>. They were instituted in honour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>, who having come to Greece in quest of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Proserpine, resided with Triptolemus at Eleusis, and instructed him in the knowledge of agriculture, and in the still more important knowledge of a future state (T). 15. About the same time, the Panathenaic were instituted in honour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, and the Dionysian mysteries in honour of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, who invented <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a> (K), and instructed the Greeks in many useful arts, but particularly in the culture of the vine (L). That the Eleusinian and Dionysian mysteries were intimately connected with the progress of the arts and sciences, is manifest from the very end for which they were formed; and that they were modelled upon the mysteries of Isis and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>, celebrated in Egypt, is probable from the similarity of their origin, as well as from the consent of ancient authors (M). If there be any plausibility in our former reasoning concerning the origin of knowledge in Egypt, it will follow, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIONYSIA">Dionysia</a> and the mysteries of Eleusis, were, like the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of free masons, formed for scientific improvement, though tinctured with the doctrines of the Egyptian mythology. 16. But it is not from conjecture only that this conclusion may be drawn. The striking similarity among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> forms of these secret associations, and the still more striking similarity of the objects they had in view, are strong proofs, that they were only different streams flowing from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fountain. Those who were initiated into the Eleusinian mysteries, were bound by the most awful engagements, to conceal the instructions they received, and the ceremonies that were performed (N). None were admitted as candidates, till they arrived at a certain age; and particular persons were appointed, to examine and prepare them for the rites of initiation (O). Those whose conduct was found <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, or who had been guilty of atrocious crimes, were rejected as unworthy of initiation; while the successful candidates were instructed, by significant symbols, in the principles of religion (P), were exhorted to quell every turbulent appetite and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> (Q), and to merit, by the improvement of their minds, and the purity of their hearts, those ineffable benefits which they were still to receive (R). Significant words were communicated to the members: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> officers presided over their assemblies (S): Their emblems were exactly similar to those of free masonry (T); and the candidate advanced from one degree to another, till he received all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and of virtue which the priests could impart (U). But besides these circumstances of resemblance, there are two facts, transmitted to us by ancient authors, which have an astonishing similarity to the ceremonies of the third degree of free masonry. So striking is the resemblance, that every brother of the order who is acquainted with them, cannot question, for a moment, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> which we have been attempting to support (X). 17. Having thus mentioned some features of resemblance between the mysteries of Eleusis, and those of free masonry; let us now attend to the sentiments of contemporaries, respecting these secret associations; and how we will find, that they have been treated with the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, liberality and influence. That some men, who, from self-sufficiency, or unfeeling dispositions, have refused to be admitted into these orders, should detract from the character of an association, which pretends to enlighten the learned, and expand the affections of narrow and contracted minds, is by no means a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of surprise; and it is equally consistent with human nature, that those, whose irregular conduct had excluded them from initiation, should calumniate an order, whose blessings they were not allowed to participate, and whose honours they (H) Herodot. lib. i. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 58. (K) Polydor Virg. de Rerum Invent. lib. iii. cap. 13. (L) Robertson's Greece, p. 59. Bacchus or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIONYSUS">Dionysus</a> came into Greece during the reign of Amphicylon, who flourished about 1497 B.C. (M) En adiun natura parentis tuis Luci admota precibus summa numinum,—cujus numen unicum, multiformi specie, ritu vario, totus veneratur orbis. This latter author has collected all the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in ancient writers, about the Eleusinian mysteries. (O) Helychius in Θεολ. (P) Clemens Alexand. Strom. lib. i. p. 325, lib. vii. p. 845. (Q) Porphyr. ap. Stob. Eclog. Phys. p. 142. (R) Arrian in Epictet. lib. iii. cap. 21. p. 440. (S) Robertson's Greece, p. 127. (T) Euseb. Prepar. Evangel. lib. iii. cap. 12. p. 117. (U) Petav. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a>. Themist. p. 414. Anacharsis tom. iii. p. 582. (X) The brethren of the order may consult, for this purpose, the article Eleusinia, and Robertson's history of Ancient Greece, p. 127. MAS Men of this description represented the celebration of the Eleusinian mysteries, as scenes of riot and debauchery; and reproached the members of the association, that they were not more virtuous and more holy than themselves (y). But it is the opinion of contemporary writers, that these rumours were completely unfounded, and arose from the silence of the initiated, and the ignorance of the vulgar. They even maintain, that the mysteries of Eleusis produced sanctity of manners, attention to the social duties, and a desire to be distinguished by virtue, as by silence. See Eleusinia. The illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> could never be prevailed upon to partake of these mysteries (z); and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a>, upon receiving a similar solicitation, replied, "That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATROCLUS">Patroclus</a>, a notorious robber, obtained initiation; and that Epaminondas and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGESILAUS">Agesilaus</a> never desired it (a)." But did not these men know, that in all human societies, the virtuous and the noble must sometimes associate with the worthless and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>? Did they not know that there often kneel in the same temple, the righteous and the profane; and that the faint and the sinner frequently officiate at the same altar? Thus did the philosophers of antiquity calumniate and despise the mysteries of Eleusis; and, in the same manner, have some philosophers of our own day, defamed the character, and questioned the motives of free masons. 18. This similarity of treatment, which the mysteries of Ceres and free masonry have received, is no small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the similarity of their origin, and their object. To this conclusion, however, it may be objected, that though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of resemblance between these secret societies are numerous, yet there were circumstances in the celebration of the Eleusinian mysteries, which have no counterpart in the ceremonies of free masonry. The sacrifices, purifications, hymns, and dances, which were necessary in the festival of Ceres, have, indeed, no <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the society of free masons. But these points of dissimilarity, instead of weakening, rather strengthen our opinion. It cannot be expected, that in the reign of Polytheism, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> sentiments of the deity should be entertained; and much less, that the adherents of Christianity should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> to the gods of the heathens. The ancients worshipped those beings, who conferred on them the most signal benefits, with sacrifices, purifications, and other tokens of their humility and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>. But when <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> had disclosed to man more amiable sentiments concerning the Divine Being, the society of free masons banished from their mysteries those useless rites, with which the ancient brethren of the order attempted to appease and repute their deities; and modelled their ceremonies upon this foundation, that there is but one God, who must be worshipped in spirit and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. 19. The mysteries of Ceres were not confined to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Eleusis; they were introduced into <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> about 1356 B.C. (b); and, with a few slight variations, were celebrated in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, Cyprus, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> (c). They had reached even to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of several countries. In short time after, they were introduced into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and other northern kingdoms (e). In the reign of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Adrian (f), they were carried into Rome, and were celebrated, in that <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, with the same rites and ceremonies which were performed in the humble village of Eleusis. They had contracted impurities, however, from the length of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, and the corruption of their adepts; and though the forms of initiation were still symbolical of the original and noble objects of the institution; yet the licentious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> mistook the shadow for the substance; and, while they underwent the rites of the Eleusinian mysteries, they were strangers to the object for which they were framed. 20. About the beginning of the fifth century, Theodosius the Great prohibited, and almost totally extinguished the Pagan theology in the Roman empire (g); mysteries and the mysteries of Eleusis suffered in the general devastation (h). It is probable, however, that these mysteries were secretly celebrated, in spite of the severe edicts of Theodosius; and that they were partly <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> during the dark ages, though stripped of their original purity and splendour. We are certain, at least, that many rites of the Pagan religion were performed, under the dissembled name of convivial meetings, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> after the publication of the emperor's edicts (i); and Pellas (k), informs us, that the mysteries of Ceres subsisted in Athens till the eighth century of the Christian era, and were never totally suppressed. (a) Plut. de aud. Poet. tom. ii. p. 21. Diog. Laert. lib. vi. § 39. (b) Playfair's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>. (c) Lucii Apuleii Metamorph. lib. xi. p. 197; 198. (d) Prais of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, or a sketch of the French capital, 1803, by S. West, F. R. S. F. A. S. This author observes, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to his work, that Paris is derived from Par Isis, because it was built beside a temple, dedicated to that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>; that this temple was demolished at the establishment of Christianity, and that there remains, to this day, in the Petits Augustins, a statue of Isis nursing Orus. (e) Omitto Eleusinam sanctam illam et augustam, ubi initiantur gentes orarum ultima. Cic. de Nat. Deorum, lib. i. sub fine. (f) A.D. 117. Encyclop. Brit. vol. vi. p. 555. Potter's Antiq. vol. i. p. 389. (g) Gibbon's History of the Decline and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">Fall</a> of the Roman Empire, &c. vol. v. p. 120. (h) Zozimus Hist. lib. iv. (i) Gibbon, vol. v. p. 110. (k) In his treatise Περὶ Ἀποκαλυψιῶν τῆς Ἐλληνικῆς, quoted by Mr Clinch in the Anthologia Hibernica, for January 1794, p. 36. 21. Having thus considered the origin and decline of the mysteries of Eleusis, and discovered in them numerous and prominent features of resemblance to those of free masonry; we may reasonably infer, that the Egyptian mysteries which gave rise to the former, had a still nearer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> to the latter; and, from this conclusion, the opinions that were formerly stated, concerning the antiquity of the order, and the origin of Egyptian knowledge, will receive very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a>. 22. Let us now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> our attention to the Dionysia, or mysteries of Bacchus, which were intimately connected with those of Ceres, and, perhaps, fill more with the mysteries of free masonry. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> (1) informs us that the solemnities, in honour of Dionysius or Bacchus, were originally instituted in Egypt; and were transported from that country into Greece, by one Melampus. But not only did the mysteries of Ceres and Bacchus flow from the same source; the one was in some measure interwoven with the other, and it is almost certain, from what we are now to mention, that those who were initiated into the former, were entitled to be present at the celebration of the latter. The fifth day of the Eleusinian festival was the most brilliant of the whole. It received the appellation of Bacchus, because it was chiefly, if not exclusively, devoted to the worship of that god. His statue, attended by the initiated and the ministers of the temple, was conducted from Athens to Eleusis, with much pomp and solemnity (m). And after it had been introduced into the temple of Ceres, it was brought back to Athens with similar ceremonies. The connection between the Eleusinian and Dionysian mysteries is manifest, also, from the common opinion, that Ceres was the mother of Bacchus (n). And Plutarch affirms us, that the Egyptian Isis was the prototype of Ceres; that Osiris was the same with Bacchus; and that the Dionysia of Greece was only another name for the Pamyria of Egypt (o). As Bacchus was the inventor of theatres, as well as of dramatical representations, that particular class of masons, who were employed in the erection of their extensive buildings, were called the Dionysian artificers (p), and were initiated into the mysteries of their founder, and consequently into those of Eleusis (q). But, from the tendency of the human mind to embrace the ceremonial, while it neglects the substantial part of an institution, the Dionysian festival, in the degenerate ages of Greece, was more remarkable for intemperance and licentiousness, than for the cultivation of virtue and of science; and he who was at first celebrated as the inventor of arts, was afterwards worshipped as the god of wine. Those who were disposed of indulging licentiously in licentious mirth and unhallowed fertility, cloaked their proceedings under the pretence of worshipping Bacchus; and brought disgrace upon those mysteries, which were instituted for the promotion of virtue, and the improvement of art. 23. About 250 years B.C., an illiterate and licentious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> came from Greece to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, and instituted the Bacchanalia, or feast of the Bacchanals (r); and with From Tuscany they were imported to Rome; but the Dionysian promoters of these midnight orgies having proceeded to the farthest extremity of dissipation and disloyalty, they were abolished throughout all <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> (s). It has been foolishly supposed, that the Bacchanalia were similar to the Dionysian mysteries, merely because they were both dedicated to Bacchus. The Liberalia of Rome was the festival corresponding to the Dionysia of Greece (t); and it is probable that this feast was observed throughout the Roman empire, similar to till the abrogation of the Pagan theology in the reign of Theodosius. The opinion which an impartial inquirer would form, concerning the nature and tendency of the mysteries of Bacchus, would not be very favourable to the character of the institution. But it should be remembered that deviations from the intentions and form of any association, are no objection to the association itself. They are rather proofs of its original purity and excellence; as it is not from the paths of vice, but from those of virtue, that we are accustomed to stray. 24. Hitherto we have considered the Dionysian mysteries under an unpropitious aspect; let us now trace them in their progress from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> to Asia, where they retained their primitive lustre, and effectually contributed to the rapid advancement of the fine arts. 25. About 1000 years B.C. (u), the inhabitants of Attica, complaining of the narrowness of their territory, and the unfruitfulness of its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, went in quest of more extensive and fertile settlements. Being joined by a number of the inhabitants of surrounding provinces, they sailed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR">Asia <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, drove out the inhabitants, seized upon the most eligible situations, and established them under the name of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, because the greatest number of the refugees were natives of that Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> (x). As the Greeks, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the Ionic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIGRATION">migration</a>, --- (1) Ελληνική γυναίκα δια τον Διονύσιον τον επιφανεστάτον και τον φιλότερον. (n) Potter, vol. i. p. 393. (o) De Idée et Oùide. Idée du Gouvernement Ancien et Modern de l'Egypte, p. 26. Paris 1743. (p) Διονυσιακοί τεχνικοί. Aulus Gellius, lib. xx. c. 4. (q) Vid. (t) Liberalia (says Festus) liberis Festis, quae apud Graecos dicuntur Dionysia. Vid. Universal History, vol. xiii. p. 262. (u) Playfair places the Ionic migration in 1044 B.C. Gillies's Hist. of Greece, 8vo. vol. i. p. 102. gration, had made considerable progress in the arts and sciences (y), they carried these along with them into their new territories; and introduced into Ionia the mysteries of Minerva and Dionysus (z), before they were corrupted by the licentiousness of the Athenians. In a short time the Asiatic colonies surpassed the mother-country in prosperity and science. Sculpture in marble, and the Doric and Ionian orders, were the result of their ingenuity (a). They returned even into Greece; they communicated to their ancestors the inventions of their own country; and instructed them in that style of architecture which has been the admiration of succeeding ages. For these improvements the world is indebted to the Dionysian artificers, an association of scientific men, who possessed the exclusive privilege of erecting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, theatres, and other public buildings in Asia Minor (b). They supplied Ionia, and the surrounding countries, as far as the Hellespont, with theatrical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a>; and erected the magnificent temple at Teos, to Bacchus, the founder of their order (c). These artists were very numerous in Asia, and existed, under the same appellation, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> (d). About 300 years before the birth of Christ, a considerable number of them were incorporated, by command of the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERGAMUS">Pergamus</a>, who assigned to them Teos as a settlement, being the city of their tutelary god (e). The members of this association, which was intimately connected with the Dionysian mysteries, were distinguished from the uninitiated inhabitants of Teos, by the science which they possessed, and by appropriate words and signs, by which they could recognize their brethren of the order (f). Like free masons they were divided into lodges, which were distinguished by different names (g). They occasionally held convivial meetings in houses erected and consecrated for this purpose; and each separate association was under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and presidents, or wardens (h). They held a general meeting once a year, which was solemnized with great pomp and festivity; and at which the brethren partook of a splendid entertainment, provided by the master, after they had finished the sacrifices to their gods, and especially to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> Bacchus (i). They used particular utensils in their ceremonial observances; some of which were exactly similar to those that are employed by the fraternity of free masons (k). And the more opulent artists were bound to provide for the exigencies of their poorer brethren (l). The very monuments which were reared by these masons, to the memory of their masters and wardens, remain to the present day, in the Turkish burying grounds, at Silverhillar and Eraki (m). The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> upon them express, in strong terms, the gratitude of the fraternity, for their disinterested exertions in behalf of the order; for their generosity and benevolence to its individual members; for their private virtues, as well as for their public conduct. From some circumstances which are stated in these inscriptions, but particularly from the name of one of the lodges, it is highly probable, that Attalus, king of Pergamus, was a member of the Dionysian fraternity. 26. Such is the nature of that association of architects, who erected those splendid edifices in Ionia, whose ruins even afford us instruction, while they excite our surprise. If it be possible to prove the identity of any two societies, from the coincidence of their external forms, we are authorized to conclude, that the fraternity of the Ionian architects, and the fraternity of free masons, are exactly the same; and as the former practiced the mysteries of Bacchus and Ceres, several of which we have shown to be similar to the mysteries of masonry; we may safely affirm, that, in their internal, as well as external procedure, the society of free masons resembles the Dionysiacs of Asia Minor (n). --- (y) According to the author of Anacharsis's Travels, the arts took their rise in Greece about 1547, B.C. (z) Chandler's Travels in Asia Minor, p. 100, 4to. 1775. The Panathenaic and the Dionysian mysteries were instituted about 300 years before the Ionic migration. The inscriptions upon them were published by Edmund Chishull, in 1728, from copies taken by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">Consul</a> Sherard in 1709, and examined in 1716. Ionian Antiquities, p. 3. (m) Dr Robison, who will not be suspected of partiality to free masons, ascribes their origin to the Dionysian artists. 27. The opinion, therefore, of free masons, that their order existed, and flourished at the building of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>'s temple, is by no means so pregnant with absurdity as some men would wish us to believe. We have already shown, from authentic sources of information, that the mysteries of Ceres and Bacchus, were instituted about 400 years before the reign of Solomon (o); and there are strong reasons for believing, that even the association of the Dionysian architects existed before the building of the temple. It was not, indeed, till about 300 years before the birth of Christ, that they were incorporated at Teos, under the kings of Pergamus; but it is universally allowed, that they arose long before their settlement in Ionia, and what is more to our present purpose, that they existed in the very land of Judea (r). It is observed by Dr. Robison (q), that this association came from Persia into Syria, along with that style of architecture which is called Grecian: And since we are informed by Josephus (r), that that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of architecture was used at the erection of the temple; there is reason to infer, not only that the Dionysiacs existed before the reign of Solomon, but that they assisted this monarch in building that magnificent fabric, which he reared to the God of Israel. Nothing, indeed, can be more simple and consistent than the creed of the fraternity, concerning the state of their order at this period. The vicinity of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> to Egypt; the connection of Solomon with the royal family of that kingdom (s); the progress of the Egyptians in architectural science; their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to mysteries and hieroglyphic symbols; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> of their being employed by the king of Israel, are additional considerations, which corroborate the sentiments of free masons, and abrogate them from those charges of credulity and pride with which they have been loaded. 28. To these opinions, it may be objected, that if the fraternity of free masons flourished during the reign of Solomon, it would have existed in Judea in after ages, and attracted the notice of sacred or profane historians. Whether or not this objection is well founded, we shall not pretend to determine; but if it can be shown, that there did exist, after the building of the temple an association of men, resembling free masons, in the nature, ceremonies, and object of their institution; the force of the objection will not only be taken away, but additional strength will be communicated to the opinion which we have been supporting. The association here alluded to, is that of the Essenes, whose origin and sentiments have occasioned much discussion among <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> historians. They are all of one mind, however, respecting the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> and observances of this religious order. 29. When a candidate was proposed for admission, History of the strictest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCRUTINY">scrutiny</a> was made into his character (t). The Essenes, if his life had hitherto been exemplary; and if he appeared capable of regulating his conduct according to the virtuous though austere maxims of their order, he was presented, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of his noviciate, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> garment, as an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> of the correctness of his conduct and the purity of his heart (u). A solemn oath was then administered to him, that he would never, even at the risk of his life, divulge the mysteries of the order; that he would make no innovations on the doctrines of the society; and that he would continue in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> course of piety and virtue which he had begun to pursue (x). Like free masons, they instructed the young member in the knowledge which they derived from their ancestors (y). They admitted no women into their order (z). They had particular signs for recognizing each other, which have a strong resemblance to those of free masons (A). They were divided into separate lodges or colleges (B). They had different places of meeting, where they practised their rites, and settled the affairs of the society; and, after the performance of these duties, they assembled in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, where an entertainment was provided for them by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, or master of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, who allotted a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> to every individual (c). They abolished all distinctions of rank; and, if preference was ever given, it was given to piety, liberality, and virtue (d). Stewards were appointed in every town, to supply the wants of indigent strangers (e). The Essenes pretended to higher degrees of piety and knowledge, than the uninitiated vulgar; and though their pretensions were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, they were never questioned by their enemies. Austerity of manners was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> characteristics of the Essenean fraternities: (o) According to Playfair's Chronology, the temple of Solomon was begun in 1016, and finished in 1008, B.C. The Eleusinian mysteries were introduced into Athens in 1356 B.C., a considerable time after their institution. (p) Robison's Proofs of a Conspiracy, p. 20. (q) Proofs of a Conspiracy, p. 20, 21.
